TI Rethinking temporalities through being with children: A dialogic
   reflection
SO GLOBAL STUDIES OF CHILDHOOD
LA English
DT Article
DE children; temporality; slow scholarship; (post-)qualitative research
ID SLOW SCHOLARSHIP; TIME; EXPERIENCE; CHILDHOOD; EDUCATION
AB Children's everyday lives are shaped by shifting rhythms of movement, suspension, and retrospection through which time becomes lived, imagined, and meaningful. This article brings together interdisciplinary and international perspectives, with members of a collective reflecting on temporality in children's lives. Across a prologue and nine reflective pieces developed through prolonged dialogue, the article explores time in children's diverse everyday contexts - including home, school, public, digital, and natural environments - in Canada, Czechia, Finland, and the USA. It also highlights the importance of slow and stretched temporalities for creative, reflective, playful, and imaginative practices. By foregrounding dialogue and deep listening, the article promotes responsive and empathetic approaches to research with children. Developed through collaborative practices grounded in an ethics of care, it also manifests slow childhood scholarship.

TI A real-world application of Lagrangian mechanics: The circular
   restricted 3-Body Problem
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB The application of advanced classical mechanics (specifically, the Lagrangian and/or Hamiltonian approaches) to real-world problems is not always straightforward, despite the mathematical rigor and elegance of this field. The objective of this work is to connect the relatively abstract concept of Lagrangian mechanics into the more familiar realm of orbital mechanics. We present a brief, yet complete and self-contained, derivation of the Jacobi integrals using the Lagrangian formulation. The result provides a useful example of how advanced classical mechanics may prove simpler and more efficient than standard methods using Newton's second law. We complement these results with two case studies in our Solar system: the Circular Restricted 3-Body Problems around Pluto and Charon and around Earth and the Moon. These examples provide useful illustrations of both unstable and stable Lagrange points. We further propose a representation of zero-velocity curves, which separate the permissible and forbidden regions of motion for the object, given a constant of the motion. This representation allows an interpretation of Jacobi constants using energy density. The use of S.I. units over normalization in our case studies departs from the traditional examples to offer a more pedagogical and intuitive approach to this problem.

TI The linear stability of Lagrange points in polar coordinates
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID CHAOTIC CAPTURE
AB In a system of two primary gravitational bodies, there are five equilibrium points known as Lagrange points. The Lagrange points exhibit widely different stability properties, such that a satellite placed at the Sun-Earth L1 or L2 points needs course corrections every few weeks, whereas Jupiter's Trojan asteroids are naturally stable on timescales of the order of 10(9) years. We analyze the stability of all Lagrange points in the circular restricted three-body problem using a matrix formulation expressed in polar coordinates. We examine the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, both of which are important for a full understanding of satellite motion near these points. Trajectories in the linearized polar representation exhibit distortions absent in the linearized Cartesian analysis, a result of geometric curvature effects that are not retained in the Cartesian formulation at first order. We include a set of questions and answers to support classroom lessons for the development of intuition about motion near Lagrange points. A set of supplementary notes provides supporting mathematical details of derivations and calculations described in the main text.

TI The Franck-Hertz experiment: Seeing cross sections
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID ELECTRON-SCATTERING; ATOMS; MERCURY; CONSTITUTION; TRANSPORT;
   PARAMETERS; EXCITATION; ENERGY
AB We re-examine the classic 1914 Franck-Hertz experiment, which was crucial both for completing the old quantum theory and for providing evidence for the quantized (Bohr) structure of atoms. Our motivation is twofold: first, to revive didactic interest in the Franck-Hertz experiment, and second, to reduce the difficulty of understanding electron-atom scattering cross sections. We perform the experiment using both neon (Ne) and mercury (Hg), accounting for the differences between measurements on the two gases using semiquantitative models. The present paper goes beyond the standard analysis of current-voltage characteristics in the Franck-Hertz experiment, which is typically used to extract the excitation energies of Hg (or Ne) atoms. The diversity and richness of electron-scattering phenomena accessible with readily available equipment underscore the enduring pedagogical value of the Franck-Hertz experiment at both undergraduate and advanced levels.

TI Calorimetric experiments for teaching energy as a crosscutting
   quantitative concept
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID HEAT
AB This paper presents a set of accessible, quantitative calorimetric experiments designed to support the teaching of energy change as a crosscutting concept across scientific domains. Building on an operational definition of energy change based on temperature variation of a standard body, the proposed approach treats calorimetry as an empirical unifying framework for studying diverse processes, including mechanical, electrical, radiative, and chemical processes. In contrast to traditional instruction that often rests on a predefined abstract concept (work), these experiments engage learners in constructing quantitative relationships empirically by identifying proportional dependencies between temperature change and relevant variables that characterize different processes. The experiments are intentionally simple to implement in classroom settings and adaptable across educational levels. Through this approach, students can develop a coherent understanding of energy change as a measurable quantity associated with a range of processes, rather than categorizing distinct forms of energy. We illustrate how this framework supports interdisciplinary connections, promotes inquiry-based learning, and provides a foundation for linking macroscopic observations with later microscopic explanations. Implications for teaching, including the role of experimental design, variable control, and the transition from temperature change to energy change, are discussed.

TI Journey from the center of the Poincaré sphere
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID POLARIZATION ANALYZER
AB We present a simple and accessible experiment to introduce the Stokes formalism and the Poincar & eacute; sphere as powerful tools for describing the polarization state of light. Within this framework, we analyze one of the earliest polarizers: a system consisting of a stack of tilted dielectric plates oriented near Brewster's angle, which acts as a progressive polarizer as the number of plates increases. We derive analytical expressions for the transmission of unpolarized light and the resulting increase in the degree of polarization using the Stokes formalism, incorporating both Fresnel coefficients and internal reflections within each plate. Finally, we validate the theoretical predictions through experiments by tracking the evolution of the polarization state via the Stokes parameters and discussing its trajectory on the Poincar & eacute; sphere.

TI The cosmological constant problem: An accessible introduction
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB We present a pedagogical introduction to the cosmological constant problem that requires only basic knowledge of quantum field theory and general relativity. A massive real scalar field is used to illustrate how the quantum vacuum energy density and pressure can be calculated both in flat spacetime and in an expanding universe. Detailed computations are provided for dimensional, cutoff, and adiabatic regularizations. No attempt is made to address quantum gravitational effects, and the expanding universe background is treated classically. We point out that although the commonly cited discrepancy of 120 orders of magnitude between theory and observation is based on an estimate that does not account for regularization and renormalization, fundamental principles of quantum field theory nevertheless lead to a huge mismatch. In addition to this large discrepancy, we emphasize that there are also conceptual challenges related to cosmic expansion, such as the choice between comoving and physical scales in certain contexts and the non-uniqueness of vacuum.

TI Extending the Schrodinger quantum field to parametrized quantum field
   theory: A variational approach using the Pavsic-Barut action
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID FORMULATION
AB This paper extends the Schrodinger quantum field-a wave function treated as a fundamental quantum field describing particle states and probabilities-to a fully relativistic framework within Parametrized Relativistic Quantum Theory (PRQT). A hallmark of parametrized theories is the use of an invariant evolution parameter, which addresses key conceptual challenges in standard quantum field theory (QFT). Feynman's path integral formulation is reviewed to illustrate the historical role of such parameters in early QFT developments. We then present a variational approach, based on the Pavsic-Barut action principle with a parametrized Lagrangian density, to derive field equations that naturally incorporate the invariant evolution parameter and yield a mass operator. The consistency of this formalism with physical measurements is demonstrated through applications to the Stueckelberg equation, including its implications for particle trajectories and mass states. The potential for resolving Standard Model anomalies is discussed.

TI Teaching decoherence by simulating quantum channels on quantum computers
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB As we move further into the second quantum revolution, it becomes increasingly important to teach modern ideas such as decoherence and to provide practical training on quantum computers. In this work, we illustrate how quantum decoherence channels can be introduced into instruction and how one can simulate these quantum channels on quantum computers. We focus on the decoherence of a single spin, because it is the simplest case to consider. Using the IBM Quantum Platform, we examine depolarizing, amplitude damping, dephasing, and thermalizing channels. These channels are first described in terms of Lindblad operators and then they are converted into quantum circuits that require mid-circuit resets. This hands-on approach to decoherence will help students learn practical concepts required for quantum information science.

TI AI Unplugged: Exploring Pathways from Physical Simulation to
   Conceptualization of AI Reasoning Processes
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI Education; Unplugged Activities; Middle School Education; AI
   Literacy; AI Reasoning
ID TANGIBLE INTERACTION; EMBODIMENT
AB Young adolescents interact with AI daily, but there is a lack of approachable, concrete opportunities for them to develop an understanding of AI reasoning processes. We leverage theories of embodied learning to design four unplugged activities-DataBites, Monster Mapping, Nature Net, and Kernel Quest-that foster young adolescents' understanding of machine learning, convolutional neural networks, and semantic networks through physical manipulation and simulation of AI reasoning. TI Process Management for Learning from Professional Source Code:
   Cultivating Experts in the Age of AI
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE program comprehension; professional development; self-directed learning;
   design patterns; scaffolding; knowledge maps; code instrumentation;
   analogical transfer; authentic learning; developer tools; sensemaking
ID DESIGN PATTERN DETECTION; PROGRAM COMPREHENSION; FRAMEWORK; SOFTWARE;
   ENVIRONMENT; NOVICE
AB Background and Context: Today's software industry increasingly values intricate conceptual knowledge (e.g., sufficient expertise to fix AI-generated code). Though program comprehension and scaffolding have mature literature, the intermediate-to-expert transition for programmers is under-researched relative to its socioeconomic impact. Learner-focused inspection tools exist (e.g., Ply, Isopleth, Python Tutor), but these often address specific problems (e.g., implicit CSS dependencies, async JS, call stacks), without systematic guidance for developing deep conceptual models of architectures and techniques across large real-world codebases or interactions. Objectives: We aim to support non-experts in learning holistically from professional code and to understand how they explore and learn in this context. Given that learners outnumber expert instructors who can teach these concepts, we propose Process Management (PM), a framework for designing tools that scaffold sensemaking on underused yet plentiful real-world code. PM addresses core obstacles learners face (code complexity, surface-level focus, and transfer challenges) through core design principles (intuitive sensemaking processes, comparison, reflection). After prototyping and piloting over 5 years, we developed 3 PM tools that surface JavaScript, CSS, and Python techniques. In this work, we seek to understand the effectiveness of PM tools, and the processes learners follow with and without PM support. Study Methods: We report on think-aloud studies conducted over 1.5 years to evaluate our 3 PM tools. Data include similar to 300 hours of remote observation of intermediate-level developers using these tools or controls (Chrome DevTools, VS Code). There were five participants in each condition for each tool. Studies consisted of tool training and pre-test, tool-use, and post-test phases, followed by a post-study interview. We qualitatively coded pre/post-and tool-use data, and present learning gains and in-task behavioral metrics. Findings: Our mixed-methods evaluations show PM tool users explored effectively (e.g., comparing, mapping) and achieved similar to 3 & times; more learning outcomes (e.g., conceptual clarity, transferable patterns). Such outcomes were observed consistently across the three programming domains under study. Our qualitative data shows how PM tools can shape learners' exploration order and process, enhance their understanding of nuanced techniques through interactive comparison, and help them uncover the domain-specific rationales behind design pattern usage through analogical mapping and reflection activities. Implications: Finally, we discuss PM's potential impact on cognitive load, the role of experts today, and a sketch for how LLMs may scale PM. In particular, we envision a world in which educators and builders can develop PM systems that provide intermediate-level engineers a process for learning holistically from open source professional code to gain conceptual expertise, which they can then use to refine AI-generated code. We also provide examples of LLM prompts that can be used to potentially automate aspects of our PM tool-use sessions, laying some groundwork for AI-driven professional development. In summary, our work contributes to computing education by introducing a scalable and forward-looking tool-building framework and design paradigm for helping intermediate-level learners extract expert-level concepts from complex, real-world code.

TI The Robot's Given Path-Embodied Representational Practices with
   Sequential Instructions
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Additional Key Words and Phrases: Embodied cognition; Young learners;
   Programming; Educational robots; Notional machines
AB This study investigates how young learners employ symbolic representations through embodied strategies to program educational robots. Drawing on video data from interviews with 22 students (ages 7-8), the analysis identifies three distinct representational practices: tool-oriented, agent-oriented, and path-oriented. In tool-oriented and agent-oriented approaches, students consistently translated arrow tiles into correct movement sequences, aligning with the robot's discrete rotation and forward commands. Conversely, pathoriented strategies, in which tiles were placed to trace the robot's physical path on a grid, sometimes led to misunderstandings of rotation commands, giving rise to disagreements and incorrect solutions. By comparing these practices, the study illuminates the role of bodily gestures, spatial reasoning, and symbolic artifacts in shaping how children conceptualize the robot's "logic." Although path-oriented strategies may appear intuitive, they can inadvertently promote a continuous-turn notion that conflicts with the robot's step-by-step command syntax. The findings underscore the importance of explicit scaffolding in early computing education, suggesting that opportunities to test, refine, and compare different representational approaches can foster deeper insights into both spatial problem-solving and computational thinking.

TI Developing Computational Thinking Skills through Embodied Dance
   Activities
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE computational thinking; computer education; dance
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; EDUCATION; EXERCISE; PERFORMANCE; COGNITION; HEALTH;
   SCHOOL; K-12
AB Objectives: There is currently no single accepted definition of Computational Thinking (CT), but abstraction, algorithmic thinking, problem solving and pattern recognition are often identified as four top skills with decomposition and spatial ability also being considered important. Physical activity has been linked to development of algorithmic thinking, visual processing and pattern recognition, while dance has been associated with ability in problem solving, visual-spatial manipulation, abstraction and pattern recognition. Dance notation has been linked to the development of skills in decomposition. This article investigates whether taking part in structured dance activities affects performance on CT tests. Participants: Fifty participants (33 girls, 17 boys) aged between 6 and 9 were recruited from schools in Scotland and out-of-school groups in Germany. Study Methods: The methods were influenced by Educational Design theory and adopted a mixed methods approach. It employed an explanatory sequential design with the aim of explaining quantitative results using qualitative methods and comprises three studies. Groups 1 and 2 used a pre-experimental design, while Group 3 used a quasi-experimental non-equivalent group design, which arbitrarily split the group in an intervention group and a control group to establish whether there was an observable change in performance on CT tasks after taking part in structured Scottish Country Dance (SCD) activities. Participants undertook the BCTt test as pre- and post-test; motivation was measured using versions of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI). Direct observation and teacher interviews provided qualitative information and were used to explore the findings. The intervention consisted of workshops that mapped physical dance and transcription activities to cognitive attributes identified as important for CT. Findings: A Related Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test found a significant difference between the median marks for pre-test (M = 18.70, SD = 4.21) and post-test (M = 20.45, SD = 3.137) (n = 20, p = 0.007) in Group 1. In Group 2, a Paired Samples t-Test indicated that the post-test score (M = 21.50, SD = 1.789) was significantly higher than the pre-test score (M = 16.69, SD = 3.945), (t(15) = 5.189, p < 0.001). However, no differences were found between scores on the pre-test (M = 20, SD = 2.00) and post-test (M = 19.67, SD = 2.160), t(5) = 0.237, p = 0.822 in Group 3A or between the pre-test scores (M = 13.75, SD = 5.898) and post-test (M = 15.13, SD = 2.997), t(7) = 0.903, p = 0.397 in Group 3B. Participants in all studies were observed Conclusions: Participants in Groups 1 and 2, who were taught by experienced SCD teachers in a classroom situation and had some prior familiarity with the dance genre, showed a significant improvement in their scores. The addition of related coding activities appears to strengthen this effect. The absence of significant results in Group 3 allows for some hypotheses about which aspects of the dance workshops may be affecting CT.

TI Designing for Engagement: A Comparison of Canvas and a Visual Peer
   Review Dashboard
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning analytics; Peer review; Visualization education; Dashboard
   design; Canvas LMS; Interaction logs; Linguistic analysis; Sentiment
   modeling; learning theories
ID LEARNING ANALYTICS; STUDENTS
AB Peer review is an underutilized yet potentially powerful strategy for fostering evaluative judgment and design literacy in visualization education. Critiquing visual work requires domain-specific competencies that extend beyond generic peer feedback; however, widely adopted platforms such as Canvas provide limited support for the cognitive and visual demands of visualization critique. We introduce VisPeerReview, a visualization-specific learning analytics dashboard (LAD) designed to scaffold peer feedback through an integrated visualization display, rubric-guided prompts, and inline annotation tools. We evaluated VisPeerReview through a threephase mixed-methods study conducted in an undergraduate data visualization course, comparing it with Canvas's default peer-review workflow. Drawing on interaction logs, peer-review text, and survey responses, we found that VisPeerReview elicited significantly longer and more linguistically rich feedback and was consistently preferred by students. Sentiment analysis further indicated more positive evaluative language and clearer reviewer intent under the dashboard-supported condition. Beyond tool evaluation, this study offers the first systematic comparison between Canvas and a visualization-specific LAD, demonstrating how theory-aligned instructional interface design-grounded in representational competence and learningsciences frameworks-can meaningfully improve the quality of peer feedback in computing education.

TI An Embodied Sense of Programming: An Anti-Ableist Framework for the
   Analysis of Learners' Developing Senses of Programming
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE programming education; inclusion; embodied cognition
ID MATHEMATICS; COGNITION; THINKING; GESTURE
AB This article proposes the Critical Embodied Sense framework, which challenges traditional, ableist assumptions in programming education that privilege abstract, decontextualised learning experiences over embodied engagement. The framework is designed to enable researchers to analyse learners' developing senses of programming concepts through an anti-ableist lens. It draws upon Vygotsky's cultural-historical theory, contemporary research from the embodied cognition field and perspectives from critical theory. We illustrate the application of the framework using a study which investigated the developing senses of visually impaired learners working with a tangible programming language. Through the application of the framework to this study we demonstrate the integral role that tools, emotions and affect play in shaping learners' senses of programming concepts. We finish by discussing potential wider applications of the framework which include researching the development of a sense of self as a programmer in under-represented groups and guiding the design of inclusive computing learning environments.

TI Program Behavior Gaps: An Extension of the Rules of Program Behavior
   Framework
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Programming education; introductory programming; rules of program
   behavior; notional machines; model of program behavior; program behavior
   gaps; learning objectives; instruc-tional design; semantics; mental
   models; conceptions
AB The Rules of Program Behavior framework notes that teachers target a model of program behavior instead of the complex semantics of the programming language, and allows describing these models as sets of rules of program behavior. When learners execute code, its behavior is defined by the semantics of the programming language, which might differ from the targeted model of program behavior. In this article, we present a theoretical framework that builds on the Rules of Program Behavior framework, while giving a more prominent role to the differences between the targeted models and the programming language semantics. We call these differences Program Behavior gaps and distinguish between incompleteness gaps-untaught parts-and conflict gaps-a semantic rule that conflicts with a rule of program behavior-, and between transparent and opaque gaps. Visualizations of the relation between the semantics of the programming language and the targeted model of program behavior are an integral part of our framework as they allow visualizing the gaps that could exist in a code fragment and whether these gaps are activated or not. On top of this, the framework contains clear definitions to distinguish between valid conceptions, misconceptions, missing conceptions, prior conceptions, fluid conceptions and program behavior gaps. The framework can be used to devise programming courses, to investigate the mental model of learners and to make a case for gradually evolving languages that are designed to have fewer program behavior gaps. To illustrate this, we (1) present a real-life progression of models of program behavior and discuss, for this progression, the program behavior gaps in 21 code fragments, and (2) present a study grounded in our theoretical framework in which we determine the mental model of each participant.

TI Children's Embodiment of Coding Concepts in an Unplugged-to-Plugged
   Learning Sequence
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational Thinking; Embodied Cognition; Elementary-aged children;
   unplugged coding; plugged coding
AB Objectives. The purpose of this study was to explore the way concepts embodied during an unplugged coding activity emerged in a plugged coding environment. Participants. A pair of 4th-grade elementary-aged children who participated in an after-school coding club over a 4-week period. Participants had no prior experience with coding. Study Method. Using a multimodal lens to frame the study, data collection and analysis focused on 3 hours of video paired with the children's coding documents in which we observed how the pair constructed meaning through both verbal and non-verbal (e.g., gestures, body movements) communication and interaction with the environment. Findings. The findings revealed unit thinking as a central concept in which the physical properties of objects in the environment were associated with units of movement. Units were then used to support the children's thinking as they planned sequences of moves with greater accuracy. This transitioned from a bodily understanding of units in unplugged towards more abstract representations in plugged. Conclusions. Findings suggest that unit thinking may be an important but somewhat overlooked mathematical concept that children embody when using physical objects to complete coding activities. Additionally, the findings support a grounded perspective of cognition in which engaging the sensorimotor system during unplugged activities can play a role in completing tasks later in a plugged environment. Implications include encouraging teachers to introduce unit thinking to children during unplugged coding activities, particularly when sequencing and measurement are required.

AB Background: The embodied cognition perspective is a collection of theories that all explicate a fundamental relationship between the perceptions, actions, and movement of the body and how humans think and reason. The application of the embodied cognition perspective to instructional interventions-often referred to as embodied learning design-has the potential to aid computing education researchers and practitioners who want to meaningfully integrate more sensory and "hands on" activities in their instruction. TI Long-term Effects of Promoting Communication and Soft Skills in Higher
   Computing Education
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; long-term study; mixed methods; qualitative content
   analysis; teamwork; professional skills; student-centered learning
AB Objectives. This work investigates students' mid-to long-term takeaways from the course "Communication and Soft Skills" conducted at a European university and relates insights to soft skills interventions in higher computing education described in the literature. A major objective was to situate findings from researching a student-centered course into a broad, international context of promoting soft skills. Research questions address the students' view on the course's lasting effects, students' memories of the course, and the identification of success factors for promoting soft skills in higher computing education based on the current study. The findings from our research contribute an evidence-based source of motivation for staff who are devoted to nourishing students' soft or professional competencies aside from knowledge and technical skills.

TI Proxy-Based Programming: Making Programming More Accessible through
   Virtual, Physical, and Social Embodiment
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Applied computing; Interactive learning environments
AB From a theoretical perspective, this article examines the role of embodiment in K-12 computer science education through three distinct perspectives: virtual embodiment for cognitive understanding, physical embodiment for emotional engagement, and social embodiment for collaborative learning. The research introduces proxy-based programming as a novel programming paradigm that helps novice programmers overcome pragmatic programming challenges by providing a visual proxy that serves as an embodiment of the object being programmed. This proxy features dual temporal representation that simultaneously shows both the present and future situations resulting from programming actions. Unlike programming approaches that primarily address syntactic challenges, proxy-based programming also mitigates semantic and pragmatic aspects of computational thinking. RULER.game, a Collaborative Computational Thinking Tool, implements four core principles of proxy-based programming, enabling safe programming experimentation while proactively preventing errors. Initial studies comparing proxy-based programming with block-based programming show significant reductions in error rates. The article explores how embodiment plays a role in making programming more accessible from both theoretical and practical perspectives. Additionally, the article explores the motivational benefits of physical embodiment, where students create games by first drawing objects on paper before importing them digitally, as well as social embodiment through awareness interfaces that make collaborators' actions and intentions visible in real-time. This comprehensive approach to embodiment presents a novel framework for making programming more accessible and engaging for K-12 students.

TI Notional Machines: Retrieving Background Practices of Perception and
   Action
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE notional machine; mental model; conceptual model; background practice;
   representational practice
ID MENTAL MODELS; ORGANIZATION
AB Notional machines have figured historically in many discussions in computing education. Under a common view in the computing education literature based on classical cognitive science, notional machines play a critical pedagogical role when they are brought into a student's mind as mental models. A mental model simplifies the phenomenon that it models and is correct to the extent that it corresponds to the modeled phenomenon. Such mental models of the notional machine are viewed as necessary for the student to program computers. In this article, I argue that this classical cognitive science view overlooks two key aspects of human cognition that are brought to the forefront in "second generation" cognitive science and recent philosophy of knowledge and language. The first is the importance of embodied perception and action to ground the meaning of language and thought. In particular, models are representational not only due to their simplification and correspondence to what they model but also require embodied representational practices by which these correspondences are constituted. The second concerns the way that these embodied practices can be sufficiently educated so that they withdraw into an unnoticed background so that reflective reasoning is not always required for skilled action. This article thus advocates a shift in pedagogical attention from the inner aspect of student mentality to the external aspect of embodied interaction between student and notional machine. This leads to a focus on the background practices by which notional machines are intelligible as models of computation and explicitly teaching these practices so that students can better leverage the benefits of notional machines to learn how to program a computer.

TI Computing Education's Superbug: Interrogating the Computer-Mind
   Metaphors
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mind-as-computer metaphor; computationalism; Cartesian dualism; habit;
   embodied cognition
ID PSYCHOLOGY; DEWEY
AB In one of the significant results from early computing education research, Pea identifies a computer-as-mind metaphor that novices use in ascribing mental properties of personhood to the computer, which causes students considerable conceptual confusion. In characterizing this as students' superbug, Pea uses a mind-as-computer metaphor, the converse metaphor to the one that students use. In doing so, he makes visible a metaphor that has become one of the predominant metaphors of mind in mid-to late-20th century theorizing in psychology and the cognitive sciences. I take both of these metaphors (computer-as-mind and mind-as-computer) to be the superbug that plagues not only student attempts to program but also computing education more broadly. The purpose of this article is to argue that these computer-mind metaphors are a steady undercurrent that runs from the cognitive sciences through computing education and the research on it, what is problematic about these metaphors, what causes this metaphorical affliction, why we might want to cure ourselves from it, and how we can do so. Key to this cure is to counter disembodied views of human reasoning and action, epitomized in first generation cognitive science, with embodied and enactive theoretical perspectives, epitomized in second generation cognitive science and in multimodal and embodied approaches to the social sciences.

TI Concreteness Fading for Primary School Computing
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Concreteness Fading; Computing Education
ID MATHEMATICS; INSTRUCTION; WORDS
AB Objectives. This article investigates the Theoretical Model of Concreteness Fading in the context of teaching children aged 9-10 about computer network structure and routing. Three between-groups, pre-test/post-test experiments were conducted to test the following hypotheses: (1) The Concreteness Fading group will have Concrete group will have higher learning gains than the Virtual Concrete group; (3) The Three-Step group will have higher learning gains than the Two-Step group; (4) The Five-Step group will have higher learning gains than the Three-Step group. Participants. Participants for all three experiments were pupils aged 9-10 at a primary school in the South of England, with 166 participants overall. Study Method. Three experiments were conducted, each with a between-groups, pre-test/post-test design using random, or blocked-random, assignment. In Experiment One (n = 59), four variations of physical and/or paper-based representational progressions were compared. In Experiment Two (n = 48), the physical and paper-based Concreteness Fading progression from Experiment One was compared against a tablet-based Augmented Reality (AR) learning environment and paper-based equivalent. In Experiment Three (n = 59), the AR learning environment from Experiment Two was extended to compare three distinct approaches to linking the concrete and abstract representations. Outcomes were measured as learning gains using two (pre/post) versions of an immediate near-transfer test in abstract, but contextualised, form. All data were collected in a primary school; pre-tests were completed in the classroom as a group, and post-tests were completed individually in a shared corridor workspace. Findings. In Experiment One, an ANCOVA test showed that differences between groups were not significant (F(3, 54) = 2.413, p = 0.077, partial ri2 = 0.118), but the Concreteness Fading group achieved significantly higher learning gains than the Concrete group (Mdiff = 1.00, 95% CI [0.26, 1.75], p = 0.010). Hypothesis 1 was not supported. In Experiment Two, a Welch t-test showed that the difference in learning gains between the Physical and Virtual Concrete groups was not significant (Mdiff = 0.47, 95% CI [-0.47, 1.41], t(41.725) = 1.015, p = 0.316). Hypothesis 2 was not supported. In Experiment Three, an ANO VA test showed significant differences between groups (F(2, 56) = 3.670, p = 0.032, partial ri2 = 0.116). The Three-Step group achieved significantly higher learning gains than the Two-Step group (Mdiff = 0.99, 95% CI [0.61, 0.99] p = 0.037). Hypothesis 3 was accepted. The Five-Step group did not achieve significantly higher learning gains than the Three-Step group (Mdiff = 0.16, 95% CI [-0.78, - 0.78, 1.09], p = 0.738). Hypothesis 4 was not supported. Conclusions. . These findings demonstrate that Concreteness Fading can be an effective method for teaching computing concepts to children , provide significant benefits over using concrete materials only. It should not be assumed that a physical manipulative is required during the initial stage of learning. Virtual manipulatives may be equally effective, enabling an increase in flexibility of design and distribution. One crucial design factor is the level of support provided to learners when translating between representations. Including at least one intermediate stage, designed explicitly to help identify and link mutual referents between concrete and abstract representations, can increase learning outcomes, particularly for those with lower prior test scores.

TI "If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It": Challenges and
   Implications for AI in Education

LA English

DE CCS Concepts; Human-centered computing-Interaction design; Computing

AB This article offers a critical analysis of the role of the body in the development of AI in the field of education. TI Coding in Virtual Reality: How Space and Movement Can Support Embodied
   Learning
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative coding; embodied learning; situated learning; virtual reality;
   computer science education
ID DESIGN; ENVIRONMENTS; CONCRETE; CHILDREN
AB This study explores how learners leverage the spatial and kinesthetic affordances of an immersive, fully 3D coding environment in virtual reality (VR). A workshop was conducted in which high school students engaged in creative coding activities using a new node-based VR coding platform. Their code histories were recorded in video format through screen casting from their headsets. Audio-free videos were subsequently annotated to characterize users' interactions with nodes and UI elements during code construction, execution, and debugging. At a minimum, creating a computer program using this platform requires loading appropriate nodes and making connections with wires between event and data ports. However, it was found that users engaged with elements of their code in much more complex ways, treating them at times as though they were tangible objects. Learners moved and rearranged nodes, hovered objects in space, fidgeted, and virtually touched, gestured, or traced over nodes and wires. These actions served to enact relational features and computational concepts underlying their code in support of planning, prediction, modeling, and other cognitive processes important for computer science (CS) learning. Preliminary outcomes suggesting growth in CS abilities. Guidelines for VR platform design are discussed.

TI Designing Embodied Metaphors and Analogies for AI Literacy: An Iterative
   Study with Experts, Teachers, and Children
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Embodied learning; Analogical learning; AI literacy; AR application;
   Design-based research; Iterative design process
ID COGNITION; FRAMEWORK
AB Teaching complex AI concepts to children presents significant challenges, as educators often struggle to both grasp nuanced mechanisms and translate them into engaging learning experiences. Drawing on embodied cognition and analogical reasoning theories, this work aims to create embodied metaphors and analogies that simplify the mechanisms and ethical issues of AI recommendation systems for middle-school students. We employed a multi-phase design pipeline grounded in the Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology to integrate feedback from key stakeholders, including domain experts, students, and teachers, for linking abstract AI concepts to concrete and familiar experiences. The resulting designs underwent mixed-method evaluations with both middle-school students and teachers, which revealed positive shifts in student attitudes and provided insights for further iteration. The design cycles ultimately uncovered key challenges, such as balancing feature fidelity with cognitive overload, and yielded design implications for developing effective embodied and analogical representations for children's AI literacy.

TI Adults' Robot Literacy-Results from a Finnish Survey
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Robot literacy; Survey; Lifelong learning; Adult education
ID SOCIAL ROBOTS; ATTITUDES; DESIGN; MIND
AB This article presents and discusses the results of a national survey on adults' media and robot literacy in Finland with a focus on robot literacy. The study addresses three pressing global challenges: population aging, increasing robotization, and a research gap concerning the skills and competencies needed for interacting with robots. The survey operationalized the authors' robot literacy framework, which focuses on physical robots and defines robot literacy across seven skill dimensions: specialIntscript Awareness of robots; specialIntscript Interaction with robots; specialIntscript Understanding and evaluating the information robots provide; specialIntscript Understanding the data security and privacy of robots; specialIntscript Programming of robots; specialIntscript Ethical reflection; and specialIntscript Providing and receiving social support on robotics-related questions. The survey addressed the following research questions: What is the scope of adults' robot literacy? How are gender, age, education, household composition, and use of the Internet connected to adults' robot literacy? The study marks the first attempt to map robot literacy across a national population. It shows that despite recent progress in AI and future forecasts of advances in the development of social and humanoid robots, awareness of robots is still limited among Finland's adult population and does not originate mainly in firsthand experiences with robots. Furthermore, the respondents exhibited uncertainty in their ethical reflection, in knowledge about interaction with robots, and in their understanding and evaluation of the information provided by robots. They also reported being entirely unprepared-or possessing low or very low skills-in providing social support related to robotics. For the field of computing education, the study offers new insights into the relatively limited robot literacy of adults, particularly older adults. A key practical implication is that adult educators-computing educators included-as well as researchers, instructional designers, the media, robotic service providers, robot developers, and other stakeholders must actively promote robot literacy among the adult population.

TI A Scalable Incremental Verilog HDL Plagiarism Detection Approach for
   Large-Scale Samples
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Incremental detection; locality-sensitive hashing; plagiarism detection;
   Verilog HDL
ID SOURCE CODE PLAGIARISM
AB Source code plagiarism detection plays an indispensable role in computer education. Over the past few decades, various tools and systems have been developed to solve software plagiarism detection with relatively satisfactory results. However, hardware description language (HDL) plagiarism detection has become a new challenge with the popularity of FPGA-based digital circuit design courses. Constructing a Verilog HDL plagiarism detection approach that supports fast incremental detection on large samples has become a thorny issue. This article proposes a scalable approach to achieve Verilog HDL plagiarism detection that supports incremental detection on large samples. The method employs a dual-layer detection strategy at both the submission-level and the module-level. At the submission-level, it conducts project-wide comparisons, while at the module-level, it calculates a project's suspicious score through a prefix matching-based risk assessment mechanism. This approach effectively distinguishes common modules from potential plagiarism, significantly reducing the false positive rate. Our method detects more plagiarism pairs with higher accuracy than the widely used Measure of Software Similarity (Moss) system. To further validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a comparative analysis with an ANTLR-based syntax-aware detector. On the dataset of Verilog HDL projects from a computer organization course (Fall 2023 and Fall 2024), our method achieved higher precision and reduced time consumption compared to the ANTLR-based model. Initially, this study leverages filtered token features and the locality-sensitive hashing algorithm to transform Verilog HDL projects into fingerprints. An efficient index is constructed to accelerate both incremental detection and batch detection. Four strategies for filtering N-Gram token sequences are used in this study. The proposed fast incremental Verilog HDL plagiarism detection approach has a logarithmic level of time complexity. Experiments were conducted to find and validate the optimal parameters for the proposed strategies on real-world datasets. The experimental results show that combining our method with Moss increases the convenience and accuracy of Verilog HDL plagiarism detection in real courses.

TI The Effects of Starter Template Scaffoldings on Coding in Courses
SO ACM TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General and reference; Empirical studies; Experimentation; Applied
   computing; Education
ID ANXIETY RATING-SCALE; COGNITIVE LOAD; MATH PERFORMANCE; SELF-EFFICACY;
   EDUCATION; VALIDATION; TOOLS
AB Programming anxiety is a well-documented challenge in introductory computing courses, particularly among students with no prior exposure to programming. Scaffolding strategies such as pair programming, Parsons puzzles, and starter code templates are widely used to reduce anxiety and build confidence during the early stages of learning. Although starter templates often include explanatory comments and partially completed code, the relative effectiveness of these different scaffold types in mitigating anxiety has not been systematically examined. This article reports findings from a controlled experiment conducted during the first laboratory session of an undergraduate C programming course for students from different engineering and science disciplines. Pairs of students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: a control group using blank templates, a comments-based scaffold group, and a code-based scaffold group. Coding anxiety was measured using a questionnaire with subscales related to self-efficacy, partner interaction, and peer judgement. Contrary to our expectations, the control group showed a greater reduction in coding anxiety than either scaffolded group, and students in the comments-based condition reported larger decreases in anxiety than those receiving code-based scaffolds. These findings suggest that for beginners, even well-intentioned scaffolds can temporarily increase the perceived difficulty in task completion.

TI LGBTQ plus Realities in the Biological Sciences
SO CBE-LIFE SCIENCES EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID GENDER; EXPERIENCES; SEXUALITY; QUEER; GAY
AB While scientific environments have been described as unwelcoming to the LGBTQ+ community, and fields such as physics have systematically documented these challenges, the climate in biology-specific workplaces has not exclusively been assessed. We conducted the largest survey to date of LGBTQ+ biologists to examine how their sense of belonging and perception of climate in the biology workplace and professional societies compare to that of their straight and cis peers. This landmark survey provides the first comprehensive analysis of the LGBTQ+ climate in biology, revealing specific challenges faced by TGNC scientists.

TI The Design of a Live Role-play Simulation Game for School Leader

AB School leaders play a decisive role in shaping teaching quality and student learning outcomes, yet their professional development opportunities often fail to address the complex, data-driven decisions required in practice. The present study seeks to address this issue by answering research questions regarding the specific elements of a live role-play simulation game and the perceived outcomes for school leader professional development derived from the game. Using a design-based research methodology across three iterative cycles, researchers, teacher educators, and simulation developers from business environment collaboratively created a simulation game that models decision making in school. The developed live role-play simulation game integrates diverse participant roles, decision-making with perceivable consequences, iterative opportunities for improvement, feedback, and structured reflection. Data from 72 school principals and vice principals, collected through questionnaires, fieldnotes, participant-produced artefacts, indicate that by the facilitation of disorienting dilemmas and subsequent critical reflection, the simulation was perceived by participants to enhance their understanding of evidence-informed decision-making and evoked various insights. Findings suggest that the developed game can serve as a part of professional development that immerses school leaders in authentic, complex scenarios, enabling them to explore the consequences of their actions in a safe environment. The study contributes to the underexplored field of simulation-based professional development for school leaders in Europe and highlights simulation game as a promising approach for cultivating leadership practices aligned with school improvement.

TI Teacher Framing and Student Mathematical Experiences During Game-Based
   Learning
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SERIOUS GAMES
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematical games; Teacher implementation; Pedagogical framing;
   Conceptual understanding; Procedural fluency; Student perceptions;
   Game-based learning
AB Mathematical games are widely used in primary classrooms and consistently associated with high student engagement, yet evidence for their effects on mathematical learning remains inconclusive. This study examines whether differences in teacher framing, conceptual versus procedural, are associated with differences in students' mathematical experiences during game-based lessons. While prior research has documented how teacher framing shapes teacher-student interactions during gameplay, this study extends this work by examining the student side of the equation: how framing is associated with students' affect, their perceptions of what they are learning, and the quality of their spontaneous mathematical reasoning with peers. Drawing on student-written reflections (n = 95), student interviews, and video-recorded student-to-student interactions (n = 20 focal students) across five Year 3/4 classrooms in Victoria, Australia, the study uses directed content analysis and interaction coding to examine students' affect, perceived mathematical learning, and student-to-student mathematical reasoning across two framing conditions. Findings indicate that framing shaped not only how much students enjoyed the games but what they believed they were learning and how they reasoned with peers. Among positive-reason responses, challenge and thinking were cited more often in conceptually than procedurally framed classrooms (34% vs. 11%). Among neutral or negative responses that included a codable reason, boredom or confusion was less common in conceptually than procedurally framed classrooms (30% vs. 72%). Students in conceptually framed classrooms also described the mathematics in richer conceptual terms, referring to factors and prime numbers (18% vs. 1%) and arrays (18% vs. 5%). Mathematical reasoning interactions were approximately 1.7 times as frequent in conceptually framed classrooms, with Connecting interactions, in which students explicitly linked gameplay to broader mathematical ideas, occurring more than six times as frequently as in procedurally framed classrooms. Conceptual framing also appeared to distribute productive challenge more equitably across the class. The findings suggest that teacher framing may function as a key mediating variable between game design and student learning, with implications for professional learning and game-based pedagogy. Findings are exploratory and best understood as generating hypotheses for more controlled future investigation.

TI Potential of Digital Game-Based Learning in Vocational Mathematics
   Education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SERIOUS GAMES
LA English
DT Article
DE Vocational students; Mathematics; Digital game-based learning;
   Expectancy value theory
AB Digital game-based learning (DGBL) has been widely recognized as a promising approach for supporting mathematics learning, yet little is known about how students in three-year vocational education and training (VET) programmes perceive its educational value. Guided by Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT), this study examined how these students perceive the value and learning potential of DGBL in mathematics. Data were collected from 469 secondary VET students using a questionnaire and analysed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, followed by descriptive and regression analyses. Students evaluated DGBL based on a brief explanation of the concept rather than direct classroom experience. The findings indicate that students expressed relatively high intrinsic value toward DGBL, whereas perceived usefulness and learning opportunities were only moderate. Gender differences were found in gaming experience and game-genre preferences, but not in value-related perceptions of DGBL. The study extends research on DGBL in mathematics to three-year VET students, a subgroup that is often insufficiently distinguished in previous research. Based on students' perceptions of a hypothetical DGBL approach, the study offers cautious design implications for DGBL in VET mathematics, suggesting that game-based activities should be connected with vocationally grounded mathematical tasks rather than relying on enjoyment alone.

TI Beyond Static Screening: Depression Symptom Indicators Using Gaze
   Behavior and Gameplay Performance
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SERIOUS GAMES
LA English
DT Article
DE Diagnostic Game; Depression; Game-based Detection; Depressive Symptom;
   Gaze Behavior; Eye Tracking
ID ATTENTION
AB This study investigates an active assessment approach for depressive symptom severity that combines eye-tracking with serious games to capture cognitive and attentional patterns during interactive tasks. Unlike traditional assessments based on self-report measures and passive viewing paradigms, this approach uses game-based cognitive challenges to examine symptom-related variations in attention and executive functioning. Fifty-three university students (25 female, 28 male; aged 20-30 years) completed the Beck Depression InventoryII (BDI-II) and played six cognitive mini-games while gaze behavior was recorded with a Tobii 4C eye tracker. Results revealed significant associations between depressive symptom severity, gaze behavior, and game performance. Higher BDI-II scores were linked to increased fixation-to-saccade ratio, longer fixation durations, reduced saccadic amplitude, and poorer performance in cognitively demanding games. Eye-tracking measures showed strong correlations with depression severity (rho = 0.702 for fixation-to-saccade ratio and rho = -0.614 for saccade amplitude, p < 0.001), while gameplay performance also showed negative associations with symptom severity. An integrated model combining eye-tracking and gameplay features explained 81.9% of the variance in depression severity (R-2 = 0.819), with oculomotor measures emerging as the strongest predictors. These findings highlight the potential of serious games and eye-tracking metrics as objective indicators of depressionrelated cognitive and attentional processes.

TI TurbeLab Serious Game for Executive Functions in Neurodevelopmental
   Disorders
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SERIOUS GAMES
LA English
DT Article
DE Executive Function; Cognitive Training; Neurodevelopmental Disorders;
   Mobile Game; User Experience
ID CHILDREN; TIME
AB Purpose: This study examined the feasibility and preliminary effects of TurbeLab, a serious mobile game designed to stimulate executive functions (EFs) in children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Methodology: Fifteen participants (aged 10-14; M = 11.3, SD = 1.3) with diagnosed NDDs completed two 20-minute gameplay sessions. EFs were assessed pre-and post-intervention using standardized neuropsychological measures of inhibitory control, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, and visuoconstructive memory; user experience was evaluated using the Game User Experience Satisfaction Scale (GUESS); data were analyzed with linear mixed models. Findings: Significant improvements were observed in inhibitory control, processing speed, and visuoconstructive memory; cognitive flexibility showed no significant change. A significant Time & times; baseline working memory interaction was found for selected outcomes. Participants reported high satisfaction and engagement. Originality: To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate TurbeLab's feasibility and preliminary efficacy using standardized neuropsychological EF assessments in a clinical NDD population, extending prior usability-focused work. Impact: Findings support TurbeLab as a feasible and acceptable brief digital intervention for EF stimulation in neurodiverse youth and motivate future controlled trials.

TI Investigating Undergraduate Student Perceptions of Classroom
   Inclusion-Emergence of the Student Perceptions of Instructor
   Practices-Inclusion/Exclusion (SPIP-I/E) Framework
SO CBE-LIFE SCIENCES EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID TEACHER IMMEDIACY; SCIENCE; RESISTANCE
AB While assertions are common about what fosters inclusive undergraduate STEM classrooms, few studies have systematically investigated student perspectives. Additionally, it is unclear how students broadly perceive active learning practices in relation to inclusion. As such, we purposefully investigated student perceptions of classroom inclusion across courses in a biology department enriched with evidence-based teaching and situated in an urban, public institution. Student perceptions were investigated using openended prompts on a department-wide, end-of-term assessment. Results revealed that students, across social identities, do indeed report active learning strategies-as well as instructor interactions and collaborative classroom culture-as fostering inclusion. Student reports about instructor practices associated with their inclusion or exclusion clustered into four mirrored categories: Building/Dismantling the Instructor/Student ReCollaborative/Non-Collaborative Classroom Culture, and Portraying Science as Inclusive/Exclusive. These categories comprise a new analytical framework, the Student Pergating student perspectives on inclusion. Intriguingly, student reports about inclusion consistently alluded to instructor language, and the emergent SPIP-I/E Framework aligns with existing Instructor Talk frameworks. We hypothesize that modest differences in instructor language-surrounding any teaching strategy-may mediate and be a predictive, explanatory variable for student perceptions of inclusion.

TI Feasibility of Learner-Led Model Building for Simulation-Based Training
   in Open Inguinal Hernia Repair: A Randomized Controlled Trial
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE open surgery; inguinal hernia; model building; simulation-based
   training; anatomical under standing; procedural performance
AB OBJECTIVES: (1) To establish the feasibility of novice learners building inguinal hernia models for simulation-based training in open inguinal hernia repairs (IHR). (2) To examine the associations between participation in model building and learners' self-reported confidence in understanding of the inguinal canal anatomy, the anatomic accuracy of learner-constructed models, and technical performance during a simulated open IHR. We hypothesized that learner-led model construction is feasible, supports acquisition of relevant anatomy knowledge, and improves performance in some steps of a simulated open IHR. DESIGN: Prospective randomized controlled trial. SETTING: Queen's University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada; institutional academic training environment. PARTICIPANTS: Forty-eight novice learners (second-year medical students) with minimal prior exposure to open or laparoscopic IHR were enrolled and randomly assigned to a didactic lecture-only group (control) or to a didactic lecture and learner-led model-building group (intervention). All study participants were then asked to complete a simulated open IHR procedure. Self-reported confidence in understanding of the 3-dimensional anatomy of the inguinal canal, as well as procedural and executional errors were assessed. RESULTS: Learner-constructed models were anatomically accurate and suitable for use in simulation-based training, and participants rated the model-building activity positively. Participants in the model-building (intervention) group demonstrated greater gains in self-reported confidence in the understanding of the 3dimensional anatomy of the inguinal canal compared to participants in the control group (p = 0.004). Participants in the model-building (intervention) group committed fewer executional errors during external oblique aponeurosis exposure (p = 0.03), fewer procedural errors during wound closure (p = 0.05), and were more likely to complete hernia sac resection within the allotted time (p = 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Learner-led construction of simulated models is a feasible, low-cost approach for simulation-based training in open IHR. This intervention improves learners' self-reported understanding of the inguinal canal anatomy and is associated with improved performance in some steps of a simulated open IHR, while requiring minimal materials and instructional resources. TI The Conclusion Assessment Rubric (CAR): A Tool to Evaluate Students'
   Ability to Make Context-Driven Claims with Appropriate Scope from
   Experimental Biological Evidence
SO CBE-LIFE SCIENCES EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID SCIENCE; VISION; GUIDE
AB Few tools exist to thoroughly assess undergraduate students' ability to generate evidence-based conclusions from research inquiries, a higher-order reasoning skill aligned with the Vision & Change Process of Science core competency. To fill this gap, we created the Conclusion Assessment Rubric (CAR), building on the experimentation competency framework developed by biology educators and literature on scientific argumentation. The CAR is a comprehensive evaluation of students' achievement of learning outcomes, integrating key aspects of knowledge building in biology. The CAR had an intraclass coefficient of 0.7 (k = 3) with raters representing a spectrum of educator experience. Papers written in the first and third semester of a three-semester process of science curriculum were evaluated; the capstone papers earned significantly higher scores (12.9 +/- 2.7 compared with 9.6 +/- 2.5; t15 = 2.53, p = 0.023), indicating that the CAR can differentiate experienced from novice learner performance in generating conclusions. We provide example student excerpts with aligned CAR scoring to demonstrate how the rubric was applied to student writing. To our knowledge, the CAR is the first tool that assesses a student's ability to generate conclusions that inform a biological rationale model within the scope of limitations inherent to the methodologies of the investigation.

TI Growth Feedback, Mastery-approach Goals, and Learning-related Outcomes:
   An Achievement Goal Perspective
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Growth feedback; Mastery-approach goals; Socioeconomic status; Learning
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; MULTILEVEL MODELS;
   SELF-EFFICACY; CLASSROOM; STUDENTS; ORIENTATION; MOTIVATION; SCIENCE;
   LEVEL
AB Growth feedback, which provides students with constructive information for personal improvement, has been identified as critical to learning. However, little is known about the underlying motivational mechanisms that explain why and how growth feedback is associated with learning. Furthermore, the impact of the broader context including the school growth feedback environment and socioeconomic status (SES) has been largely neglected. Drawing on achievement goal theory, this study aimed to explore (1) whether and how growth feedback is associated with mastery-approach goals and focal learning-related outcomes and (2) whether the school growth feedback environment and socioeconomic conditions moderate the relationships among these variables. Data were drawn from 271,874 15-year-old students from 36 OECD countries. Multilevel moderated mediation analyses were used to analyze the data. Results indicated that students who received growth feedback from their teachers were more likely to endorse mastery-approach goals, which in turn led to better learningrelated outcomes. Furthermore, the association between growth feedback and mastery-approach goals was stronger in schools where growth feedback was more prevalent. Students from different SES backgrounds benefited equally from receiving growth feedback. However, students from low-SES schools appeared to gain more from growth feedback than their peers from high-SES schools. Our study demonstrates the importance of bridging the separate lines of research on feedback, motivation, and SES to better understand how growth feedback is associated with achievement goals and learning, and how school growth feedback and SES contexts shape the associations among these crucial variables.

TI Applying emotion regulation strategies in complex tasks
SO KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT & E-LEARNING-AN INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotion regulation; Complex task; Cloze task
ID ACHIEVEMENT; ANXIETY
AB Students often experience negative emotions, such as anxiety and frustration, when engaging in complex tasks, which may influence both their learning experiences and task performance. Although emotion regulation (ER) strategies have been shown to have positive effects on student learning, evidence regarding their effects in complex task situations remains underexplored. This study investigated students' use of ER strategies to support complex tasks and how their task performance and emotional experiences changed after applying these strategies. The participants were 24 ninth-grade students, who were learning English as a foreign language. They received instruction on applying three types of ER strategies (emotion-focused, task-focused, and regulation-focused) to support their cloze tasks. Results show that among the three types of ER strategies, students most frequently used task-focused strategies, followed by regulation-focused strategies, while emotion-focused strategies were used the least. Low-achieving students improved their task performance, whereas higher-achieving students did not show this change. Students' positive emotions increased and their negative emotions decreased after applying ER strategies. Many students reported that they still experienced negative emotions (such as anxiety and frustration) even when they applied ER strategies, mainly due to the challenging nature of tasks and the time pressure; these negative emotions distracted their attention and affected their performance. Implications of the findings are discussed.

TI From threat to tool: AI self-efficacy and user profiles in higher
   education
SO KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT & E-LEARNING-AN INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; AI self-efficacy; Academic integrity; Student profiles; Higher
   education
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has brought both challenges and opportunities for teachers in higher education. This study does not focus on restrictive methods; instead, it explores how educators can actively promote academic integrity. We contend that AI self-efficacy, characterized as a student's confidence in their capacity to employ AI ethically and efficiently, constitutes a substantial determinant. This paper delineates significant findings derived from a survey administered by 177 university students. A moderation analysis indicates that the adverse correlation between AI usage frequency and academic integrity is markedly diminished among students exhibiting high AI self-efficacy. Moreover, a cluster analysis clearly delineates three distinct AI user profiles: Confident and Cautious Users, Pragmatic High Users, and Dependent Users. Demographic studies reveal a significant correlation between these profiles and the students' academic disciplines. The results suggest that the focus of instruction should transition from a "one-size-fits-all" approach to tailored interventions designed to enhance student empowerment. This article outlines practical implications and customized strategies for each student profile.

AB The purpose of this study is to determine the experiences, opinions, and achievements of prospective science teachers (PST) regarding the process of developing digital instructional materials using Web 2.0 tools based on student-led instruction (SLI) activities. TI Mining and modelling the cognitive strategies students use to construct
   higher quality causal maps
SO KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT & E-LEARNING-AN INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive strategies; Causal maps; Learning analytics
ID CRITICAL THINKING; SKILLS
AB This study examines the cognitive strategies students employ when constructing causal maps and investigates whether specific processing methods-backward versus forward and breadth-first versus depth-first-affect map quality. Building on prior research that linked backward and depth-first processing to stronger argument maps, the study applied similar analytical tools to causal mapping, a task with distinct cognitive demands. Using jMAP software, 37 causal maps were created by students at a Southeastern university in the United States. Within the first five nodes placed, students used backward, forward, breadth-first, and depth-first processing an average of 0.81, 1.84, 1.73, and 1.95 times, respectively, producing maps with a mean score of 125.82 (SD = 55.13) out of a possible 340. Regression analysis revealed that neither backward nor breadth-first processing significantly predicted map scores, though a non-significant trend suggested that more frequent backward processing may support higher-quality maps, consistent with prior findings on argument mapping. While not definitive, these results carry instructional implications: encouraging backward processing and designing diagramming tools that facilitate this strategy without inadvertently biasing students toward less effective approaches. Ultimately, the study highlights that predominant reliance on forward, backward, or breadth-first processing does not necessarily yield higher-quality causal maps as it does in argument mapping, underscoring the importance of understanding task-specific demands to inform instructional design and the development of tools that better support student reasoning and problem-solving.

AB This study analysed how the use of sensorised 3D models and advanced technologies can promote accessible and inclusive environments for visually impaired people. TI The impact of computer-based testing on EFL university students' reading
   and listening skills test performance and test anxiety levels
SO KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT & E-LEARNING-AN INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Computer-based testing; Paper-and-pencil testing; Language assessment;
   Anxiety; University students
ID PAPER; EQUIVALENCE; ADMINISTRATIONS; COMPARABILITY; ATTITUDES; VERSIONS;
   INTERNET; VDT
AB This study investigated the impact of computer-based testing (CBT) on upper-intermediate EFL university students' test performance in reading and listening, and on their test anxiety levels. Forty students at the English Language Centre of Pharos University in Alexandria (N = 40) were randomly assigned to a control group taking paper-and-pencil tests or an experimental group taking the same tests in a computer-based format. Three reading and three listening tests, each developed according to Cambridge B1 specifications, were administered over eight weeks. Students' text anxiety was assessed using the Test Anxiety Inventory questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The results revealed no statistically significant differences in reading or listening performance between groups; however, test anxiety levels were significantly higher among CBT participants (t = -8.99, p < 0.001). The findings suggest that while CBT can be used interchangeably with traditional paper-based tests, additional measures such as pre-test orientation and digital familiarization sessions are essential to mitigate increased anxiety from CBT. For practitioners, this study highlights the importance of preparing and orienting EFL learners before transitioning to computer-based assessment environments.

TI Initial Development of an Instrument Measuring Teachers' Mindsets in a
   Professional Development Context
SO ELEMENTARY SCHOOL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
ID STRUCTURE STRATEGY; HIGH-EXPECTATION; BELIEFS
AB Professional development (PD) is crucial for educators, offering continuous learning opportunities to enhance teaching effectiveness. Effective reading comprehension hinges on teachers' ability to guide student learning, necessitating robust PD to enhance their knowledge of evidence-based reading comprehension strategies. Regrettably, many PD efforts fall short in transforming teaching practices, prompting an inquiry into the factors within PD that either facilitate or impede pedagogical change among educators. Variables such as teachers' mindsets, self-perceptions of teaching abilities, attitudes toward PD, and readiness for change are pivotal. Understanding these factors can illuminate why some teachers struggle to implement evidence-based reading comprehension practices acquired from PD.

TI Examining the Role of Rehearsals in Preservice Teachers'
   Mathematics-Related Teaching Identity Development
SO ELEMENTARY SCHOOL JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
ID EDUCATION; EXPERIENCES; COMMITMENT; KNOWLEDGE; SELF
AB This study explores the development of elementary preservice teachers' (PSTs') mathematics-related teacher identity through participation in rehearsals as a practice-based pedagogical tool. Data were collected from two cohorts of PSTs: one cohort engaged in rehearsals, and the other did not. Using a single-item identity measure, we quantitatively analyzed shifts in PSTs' identities and qualitatively examined the reasons underlying these shifts. TI Mapping longitudinal trajectories of personal values in elementary
   school: unveiling roles of the classroom
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Value change; Classroom impact; Classmates' values; Value development
ID YOUNG-CHILDREN; FAMILY; ADOLESCENT; PRIORITIES; PARENTS; TRANSMISSION;
   ACHIEVEMENT; COMPETENCE; TEACHERS; BEHAVIOR
AB Value transmission is a key societal responsibility, and value education has gained increasing global attention. Although classrooms represent important developmental environments for children's values, comparatively little is known about how different social actors within classrooms contribute to value development. This longitudinal study examined how classmates, teachers, and classroom relationships contribute to children's value development over time. A total of 1342 Swiss children (ages 5.8-7.3 years, Matt1 = 6.82, SD = 0.50) were followed for 1.5 years from the onset of elementary school. We analyzed trajectories of four higher-order value types. Our results showed that self-transcendence (close to compassionate values) and openness-to-change values increased in priority over time, as did conservation values, although the latter increase leveled off at later time points. In contrast, self-enhancement values' priority decreased. Children's values became more similar to those of their peers over time. Children's perceptions of classroom dynamics also predicted value change: Perceiving the teacher as warm predicted later increases in self-transcendence and decreases in self-enhancement value priority; feeling close to the teacher predicted increases in conservation and decreases in openness to change value priority; and feeling close to classmates predicted increases in self-transcendence and decreases in openness to change value priority. Teachers' value-related educational goals did not predict changes in pupils' values. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of a multilayered social perspective for understanding value development and suggest that peers and teacher-pupil relationships play distinct roles in children's moral and social growth.
