TI Discourse as critical thinking: A focus on disposition
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking disposition; Discourse-centred reasoning; Inquiry;
   Argumentation; Quality Talk; High-level comprehension
ID ARGUMENTATION; LEVEL; COMPREHENSION; ADOLESCENTS; INQUIRY; SKILLS; TALK;
   TEXT
AB The normative orientation of many established definitions of critical thinking has given way to an inevitable shift towards conceptions seeking to incorporate and highlight the construct's implications for practice. Kuhn's (2019) framing of critical thinking as discourse is a case in point, and one which largely informs the conceptual approach adopted in this study. The conditions of our study, however, specifically its focus on the dynamics of in-person dialogic discussion in the context of a university classroom, necessitated a slight adjustment of Kuhn's term to discourse as critical thinking. Modified thus, the term ascribes at least as much agency to collective interaction as it does to individual cognition in generating elements of critical thinking. Discourse as critical thinking also reflects the ethos of Quality Talk, the discussion model employed in the study. Against this background, the present article documents an unconventional research and pedagogical approach to developing students' propensity to collective inquiry, informal reasoning and argumentation. To illustrate this approach, we focus on a single student's performance within a classroom reading circle of peers, foregrounding her disposition to critical and creative thinking. In tracking the group's verbal engagement with each other about and around issues arising from given texts, we advance theorised explanations of the focal participant's individual discourse as displaying elements of critical thinking.

TI Enhancing a large language model with a chain-of-metacognitive reasoning
   approach increases argumentative writing evaluation accuracy, student
   writing outcomes, and mental effort
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Automated writing evaluation; Large language models; Argumentative
   writing; Metacognition; Explainable AI
ID POWER; INSTRUCTION; AI
AB Effective feedback is crucial for learning, especially in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing context. However, teacher feedback is often delayed and difficult to scale, while automated writing evaluation systems may struggle to address complex reasoning skills such as argumentation. Although large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities because of their ability to interpret context, their feedback remains generic, lacks transparency, and can diminish students' mental effort. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel chain-ofmetacognitive reasoning (CMR) framework, implemented through group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using reward functions. This training procedure was used to fine-tune a small-scale open-source LLM. The resulting CMR-GRPO system, ArguCoach, generates structured reasoning chains that assess argumentative writing. Unlike existing systems, ArguCoach drives the model to "think aloud," modeling metacognitive strategies such as planning, monitoring, and evaluation. In the first stage, ArguCoach achieved higher agreement and fewer errors than did leading LLMs on over 5000 argumentative essays. In the second stage, undergraduate EFL students (n = 50) receiving ArguCoach feedback exhibited significantly greater writing performance and mental effort than did those (n = 60) with traditional teacher feedback in an eight-week quasi-experiment; notably, the writing performance gains persisted even after the intervention concluded. Feedback acceptance was similar across groups. However, students who received ArguCoach feedback were more likely to elaborate on suggestions with new content, whereas those who received teacher feedback were more likely to adopt suggestions directly. These findings indicate that aligning LLMs with metacognitive reasoning via reinforcement learning enables them to serve as effective partners in human-AI collaborative language education.

TI The Discourse Mapping Tree as a tool for mapping classroom discussions
   in linear algebra
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Linear algebra; Classroom discussion; Commognition; Realization trees;
   Mathematical discourse
ID KNOWLEDGE SHIFTS; PARTICIPATION
AB Mathematical discussions, along with other learner-centered teaching practices, are becoming more prevalent in tertiary mathematical education, yet the mathematical content of these discussions and the learning involved remain less explored. We developed the Discourse Mapping Tree (DMT), a commognitive based tool for mapping mathematical content during discussions, which allowed us to examine learning of a class as a whole in linear algebra discussions.    research project
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative teaching; AUT; Action research; Student creativity; Vocational
   education
ID SELF-EFFICACY; TEACHERS; THINKING
AB The aim of the study was to investigate how students' creativity can be developed through a creative teaching program. A total of 56 students from a Chinese higher vocational college took part in an 18-week action research project. This study employed an action research design combining quantitative pre-post assessments and qualitative reflections to investigate the program's impact on students' creativity. Creativity was assessed through the Alternative Uses Task (AUT), focusing on four key dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration. These findings highlight the importance of adopting a multifaceted pedagogical approach to nurture creativity. They also offer practical implications for designing creative teaching frameworks that foster students' creativity and support its transferability to real-world scenarios.

TI Visual attention and perceived attractiveness in scientific posters: An
   eye-tracking study
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Eye-tracking technology; Educational technology; Communication; Eye
   movement measurements; Visual perception; Cognition
ID PERFORMANCE; MOVEMENTS; FIXATION
AB Background Scientific posters are widely used in medical conferences to share research findings visually and interactively, yet many fail to communicate effectively due to excessive text, poor structure, and a lack of visual appeal. Objective To evaluate how the design of scientific posters, focusing on Text-density, Figure-ratio, and Margin-spacing, influences visual attention and perceived attractiveness. Methods Forty-six participants viewed fifteen scientific posters in one session, divided into three layout conditions (Text-density, Figure-ratio, Margin-spacing). Eye-tracking metrics such as the Time to First Fixation (TTFF), Total Duration of Fixations (TDF), and Number of Fixations (NF) were analyzed to measure visual attention. After the display of each condition, the participants were asked to select the most visually attractive poster. The results were analyzed with a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, and a P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results The results showed that the participants preferred the Moderate layout in the Margin-spacing condition (37 %), the Overloaded layout in the Figure-ratio condition (41 %), and the Light layout in the Text-density condition (48 %). Repeated measures ANOVA showed significant effects of condition (P = 0.019) and Area of Interest (AOI; P < 0.001) on TDF, which was highest in the Text-density condition. Moderate AOIs consistently received the longest TDF (P < 0.001). NF was significantly higher in Overloaded AOIs within the Figure-ratio condition (P < 0.002). TTFF was shorter in Sparse, Light, and Dense AOIs for the Figure-ratio condition compared to the others (P < 0.018), indicating that image-rich designs captured attention more quickly. Conclusion Poster design strongly influences visual attention. Layouts with balanced Figure-ratio, moderate Text-density, and structured spacing promote engagement and readability, while extreme designs may hinder attention. These results highlight the importance of visual design in optimizing educational materials and support its integration into instructional strategies in medical education.

TI Construction of the connection between Cavalieri's principle and the
   Riemann sums
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Cavalieri's principle; Riemann sums; Argumentation; Toulmin's model; cK
   cent model
ID GEOGEBRA; PROOF; TEACHERS; SOFTWARE
AB This study aims to explore how university students construct the connection between Cavalieri's principle and Riemann sums through arguments generated with dynamic mathematics software within a collaborative learning methodology. Seven university students took part in the study, which lasted four weeks. Data collection included tasks, field notes, audio-video recordings, and screen recordings. Data analysis was based on the integration of the Toulmin model and the cK cent model. The specific approach helped students realize that the rectangles in the Riemann sum approach line segments as their limit approaches infinity. It also supported students in developing the concept of line segments in Cavalieri's principle based on their understanding of the rectangles in Riemann sums. It was observed that understanding line segments helped students explain the geometric rationale behind some calculus rules. In this way, students were able to move from algebraic to geometric representations within a social interaction environment. The ability to switch between representations fostered a deeper understanding of the connection between Cavalieri's principle and Riemann sums. Integrating dynamic software into a collaborative learning methodology enabled students to construct Cavalieri's principle from a more dynamic perspective.

TI Designing attention: temporal structuring and visual cognition in
   undergraduate design observation
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Slow looking; Designed attention; Visual literacy; Design pedagogy;
   Time-based learning; Observational cognition
ID TEACHERS
AB Accelerated production cycles and the widespread use of generative AI tools in design education have intensified a focus on rapid visual output, often at the expense of deep visual literacy. In studio-based curricula, the cognitive skill of sustained observation has become increasingly rare. To address this, this study examines how prolonged, time-structured observation can foster perceptual depth, metacognitive awareness, and design vocabulary in undergraduate design students. It formally introduces and operationalizes "Designed Attention," a pedagogically structured method of visual engagement grounded in time, reflection, and constraint. Using coursework archived from 50 first-year design students, the study analyzed minute-by-minute observation logs, pre- and post-observation essays, and voluntary reflective self-reports generated during a continuous three-hour viewing of a single artwork. A mixed-methods approach integrated time-series frequency analysis, qualitative thematic coding, and comparative concept mapping. Findings reveal a temporal evolution from recognition of basic Art Elements (e.g., line, color) toward higher-order Design Principles (e.g., unity, hierarchy), with a perceptual threshold emerging at approximately 60-75 min. Additionally, reflective writing often omitted concepts observed in real time, indicating a perception-articulation gap. It also observed symbolic and narrative compositions with richer relational cues sustained engagement more effectively than minimal works. Consequently, Designed Attention reframes attention as an emergent property of intentionally structured educational environments rather than a prerequisite for learning. This model offers a replicable, evidence-based framework for cultivating visual literacy and critical interpretation, countering accelerationist tendencies in contemporary studio culture and AIenhanced workflows.

TI A step towards understanding systems thinking as mental self-renewal
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-renewal; Systems thinking; 4E paradigm of cognition; Enaction;
   Adult cognitive development; Postformal thinking; Dynamic systems
   paradigm
ID PARADIGM
AB This article is a critical theoretical review on underlying theoretical concepts of the mind behind St & aring;hle's self-renewal model of systems thinking. Previous research has claimed that self-renewal meaning systems inherent and autonomous ability to constantly renew oneself - can explain systems thinking in social contexts, such as group and organisational settings. This research aims to analyse self-renewal in light of existing research on the 4E paradigm of cognition and adult cognitive development, to understand it as a part of individual thinking and development. The aim is to reach a theoretical synthesis in order to construct a working definition of mental selfrenewal. The article concludes by arguing that mental self-renewal is an effective conceptualization for systems thinking, which can describe its inherent creativity and cognitive development. However, there is a need to include more concepts from phenomenology in order to fully explicate it as a mental phenomenon. There are many directions for future research due to the infancy of this topic.

TI Contributions of an APOS theory-based instructional module supporting
   the action-to-process transition in eighth grade students' understanding
   of geometric reflection
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Geometric reflection; Thinking styles; APOS theory; Motion view; Mapping
   view
AB This study investigates the impact of an instructional module, developed within the framework of APOS theory, on enhancing eighth-grade students' conceptual understanding of geometric reflection. The module emphasizes three fundamental components of reflection-line of symmetry, domain, and plane-with the goal of deepening students' comprehension of these concepts and their interrelationships. Changes in students' modes of thinking were analyzed through the lens of APOS theory. Findings revealed that all participating students progressed from the action level to the process level, indicating a shift from viewing reflection merely as a physical movement of shapes to engaging in more sophisticated reasoning based on point correspondences and underlying geometric principles. The module's constructivist, inquiry-based, and discussioncentered activities were found to be effective in promoting this conceptual development. The results suggest that this approach offers valuable implications for mathematics education, particularly in teacher preparation and the cultivation of students' mathematical thinking.

TI AI delivers creative output but struggles with thinking processes
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative thinking; Artificial intelligence; Human-AI comparison
ID IDEA GENERATION; INSIGHT; MODEL
AB A key objective in artificial intelligence (AI) development is to create systems that match or surpass human creativity. Although current AI models perform well across diverse creative tasks, it remains unclear whether these achievements reflect genuine creative thinking. This study examined whether AI models (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and GPT-4o) engage in creative thinking by comparing their performance with humans across various creative tasks and core cognitive processes. Results showed that AI models outperformed humans in divergent thinking, convergent thinking, and insight problem-solving, but underperformed in creative writing. Compared to humans, AI generated lower forward flow values in both free and chain association tasks and showed lower accuracy in the representational change task. In creative evaluation, AI exhibited no significant correlation between the weights of novelty and appropriateness when predicting creative ratings, suggesting the absence of a human-like trade-off strategy. AI also had higher decision error scores in creative selection, suggesting difficulty identifying the most creative ideas. These findings suggest that while AI can replicate-or even exceed-human performance on creative tasks, it does not exhibit a corresponding ability in the core thinking processes that drive such performance in humans.

TI The impact of virtual reality-assisted learning on students' critical
   thinking: A meta-analysis of 37 experimental and quasi-experimental
   studies
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; Critical thinking; Critical thinking Skill critical
   thinking disposition; Meta-analysis
ID SKILLS
AB Critical thinking is significant in talent cultivation as a form of higher-order thinking. Virtual reality (VR), leveraging its "3I" technology matrix (i.e., Immersion, Interaction, and Imagination), is regarded as a potential tool for fostering critical thinking. Consequently, numerous researchers worldwide have conducted empirical studies focusing on utilising VR-assisted learning to enhance students' critical thinking. However, the impact of such interventions remains contentious, with research findings scattered and lacking unified evaluation criteria and methodologies. This meta-analysis of 37 empirical studies from 2014 to February 2026 reveals that the deep integration of VR and pedagogy yields a significant, moderate-to-large positive effect on students' critical thinking development (Q = 312.14, I & sup2; = 88 %, z = 6.23, df = 36, p<0.00001). The findings indicate a low likelihood of publication bias (Egger's regression test = 0.067, p > 0.05). Furthermore, the teaching cycle, education level, critical thinking dimension, teaching method, and knowledge domain were found to moderate the overall effect size significantly. Based on this comprehensive assessment, this study proposes a mechanism of action for how VR-assisted learning promotes students' critical thinking and discusses applicable scenarios for effectively enhancing this ability.

TI The impact of toolkit-based maker activity model (IPRCV model) on senior
   high school students' maker literacy and learning experiences: A
   quasi-experimental study
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Maker education; New-form maker textbook; Toolkit; Maker activity model;
   Learning experience; Maker literacy
AB Maker education serves as an effective approach to cultivating learners' 21st-century core competencies and has garnered significant attention in senior high school education. However, there remains room for improvement in designing maker textbooks and implementing maker activities that enhance students' learning experiences and foster their maker literacy. To address this, this study designed a new-form maker textbook (toolkit) and its corresponding activity model (IPRCV model), aiming to investigate the impact of the IPRCV model on the maker literacy and learning experience of first-year senior high school students. A quasi-experimental design with pre-and post-tests for both experimental and control groups was adopted. The experimental group (n = 67) received the IPRCV model, while the control group (n = 68) followed a traditional teaching model. Questionnaires and maker project evaluations were used to assess students' maker literacy, activity satisfaction, and learning experience before and after the intervention. Results indicate that the IPRCV model significantly and positively influenced both maker literacy and learning experience among senior high school freshmen. This study demonstrates that toolkit-based maker activity interventions are an effective method for enhancing maker literacy and learning experience among senior high school students.

TI Beyond the entity perspective: Exploring the internal development
   mechanism of high school students' geospatial thinking based on network
   analysis
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Geospatial thinking; Complex system; Network comparison; Cross-lagged
   panel network
ID SPATIAL THINKING; TEXTBOOK QUESTIONS; GEOGRAPHY; ABILITY; CURRICULUM;
   KNOWLEDGE; TECHNOLOGIES; ORIENTATION; EXPERIENCE; EDUCATION
AB Geospatial thinking (GST) is essential for high school students to understand spatial relationships and address complex geographic problems. This study approaches GST from a complex-system perspective and examines the dynamic interactions among its components using longitudinal network analysis. Two-wave data were collected from 1,608 Chinese high school students using the Spatial Thinking Ability Test (STAT). Network comparison and cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) analysis were employed to examine the dynamic characteristics, interrelationships, and internal development mechanisms of GST's components. The results show that GST forms an interconnected structure in which different components play distinct roles at different developmental stages. These findings provide a systemic perspective on GST development and offer implications for targeted geospatial instruction and spatial thinking training.

ID SELF-EFFICACY; VALIDATION; TRAITS; SCALE; MODEL
AB Understanding how AI-Generated Content (AIGC) tools are associated with student creative expression requires exploring a complex interplay of factors. This cross-sectional study (N = 374, art and design students) used a hybrid SEM-fsQCA approach to examine AIGC usage characteristics, creative psychology, creative ability, digital literacy, and university support. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) revealed that while creative psychology, ability, and external supports positively predicted creative expression, AIGC usage had a complex dual role. It directly boosted expression and indirectly promoted it by enhancing creative psychology (e.g., motivation). Furthermore, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) identified 5 distinct configurations (Overall Coverage=0.739) for high creative expression, highlighting digital literacy and university support as core conditions. These findings reveal AIGC's dual-pathway mechanism, showing its benefits are contingent on psychological and environmental factors, holding key implications for education.

TI Possibilities Literacy: Empowering learners for an uncertain world
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Possibility; Literacy; Futures; Creativity; Ethical imagination;
   Education for uncertainty
ID POSSIBILITY THINKING
AB In an era of rapid change, uncertainty and complexity, individuals and societies must develop new capacities to engage with the possible. This article introduces Possibilities Literacy as the cluster of inter-related competencies that allow individuals and groups to understand, generate and ethically act on diverse possibilities across personal, social, and cultural contexts. Drawing from cognitive and sociocultural perspectives, we propose a distinctive five-dimensional framework-Perception, Crafting, Engagement, Stewardship, and Mindsets-each explored through three orientations: Constraints, Alternatives, and Agency. At each intersection, we identify key competencies such as reframing constraints, playful generation, co-creation, futures deliberation, and self-authorship. Together, these enable learners to recognize limitations as invitations, map emerging possibilities, act with resilience, and steward futures aligned with shared values. We offer a rubric to support the development and assessment of Possibilities Literacy across contexts and conclude by rethinking literacy itself not as content mastery but as the evolving capacity to navigate uncertainty and co-create shared spaces of possibility.

TI Biomimicry-Inspired Urban Design Transformation in the Grand Paris
   Express: Exploring Cross-Disciplinary Thinking in Architecture Education
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Biomimicry education; Cross-disciplinary thinking; Architectural
   pedagogy; Biomimetic design processes; Urban-scale design; Sustainable
   architecture; Design thinking methodology; Cognitive development;
   Systems thinking; Interdisciplinary learning; Creative problem-solving;
   Architecture students
AB Architectural education faces unprecedented challenges as climate change and resource scarcity demand innovative cross-disciplinary approaches that transcend traditional boundaries. This study examines how structured biomimicry education develops cross-disciplinary thinking skills in architecture students, addressing urban-scale sustainability challenges. Through a qualitative case study of 17 fourth-year architecture students at California Polytechnic State University, we analyze biomimicry-based projects for the Grand Paris Express infrastructure using an integrated analytical framework combining Bloom's Taxonomy, Design Thinking methodology, and Creativity Metrics. This research provides the first comprehensive pedagogical framework for integrating biomimicry into architectural education at urban scales. Findings demonstrate that structured biomimicry education cultivates the interdisciplinary and collaborative competencies increasingly demanded by contemporary architectural practice, while identifying specific conditions- particularly biological model complexity management, iterative refinement support, and foundational science education-that support or hinder successful knowledge transfer from biological observation to architectural implementation.

TI Did students really care about creative thinking assessment in PISA
   2022?
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative thinking; Engagement; Careless responding; PISA 2022;
   Evaluative stakes
ID EXTERNAL EVALUATION; SELF-EFFICACY; STAKES; MOTIVATION; RESPONSES;
   TESTS; TIME; SPECIFICITY; PERFORMANCE; PSYCHOLOGY
AB The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 assessed creative thinking (CT) skills for the first time. While this assessment offers a unique snapshot of the creative abilities of 15-year-olds worldwide, it also raises questions about the influence of the low-stakes school context in which it was administered, where academic domains are more routinely assessed than creativity. This study examined differences in careless responding across PISA domains and within CT subdomains and facets. Within CT, it also tested whether cognitive and behavioral engagement and self-reported disengagement due to PISA's low-stakes nature predicted itemlevel performance. It further investigated whether school-level testing practices moderated the link between disengagement and performance. Within CT, careless responding also varied across subdomains and facets, with the lowest rates observed for the Social Problem Solving (SoPS) domain and the Generate Creative Ideas (GCI) facet. Performance on CT items was positively associated with both cognitive and behavioral engagement, and negatively associated with disengagement. Finally, among students in schools that routinely use tests for promotion or retention, the negative impact of disengagement on CT performance was weaker. These findings suggest that students took CT tasks at least as seriously as traditional academic ones. We discuss how, despite their potentially more engaging nature, CT assessments are not immune to the same engagement-related issues that affect core domains in low-stakes contexts.

TI A realist synthesis review of algorithmic approaches to developing
   multiple-choice questions in the natural sciences
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Standardized assessment; Artificial intelligence; Test construction;
   Multiple-choice test; High-order thinking skills; Natural sciences;
   Higher education
ID COEFFICIENT; DESIGN
AB This review study aimed to identify factors influencing the effectiveness of algorithmically generated test items, the quality of the tasks generated, and their broader impact on education when algorithmic procedures are implemented. The applied method of realist synthesis enabled the integration of evidence from previous studies to identify successful and unsuccessful configurations within the system Mechanism - Context - Outcomes. The mechanism encompasses diverse components of the algorithmized MCQ development, from the theoretical basis to workflow procedures. The context is understood as the specific conditions in which these mechanisms operate, while the outcomes are the results of the interaction between mechanisms and context. The findings obtained from 19 selected articles suggested that in creating test items, the design of algorithmic definitions plays a more critical role than their technical implementation. Of the measured outcomes, productivity was the only area in which automated multiplechoice question (MCQ) generation outperformed manual creation. However, it struggled to produce test items with sufficient complexity. The least favourable conditions arise when developers pursue "universality," producing algorithms that are not tailored to specific assessments, disciplines, or item banks. The most effective approach involves a team of developers with diverse expertise, equipped with well-defined algorithms, collaboratively creating MCQs for structured item banks under state or university regulations. Algorithmizing improves assessment techniques. It contributes to the reliability, transparency, and trustworthiness of examinations, enhancing their societal value, and also teachers' expertise in creating educational materials for more differentiated, personalized, and targeted learning.

TI Fostering Critical Thinking Through STEM Undergraduate Research:
   Mechanisms and Challenges in a Chinese Research University

LA English

   Research; Constructivist mechanisms; Cross-cultural pedagogy
AB Critical thinking (CT), a core learning objective in Western higher education, has seen limited integration into the curriculum of Chinese higher education (CHE). This study investigates how CT is inadvertently fostered within STEM authentic undergraduate research practices (AURPs) at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), a leading Chinese university that affords research opportunities to all undergraduates. By bridging Western CT principles within CHE's pragmatic practices, the study further provides actionable insights for designing learning environments that synergize disciplinary expertise and CT development.

TI Exploratory behaviour during improvisation tasks: A comparison between
   professional dancers and inexperienced individuals
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Dance; Constraints; Expertise; Dance training
ID CREATIVITY; EMERGENCE; CONSTRAINTS; THINKING; PLAY
AB The study of creativity in physical activity and sport sciences has increased in recent years, reflecting a growing interest in understanding how creative behaviour emerges in practice. In this line, particular attention has been paid to how different constraints shape individuals' exploratory behaviour, understood in terms of the speed of transitions between motor patterns and the diversity of those patterns. In the specific context of dance, the impact of task constraints (such as using a mirror or working with a partner) during improvisation situations, particularly in relation to participants' expertise, remains largely unexplored. Therefore, the aim of the study was to compare the exploratory behaviour of professional dancers and inexperienced individuals during improvisation under different task constraints (solo versus duo and mirror presence versus absence), in order to examine how this combination shapes creative exploration rather than performance outcomes. Twelve professional dancers and twelve inexperienced individuals were recorded while improvising under four conditions: a) Individual improvisation Without Mirror (IWOM), b) Individual improvisation With Mirror (IWM), c) Pair improvisation Without Mirror (PWOM), and d) Pair improvisation With Mirror (PWM). Exploratory behaviour was analysed using an observational instrument, and intra observer and inter observer reliability were assessed prior to data analysis. A linear mixed model was applied. The results reveal expertise related differences in exploratory strategies, with inexperienced participants showing quicker transitions between motor patterns and professional dancers demonstrating lower variability. Furthermore, improvisation with a mirror appears to produce slowed transitions, while pair improvisations seem to reduce the mirror's influence in favour of collaborative dynamics. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of creativity in dance as a situated and dynamic process and offer relevant insights for artistic and educational practice.

TI Applying image similarity analysis to coursework in visual design
   education
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Visual literacy; Sociocultural learning; Collaboration; Image
   similarity; Visual plagiarism; Plagiarism detection; Plagiarism
   prevention; Document similarity
ID PLAGIARISM DETECTION; INFORMATION; TOOL
AB Text similarity tools are widely used by educators for plagiarism prevention and detection in coursework, home exams, theses, and portfolios. Although most university-level subjects are text-oriented, there are also several subject areas that rely on visual elements, such as design, architecture, and engineering. In visually oriented subjects, it is natural to use images alongside text. However, there are few practical tools for, or documented studies on, applying image similarity analysis in educational contexts, despite a vast literature on image similarity and image plagiarism detection. The objective of this study was therefore to explore the opportunities offered by image similarity analysis within an educational context. Six use-cases were identified. A simple image analysis prototype was implemented as an experimental platform. The ideas were tested in a human-computer interaction course with around 250 undergraduate students where the coursework comprised more than 1,000 reports with more than 8,000 images. The results confirm that group efforts lead to more figures than solo efforts. The portion of individual images was inversely related to the group size. Increased figure counts were also observed with revised reports. Next, image similarity could be used to provide visual overviews, detect legitimate collaboration structures, detect possible unethical image borrowing, identify cases of potential lack of appropriate image attribution, and detect other anomalies that otherwise would be hard to detect. It is argued that image similarity tools hold potential for directing the teachers' attention towards relevant cases that help provide timely formative feedback to students and thus promote learning. It is concluded that state-of-the-art educational technology should be extended to also include similarity analysis of visuals.

AB Instructional designs simultaneously targeting the development of computational thinking (CT) skills and English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) knowledge have been implemented. These findings yielded pedagogical suggestions for educators integrating CT into EFL instruction.

TI Applying the torrance test: Developing a rubric to evaluate function art
   in educational settings
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE STEAM education; Function art; Torrance test; of creative thinking; Art
   and math integration; GeoGebra and art
ID CREATIVE-THINKING; STEAM
AB Function art is an art form that uses graphs of mathematical functions in creating artwork. It integrates mathematical functions, art, and technology within the STEAM framework. Despite its potential, a standardized method for evaluating function art remains lacking. This study develops and validates a rubric based on the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking (TTCT) to assess function art, focusing on Fluency, Flexibility, Originality, and Elaboration. This paper explores the development and validation of this rubric in an educational context. The rubric was designed for our specific setting, but it can be generalized. To create this rubric, the researchers adapted the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking. The rubric was tested on 51 function art pieces created by Grade 11 students in the Philippines. The psychometric evaluation of the function art task using Rasch measurement revealed robust reliability and validity. Correlation analysis identified a positive relationship between Fluency, Flexibility, and Originality. Regression analysis highlighted significant reciprocal influences between Fluency and Originality. Findings suggest that the framework can be used to objectively get a score on a single piece of artwork. The study contributes to the pedagogical landscape by providing educators with a tool for evaluating function art.

TI Creative minds in motion: The role of motor creativity in skill transfer
   among kindergarten children
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Motor creativity; Learning transfer; Creative thinking; Invented letter
   task; Kindergarten children; Early childhood development
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; DOMAIN-SPECIFICITY; GENDER-DIFFERENCES;
   YOUNG-CHILDREN; SCHOOL; MODEL
AB This study examined whether creativity is associated with the transfer of fine motor skills in kindergarten-aged children. Using Torrance's (1981) Thinking Creatively in Action and Movement (TCAM), we assessed creativity in 120 children, who were also evaluated on perceptualmotor and memory abilities. After training on the Invented Letter Task (ILT), transfer performance was tested at 24 h (consolidation) and 4-5 weeks post-training (retention). All facets of creativity, especially imagination, were significantly correlated with transfer speed and accuracy. Moderated regression analyses showed that creativity predicted transfer speed and accuracy independently of cognitive and perceptual-motor abilities and post-training skill levels. A significant Creativity & times; Time interaction for transfer speed revealed that creativity predicted faster transfer performance at both time points, with a more pronounced effect at long-term retention. Creativity, short-term memory, and task-specific skill independently contributed to the prediction of transfer performance without joint effects. These findings support the hypothesis that creativity may play a unique role in skill transfer, likely reflecting cognitive flexibility and adaptive problem-solving abilities. The results have implications for early childhood education, as they pave the way for intervention studies aimed at testing the potential of creative movement activities to enhance the generalization of motor learning necessary to promote lifelong learning and adaptability in children.

TI A Case Study of HEI Students' Experiences and Preferences Regarding Mode
   of Delivery: The Role of Socio-Economic Circumstances
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE mode of delivery; socio-economic circumstances; online learning;
   hybrid/blended learning; work-study balance; inclusivity
AB Students in higher education face diverse financial, employment and technological circumstances that may influence the suitability of different modes of delivery. This study explored students' preferences for and experiences of online, face-to-face and hybrid/blended delivery, with particular attention to the role of socio-economic circumstances in these preferences and experiences. A concurrent mixed-methods case study design was employed. Forty-four senior undergraduate and postgraduate students completed an online questionnaire comprising five-point Likert-scale items and open-ended narrative responses. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis and reliability analysis, while qualitative responses were analysed thematically and integrated with the quantitative findings. The results indicated a clear preference for online delivery, with 93.2% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that they preferred this mode and 75.0% preferring to remain online rather than change to an alternative mode. Flexibility, financial considerations and the ability to combine employment and study emerged as prominent considerations, particularly in a sample in which 95.5% of respondents combined employment with their studies. Transportation, accommodation and daily living expenses were also perceived as relevant to mode-of-delivery decisions. However, no single mode was perceived as universally inclusive, with students from very poor to poor socio-economic circumstances considered particularly vulnerable to exclusion. The findings demonstrate that mode-of-delivery preferences should be understood within students' broader socio-economic circumstances rather than solely as pedagogical preferences. Thus, it is recommended that higher education institutions consider adopting flexible and differentiated delivery approaches accommodating students' financial, employment and access circumstances while promoting equitable participation.

TI Is Artificial Intelligence a New Pillar of Higher Education? Exploratory
   and Confirmatory Factor Analysis of the Student Academic Experience
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; higher education; academic
   experience; psychometric validation; factor analysis
AB Traditional frameworks evaluating the university academic experience often give limited attention to students' reported use of Artificial Intelligence. This study psychometrically validates a novel measurement model, testing whether AI-related academic practices emerge as a distinct component of students' perceived academic experience. Using a cross-validation design, 2403 undergraduate students from a private university in Bolivia were surveyed. The dataset was randomly split for Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA, n = 1200) to uncover latent variables and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA, n = 1203) to validate the structural stability of a refined 31-item scale. The EFA revealed a cohesive five-factor structure: (1) Academic Engagement and Student Life, (2) Student-Reported AI Use in Academic Learning, (3) Communication and Critical Thinking Skills, (4) Teaching Quality, and (5) Academic Dedication. The CFA confirmed an excellent model fit (CFI = 0.954, RMSEA = 0.046), supporting strong construct validity. Furthermore, inter-factor correlations showed that student-reported AI use was positively associated with academic engagement and with the broader Communication, Ethical, and Critical Thinking Skills domain. These empirical results suggest that, within this institutional context, students perceive AI as a relevant element of their academic routines. By validating the University Academic Experience and AI Integration Survey, this study provides a context-specific framework for assessing students' self-reported use and perceived integration of AI in academic learning as a distinct dimension of their academic experience. The validated instrument is not intended for directly measuring learning outcomes, educational effectiveness, teaching effectiveness, or institutional quality.

TI An Analytic Developmental Rubric for AI-Enabled Integrated STEM
   Instructional Design: Development and Validation with Preservice
   Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; integrated STEM; instructional design; rubric
   development; instrument validation; preservice teachers
ID CORRELATION-COEFFICIENTS
AB Teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) competence is increasingly important in China's educational modernization. Yet in contexts related to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), how AI integration at the pedagogical level can be made observable in instructional design remains underexamined. This mixed-methods study developed an analytic developmental rubric that integrates the AI pedagogy aspect of UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Teachers with seven key characteristics of integrated STEM. The rubric uses gates to define the minimum evidence required for each STEM characteristic and uses verifiable descriptors and hallmarks to assign a competency level within each characteristic for preservice teachers' use of AI to enable integrated STEM instructional design. Then, the rubric underwent a series of validation procedures. Eight experts from two universities conducted expert review and content validity assessment. A total of 108 preservice teachers from six teacher education degree programs spanning mathematics, science, and technology at a normal university in China completed integrated STEM instructional designs on the same topic. Three raters from the two universities independently scored the artifacts, and the resulting scores were used to estimate inter-rater reliability, examine intercorrelations and internal consistency, and assess known-group validity. The findings provided evidence supporting the rubric's reliability and validity and indicated that it could consistently distinguish preservice teachers across training stages ordered a priori by expected competency. In this way, this rubric begins to fill the gap in the assessment of AI-enabled integrated STEM instructional design, and its scope of application is not confined to any particular STEM subject or instructional design framework.

TI STEM Motivation, Identity and Interest Among Students in Two Flemish
   Secondary Schools: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Survey
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM motivation; STEM interest; STEM identity; basic psychological
   needs; gender differences; study track; grade level; secondary
   education; comparative cross-sectional survey
ID SCIENCE IDENTITY; CAREER; CHOICE; INTERVENTION; EXPERIENCES;
   MATHEMATICS; TECHNOLOGY; PIPELINE; MODEL
AB Rapid technological innovation and digitalization have intensified the demand for STEM-related skills, yet many educational systems face stagnant or declining student engagement in STEM, particularly in the later years of secondary education. This study examined how gender, study track (STEM versus non-STEM) and grade level are related to secondary school students' STEM motivation, interest and identity. The study also examined the role of perceived autonomy, relatedness and competence support from mathematics teachers in these associations. Using a comparative cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 317 students in two secondary schools in the Kempenrand region of Antwerp, Flanders (Belgium). Linear regression models and school-specific simple-effects analyses were used to examine school and subgroup differences. Concurrent indirect-association and moderation analyses were performed to examine the role of perceived need support with Benjamini-Hochberg corrections applied for multiple testing. The results revealed variation between school contexts. The association between gender and STEM identity differed between schools, while study-track differences in STEM interest, identity and intrinsic motivation were greater in one school than in the other. The clearest contextual variation concerned grade level. In one school, 5th-year students reported higher STEM identity and identified regulation, whereas 6th-year students reported higher levels of these outcomes in the other; 6th-year students in the latter school also reported higher STEM interest and intrinsic motivation. No total concurrent indirect associations through perceived need support remained statistically significant after correction. However, the association between study track and STEM identity varied significantly as a function of perceived autonomy and relatedness support, with both forms of support positively associated with STEM identity among STEM track students but not among non-STEM students. These findings indicate that subgroup differences in STEM-related outcomes are not uniform across school contexts and that pooled estimates may obscure meaningful contextual heterogeneity. Context-sensitive analyses are therefore important when identifying groups with lower STEM motivation, interest or identity.

TI Artificial Intelligence Integration in Teacher Education: Institutional
   Readiness and Curriculum Pathways in a Fourth Industrial Revolution
   Context
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; teacher education; curriculum integration;
   institutional readiness; Fourth Industrial Revolution; higher education;
   Namibia
AB Despite growing global interest in Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, limited empirical research has examined how teacher education institutions in developing-country and resource-constrained contexts can sustainably integrate AI into their curricula. This gap is particularly significant because many existing AI integration frameworks assume levels of technological infrastructure, institutional capacity, and digital readiness that may not reflect the realities of higher education institutions in the Global South. Against this backdrop, this study explored institutional readiness, curriculum integration pathways, and implementation strategies for Artificial Intelligence within teacher education programmes in Namibia. Guided by an interpretivist paradigm, a qualitative exploratory design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with 25 teacher educators across six university campuses. Data were analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's framework. The findings indicate that AI integration extends beyond technological adoption and requires coordinated curriculum transformation, institutional preparedness, and pedagogical redesign. Key integration pathways include embedding AI within faculty courses, curriculum-wide integration of AI competencies, simulation-based learning, and support for online teaching environments. Institutional readiness, particularly in terms of infrastructure, faculty capacity, and curriculum alignment, emerged as a critical determinant of implementation. While participants highlighted benefits such as improved instructional efficiency, enhanced teacher capacity, and increased learner autonomy, they also expressed concerns regarding overreliance on technology. By integrating Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this study advances a multi-level framework linking institutional and individual dimensions of AI adoption in teacher education. This study contributes context-specific insights to AI curriculum transformation in the Global South and provides practical implications for curriculum design, institutional strategy, and policy development.

TI Negative Campus Climate as an Institutional Risk Indicator for Student
   Success and Wellbeing in Higher Education: A Covariate-Adjusted Analysis
   of Open Survey Data
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE campus climate; student success; psychological wellbeing; intention to
   remain; higher education; diversity, equity and inclusion;
   propensity-score weighting; augmented inverse probability weighting;
   institutional risk; learning analytics
AB Campus climate surveys are widely administered in higher education, but their results are rarely integrated into student-success analytics. This study examines negative campus climate as an institutional risk indicator for academic satisfaction, intention to remain, and psychological wellbeing. Open student microdata from the 2016 University of Michigan Campus Climate Survey on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (ICPSR 37096) were analyzed. A negative climate factor was constructed from perceived DEI climate, general climate, fair treatment, and institutional communication and showed satisfactory psychometric properties (KMO = 0.780; alpha = 0.846; omega = 0.850; AVE = 0.587). Survey-weighted analyses combined inverse probability weighting, five-fold cross-fitted augmented inverse probability weighting, continuous models, cluster analysis, mediation, and spline-based risk curves. High negative climate was associated with reductions of 0.734, 0.752, and 0.656 points on the original five-point scales for academic satisfaction, intention to remain, and wellbeing, respectively; standardized AIPW contrasts were -1.029, -1.017, and -0.951 SD. Each one SD increase in negative climate was associated with decreases of 0.764, 0.725, and 0.661 SD in the respective outcomes. Wellbeing statistically mediated 21.4% of the association with academic satisfaction and 19.3% of the association with intention to remain. Three interpretable climate profiles showed substantial outcome gradients. The predicted probability of very low outcomes reached 25% at climate scores between 1.80 and 2.42 SD above the mean, depending on the outcome. These context-specific findings support campus climate as a potentially useful institutional monitoring signal, while not establishing temporal or causal effects.

TI Generative Artificial Intelligence as a Collaborative Designer for
   Elementary Computer Science Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DE GenAI; human-AI collaborations; instructional design; K-12 education;

ID DUAL-CODING THEORY
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming ubiquitous in our everyday lives. In the United States, AI has increasingly been recognized as an important part of computer science (CS) standards for elementary school students. Prior research work has shown that AI-related content can be taught at upper elementary grade levels. However, classroom-ready, standards-aligned materials for CS in the context of AI remain limited at the elementary level. This paper showcases how educators may use generative AI to design standards-aligned materials for teaching CS and AI in elementary schools. TI Mapping Teachers' Environmental Attitude, Engagement, and Education
   Practices in South Sudanese Schools
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE environmental education; educational practice; primary schools; South
   Sudan
ID BEHAVIOR; MODERNIZATION; PARADIGM; SCALE
AB This study examines the relationship between teachers' level of environmentalism and their pedagogical practices across South Sudan, using a survey conducted among 254 primary school teachers in the Yei and Juba counties of Central Equatoria State, South Sudan. Through a statistical analysis of the survey data and use of relevant theory, the findings reveal pro-environmental attitudes and engagement among teachers; however, these are more focused on context-bound environmental issues, unlike in Western countries, where more abstract types of environmentalism often dominate engagement. In contrast, strong correlations were found between environmental engagement and teachers' efforts to motivate and support pupils. Thus, the study contributes to the understanding of context-bound environmentalism and the attitude-pedagogy gap within a resource-based, post-conflict educational setting.

TI Beyond Acceptance: How Early Childhood Preservice Teachers Critically
   Engage with GenAI Feedback in Lesson Planning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE critical engagement with AI; developmentally appropriate practice; early
   childhood education; pedagogical adaptation; reflective decision-making
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being investigated as a pedagogical tool in early childhood education, particularly for lesson planning and professional learning. This study examined preservice teachers' reflections on GenAI-generated feedback during sustainability focused lesson planning. Fifty preservice teachers were involved in developing two lesson plans, receiving GenAI feedback, and revising their plans. Data collection included written reflections about two lesson plans.    Residential Camp
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

AB Math walks, where participants explore physical spaces and make connections to mathematics, have been implemented in a wide variety of ways in different learning settings. Math walks connect place-based learning, the development of interest in STEM fields, and opportunities for students to exercise agency over their STEM learning. AB Teacher education programs increasingly recognize emotion regulation as central to teachers' professional functioning, particularly in settings serving at-risk youth. TI Promoting Inclusive Education Through School Leadership: The Mediating
   Role of Principal Self-Efficacy
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive education; inclusive school leadership; principal
   self-efficacy; transformational leadership; transactional leadership;
   school culture; mediation analysis
ID TRANSFORMATIONAL LEADERSHIP; TEACHERS; WORK
AB Inclusive education depends not only on policy frameworks but also on school leaders' capacity to translate inclusive principles into sustained organisational practice. This study examined the relationships among principals' transformational and transactional leadership, self-efficacy, school culture, and the implementation of inclusive policies and practices. The study employed a cross-sectional quantitative design involving 452 principals of primary and lower-secondary schools in Greece. Data were collected using the Leadership for Inclusion Questionnaire (LEI-Q), the School Culture Survey (SCS), the Principals' Self-Efficacy for Inclusive Leadership Scale, and the Transformational and Transactional Leadership Scale (TATL). TI How strong is the evidence in generative AI-related academic misconduct
   allegations? A mixed-methods analysis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic misconduct; Generative AI; Evidence quality; Probative value;
   Evidence taxonomy
AB Since the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, higher education institutions have experienced an increase in academic misconduct allegations related to suspected generative AI (GenAI) misuse. A necessary part of these processes is the inclusion of evidence to support and strengthen allegations. To date, no systematic framework exists for understanding trends and patterns in GenAI student academic misconduct and classifying the types and probative value of evidence presented in these allegations. This study addresses that gap through a mixed-methods analysis of 1,162 GenAI-related misconduct case records spanning January 2023 to December 2025 at one regional Australian university. Analysis confirmed an increase in case volumes over the study period and produced an empirically derived 15-code evidence taxonomy, which was applied across the 1,855 evidence items against three probative quality credentials drawn from legal evidence scholarship: relevance, credibility, and inferential force. Results point to patterns across time that differ across evidence types, including an increasing use of fabricated references and student admissions of AI use, and a decrease in allegations being raised without support. These findings highlight a critical gap in current misconduct policies: institutions lack explicit criteria for determining what constitutes reliable evidence in GenAI misconduct cases. To address this, the study offers three contributions: first, an empirically derived taxonomy that categorises the types of evidence used in GenAI misconduct proceedings. Second, a structured framework for assessing the quality and reliability of that evidence, designed for direct application in institutional decision-making. Third, the first empirical analysis at scale of how evidence is currently gathered and evaluated in GenAI misconduct cases.

TI The relationship between coping response and adjustment to university
   life among university students: Indirect associations through the impact
   of music
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Coping skills; Music; Adaptation; University; Indirect effect
ID EMOTION REGULATION; STRATEGIES; STRESS; STYLES; SAMPLE; SIZE
AB The transition to university presents academic, social, and personal challenges. Although approach coping responses are associated with university adjustment, the processes linking them to different adjustment dimensions remain unclear. Music may serve as a resource for emotion regulation and stress management, but its statistical role in these associations has received limited attention. This cross-sectional study examined whether approach coping responses were indirectly associated with social, personal, and academic adjustment through the impact of music among first-year university students. Data were collected from 507 domestic undergraduate students (mean age = 19.7, SD = 3.50; 58.4% female). Three regression-based indirect-effect models were tested using ordinary least squares regression and 5000 bootstrap resamples. Approach coping responses were positively associated with the impact of music (B = .354, p < .001) and with all three adjustment dimensions. In the primary unadjusted analyses, indirect associations through the impact of music were supported for social adjustment (ab = .069, 95% bootstrap CI [.042, .103]) and academic adjustment (ab = .038, 95% bootstrap CI [.011, .070]), but not for personal adjustment (ab = .015, 95% bootstrap CI [-.008, .041]). Post-hoc sensitivity analyses adjusting for gender and academic discipline showed that the social-adjustment finding remained supported (ab = .057, 95% bootstrap CI [.032, .088]), whereas the academic-adjustment estimate was attenuated and its confidence interval included zero (ab = .023, 95% bootstrap CI [-.001, .054]). The personal-adjustment estimate remained nonsignificant (ab = .011, 95% bootstrap CI [-.011, .037]). These findings indicate that the social-adjustment result was robust to demographic adjustment, whereas the academic-adjustment result should be interpreted cautiously. Because of the cross-sectional design, the findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation.

AB This study evaluated Kahoot!-supported collaborative learning in a first-year chemical engineering fluid mechanics module delivered within an outcome-based education framework aligned to the Malaysian Qualifications Framework (MQF 2nd Edition) and current Malaysian engineering accreditation standards. TI Long-term effects of online education: Evidence from Kazakhstan's
   COVID-19 policy cutoff
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Online education; Student performance; Kazakhstan; Long-term effects;
   Unified National Testing; Rural schools
AB This study exploits a unique policy cutoff in Kazakhstan during the COVID-19 pandemic to estimate the effect of online education on student performance. In 2020, small rural schools were permitted to continue offline instruction, while others transitioned to online learning. We estimate the effect of online learning on Unified National Testing (UNT) scores in mathematics and reading for the full population of rural students from 2021 to 2024. SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   pediatric trauma; pelvic binding; pelvic trauma
ID PERFORMANCE; SPEED
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility and impact of a gamified, low-fidelity simulation activity for pediatric pelvic sheet binding, focused on improving trainee procedural speed, technical proficiency, and self-efficacy through deliberate practice and mastery learning. DESIGN: This was a prospective educational pilot study utilizing a pretest/posttest design and a low-fidelity simulation mannequin with haptic feedback. The intervention was developed using Kern's 6-Step Framework and designed to address American Board of Surgery (ABS) Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs). The activity followed a structured progression to track performance across assessment phases and 2 successive attempts separated by a structured educational session (debriefing with focused feedback, video demonstration, and live demonstration) to evaluate short-term skill acquisition. TI Filters, frames, and guides: How institutional contexts organize
   teachers' beliefs about inclusion
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusive education; Teacher beliefs; Belief functions; Activity
   settings; Institutional organization; Policy implementation; Cayman
   Islands
ID ATTITUDES; EDUCATION
AB Elementary teachers across seven schools in the Cayman Islands converged on strikingly similar interpretations despite diverse international training: filtering inclusion through ability differences, framing effectiveness as support-dependent, guiding practice toward ability-based differentiation. AB Although language teacher immunity has been widely studied in relation to how teachers navigate professional challenges, little is known about how immunity configurations are retrospectively interpreted and reorganised across extended careers. TI The secondary-tertiary mathematics transition: a visionary research
   agenda for the field
SO TEACHING MATHEMATICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENTS; ENGAGEMENT; UNIVERSITY; SCHOOL
AB The secondary-tertiary mathematics transition remains a persistent challenge across educational systems. Despite decades of research, reforms often oscillate between deficit narratives ('students are underprepared') and narrow curriculum fixes ('more algebra, more rigour'). In this paper, I argue for a different framing: the transition is a shared design problem distributed across institutions, curricula, pedagogies and assessments. I synthesize key lines of work: early studies on proof, formalization and advanced mathematical thinking; institutional analyses emphasizing didactical contract and discontinuities in mathematical organizations; and more recent socio-cultural, socio-political and affect-oriented research examining belonging, identity, norms and equity. I identify unresolved issues, including theory fragmentation, limited comparative curricular evidence, weak causal claims about interventions at scale, and insufficient attention to diverse student pathways and service mathematics. I propose a future research agenda structured around (i) theory networking, (ii) curriculum-assessment coherence, (iii) design-based and programmatic intervention research, (iv) equitable participation and identity-safe teaching, (v) cross-institutional teacher education, (vi) data infrastructures for transition monitoring and (vii) international and intra-national comparative studies. The argument is intentionally visionary: we need to move from diagnosing transition 'problems' to designing transition 'handovers' with shared responsibility and stronger evidence.

TI Individual Differences in the Sub-Lexical Perception and Production of
   L2 Chinese Tones
SO CHINESE JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 Chinese tones; sub-lexical perception; sub-lexical production;
   individual differences; auditory processing
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE ACQUISITION; MANDARIN; REPRESENTATION; LEARNERS
AB This study examines sub-lexical Chinese tone perception and production, considering the role of individual differences. We recruited 27 native speakers of Portuguese learning Chinese at university in Portugal, ranging from beginner to intermediate-advanced. We assessed their categorical perception and acoustic sensitivity to lexical tones using three synthesized 8-step continua-T1-T2, T2-T4, and T3-T4-in AXB identification and AXB discrimination tasks (from Hall & eacute; et al., 2004). Tone production was assessed using a pinyin reading task with monosyllables. Chinese proficiency was measured through the Chinese version of LEXTALE (Chan & Chang, 2018). Auditory processing was tested using pitch and rise-time discrimination tasks and melody reproduction tasks (Saito et al., 2020). Results showed that learners' perceptual accuracy varied across tone continua, and that T3-T4 was the most challenging. Learners' categorical perception and acoustic sensitivity in tone perception were not completely consistent. This may reflect a greater sensitivity to pitch rate variation, which learners may have relied on when processing acoustic information. Tone production difficulty aligned with categorical perception ability, with T3 being the most problematic and T1 the most accurate. Additionally, proficiency showed no clear effect on categorical perception, but it was associated with better performance in acoustic discrimination, whereas perceptual acuity in spectral and temporal dimensions played a crucial role in sub-lexical tone processing.

TI Testing the Activation of Embodied Experience During First and Second
   Language Comprehension: A Sentence-Picture Verification Study
SO CHINESE JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE embodied cognition; second language; sentence comprehension; shape
   information; sentence-picture verification
ID MENTAL SIMULATION; MOTOR SYSTEM; LANGUAGE; REPRESENTATIONS; PERCEPTION;
   WORD
AB Embodied cognition theory posits that language comprehension is grounded in sensorimotor experience. However, it remains unclear to what extent embodied experience-particularly visual information-is activated during first-language (L1) and second-language (L2) processing. To address this gap, we investigated whether L1 and L2 speakers of Chinese could activate object shape information implied by sentence during real-time comprehension. Two sentence-picture verification (SPV) tasks were used: a time-constrained version (Experiment 1) and a self-paced version (Experiment 2). In both experiments, L1 speakers responded significantly faster when the pictured object matched the shape implied by the sentence, demonstrating robust embodied effects. In contrast, L2 speakers did not show a significant embodied effect under time pressure (Experiment 1) but exhibited a trend toward shape simulation in the untimed task (Experiment 2). Moreover, under the untimed condition, L2 proficiency significantly predicted reaction times (RTs) but did not interact with shape congruency. Taken together, our findings suggest that while embodied experience reliably supports L1 comprehension, such effects are less robust in L2 processing, potentially due to limited or qualitatively different sensory-motor grounding during L2 acquisition.

TI Resonance Alignment in the Naturalistic Interaction Between Chinese
   Native and Non-Native Speakers
SO CHINESE JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE resonance alignment; naturalistic interaction; interactional competence
ID SOCIOCOGNITIVE APPROACH; 2ND-LANGUAGE; COMPETENCE
AB The notion of resonance alignment has been used in the present study to describe the process by which interlocutors synchronize their situation models and linguistic representations, and engage in the dynamic echoing and transformation of discourse elements to construct shared meaning during interaction. TI Statistical Learning of L2 Chinese Characters: The Role of Phonological
   Similarity and Explicit Instruction
SO CHINESE JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS

DT Article
DE Chinese character learning; cross-situational statistical learning;
   explicit instruction; lexical tone; second language acquisition
ID NONNATIVE LEARNERS; RADICAL AWARENESS; WORD ACQUISITION; IMPLICIT;
   SENSITIVITY; READ; KEY
AB Learning to read in Chinese requires learners to map phonological forms not only to meaning but also to visually complex logographic characters. The present study examined whether native English speakers can acquire novel Chinese characters through cross-situational statistical learning (CSSL), and whether phonological similarity constrains this process. Phonological similarity was manipulated such that some character pairs were associated with tonal minimal pairs, whereas others involved phonologically distinct words. In addition, half of the participants received brief explicit instruction on Chinese lexical tones prior to the task. Results showed that learners successfully acquired character-sound mappings after a short exposure period, demonstrating that statistical learning mechanisms can support early stages of Chinese character acquisition. However, learning was significantly constrained by phonological similarity, with tonal minimal pairs proving especially difficult. No significant differences emerged between the instructed and implicit learning groups. Nevertheless, post-task questionnaires revealed that participants who reported greater awareness of lexical tones achieved higher overall accuracy. These findings highlight the importance of phonological distinctiveness in character learning and suggest that learners' sensitivity to tonal information may facilitate acquisition even in predominantly implicit learning contexts. The study contributes to current research on the integration of phonological and orthographic learning in Chinese second language acquisition.

TI Variable-Length Calibration Stopping Rules for Multidimensional
   Computerized Adaptive Testing
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID ONLINE CALIBRATION; MODEL
AB Multidimensional computerized adaptive testing (MCAT) has gained increasing attention, as has online calibration for MCAT. As an essential component of online calibration, the calibration stopping rule determines the conditions for ending calibration and affects its accuracy and efficiency. Current MCAT online calibration studies predominantly employ fixed-length calibration stopping rules. This study introduces four novel variable-length calibration stopping rules (designated as D-rule, E-rule, T-rule, and DI-rule), all derived from the Fisher information matrix of item parameters. The D-rule and E-rule quantify calibration information through the determinant and the minimum eigenvalue of the Fisher information matrix, respectively; the T-rule and DI-rule quantify item parameter estimation error variances using the trace and the maximum diagonal element of the inverse of the Fisher information matrix, respectively. To obtain appropriate termination thresholds, two methods were employed: the empirical method and calibration reliability. Results showed that the four variable-length calibration stopping rules could terminate calibration as expected and achieve satisfactory calibration accuracy.

TI GutDigest: a new game to enhance active learning and assessment of
   gastrointestinal digestion of macromolecules
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digestion; gamification; gastrointestinal physiology; macromolecules;
   teaching innovation
ID EDUCATIONAL GAME; LINGUAL LIPASE; PHYSIOLOGY; PUZZLE; MECHANISM;
   INSIGHTS; ENZYME; TEACH; KEY
AB Several educators have developed educational games to promote the teaching and learning of complex concepts in physiology and other biomedical sciences. However, none of the currently available games specifically addressed the digestion of macromolecules across the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. In this study, we describe our new initiative of developing an online educational game (GutDigest) that helps students understand this complex topic. GutDigest has 3 sections (section 1 for carbohydrate, section 2 for lipid, and section 3 for protein digestion) across which 17 immovable e-tokens (representing the enzymes) are placed in the first column of the board on the left side (6 for carbohydrates, 5 for lipids, and 6 for proteins). Likewise, it has 122 movable e-tokens (representing enzyme source, classification, substrate, major site of action, end product of digestion, and means of enterocyte absorption of the corresponding end products) scattered in the repository on the right side (43 for carbohydrates, 36 for lipids, and 43 for proteins). Matching from right to left sides can be done either by dragging or by tapping and dropping. The results of the 3 sections are displayed to the player after each trial, and the e-tokens are reshuffled for the next trials. We recommend the use of this game by tutors to complement the teaching of this complex topic, assess the knowledge of students, and support practical simulation sessions in resource-limited settings. With its formative assessment-like feedback, this game enhances personalized learning for students compared to traditional study methods.

TI Medical physiology faculty overpredict assessment question complexity
   and alignment with national board expectations
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment alignment; board preparation; curriculum design; educational
   measurement; medical physiology education
ID MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS; ACHIEVEMENT; IMPACT; FLAWS
AB Medical licensing exams require students in allopathic and osteopathic programs to apply foundational science knowledge to board-style patient presentations. This study aimed to assess Medical Physiology course questions and their alignment with the National Board of Medical Examiners' (NBME) Item-Writing Guide. The research team obtained practice and exam questions written by 5 physiology faculty members, totaling 316 practice and 187 exam questions. Questions were reviewed by the research team and assessed for word count and then coded into three categories: basic science (lowest complexity), clinical scenario (moderate complexity), or NBME style (highest complexity). A Step-1 practice exam was obtained from the NBME, and questions were assessed for word count and then coded into the same categories. Faculty members completed a survey that assessed NBME-style question familiarity and estimated the percentages of their practice and exam questions in each category. Faculty predicted their practice and exam questions included 14% and 23%, respectively, of NBME-style questions. However, the research team coded and found that only 3% of the practice and 7% of the exam questions met NBME-style criteria. In contrast, the Step-1 practice exam contained 92% NBME-style questions. Significantly lower word counts were identified in course exams compared to practice Step-1 questions. Survey results indicate a high degree of concern over student success on Step-1 licensure. Faculty predictions highlight extensive overprediction of NBME-style questions and may contribute to gaps in student Step-1 preparedness. Training with the NBME's Item-Writing Guide may be needed to help address this gap. NEW & NOTEWORTHY As national board examinations emphasize patient-centered application, are course exams missing the mark? Analysis of 500+ physiology questions revealed a striking disconnect: faculty believed up to 23% of their exam questions were board style, but fewer than 7% met the standard. Shorter, less complex practice and exam questions may be undermining readiness. These findings expose a hidden gap in assessment design and point to faculty development as a critical step toward improving student success.
