TI Adaptations to intertidal life: divergence of energy metabolism enzyme
   pathways in marine polychaetes
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Alitta virens; energetic metabolism; Nephtys caeca; opine
   dehydrogenases; physiological adaptation
ID NEREIS-VIRENS SARS; ANAEROBIC METABOLISM; NEPHTYS-CECA; NEANTHES-VIRENS;
   DEHYDROGENASE; ORGANIZATION; ANNELIDA; MUSCLE; OXIDOREDUCTASES;
   INVERTEBRATE
AB To engage undergraduate marine biology students and demonstrate the relevance of energy metabolism to their field, we developed laboratory activities that integrate cellular metabolism with the biology of marine invertebrates. Our approach has the potential to uncover specific adaptations in energy pathways associated with hypoxia tolerance. A key difference between marine invertebrates and vertebrates lies in their anaerobic metabolism. Whereas vertebrates typically utilize lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to produce lactate as the end product of anaerobic glycolysis, marine invertebrates employ a variety of dehydrogenase pathways. This diversity enables efficient anaerobic energy production and reduces the accumulation of harmful by-products. We used two abundant polychaete species (Nephtys caeca and Alitta virens) found on the eastern Atlantic coast of Canada. Students measured the maximal activities of key enzymes of anaerobic (LDH, pyruvate kinase, and opine dehydrogenases) and aerobic (electron transport system, pyruvate kinase, malate dehydrogenase, and aspartate aminotransferase) metabolism. The presence of two opine dehydrogenases (strombine and alanopine) was observed in N. caeca, whereas LDH activity was marginal. Opine dehydrogenases are homologous to LDH and help buffer acidification during hypoxia. In A. virens, only LDH is present. As a general marker of aerobic capacity and hypoxia tolerance in invertebrates, malate dehydrogenase activity was high in both species. This laboratory activity introduces undergraduate students to metabolic adaptations and alternative energy pathways in marine life, particularly in the intertidal zone. This activity, conducted at the beginning of the semester, captured their interest and motivated them to study the key theoretical concepts governing animal energetic metabolism.

TI How drawing unlocks students' developing mechanistic reasoning about
   complex systems in physiology
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION

DT Article

AB In science education, student-generated drawings provide valuable insights into students' developing understanding of complex systems. TI Diagnostic instruments in extended curriculum programs: a scoping review
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic readiness; academic support; diagnostic assessment; extended
   curriculum program; health sciences education
ID ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; MEDICAL-STUDENTS; UNIVERSITY; SUCCESS
AB This study maps and synthesizes the existing body of literature on diagnostic tools and tests used within extended curriculum programs (ECPs) in higher education. Diagnostic assessment plays an important role in informing admission, placement, and early academic support within ECPs. The evidence based on the types, uses, and quality of diagnostic instruments, particularly within the South African higher education system, remains fragmented. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O'Malley framework, as refined by Levac et al. (Levac D, Colquhoun H, O'Brien KK. Implement Sci 5: 69, 2010). Five electronic databases were systematically searched for empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025. Studies examining diagnostic assessment instruments used for admission, placement, or academic support in higher education were eligible for inclusion. Nine empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Quantitative designs were utilized eight times (n = 8; 88.88%), representing diverse regions of the world. Three studies (33.33%) focused explicitly on health sciences education, primarily within medical training contexts. Diagnostic instruments commonly assessed cognitive or discipline-specific knowledge, as well as academic literacy or language proficiency. Diagnostic scores were predominantly used to predict how prepared students are for higher education or identify students at risk of academic difficulty. Only one study focused explicitly on ECP students. Evidence supporting the validity and reliability of diagnostic instruments was inconsistently reported, and limited attention was given to fairness, cultural responsiveness, and contextual relevance. The study findings highlight the need for validated ECP-specific diagnostic tools to support equitable student success.

TI How Generative AI Influences Learning Outcomes in Programming Education:
   A Three-level Bayesian Meta-analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Programming education; Learning outcomes; Meta-analysis
ID COMPUTATIONAL THINKING; EFFECT SIZES; CHATGPT; MODELS; IMPACT; SKILLS;
   TESTS; POWER
AB Generative AI (GenAI) has shown promise in programming education, yet empirical evidence remains inconsistent due to varied pedagogical and technical contexts. This research addressed this inconsistency through a three-level Bayesian meta-analysis of 35 empirical studies with 131 effect sizes published between 2022 and 2025. Learning outcomes were classified into AI-assisted programming outcomes (AIPO), independent programming outcomes (IPO), higher-order skills (HOS), and motivational-emotional outcomes (MEO). Results demonstrated credible small-to-medium positive effects of GenAI on all four outcome categories, and no credible difference among categories was detected. The moderator analyses did not detect credible moderation by educational contexts, instructional designs, or GenAI system designs in any outcome category. A few exploratory pairwise differences were credible for MEO under specific educational contexts and strategy-training conditions. Within the current evidence, GenAI shows consistent positive average effects, whereas the conditions that strengthen or weaken these effects remain undetermined. Because the corpus is small and unevenly distributed across moderator levels, the absence of detected moderation may reflect limited statistical information rather than equivalence across conditions. Larger and more balanced studies with more complete reporting of implementation details are needed to identify these conditions.

DE autoethnography; hybrid semiotic practice; Korean-English; Kyopomal;
   multilingual children; translanguaging; two-way immersion
ID LANGUAGE; ENGLISH; IDEOLOGIES
AB In bi-/multi-lingual and Two-Way Immersion (TWI) programs, strict language-separation policies often inadvertently marginalize the natural, fluid communication of emergent multilinguals, reducing their complex hybrid talk. Bridging the author's lived experience as a multilingual child with qualitative classroom research of first-grade Korean-English students, this article challenges the monolingual gaze. Utilizing translanguaging as an overarching framework and Hybrid Semiotic Practice (HSP) as an analytical lens, the study documents how children strategically deploy their full linguistic, cultural, and embodied repertoires in peer interactions. The findings reframe these highly metacognitive, audience-aware, and rule-governed practices not as errors, but as Kyopomal-an agentive, community-normed linguistic repertoire. By shifting the paradigm from "Konglish" to Kyopomal, this article offers actionable pedagogical implications for elementary literacy instruction, including cross-linguistic wordplay. This research demonstrates that affirming these hybrid literacies is not merely an instructional scaffold, but an act of sociolinguistic justice that celebrates what it truly means to be multilingual.

TI Home Writing Environments of At-Risk and Typically Developing Children
   in Spain: Implications for Preventing Writing Difficulties
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE home writing environment; formal and informal practices; family support;
   at-risk writers; primary education; inclusive education; writing
ID LITERACY PRACTICES; EMERGENT LITERACY; READING-COMPREHENSION; PARENTAL
   INVOLVEMENT; FAMILY-RISK; INTERVENTION; LANGUAGE; SKILLS; SUPPORT;
   GROWTH
AB Writing is a key competence for academic and social success, and for future employability. From a sociocultural perspective, writing development is shaped by both school instruction and literacy-related experiences within the home. However, little is known about what specific writing practices and support families naturally provide, particularly for children at-risk of writing difficulties in early primary education. This study examines home writing practices and family support for 296 typically developing and at-risk children in Spain in grades 1 and 2. Students' writing performance was monitored longitudinally using curriculum-based writing measures, identifying 48 at-risk writers. Parents completed the Home Writing Environment Questionnaire, assessing the frequency of formal and informal writing practices and types of family support, including procedural, motivational and material support. The results showed similar patterns of home writing environments between groups; however, at-risk children engaged in writing activities less frequently, especially those involving higher-level processes such as planning, composing and revising. Families of at-risk children reported slightly higher levels of contingent support, suggesting adaptive involvement. These findings highlight the importance of promoting systematic family engagement in early writing to support inclusion and prevent difficulties.

TI Comparing Student Reasoning on Graphical Problems in Chemical Kinetics
   and Physics Motion Using Eye-Tracking
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE graph comprehension; eye tracking; chemistry education; physics
   education; kinetics; kinematics; rate of change
ID MOVEMENTS; FRAMEWORK; EXAMPLES
AB Graphs are essential tools in introductory STEM courses, yet students often read them as pictures rather than quantitative representations of changing quantities. This study examined how 18 first-semester general chemistry students interpreted two structurally parallel, three-question graphs in chemistry and physics: a concentration-time graph of a chemical reaction and a position-time graph of a walking person. Using eye-tracking, written work, and accuracy data, we found high but asymmetric performance (82% in chemistry; 89% in physics), with rate calculations as the most challenging items in both domains. Students commonly conflated value with rate and sometimes averaged from the origin across discontinuities, with these difficulties more prevalent in chemistry. Trials resulting in correct answers typically followed a question -> axes -> curve pattern with brief returns to the prompt, whereas trials resulting in incorrect answers often showed early and repeated attention to salient non-target graph features without careful attention to axes. These findings support teaching graph comprehension as a discipline; it is a general but context-sensitive skill and has potential value in an axes-first, rise-over-run-based protocol for rate-of-change reasoning.

TI Explaining ChatGPT Adoption in Higher Education: Insights for AI
   Literacy, Educational Practice, and Responsible AI
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; generative artificial intelligence; higher education;
   explainable artificial intelligence; educational technology adoption;
   UTAUT2; machine learning; digital literacy; learning analytics;
   responsible AI
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly ChatGPT, is transforming teaching and learning in higher education. This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework that integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), machine learning, and explainability techniques to examine students' intentions to use ChatGPT in academic contexts. Survey data were analyzed using Ordinary Least Squares regression, Random Forest, SHAP, Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Importance-Performance Map Analysis (IPMA), and K-Means clustering. The results indicate that Habit, Performance Expectancy, Hedonic Motivation, Social Influence, and Facilitating Conditions significantly influence behavioral intention, explaining 67.6% of the variance. Habit emerged as the strongest predictor, whereas Price Value had negligible influence. XAI analyses revealed that Effort Expectancy acts as a necessary condition for high adoption levels despite its limited direct effect. Four distinct student profiles were identified, highlighting heterogeneous patterns of AI integration and informing strategies for responsible and effective educational adoption. These findings provide evidence-based guidance for integrating AI literacy, responsible AI practices, and pedagogically meaningful ChatGPT use in higher education curricula.

TI A New Conceptual Framework for Data Science Education in
   Interdisciplinary Contexts: The Apian Model
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE interdisciplinary teaching; models of teaching and learning; data
   science education; teaching and learning
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB Integrating data science into undergraduate teaching in the United States requires educators to navigate disciplinary boundaries, integrating knowledge in ways that reshape teaching practices and disciplines themselves. While existing models of teaching and learning effectively describe expertise within single disciplines, they do not account for interdisciplinary knowledge movement or the specific challenges of bringing data science into established curricula. The Apian Model addresses this gap using bee behavior as a metaphor: instructors (bees) gather insights (nectar) from diverse curricular domains (flowers), transform them into learning experiences (honey), and disseminate them within and beyond their disciplines (hives). Through incorporation, communication, pollination, and hive splitting dynamics, this model explains how teaching evolves from individual learning to broader disciplinary change, processes especially relevant for navigating the complexity and interdisciplinarity of data science education. The model was developed with data science education in higher education in mind, but future research may establish its broader utility for interdisciplinary education more generally, particularly as a complement to existing models designed for single-discipline instruction.

TI Visual Literacy in Teacher Education: Narrative Reconstruction and AI
   Mediation in Warja Lavater's Cendrillon
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE coded picturebooks; Warja Lavater; visual literacy; folk literature;
   creative writing; generative AI; artificial intelligence
AB This study examines the development of visual literacy in teacher education through a classroom experience based on Cendrillon, the coded picturebook by Warja Lavater. The activity required students to reconstruct the sequence of the book's twenty scenes, assign each scene to a narrative phase, provide a verbal description, and generate a new version of the story using generative artificial intelligence. The participants were 234 students from undergraduate teacher education degrees and the Master's Degree in Educational Research, organized into 52 subgroups and classified according to their reading habits and self-reported familiarity with traditional fairy tales. Data were analyzed using indicators of sequential reconstruction, distribution of narrative phases, verbal description, and AI-mediated narrative reformulation. The results showed that, descriptively, groups with stronger reading habits achieved higher overall scores in the sequential reconstruction task; however, these differences did not reach statistical significance in the exploratory inferential models, and self-reported familiarity with traditional folktales alone did not guarantee greater accuracy. Narrative phase assignment was predominantly concentrated in the development of the story, while verbal descriptions followed a different pattern from the sequential ordering. The AI-generated stories retained part of the students' original vocabulary but incorporated a greater proportion of newly generated lexical items. The findings suggest that coded picturebooks provide a valuable framework for examining visual literacy as a process involving narrative reconstruction, verbal transduction, and critical engagement with generative artificial intelligence.

TI Bilingualism and Background Factors as Predictors of Perceived
   21st-Century Skills in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE bilingualism; 21st-century skills; higher education; cognitive skills;
   demographic factors; academic factors
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; DISABILITIES
AB This study examines differences between monolingual and bilingual students' self-reported 21st-century skills in higher education, with attention to the contributions of demographic and academic factors. Drawing on data from a linguistically and socioeconomically diverse sample of higher education students, the study considers these skills as part of broader educational concerns related to students' preparation for academic, social, and labor market demands. Data were collected through an online questionnaire completed by 564 Israeli undergraduate students. The analysis focused on differences between monolingual and bilingual students and on the role of socioeconomic indicators, including family income and mother's education, as well as academic degree, year of study, and employment status. Results showed that bilingual students reported higher levels in selected subscales, including cognitive processes such as critical thinking and problem-solving, intellectual openness, and interpersonal skills such as teamwork. No significant differences were found for creativity. Hierarchical regression analyses showed that demographic, socioeconomic, academic, and employment variables were associated with perceived skill levels, with different patterns for monolingual and bilingual students. Overall, the findings point to domain-specific differences between bilingual and monolingual students and highlight the importance of contextual and demographic factors. They suggest that bilingual experience may be associated with specific cognitive, intrapersonal, and interpersonal skill domains, although these associations should be interpreted with caution, given the cross-sectional, self-report design. The findings also suggest the value of creating structured opportunities for multilingual engagement in educational settings as one possible way to support 21st-century skills among students from diverse linguistic and socioeconomic backgrounds.

TI How AI Empowers the Double-Helix Approach: Examining a Decision Support
   Framework for Personalised Learning Trajectories in Gifted Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; gifted education; personalised learning;
   adaptive learning; learning analytics; talent development; UTAUT;
   Education 4.0; Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding opportunities for adaptive and personalised learning that responds to learners' abilities, interests, and educational needs. However, formal gifted education programmes may still offer limited opportunities for individualised learning pathways. In this study, gifted education programmes refer to formal provision for identified gifted students that supports differentiated depth, complexity, pace, challenge, enrichment, and talent development. This study proposes an AI-Supported Double-Helix Framework for Personalised Learning in Gifted Education and examines preliminary empirical support for its hypothesised relationships. The framework integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), AI-Supported Adaptive Learning (ASAL), Personalised Learning Experience (PLE), and curriculum integration. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, PLS-SEM was applied to data from 437 gifted secondary school students. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and measurement invariance. Performance Expectancy showed the strongest positive association with ASAL, which was positively associated with PLE. PLE was positively associated with perceived Double-Helix Framework Implementation (DHFI), which was subsequently associated with perceived Learning Effectiveness, Talent Development, and Future Readiness. A secondary multi-group analysis indicated that most structural relationships were comparable across gender groups. The study extends UTAUT by linking technology adoption factors with AI-supported adaptation, personalised learning, curriculum integration, and perceived developmental outcomes. It also situates these processes within the context of Education 4.0 through adaptive, data-informed, and future-oriented learning. However, the cross-sectional self-report design provides preliminary empirical support only for statistical relationships among the measured constructs. It does not establish the framework's educational effectiveness or causal effects on learning. Longitudinal, experimental, behavioural, and performance-based studies are needed to evaluate its educational effectiveness and practical implementation.

TI Educator-Infant Mealtime Interactions in Early Childhood Settings in
   Australia and China: A Systemic Functional Multimodal Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE educator-infant multimodal interactions; language and gesture; mealtime
   talk; cultural comparison
ID TODDLERS; QUALITY; QUANTITY; GESTURES; NORWAY; TALK
AB Previous studies suggest that educator-infant interactions during mealtime have significant potential to promote early language learning. As most of this research has focused on Western contexts, little is known about whether and how educators' interactions with infants during mealtime in early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings vary across cultures. To address this knowledge gap, using a multi-case study approach, we compared the natural mealtime interactions of 12 educators with infants in ECEC settings in Australia and China, with six educators participating in each country. Drawing on systemic functional linguistic (SFL) theory and multimodal discourse analysis (MDA), this study examined (1) the situational context of the mealtime practices (each meal's duration, educators' movement and whether they modelled eating behaviours, and infants' eating behaviours); (2) educators' infant-addressed language and gesture use; and (3) infants' use of vocalisation and gesture. The analysis revealed several differences: (1) the Australian educators sat with the infants, while the Chinese educators moved around the tables and served the infants; (2) the Australian educators' talk included a higher percentage of mental processes, statements, and gestures, while the Chinese educators used more material processes and commands in their speech and fewer gestures; and (3) the Australian infants vocalised more and used more gestures. Adopting a systemic functional and multimodal discourse analysis (SF MDA) approach enabled us to relate such differences to both the situational and broader cultural context of educator-infant interactions. This study thus contributes to a richer, more nuanced understanding of the factors that shape educator-infant interactions and the potential of mealtime in ECEC settings to provide infants with opportunities for language learning across cultures.

TI A Global South Perspective on Mediated Intercultural Experiences in
   China's Small-City International Schools: A Qualitative Case Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE intercultural learning; Global South; international schools in China;
   mediated intercultural experience; cultural capital
ID ELITE; FRAMEWORK; LANGUAGE; CULTURE
AB International schools in China are showing a trend of rapid expansion from major cities (Tier-1) to small cities (Tier-2 and lower tiers). Examining the intercultural experiences of students at international schools in small cities is of great significance for understanding the unequal distribution of resources for intercultural learning across international schools in different regions; however, there is a scarcity of relevant research. This qualitative case study draws on six months of fieldwork at an international school in a small city in China, using semi-structured interviews and classroom observations. Following a thematic analysis of the full dataset, the study examines mediated intercultural experiences across the student cohort and then selects a representative student-teacher pair as a focal case for more detailed analysis. From a Global South perspective, it examines how inequalities in intercultural resources shape the development of students' intercultural competencies. This study finds that the teacher and student view limited face-to-face intercultural experience as a barrier to understanding other cultures. However, the student attributes the limited opportunities to families' preferences, without noticing the influence of geographical location. In the absence of authentic lived experience, students rely on mediated sources. Due to differences in the types of mediated experiences involved, a gap may exist between teachers' expectations of mediated intercultural learning and students' actual mediated experiences. This may make it difficult to identify certain problematic cultural perceptions in a timely manner. This study further suggests that differences in intercultural learning among students at international schools in small cities are linked to the uneven spatial distribution of intercultural resources as cultural capital.

TI Toward a Digital Emotional-Intelligence Tool for Faculty Motivation: A
   Self-Determination Theory-Grounded Feasibility Study of Theory-Guided
   Message Personalization
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emotional intelligence; digital intervention tool; chatbot; faculty
   motivation; higher education; artificial intelligence;
   Self-Determination Theory; large language models; natural language
   processing; design science research
ID DESIGN SCIENCE
AB Most computational work on emotional intelligence in education targets students; where the emotional states of teaching staff are modeled at all, the signal is typically a static questionnaire score rather than an input to an automated response. This study asks a narrower question: does routing a detected emotion through Self-Determination Theory-rather than naming the emotion, or using generic language-produce a message that university faculty themselves rate as better, and does that advantage survive once the underlying emotion classifier is realistically imperfect? Using two public emotion corpora (GoEmotions and ISEAR), a 75-item researcher-authored and independently unvalidated set of faculty-oriented stress vignettes, four classifier families spanning lexicon counting to large-language-model few-shot prompting, a four-level message-personalization ablation (generic, emotion-only, need-only, full situational context), and blind ratings from 30 higher-education faculty and researchers, two findings are reported. First, when classifiers are compared on a matched label space, the few-shot large-language-model classifier performs best on both out-of-domain evaluations without fine-tuning, including 0.893 accuracy on the synthetic faculty-oriented vignette set. Second, the human evaluation does not support a uniform monotonic benefit from progressively adding personalization. Need-only routing does not yield a consistent gain over emotion-only messages, whereas the full-context condition shows its clearest positive signal for relevance and motivational usefulness; these two contrasts are significant in the crossed mixed-effects analysis but are not uniformly significant under the rater-level paired tests. The automatic text-similarity proxy does not detect this contextualized-condition advantage. Because the faculty vignettes are synthetic and were not independently content-validated, the results should be interpreted as evidence of technical and methodological feasibility rather than ecological validity or deployment effectiveness.

AB The faculty is the core academic unit of a university, with faculty deans occupying a pivotal role as chairs of academic departments and leaders of academic staff. TI Disruptive change: institutionalising interdisciplinarity in Chilean
   state universities
SO JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION POLICY AND MANAGEMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Interdisciplinarity; academic capitalism; university governance;
   organisational change
AB This article examines how interdisciplinarity is being institutionalised in Chilean state universities operating under a dual governance regime shaped by academic capitalism and commitments to public service. Drawing on document analysis and 27 interviews across five institutions, the study identifies four interrelated dimensions-organisational, cultural, epistemic and strategic leadership-through which interdisciplinarity is structured and contested. Findings show that interdisciplinarity has been incorporated through managerial instruments such as strategic plans, funding schemes and accreditation frameworks, which enable visibility and coordination but leave disciplinary hierarchies largely intact. Academic cultures and evaluation systems continue to privilege disciplinary specialisation, limiting epistemic integration and cultural transformation. Strategic leadership emerges as a mediating force that facilitates adoption but struggles to generate structural change. The Chilean case illustrates a broader paradox: interdisciplinarity becomes administratively viable through managerial governance, yet constrained by the same logics that enable it.

AB Differences in how teaching-focused roles are envisaged are evident in two main narratives, deficit-based and strength-based, that appear in the literature, often together. TI Developing students' mathematical literacy through STEM-PBL: a
   quasi-experimental study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital technologies; geometry education; mathematical literacy; PISA;
   problem-based learning; secondary education; stem education; STEM-PBL
AB Introduction Kazakhstan's performance in mathematics in the PISA 2022 assessment remained below the OECD average, highlighting the need for more effective pedagogical approaches to improve students' mathematical literacy. This study examined the effectiveness of a STEM-problem-based learning (STEM-PBL) approach in developing the mathematical literacy of Grade 11 students in geometry. Methods A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design was implemented during the 2025-2026 academic year at a secondary school in Almaty, Kazakhstan. The experimental group (n = 22) participated in STEM-PBL lessons centered on real-world engineering tasks related to the volumes of solids of revolution and supported by digital tools, including GeoGebra 3D, Desmos, Mathigon Polypad, and CalcPlot3D. The control group (n = 21) received conventional instruction. Prior to the intervention, a needs assessment survey was conducted with all Grade 11 students (n = 60) to inform the instructional design. Results The survey showed that 61.7% of students favored collaborative and project-based learning and expressed a strong preference for practical and visual learning materials. The experimental group achieved significantly higher mathematical literacy outcomes than the control group (82% vs. 70%, p < 0.001, d = 0.825). The greatest improvements were observed in students' ability to formulate mathematical problems and engage in mathematical reasoning. Students also showed an enhanced ability to identify geometric objects in authentic real-world contexts, decompose complex three-dimensional figures into simpler components, and interpret mathematical results in relation to practical situations. Discussion The findings suggest that STEM-PBL has the potential to foster mathematical literacy in Grade 11 geometry. However, further research with larger and more diverse samples is needed to establish its broader applicability.

TI Self-regulation skills as statistical predictors of environmental
   awareness and consciousness in preschool children: a cross-sectional
   study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attention; early childhood development; environmental awareness;
   environmental consciousness; executive function; preschool education;
   self-regulation; sustainable behavior
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS
AB This cross-sectional study examined the extent to which self-regulation skills (attention, inhibitory control, and working memory) statistically predict sustainable environmental behaviors (consciousness and awareness) in 224 preschool children aged 61-72 months. The Self-Regulation Skills Scale (Teacher Form) and the Environmental Sustainability Scale for Children 60-72 Months Old were administered. Curriculum implications and directions for confirmatory longitudinal research are discussed.

TI Understanding artificial intelligence adoption among university students
   in South African higher education: a technology acceptance model
   approach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI adoption; artificial intelligence; higher education; TAM; university
   students
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly transforming higher education by supporting teaching, learning, and academic productivity. Despite the use of AI tools among students, limited evidence exists on factors associated with AI adoption within South African higher education institutions. This study investigated factors associated with AI adoption among university students at a selected South African university using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework. Specifically, the study examined the associations among perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, attitudes towards AI, and actual AI use, as well as differences in AI adoption across demographic and academic characteristics. A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among students at a selected South African university. Data were collected using a structured self-administered questionnaire adapted from the TAM and existing AI adoption literature. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling approach, and 216 students participated in the study. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed, with statistical significance assessed at the 5% level. Students generally perceived AI technology as beneficial for improving academic performance, saving time, facilitating learning, and supporting academic tasks. All four hypothesised relationships were statistically significant: perceived ease of use was positively associated with perceived usefulness (r(s) = 0.728, p < 0.001), perceived usefulness with actual AI tool use ( r(s) = 0.647, p < 0.001), subjective norms with attitudes towards AI use ( r(s) = 0.548, p < 0.001), and attitudes towards AI use with actual AI tool use ( r(s) = 0.589, p < 0.001). Significant differences in AI adoption were observed across study levels [Kruskal-Wallis H test statistic (H) = 15.47, p = 0.009] and faculties (H = 8.74, p = 0.013), but not by gender, age, or race. University students demonstrated generally positive perceptions and moderate adoption of AI technologies. The findings suggest that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, and attitudes towards AI are significantly associated with AI adoption. Higher education institutions should strengthen AI literacy, provide guidance on responsible and ethical AI use, and develop targeted strategies that address differences across academic disciplines and levels of study.

   preservice mathematics teachers: evidence from a Ghanaian University
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mathematics education; mathematics teaching practices; ontological
   beliefs; pre-service mathematics teachers; teacher beliefs
ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB Although teachers' beliefs about mathematics are widely recognized as important influences on instructional decision-making, empirical evidence regarding the role of ontological beliefs in shaping mathematics teaching practices remains limited, particularly in Sub-Saharan African contexts such as Ghana. This study therefore examined whether pre-service mathematics teachers' ontological beliefs were significant statistical predictors of their mathematics teaching practices. Guided by Ernest's Philosophy of Mathematics Education, the study employed a quantitative cross-sectional survey design involving 312 Level 300 pre-service mathematics teachers from a public university in Ghana. The study concludes that ontological beliefs constitute an important explanatory factor associated with pre-service mathematics teachers reported instructional practices.

TI Transformative leadership and the implementation of digital education
   policy in Zanzibar: a sequential explanatory study of implementation
   barriers, challenges and enabling strategies
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital education policy; mixed methods; policy implementation;
   small-island developing states; transformative leadership; Zanzibar
AB The digitalization of education requires leadership that can reframe institutional purpose rather than merely administer technology. Drawing on Shields' theory of transformative leadership, this study examines the implementation environment that educational leaders in Zanzibar must navigate, and asks which implementation conditions are most amenable to transformative leadership action. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. In the quantitative phase, 30 learners drawn from primary, secondary and university levels completed a 31-item instrument measuring perceived implementation barriers, challenges and strategies; in the qualitative phase, 20 teachers, lecturers and public servants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, one-sample t-tests against the scale midpoint with Holm correction for multiple comparisons, 95% confidence intervals and Cohen's d; qualitative data were analysed using six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. The two strands were integrated through a connecting strategy and displayed jointly. Internal consistency of the quantitative instrument was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha = 0.77). Three conditions were endorsed with large effect sizes and survived correction for multiple testing: internet infrastructure (M = 4.50, d = 2.95), stakeholder resistance (M = 4.47, d = 2.89) and delayed disbursement of digitalization grants (M = 4.90, d = 6.23). Institutional and leadership barriers were also strongly endorsed (M = 4.40, d = 2.81), while items concerning equity between rural and urban settings were rejected (M = 2.17, d = -0.79), a divergence the qualitative strand attributes to the urban location of the sampled institutions. The study contributes to the international literature by specifying which of the four transformative-leadership dimensions is load-bearing under which implementation constraint, and by showing that in a small-island developing state the binding constraint is fiscal timing rather than fiscal volume. Findings are exploratory and constrained by a small, single-jurisdiction sample.

TI An Internet of Behaviors ecosystem for adaptive, inclusive, and
   explainable e-learning: empirical validation on the OULAD corpus
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive e-learning; algorithmic fairness; blockchain audit; disability
   inclusion; explainable AI; Internet of Behaviors; multi-task BiLSTM;
   OULAD
ID ANALYTICS
AB Virtual Learning Environments now record behavioral data at a scale traditional classrooms never reached, yet most online platforms still serve every student the same content, pacing, and evaluation. The learners who most need adaptive support pay the highest price for this uniformity. In the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), students who self-declare a disability pass 10.0 percentage points less often than their non-disabled peers and withdraw 9.1 points more often. We present an Internet of Behaviors (IoB) analytics ecosystem for adaptive e-learning that turns this behavioral record into timely, accountable support, closing the loop between observation and intervention. The ecosystem links four working parts: a forecasting model that predicts drop-out, pass/fail, and near-term disengagement from routine course activity; an explanation layer that makes each prediction legible to the instructor who has to act on it; a fairness audit centered on students with a declared disability; and a tamper-evident record of every automated decision, so that actions affecting a learner's path can be reviewed under GDPR Article 22 and FERPA. We evaluate the analytical layers on OULAD using multi-seed runs with confidence intervals and cross-validation across unseen course presentations. The model holds up on those presentations (drop-out AUC 0.916), and its explanations agree closely across methods. The fairness gaps it leaves stay small. Three results complicate the story: a strong gradient-boosting baseline outperforms the deep model on drop-out; an external sentiment signal adds nothing over a simple week indicator; and the multi-task design is smaller and faster rather than more accurate. On a public blockchain testnet, each decision was anchored within a single block at a median 23,965 gas. Inclusion and accountability can be designed into an e-learning analytics pipeline and then measured.

TI Qualitative and probability-based analysis of student open-ended
   responses on academic stress and mental health
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic stress; conditional probability; gender differences; graduate
   students; India; locus of control; sentiment analysis; thematic analysis
ID DEPRESSION; ANXIETY
AB Likert-scale instruments capture how much stress students report, but not what shape that stress takes. We present a thematic and probability-based analysis of open-ended survey responses from 217 graduate students at a private university in central India, collected in July 2025. Students described how academic stress had affected their mental health and proposed institutional changes they considered necessary. Seven stressor themes were extracted through inductive coding following the Braun and Clarke framework. Anxiety symptoms and assignment accumulation each appeared in close to 29% of valid narratives. Female students reported higher rates on five of seven themes; the gap was largest for sleep and physical health (28.1% against 16.2% for male respondents). Conditional probability analysis placed the lift for exam scheduling stress co-occurring with sleep disruption at 1.31. VADER sentiment scoring identified anxiety narratives as carrying the most negative polarity. Classification of student-proposed solutions by locus of control showed that students reporting structural stressors (scheduling, attendance rules, faculty relations) consistently demanded structural remedies. The probability framework provides a replicable method for extracting granular stressor profiles from open-ended feedback.

TI The influence of expressive vs. conventional typography on parent-child
   shared book-reading
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE book characteristics; parental attitudes; shared book-reading; tone;
   typography
ID VISUAL-ATTENTION; PRINT; TEXT; PRESCHOOLERS; FEATURES; MOTHERS
AB Introduction Typography, that is, the typeface, size, style, color, or position of the type of the book, is considered an element of meaning-making. As such, it has been suggested that typography may relate to the nature of parent-child shared book-reading. This study examined parents' attitudes towards expressive typography (changes in font, size, added letters, flipped letters), and how this relates to shared reading of books with expressive vs. conventional typography.Methods Participants included 72 parents (59 mothers, 13 fathers) and one of their children (41 girls, 31 boys) whose average age was 61.86 months (SD = 8.69 months). All parent-child dyads read two books with conventional typography and the same two with expressive typography in a counterbalanced order; all interactions were recorded and analyzed.Results Results revealed that parents were generally aware of a book's typography but didn't necessarily see it as influencing how they read. Negative binomial regressions with generalized estimating equations indicated that the presence of expressive typography related to longer shared reading interactions and changes in parents' tone and pace during shared reading.Discussion The study suggests that attitudes towards a book's characteristics may act more implicitly in terms of parents' reading behaviors. Parents can be guided to look for typographic features in books and encouraged to consider them when selecting books for shared reading.

TI HarmonicThreads: a formative evaluation of a fabric-based digital
   musical instrument toward inclusive music-making
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accessible digital musical instruments; fabric-based interfaces;
   formative evaluation; inclusive music practices; multimodal feedback;
   musical agency; textile interaction
AB Background Inclusive music-making requires instruments that support varied bodies, abilities, musical backgrounds, and forms of participation. Digital musical instruments provide diverse approaches to sound creation, and fabric-based interfaces offer an alternative interaction modality that may support participation for some users and contexts. Their tactile and deformable properties enable forms of interaction that differ from conventional rigid or screen-based controllers and may offer inclusive possibilities in particular settings.Objective This paper presents HarmonicThreads as a formative interaction-design case of a fabric-based digital musical instrument. The prototype explores how tactile cues, fabric deformation, projected visual feedback, and assisted accompaniment can support low-barrier music-making. We examine first-use discovery, perceived musical agency, and design considerations intended to inform the development of future fabric-based, accessible digital musical instruments.Methods We conducted a formative mixed-methods evaluation with 20 adult participants. Participants used HarmonicThreads in independent play, where conductive threads directly triggered notes, and assisted play, where sustained contact generated automated melodic accompaniment. Data included observations, SUS and UEQ-S responses, semi-structured interviews, and participant-generated design sketches.Results Participants treated the fabric surface as an instrument, using raised threads to identify playable regions, form spatial pitch expectations, and experiment with chords, rhythm, and sustained notes. Qualitative results show that assisted play supported immediate musical engagement, while independent play supported greater perceived control. The study also revealed accessibility-relevant barriers, including uncertain activation thresholds, perceived fragility, thin and closely spaced threads, posture and fatigue, ambiguous visual feedback, and limited expressive mappings.Conclusion HarmonicThreads contributes a formative design case for inclusive digital music technology. We identify design considerations for tactile legibility, low-effort activation, ergonomic support, transparent multimodal feedback, configurable scaffolding, richer sonic mappings, and future participatory evaluation with intended users and real music-making contexts.

TI Educational exclusion of persons with disabilities in the Philippines:
   documentary narratives and the challenges of inclusive education
   governance
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE disability rights; documentary narratives; educational exclusion;
   implementation gap; inclusive education; inclusive education governance;
   media accountability; persons with disabilities
ID STUDENTS
AB Despite comprehensive disability rights legislation and inclusive education policies in the Philippines, cases of prolonged educational exclusion among persons with disabilities (PWDs) continue to emerge. Documentary investigations have exposed individuals experiencing extreme domestic confinement, absence from schooling, and limited access to educational and support services, revealing persistent gaps between policy commitments and implementation. This study examines how documentary narratives portray educational exclusion, identify contributing structural and familial factors, reference disability rights and inclusive education frameworks, and depict institutional responses to deprivation. Using a meaning-centered qualitative content analysis of five investigative documentaries, the study analyzed representations of educational access, governance dynamics, and post-exposure intervention. Findings indicate that educational exclusion is constructed as a multidimensional process encompassing physical confinement, social isolation, institutional neglect, and disrupted access to educational opportunities. Exclusion was associated with intersecting factors including poverty, limited access to special education and mental health services, caregiver burden, stigma, and weak monitoring mechanisms. The findings further reveal that institutional responses were largely reactive, with intervention typically occurring only after media exposure. Documentary narratives therefore position media visibility as a form of reactive accountability infrastructure that temporarily exposes governance failures without addressing the structural conditions that sustain educational exclusion. The study highlights the need for proactive identification of at-risk learners, strengthened inter-agency coordination, expanded school-based support services, and sustained governance mechanisms capable of translating disability rights into meaningful educational inclusion.

TI Associations between student organization involvement and college
   student mental health in the United States
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE belonging; college students; loneliness; student involvement;
   undergraduates
ID SENSE; POPULATION; LONELINESS; 1ST-YEAR; PERCEPTIONS; TRANSITION;
   ENGAGEMENT; SCALE
AB Introduction The mental health of college students is a growing concern. Loneliness, belonging, and psychological distress are associated with stress, anxiety, and depression among college students. Student organization involvement is positively associated with student mental health, including lower depression. Therefore, it is worthwhile to explore the relationship between mental health and student organization involvement. This study examines the associations between student organization involvement, loneliness, belonging, and psychological distress among college students in the United States using the National College Health Assessment for secondary data analysis.Method Over 78,000 students from 125 institutions participated in the Spring 2023 NCHA. Loneliness decreased modestly across participation levels. Psychological distress showed a curvilinear pattern, with lower distress at low to moderate involvement and slight increases at the highest levels.Conclusion Recommendations for institutions of higher education are presented to help address student belonging, loneliness, and psychological distress.

TI Integrating AI into pre-service teacher training for reflective
   interpretation of fine art: a qualitative study in Kazakhstan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE art education; artificial intelligence; multimodal reflection;
   pre-service teachers; reflective practice
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into education, yet its role in supporting multimodal reflective processes in discipline-specific learning, particularly in fine arts, remains underexplored. This study examines how AI can mediate reflective engagement among pre-service teachers in the interpretation of paintings within a pedagogically structured framework. A qualitative design was employed with 28 pre-service teachers in Kazakhstan. Data were generated through an iterative multimodal reflective process, including individual reflection, AI-mediated interpretation, reflective comparison, and focus group discussions. A four-dimensional framework-descriptive-contextual, formal-compositional, technical-spatial, and individuality and uniqueness-guided reflective engagement, and thematic analysis with triangulation was applied. Findings indicate that the role of AI is dimension-dependent. It most effectively supports reflection on formal-compositional and technical-spatial aspects of paintings by structuring attention to visual elements, but shows clear limitations in enabling culturally grounded and symbolic meaning-making. AI primarily functions as a mediating tool that facilitates structured reflective engagement rather than replacing human interpretive processes. The study contributes by conceptualizing artistic interpretation as a multimodal reflective process and by positioning AI as a mediator within reflective practice. It further proposes a model for integrating AI into fine arts teacher education as a supplementary resource that supports, but does not replace, human-centered meaning-making. Effective AI integration requires alignment between reflective frameworks, technological affordances, and the interpretive nature of disciplinary learning.

TI Motivational pathways into physical education teaching: a cross-cultural
   analysis of intrinsic motives, career transitions, and minority group
   dynamics
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE career changers; FIT-choice; minority students; physical education
   teaching; self determination theory; teacher motivational profiles
ID CHOICE
AB Introduction This study examined the motivational factors influencing the decision to pursue a career in teaching physical education (PE) among 256 preservice and in service teacher education students in Israel, including both undergraduate students and academic career changers.Methodology Using a newly adapted questionnaire derived from the AFPE instrument, we assessed five motivational dimensions: work, mission, personal fit, self-development, and family influence. A series of repeated-measures General Linear Models were conducted to explore within-subject differences across motivational domains and between-group differences based on sex, ethnicity, and program type. We also performed a thematic content analysis of open-ended responses from academic career changers to further illuminate the personal narratives underlying their decisions to retrain in PE.Results Findings revealed a clear motivational hierarchy across all participants: mission- and value-driven motives were the strongest, followed by personal fit, self-development, and work-related factors, whereas family influence was consistently the weakest motivator. Minority students (Druze, Muslim, Christian) reported significantly higher overall motivation than the majority (Jewish) students, particularly in self-development and work-related dimensions. Sex showed no significant effect on overall motivation. Comparison between undergraduate students and academic career changers revealed broadly similar overall motivation levels, although academic career changers reported a slightly higher overall motivation, reflecting a small but statistically significant effect. Despite between-group differences in motivational intensity, the shape of the motivational profile remained stable across demographic groups and program types. Qualitative themes further supported these findings, highlighting motives related to personal meaning, long-standing aspirations, and employment stability among career changers.Discussion This study contributes to theoretical understandings of teacher motivation by providing findings that are consistent with the centrality of autonomous, intrinsic, and value-based motivations proposed by Self-Determination Theory, and by extending findings from the Factors Influencing Teaching Choice model to a culturally diverse Middle Eastern context. Practical implications include the need for selection of strategies emphasizing mission, personal fit, and opportunities for growth, as well as targeted support for minority students and career changers.

TI External support and university faculty's AI-TPACK: a serial mediation
   model of perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and behavioral
   intention
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-TPACK; behavioral intention to use AI; external support; perceived
   ease of use; perceived usefulness; technology acceptance model
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL; BARRIERS
AB Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly requires university faculty to integrate technology, pedagogy, and disciplinary content, as reflected in the Artificial Intelligence-enhanced Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK) framework. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and AI-TPACK research, this study examined how external support (ES) is associated with faculty's self-reported AI-TPACK through perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), and behavioral intention to use AI (BI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 593 university faculty members in China. The measurement structure was evaluated using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, followed by structural equation modeling. Indirect effects were assessed using 5,000 bootstrap resamples and 95% confidence intervals. Results The five constructs demonstrated acceptable reliability and a distinguishable five-factor measurement structure. ES was positively associated with self-reported AI-TPACK (beta = .238, p < .001). The total indirect effect of ES on AI-TPACK through the specified mediators was also statistically supported (B = .287, 95% bootstrap CI [.203, .386]). The specific indirect pathway through BI alone was not supported, whereas several pathways involving PEOU and PU had bootstrap confidence intervals that excluded zero. Discussion The findings indicate that institutional support, technology-acceptance beliefs, behavioral intention, and AI-TPACK are statistically connected within the proposed structural framework. In particular, PEOU and PU appear to play important roles in the indirect associations between ES and AI-TPACK.

TI Temporal and intensity-distribution differences in physical activity
   among schoolchildren and adolescents from the Basque Country:
   weekday-weekend and school-after-school comparisons
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accelerometry; adolescents; children; intensity gradient; physical
   activity; school time; weekend
ID CHILDREN
AB Introduction This study examined temporal and intensity-distribution differences in objectively measured physical activity among schoolchildren and adolescents from the Basque Country, Spain, comparing weekdays with weekend days, Saturday with Sunday, and school time with after-school time. Methods Raw wrist-accelerometer data were reprocessed for 540 participants in the Mugikertu study. The final exact-linked regional sample comprised 503 participants aged 6-17 years from 42 schools, contributing 2,979 valid days. Euclidean Norm Minus One (ENMO), waking average acceleration, intensity gradient, M30, M60, and time in moderate (MPA), vigorous (VPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) were derived in GGIR. Pediatric non-dominant-wrist thresholds were applied (MPA 201.4-<707 mg; VPA >= 707 mg). Paired comparisons and multilevel models examined day-type differences, with days nested within participants and participants within schools. Results Mean MVPA was 65.19 +/- 34.85 min/day, and 51.1% of participants accumulated an average of >= 60 min/day. Weekday values exceeded weekend values for 24-h ENMO (47.97 +/- 17.82 vs. 41.28 +/- 20.46 mg) and MVPA (68.25 +/- 35.31 vs. 59.12 +/- 41.94 min/day; mean difference 9.13 min/day, 95% CI 6.51-11.75). During weekdays, MVPA density was lower in the 09:00-14:30 school window than in the 14:30-22:00 after-school window (4.49 +/- 2.82 vs. 5.12 +/- 2.89 min/h). The weekday-weekend association varied by age but not by sex or socioeconomic context for MVPA. Conclusion In this Basque regional sample, activity volume and intensity were lower on weekends, particularly Sundays, and declined sharply with age. School time contributed meaningfully to daily activity, but after-school time showed slightly higher MVPA density. The regional context and the age-specific pattern should be considered when transferring these findings to other settings.

TI Building confidence about inclusive teaching through identity-focused
   professional development
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE confidence; identity; inclusive teaching; STEM faculty development;
   teaching and learning; higher education
ID TEACHERS; EXPERIENCE; PRIVILEGE; STUDENTS; RACE
AB Introduction Despite global investments in improving STEM education, retaining students remains challenging, often attributed to learning environments that do not adequately support all students. While many higher-education institutions offer teaching development programs that focus on student-centered practices and reflection on practice, these approaches may insufficiently address inclusive teaching, which emphasizes awareness of student and instructor identities and lived experiences. Moreover, limited empirical research examines how professional learning emphasizing instructor and student backgrounds, coupled with structured identity-based reflective practice, impacts instructors' confidence in implementing inclusive practices or designing learning environments. We investigated, after being exposed to identity-based inclusive teaching development, (1) how educators described increases in their confidence to engage in inclusive practices, and (2) what challenges educators identified requiring continued learning or support.Methods We analyzed responses from 545 higher-education educators who participated in an asynchronous, self-paced, open-access online course, focusing on identity and lived experiences using structured identity-based self-reflection. Participants identified areas where they had "increased confidence" and were "still gaining confidence" following the course. We used inductive content-analysis methodology to identify five emergent themes: course structure, course climate, identity awareness, conceptual understanding, and future implementation.Results Educators most frequently described confidence development in course structure, course climate, and identity awareness, while reporting continued uncertainty in these same areas. These findings reveal a gap between awareness of inclusive teaching principles and the ability to enact them in practice, highlighting that confidence develops iteratively rather than linearly.Discussion These findings suggest that participants perceived identity-centered reflection as important to developing their confidence for implementing inclusive teaching practices. Their responses suggest that sustained, structured opportunities for reflection, practice, and feedback may be needed to support translating awareness into action. By conceptualizing confidence as a recursive developmental process, this study provides insight into how educators perceive the role of identity-centered professional learning in supporting their development as inclusive instructors. We offer practice-informed recommendations that faculty and faculty developers may implement to help bridge this critical gap.

TI Application of the BOPPPS model combined with flipped classroom in
   clinical practice competency training for gastroenterology residents in
   standardized residency programs
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; BOPPPS model; clinical practice competency; flipped
   classroom; gastroenterology; standardized residency training
ID LEARNING READINESS SCALE; CONTROLLED-TRIALS; ACQUISITION; PERFORMANCE;
   EDUCATION
AB Background The bridge-in, objective, preassessment, participatory learning, postassessment, summary (BOPPPS) instructional model and flipped classroom pedagogy are increasingly recognized as effective active learning strategies in medical education. However, their combined application in gastroenterology residency training has not been systematically evaluated. This study investigated the impact of the BOPPPS + flipped classroom model on clinical practice competency, clinical thinking, self-directed learning, and teaching satisfaction among gastroenterology residents. Methods A randomized controlled design was employed. A total of 120 first-year undergraduate-degree residents who completed their gastroenterology rotation at the Third People's Hospital of Yunnan Province between January 2025 and December 2025 were enrolled and randomly assigned to an observation group (n = 60; BOPPPS + flipped classroom) or a control group (n = 60; traditional lecture-based teaching). The intervention lasted 12 weeks (one session per week, two class hours per session). Teaching effectiveness was assessed using standardized clinical practice simulations (admission interview/consultation, clinical reasoning case analysis, and procedural skills), the primary trait analysis (PTA) clinical thinking scale (eight domains), the Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale (SDLRS), and a validated satisfaction questionnaire. Primary analyses employed analysis of covariance adjusting for corresponding baseline values, with effect sizes reported as adjusted Cohen's d. For multiple secondary comparisons, the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied. Ordinal PTA scale data were additionally analyzed using non-parametric Mann-Whitney U-tests as sensitivity analyses. Results The observation group achieved significantly higher scores than the control group across all clinical performance measures: admission interview [adjusted mean difference (aMD) = 3.02, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.46-4.58, P < 0.001, adjusted d = 0.69], clinical reasoning (aMD = 6.85, 95% CI: 4.75-8.95, P < 0.001, adjusted d = 1.36), and clinical skills (aMD = 9.52, 95% CI: 7.22-11.82, P < 0.001, adjusted d = 2.18). PTA scores were significantly higher in the observation group for all eight clinical thinking dimensions (all P < 0.001 after FDR correction). SDLRS total scores were also markedly higher in the observation group (aMD = 13.82, 95% CI: 10.35-17.29, P < 0.001, adjusted d = 1.38). Satisfaction rates exceeded 86% across all domains in the observation group, compared with 34.3%-54.3% in the control group (all P < 0.05). Conclusions The BOPPPS + flipped classroom model significantly enhances clinical practice competency, clinical thinking, self-directed learning, and teaching satisfaction among gastroenterology residents compared with traditional instruction. However, the very large effect sizes observed should be interpreted with caution, as the intervention combined multiple instructional components (preclass preparation, supervised hands-on practice, and structured feedback) that were not isolated. Implementation decisions should consider local resources and the specific training contexts.

TI When more technology does not mean better learning: digital tool use,
   instructional quality, and mathematics achievement in everyday classroom
   settings
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE everyday classroom settings; longitudinal study; mathematics
   achievement; multilevel analysis; perceived frequency of digital tool
   use; perceived instructional quality
ID TEACHING QUALITY; FRAMEWORK; METAANALYSIS; KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS; IMPACT;
   MODEL
AB Meta-analyses highlight that digital tool use can positively affect students' mathematics achievement. However, these findings mainly derive from controlled studies with well-orchestrated technology integration, whereas evidence from regular classrooms remains scarce-particularly regarding how often digital tools are used in everyday settings and how this relates to students' mathematics achievement. At the same time, instructional quality-encompassing basic dimensions such as classroom management, cognitive activation, and student support-is widely acknowledged as a key determinant of learning outcomes, but it has rarely been examined alongside digital tool use within the same study. To address these gaps, we examined both the frequency of digital tool use and instructional quality as predictors of mathematics achievement in everyday classroom settings, and additionally explored their association at the classroom level. In an exploratory extension, we investigated whether the relationship between digital tool use frequency and mathematics achievement varies across levels of instructional quality, implying a potential moderating role. To this end, we tested interaction effects between digital tool use frequency and each of the three basic dimensions. We applied a multilevel analysis of longitudinal data from 1,627 eighth-grade students across 72 classes from 30 German secondary schools. Mathematics achievement was assessed through curriculum-based pre- and post-tests and analyzed in relation to student-reported digital tool use frequency and student-reported instructional quality at both the student and class levels. Contrary to meta-analytic findings, we identified a small but statistically significant negative association between everyday digital tool use frequency and mathematics achievement. In line with prior research, instructional quality was positively associated with achievement. At the class level, the exploratory analyses provided no evidence that instructional quality moderates the relationship between digital tool use frequency and mathematics achievement. At the student level, however, a significant interaction effect between classroom management and digital tool use frequency occurred, indicating that the negative association between frequent digital tool use and achievement was weaker when classroom management was perceived as strong. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of these relationships, future research should develop more refined and integrated models of digital tool use and instructional quality.

TI Theory vs. praxis: what [should] mathematics offender-educators know and
   why it matters?

LA English
DT Article
DE adult offenders; andragogical strategies; mathematics adult
   offender-educators; neuroscientific realities; translingual andragogy
ID HIPPOCAMPUS; MEMORIES; BRAIN
AB Several studies indicate that adult offenders' mathematics performance is dire. Bedeviling scholars has been the question of whether adult offender-educators know andragogical strategies pertinent to teaching mathematics in correctional center classrooms. TI Semiotic meanings in mathematical modeling: an analysis of videos
   produced by prospective teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital videos; mathematical modeling; prospective mathematics teacher;
   replication; using mathematics
AB Mathematics teacher education remains a major challenge within the mathematical modeling community. More exploration of practices, contexts, resources, problems, and tasks is also needed. This study examined how creating mathematical modeling videos can support semiotic meanings by prospective mathematics teachers (PMT). The study took place in a course in which 15 pre-service teachers worked in groups to create digital videos. TI Teacher educators' understanding of pedagogical innovation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational change; pedagogical innovation; pedagogical risk; teacher
   education; teacher educators
ID PRESERVICE
AB Introduction Pedagogical innovation has become a key concept in educational discourse. However, its meaning remains contested, and the concept is often used vaguely to denote new practices. Within teacher education policy and research, teacher educators (TEDs) are frequently positioned as change agents who, through innovative practice, are expected to prepare future teachers for contemporary classrooms. In light of this, the study aims to conceptualize pedagogical innovation from the perspective of teacher educators and their pedagogical practice.Methods The study employs a qualitative approach based on three focus group interviews with thirteen TEDs from six Norwegian teacher education institutions.Results Thematic analysis yielded four themes: creative adaptations, benefit to student teachers, relevance to school practice, and risk of failure.Discussion The findings show that TEDs primarily conceptualize pedagogical innovation as adaptations of existing practices aligned with their own pedagogical objectives. This conceptualization foregrounds clear benefits for student teachers, while highlighting the context-specific and experimental nature of pedagogical innovation. Such an understanding requires TEDs to accept uncertainty and the possibility of negative outcomes. The study offers important implications for the implementation of pedagogical innovation in TEDs' practice. The findings emphasize the need to weigh anticipated benefits against potential costs. Accordingly, the risk of failure associated with pedagogical innovation should be made more explicit in educational policy and institutionally recognized as integral to the continuous development of pedagogical practice. Such a shift may support greater engagement in pedagogical innovation and contribute to the modernization of teacher education in response to contemporary educational challenges.

TI A longitudinal core curriculum to strengthen interprofessional
   competencies in German undergraduate nursing education: a mixed methods
   study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interprofessional education; Healthcare; Core curriculum; Nursing
   education; Mixed methods; Interprofessional collaboration
ID GUIDANCE; CONDUCT
AB Aim Interprofessional education is considered an important strategy for improving interprofessional collaboration in healthcare practice. The aim of the interEdu project was to develop a longitudinal core curriculum to strengthen interprofessional competencies in undergraduate nursing education.Methods The study was conducted using a mixed methods design with qualitative and standardized interviews and evidence syntheses. The results were triangulated via joint displays and were discussed in an expert workshop. The curriculum was designed by the interprofessional project team based on these results.Results The interEdu curriculum comprises nine chapters. The central element is a framework of interprofessional competencies, which forms the basis of competence descriptions that are formulated over three years of nursing education. It has a spiral structure and offers modules and learning units based on the situational principle. In order to facilitate a transfer between the different learning venues, appropriate learning methods are recommended. These are learner-centered to support collaborative learning and self-directed learning.Results The interEdu curriculum comprises nine chapters. The central element is a framework of interprofessional competencies, which forms the basis of competence descriptions that are formulated over three years of nursing education. It has a spiral structure and offers modules and learning units based on the situational principle. In order to facilitate a transfer between the different learning venues, appropriate learning methods are recommended. These are learner-centered to support collaborative learning and self-directed learning.Conclusions The interEdu curriculum will be used to longitudinally integrate interprofessional education into educational programs for nursing and other healthcare professions. In particular, the spiral structure and the interprofessional competencies formulated longitudinally over the whole undergraduate education cycle should contribute to the continuous development of competencies.

TI Preferred scaffolding does not lead to better learning performance:
   Empirical evidence from AI-supported mathematical modelling
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Mediated interaction; Learning preference; Mathematical modelling;
   Modelling competency; Scaffolding
ID EDUCATION; ITEM
AB Mathematical modelling (MM) is widely recognized as a key competency for addressing complex real-world problems, which requires learners to engage in higher-order processes such as abstraction, representation, and iterative reasoning. However, students often experience difficulties in coordinating these processes within mathematics modelling tasks. While recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer new possibilities for supporting mathematical modelling, limited research has examined how different forms of AI-mediated interaction shape students' learning processes in MM. To address this gap, the present study investigates five AI interaction roles, Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer, Excellent Student, and Struggling Student, as distinct pedagogical scaffolding strategies in AI-assisted learning environments. To evaluate the effectiveness of these roles, we conducted a randomized within-subjects experiment with 26 university students to compare modelling competency, learners' role preferences, and learning experiences across the five conditions. A randomized withinsubjects experiment with 26 university students was conducted to examine differences in modelling performance and learners' role preferences across conditions. The findings reveal a notable divergence between mathematical modelling performance and pedagogical roles preference. Students demonstrated higher modelling competency when interacting with Peer and TA roles, which fostered collaborative reasoning and co-construction of ideas. In contrast, students expressed stronger preferences for Tutor and Excellent Student roles, which provided more explicit guidance and structured explanations. The Struggling Student role was consistently perceived as least supportive across both performance and preference measures. These findings examine how interactional structures influence students' engagement in mathematical modelling. The study highlights the importance of balancing cognitive scaffolding with opportunities for collaborative sense-making, and provides design implications for developing adaptive, learner-centered AI-supported modelling environments in mathematics education.
