TI Integrating deep learning framework into chemical engineering education:
   A case study on reactor selection and design
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted teaching; Reactor Design; Deep Learning Surrogate Modeling;
   Cloud-Based AI Notebook
AB Embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in chemical engineering curricula is often constrained by software deployment barriers and limited evidence about how students engage with AI-enabled workflows. This preliminary implementation and feasibility study integrated a neural processing unit (NPU)-powered cloud AI Notebook into two chemical engineering courses using fixed-bed reactor design as the central case. The instructor provided a functional multilayer perceptron (MLP) workflow, while students modified model architecture and hyperparameters, compared catalyst geometries, and interpreted predictions against computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-derived reference data. The teaching and survey cohort comprised 72 students (22 undergraduates and 50 postgraduates), all of whom provided matched pre-intervention and post-intervention questionnaire data. A 28-student course-assessment subset (22 undergraduates and six first-year master students) completed a final-examination item and presentation assignment. The cloud NPU reduced single-epoch training time from 114.2 s on a local CPU to 5.8 s and enabled repeated model exploration within a 45-minute session. Questionnaire scores increased descriptively across the four self-reported dimensions, while the final-examination item yielded a mean score of 8.36 out of 10 (SD 1.54). These findings support the technical feasibility and short-term educational relevance of the module. However, the absence of an objective pre-test, control group, and longitudinal follow-up precludes causal claims about learning gains.

TI What makes rural tourism tick in Portugal? Word of mouth, experiential
   learning, and individual performance examined
SO JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY LEISURE SPORT & TOURISM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Rural tourism; UTAUT2; Individual performance; Perceived mental health;
   Experiential learning; Tourism education
ID COMMON METHOD VARIANCE; INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; CONTINUANCE; INTENTION;
   SATISFACTION; ACCEPTANCE; DIMENSIONS
AB Positioning rural tourism as a site of informal, experiential education, this study examines how experiential learning and perceived mental health (PMH) shape rural tourists' post-visit performance in Portugal. The learning construct, with word-of-mouth (WoM), is embedded in an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) framework, tested on 308 tourists. PMH mediated the WoM-performance link, and experiential learning emerged as the strongest driver of post-visit performance, revealing rural tourism as a learning-rich experience rather than mere leisure. The study informs tourism education, showing how rural experiences can shape curriculum design and the training of tourism professionals.

TI The impact of gamification on learning outcomes in virtual museums
SO JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY LEISURE SPORT & TOURISM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; Virtual museum; Perceived cultural attractiveness;
   Learning outcomes; Digital library cave of Mogao Grottoes
ID NOVELTY-SEEKING TENDENCIES; DESTINATION ATTRACTIVENESS; MODERATING ROLE;
   SERIOUS GAMES; TOURISTS; SATISFACTION; ENGAGEMENT; EXPERIENCE;
   USABILITY; SCALE
AB This study explores gamification potential in virtual cultural heritage museums, addressing a gap in empirical evidence on its educational impact among young people, particularly students. Using gamification learning and self-determination theories, we examined 398 young participants experiences in the Digital Library Cave. Results show that perceived cultural attractiveness fully mediates the effects of gamification mechanics and technology implementation on learning outcomes, partially mediating aesthetic performance, storyline effects. Novelty seeking positively moderates the relationship between gamification elements and perceived cultural attractiveness. These findings enhance understanding of gamified virtual museum experiences, offering insights for cultural heritage curators and digital content creators.

TI Micro-level advocacy toward socially just multi-tiered systems of
   support: Action steps
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Advocacy; MTSS; Social justice; Systems change; Qualitative content
   analysis
ID SCHOOL-PSYCHOLOGY; MENTAL-HEALTH; JUSTICE; CONSULTATION; EQUITY;
   PERCEPTIONS; CHALLENGES; FAMILIES; STUDENTS; SKILLS
AB Advocacy is a critically important skill in applied psychological service delivery, however, little is yet understood about what it means to advocate effectively, especially within school and district settings (e.g., micro-level advocacy). By examining literature related to advocacy and systems change, with a focus on efforts to advance social justice and multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) in schools, we identified practices that can be used to create widespread, equitable deployment of effective services at the school and district level. Using conventional content analysis methods, we analyzed 81 articles from journals in school psychology and related professions related to social justice, advocacy, and/or MTSS. Findings yielded eight potential areas of micro-level advocacy practice that are important to advancing socially just MTSS: community consultation, data and assessment, family collaboration, graduate education, school/district policy change, mental health service delivery, working with school teams, and teacher consultation. Many of these areas reflect core school psychology work, whereas other actions cut across traditional practice areas. Overall, the results of this content analysis have broad implications for future research, graduate training, continuing education, and professional practice.

TI Rise of the Gap Year: Unintended Consequences of Evolving Assessment
   Systems
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE medical student assessment; surgical education; gap year; residency
   selection; research productivity; Step 1
ID USMLE STEP 1; PERSPECTIVES; TRANSITION; CRITERIA
AB OBJECTIVE: Recent changes have substantially impacted the assessment of medical students, including adjustments in clerkship grading and the transition of Step 1 to a pass/fail grading system in 2022. This study examines factors influencing students' decisions to take a gap year and the potential impact of assessment changes on the landscape of these decisions. DESIGN: This qualitative study used semi-structured interviews of medical students applying to surgical specialties to gather in-depth perspectives regarding their decision-making processes around taking or not taking a gap year. SETTING: We conducted virtual interviews with students from 5 U.S. medical schools located in the West, Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, and South. PARTICIPANTS: Interviewees comprised 25 senior medical students pursuing surgical specialties including general surgery, orthopedic surgery, neurosurgery, plastic surgery, and otolaryngology-head and neck surgery. RESULTS: We identified 5 main themes related to students' gap year decisions. Local institutional and specialty cultures set background expectations around gap years. Within these contexts, 3 dominant and often interrelated reasons motivated gap year decisions: the anticipated potential of a gap year to affect residency application competitiveness; personal, nonacademic circumstances; and the desire for professional growth. Regardless of students' gap year wishes, logistics ultimately dictated decisions for many students. CONCLUSIONS: In the context of evolving assessment systems, residency application competitiveness emerged as a primary factor influencing students' decisions to take a gap year. Students described that the transition of Step 1 to pass/fail led to fewer objective application metrics, with an ensuing focus on increased research productivity as a perceived differentiating factor amongst applicants. Personal and professional growth motivations remained present, but often played secondary roles in decision-making. For both gap year and traditional students, concerns regarding research years included variable access to funding, financial and temporal costs, and implications for delayed career and family timelines. TI From images to interaction: Examining the relationship between
   children's photography and types of dialogic interactions
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Types of dialogic interactions; Photo elicitation; Photography
   assignments and themes; Early childhood education and care
ID PERSPECTIVES; PLAYSCHOOL; CLASSROOM; QUALITY; VOICE; TALK; CARE
AB Photo elicitation in early childhood education and care (ECEC) can facilitate various types of dialogic interactions between teachers and small groups of children. However, little is known about how the content of children's photographs and their perspectives on them relate to different forms of interactions. In the present study, we explored the themes of photographs taken and discussed by children and the extent to which photography assignments and identified themes were associated with types of dialogic interactions in related small-group discussions. The interaction types examined were drawn from prior work by Muhonen et al. (2026): individual interview, group interview, child-centred dialogue, and teacher-directed dialogue. The analytical strategy employed a mixed-methods approach, combining thematic analysis and multinomial logistic regression. Eight photography themes were identified, with play, social relationships and rules, and physical surroundings emerging most frequently in the photographs and discussions. Both the photography assignments and the identified themes significantly influenced the likelihood of different types of interactions. These findings extend prior research by demonstrating variations in how different photography assignments and themes contribute to the emergence of both more segmented initiation-response-feedback sequences and more extended, collective forms of interaction in ECEC.

TI Cases of collective learning? Combining Value Creation and Multilevel
   Boundary Crossing in cross organizational Professional Learning
   Communities
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional Learning Communities; Multilevel Boundary Crossing; Value
   Creation; Collective learning; Longitudinal case study
ID SCHOOLS
AB In gaining insight into the complex process of learning in Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) both the Value Creation (VC) Framework and Multilevel Boundary Crossing (MBC) were combined as method of analysis in a multiple case study. The members of two heterogenic educational PLCs were interviewed yearly using a semi-structured interview approach over the course of three years, to answer the question: 'How do VC and MBC clarify the outcomes that sustain the long-term functioning of a cross-organizational PLC?'. The combination of the VC and MBC frameworks yielded insights into both PLCs, one well-functioning, the other struggling. It first underscored the defining influence of strategic and enabling value. These insights enable PLCs and their facilitators to address these mechanisms more intentionally in order to strengthen collective learning.

TI Educational inequalities in primary and secondary education across the
   European Union: Evidence from PISA, PIRLS, and TIMSS
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational inequalities; European Union; PISA; PIRLS; TIMSS
ID ACHIEVEMENT
AB This study examines educational inequalities in primary and secondary education across the European Union (EU) using data from PISA, PIRLS, and TIMSS. Drawing on data from 934,263 students in 34,060 schools across EU countries that participated in one or more of these assessments between 2016 and 2023, it investigates trends in both inequality of achievement, captured through variation in performance, and inequality of opportunity, captured through associations between performance and student gender, country of birth, and socioeconomic background. Over time, average performance declined or stagnated, while performance variability increased, indicating widening inequality of achievement. Inequality of opportunity was also evident, with socioeconomic background emerging as the strongest predictor of performance, an association that was particularly strong for school socioeconomic composition at secondary level. Less consistent differences by gender and country of birth were also observed. While these patterns were evident at the EU level, country-level analyses revealed considerable cross-national variation.

TI Evaluating Emergency Medicine Resident Salary Adequacy: Inflation Trends
   and Cost-of-Living Adjustment Across US Programs
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Objectives To determine whether US emergency medicine (EM) postgraduate year 1 (PGY-1) resident salaries kept pace with inflation from 2021 and 2022 to 2025 and 2026 and to assess how adjustment for local cost of living altered their relative value. Methods We conducted cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses of ACGME-accredited EM residency programs. Publicly reported 2025 and 2026 PGY-1 base salaries were collected from program websites, and paired 2021 and 2022 salaries were available for a subset. Salaries were adjusted using the Council for Community and Economic Research Cost of Living Index (C2ER COLI), Quarter 3 2025. Salary growth was compared with the 18.331% increase in CPI-U from July 2021 to July 2025. Regional differences were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis tests, and the relationship between COLI and nominal salary was evaluated using simple linear regression. Results Of 295 programs identified, 271 had 2025 and 2026 salary data and 209 had paired salary data. Mean PGY-1 salary increased from $59,115 to $69,184, a mean increase of 17.0%, slightly below cumulative inflation. 70 programs (33.5%) met or exceeded the inflation benchmark, whereas 139 (66.5%) did not. Across all programs, mean nominal salary was $68,839 and mean COL-adjusted salary was $65,100. The West and Northeast had the highest nominal salaries but the lowest COL-adjusted salaries, whereas the Midwest and South showed the opposite pattern. Each 1-point increase in COLI was associated with a $212 increase in nominal salary (95% CI, $188-$236; R-2 = 0.53; p < 0.001). Adjusted mean salaries ranged from $37,510 for New York City programs in Manhattan to $82,600 in Akron, Ohio. Conclusions Mean EM PGY-1 salary growth slightly lagged inflation, and two-thirds of programs did not meet the inflation benchmark. Although higher-COL markets paid higher nominal salaries, these increases did not fully offset local costs. COL-adjusted salary reporting may improve transparency and support more informed residency selection and compensation review.

TI A Spatial Analysis of Parks in King County, Washington: Identifying
   Access Disparities Through Isochrone-Based Cluster Analysis
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE park access; urban planning; isochrones; spatial analysis; cluster
   analysis
ID FEATURES; RACE/ETHNICITY; ACCESSIBILITY; ASSOCIATION; QUALITY; CITIES;
   PEOPLE; HEALTH; SPACES
AB Washington's King County Parks agency seeks to "steward, enhance and acquire parks to inspire healthy communities." To aid planning, we identify regions of relatively low park access using a walking-based approach. We define access as the number of parks reachable within a 10-, 20-, or 30-minute walk from the centroid of each Census block group. Cluster analysis reveals distinct spatial patterns: high-access clusters are concentrated in Seattle's urban core, while low-access clusters are primarily in eastern and southern King County, highlighting regions for potential targeted infrastructure investment. This case demonstrates the importance of measuring "access" using walking distances that account for local road networks. Our methodology, implemented with open-source R packages and publicly available data, provides a reproducible framework for both practitioners and educators. Additionally, the supplemental code vignette (nepf_iso_vignette) offers a step-by-step walkthrough of the analysis. Planners can apply these methods to assess access to parks or other local amenities, while students can follow the vignette to develop their own spatial analyses. Our results inform future park development and offer a foundation for further research on equitable access to parks and green space across King County's diverse communities.

TI Academic Integrity in Unsupervised Digital Environments: The Role of
   Interdisciplinary Task Design and Peer Assessment
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic cheating; academic integrity; assigned learning tasks; digital
   environment; interdisciplinary approach; peer assessment
ID REASONS; CHEAT
AB Academic cheating remains a persistent challenge in education across all levels despite various proposed solutions. This study is the first to investigate the integration of an interdisciplinary assessment approach and peer assessment as proactive strategies to enhance academic integrity in unsupervised digital learning environments. A quasi-experimental study with control and experimental groups was conducted with N = 110 students enrolled in primary teacher education, including a control group (n = 55) and an experimental group (n = 55) over one semester. These findings suggest that the intervention was effective in reducing cheating behaviours and strengthening academic integrity in unsupervised digital learning environments. The study highlights the potential of integrating interdisciplinary assessment and peer assessment into contemporary teaching and assessment practices to promote more responsible learning behaviours.

TI Teacher- Versus Video-Delivered Classroom Activity Breaks and Student
   Physical Activity: The PAAC-3 Trial
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom; elementary students; physical activity; technology
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; CHILDREN; CALIBRATION; TIME; TASK
AB Background Classroom activity breaks may increase moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA); however, few studies have compared teacher and video-delivered approaches under real-world conditions. Methods In this cluster randomized trial, 11 elementary schools were assigned to teacher-delivered (PAAC-T; 5 schools, 192 students) or video-delivered (PAAC-V; 6 schools, 276 students) classroom activity breaks across one academic year. Teachers were trained to deliver two 10-min breaks daily. Intervention delivery was tracked via a web-based platform, and classroom MVPA was assessed using accelerometers at baseline and follow-up. Results Implementation fidelity was low and highly variable, but comparable between PAAC-T (42.3 +/- 57.1 activity breaks/teacher/year) and PAAC-V (39.2 +/- 33.9; p = 0.96), with teachers delivering similar to 50% of the intended daily activity. Classroom MVPA increased significantly in both groups (PAAC-T: 9.8 +/- 15.9; PAAC-V: 9.1 +/- 15.3 min/day; p < 0.001), with no intervention arm-by-time interaction (p = 0.43). Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Classroom physical activity breaks may increase student MVPA, but effectiveness in elementary schools appears to depend on implementation fidelity, administrative support, and equitable system-level infrastructure. Conclusions Modest increases in classroom MVPA were observed across both delivery formats, although low and variable implementation fidelity limited conclusions regarding effectiveness and highlighted the need for stronger implementation supports.

TI Closing the Gap From Both Sides: Why Empowering Educators and
   Researchers Is More Promising Than Engineering a New Field
SO MIND BRAIN AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE dyslexia; evidence-based practice; implementation; practitioner
   knowledge; research literacy; research-practice gap; science of reading
AB The persistent gap between reading science and classroom practice remains one of the most consequential challenges in education. A recent proposal in this issue calls for the creation of a new "engineering of reading" field to bridge this divide. This commentary argues that the central issue is not a lack of translation but a lack of capacity on both sides. Educators are rarely trained to evaluate research as informed consumers, and researchers are often insufficiently prepared to design work that functions within real educational systems. Addressing this gap requires building complementary forms of expertise rather than introducing new intermediary roles. While grounded in reading, this argument extends to other disciplines pursuing evidence-based reform. Drawing on the author's experience and the mission of The Dyslexia Foundation, this commentary outlines a framework for strengthening research literacy among educators and systems literacy among researchers as a more sustainable path forward.

TI Advancing contemporary self-determination research and practice in
   Arabic contexts: Validation of the self-determination inventory:
   Parent/teacher report
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Students with disabilities; Self-determination; Assessment;
   Self-Determination Inventory; Arabic contexts
ID QUALITY-OF-LIFE; STUDENT REPORT
AB Self-determination is a critical construct for people with disabilities across languages and cultures. However, limited research has examined how self-determination is expressed, measured, and supported in Arabic contexts. This study represents the first phase of the Self-Determination Inventory Translation Initiative, a multi-phase project to extend and build culturally responsive measurement and an implementation knowledge base for self-determination in Arabic contexts grounded in Causal Agency Theory. Using a Bayesian Three-Part Beta Item Response Theory model, we examined the validity of the Self-Determination Inventory: Parent/Teacher Report (SDI: PTR) Arabic Translation. Results provided initial evidence supporting the validity of the SDI: PTR Arabic Translation and indicated notable variability in parent and teacher reports of self-determination in Arabic context. Future oriented goal-directed self-determination skills and abilities were reported by parents and teachers less frequently than everyday routine aspects of self-determination, suggesting differences in opportunities across school contexts. The results highlight the value of proxy reports for understanding contextual supports and opportunities while recognizing the importance of continued work that centers student self-report data to more fully represent student voice in Arabic self-determination research. Implications for future research and practice focusing on advancing self-determination in Arabic educational contexts are discussed.

TI Manipulating task order by cognitive task complexity: Associations with
   feedback-seeking behavior and L2 writing quality
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Task complexity; Feedback-seeking behavior; L2 writing quality; TBLT
ID SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; LEXICAL COMPLEXITY; SELF-REGULATION; ACCURACY;
   MINDSETS; FLUENCY; GROWTH
AB This study examines whether task order, based on Cognitive Task Complexity (CTC), predicts second language (L2) writing quality and moderates the predictive relationship between learners' Feedback-Seeking Behavior (FSB) and writing quality following written corrective feedback (WCF). Although research has examined CTC in relation to dimensions of L2 performance, including syntactic complexity, accuracy, lexical complexity, and fluency (CALF), less is known about its predictive relationship with broader dimensions of L2 writing quality. The role of FSB in predicting post-feedback writing quality across tasks of different complexity has also received limited attention. Seventy-six ESL learners in a first-year writing course completed an FSB questionnaire and performed simple and complex argumentative writing tasks in counterbalanced order. In a subsequent session, they received WCF on content, organization, vocabulary, language use, and mechanics and revised their essays. Feedback Monitoring, Value, and Growth Mindset predicted overall post-feedback writing quality. At the dimension level, Feedback Inquiry predicted content; Fixed Mindset predicted content and language use; Feedback Monitoring predicted vocabulary; and Cost, Value, and Growth Mindset predicted mechanics. Task order predicted content and language use, with simple-first learners outperforming complex-first learners on the subsequent complex task. Task order also moderated FSB-writing quality relationships for vocabulary and mechanics. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing task-level and learner-level predictors when examining L2 writing quality.

TI Emotional pathways of Chinese university EFL teachers during AI
   integration: An ecological multiple-case study
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Circumplex model of affect; Bronfenbrenner's
   bioecological model; Teacher emotion; Emotional pathways; University EFL
   teachers
ID CIRCUMPLEX MODEL
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in language education, yet little is known about how English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' emotions unfold over time as they integrate AI into their teaching. Guided by the circumplex model of affect and Bronfenbrenner's bioecological model, this retrospective qualitative multiple-case study examined the emotional pathways of three Chinese university EFL teachers at different career stages. Data came primarily from semistructured interviews, supplemented by retrospective reflective entries and platform-based teaching artefacts that clarified and contextualised reported incidents. Textual data were analysed through narrative reconstruction, coding at the episode level, interpretation of valence, arousal, and ecological conditions, and comparison across cases. The analysis identified three case-based interpretive pathways: volatility, characterised by high arousal and fluctuating valence; equilibrium, marked by moderate arousal and a stable positive orientation; and composure, reflected in low arousal and a neutral-to-positive orientation. These pathways were associated with case-specific configurations of teachers' appraisals, interactions with students and colleagues, institutional arrangements, sociocultural narratives, career timing, and changing AI tool ecologies. The study contributes an ecological account of AI-related teacher emotion and highlights the value of context-sensitive, pathway-responsive support focused on technical reliability, pedagogical judgement, ethical use, and collegial learning.

TI Harmony or dissonance? Teacher-Student congruence in generative AI
   adoption and perceived English learning gains
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher-student congruence; Continuance intention; Perceived usefulness;
   Response surface analysis; GenAI-assisted language learning
ID EXPECTATION-CONFIRMATION MODEL; USER ACCEPTANCE; PERCEPTIONS;
   SATISFACTION; CONTINUANCE; TECHNOLOGY; CONSEQUENCES; ANTECEDENTS;
   MOTIVATION; INTENTION
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet research has largely examined teachers' and students' perceptions separately. This leaves unresolved whether alignment or discrepancy between classroom stakeholders' post-adoption perceptions is associated with students' perceived English learning gains. Addressing this problem is theoretically important because technology-continuance research remains predominantly individualcentred, and practically important because teacher-student differences may complicate the coordination of GenAI-supported learning activities within classroom settings. Adopting an ECMderived relational perspective, this study examined teacher-student configurations of perceived usefulness and continuance intention using matched classroom-level data from 61 teachers and 1189 students across 61 classrooms in 36 Chinese universities. Response surface analysis modelled nonlinear associations between these configurations and students' perceived learning gains. Students reported the highest perceived learning gains when their continuance intention exceeded that of their teachers, suggesting that student-led persistence may remain educationally meaningful when teacher uptake is more cautious. For perceived usefulness, both high-high and low-low alignment were associated with higher perceived learning gains than mismatched evaluations, indicating that shared appraisals may support more coherent GenAI use. The study shows that teacher-student congruence is construct-specific: shared usefulness appraisals and directional discrepancies in continuance intention correspond to different patterns of perceived learning gains. Practically, educators should distinguish disagreement about GenAI's perceived value from disagreement about willingness to continue using it when coordinating AI-supported language-learning activities.

TI Exploratory study of protective factors against belief in neuromyths in

DT Article
DE Neuromyth; Knowledge about the brain; Vocational-technical high school;

SO DYSLEXIA

DE dyslexia; dyslexia legislation; pseudoscientific treatments; reading

ID VISUAL-ATTENTION SPAN; WORKING-MEMORY; LEARNING-DISABILITIES;

   LANGUAGE DEFICITS; COLORED OVERLAYS; ORTON-GILLINGHAM; DECISION-MAKING
AB Despite a strong base of scientifically supported research on dyslexia, pervasive misunderstandings continue, particularly in the United States, where state legislation, instructional practices and parent advocacy intersect in ways that influence how dyslexia is identified and treated. AB This collective autoethnography emerged from our experiences at the Emotions in Engineering Education Symposium 2025. TI The Role of Science Course Pathways in Predicting College Enrollment:
   Insight From A Large Urban School District
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE college enrollment; science course-taking; science pathways; STEM; STEM
   participation; tracking
ID COURSE-TAKING; MATHEMATICS; TRACKING; MATH
AB Although high school science course-taking is highly valued in college admissions, its predictability for college enrollment, a key step in access to many STEM fields, has not been sufficiently investigated in the context of wide variability in science courses and updated standards. Furthermore, while ability group tracking in science has declined, tracking can persist in the levels, type, and breadth of science courses taken. The study analyzes students' science course-taking pathways from ninth through eleventh grade and examines their relationship with college enrollment. We use cross-classified hierarchical logistic regression modeling of students nested within both course pathways and schools in a large urban school district, examining school and course pathway features and controlling for academic performance and student characteristics. Completing the three core science courses-biology, chemistry, and physics-remains a strong predictor of college enrollment, even in the context of updated science standards, but the presence of advanced science coursework in the pathway showed the strongest association with college enrollment. Greater school STEM-orientation was associated with increased likelihood of college enrollment.

TI Gainers give: a social exchange analysis of teachers' interpersonal
   emotion regulation, faculty trust, and work engagement
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher; Interpersonal emotion regulation; Faculty trust; Work
   engagement; Social exchange theory
ID QUESTIONNAIRE; PRINCIPAL; SCHOOL
AB Teaching is fundamentally an interactive endeavor, involving continuous emotional exchanges. Drawing on social exchange theory, this study examined how teachers' perception of faculty trust influences their work engagement through interpersonal emotion regulation. Teachers' interpersonal emotion regulation is differentiated between intrinsic (self-targeted) and extrinsic (other-targeted) interpersonal emotion regulation to capture both internal and relational dimensions of emotional exchange. A sample of 987 primary and secondary school teachers in China participated in an online survey. Structural equation modeling with mediation analysis revealed that teachers' faculty trust was positively associated with intrinsic and extrinsic interpersonal emotion regulation, as well as with work engagement. By conceptualizing interpersonal emotion regulation as a social exchange mechanism, this study provides a novel theoretical perspective on understanding teachers' emotional interactions at school, offering practical implications in teachers' professional relationships and work engagement.

TI Adaptive constructive support in teacher-student interactions:
   differences in support duration depending on individual student
   characteristics
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Adaptive teaching; Constructive support; Socioemotional support;
   Instructional support; Diverse students' needs; Bayesian statistics
ID MULTILEVEL MODELS; CLASSROOM; SCHOOL; ACHIEVEMENT; QUALITY;
   ASSOCIATIONS; ENGAGEMENT; CHILDREN; IMPACT
AB This paper examines teachers' constructive support in dyadic teacher-student interactions and explores interindividual differences in teacher support depending on student characteristics. We developed an observational tool that assesses the duration and valence of teachers' constructive support according to two facets: socioemotional and instructional support. Observational and survey data from 192 third- and fourth-grade students from 14 classes in 5 award-winning elementary schools in Germany were analyzed. The results show that 74% of the students were involved in teacher-student interactions during the observed 30-minute period of teacher-assisted learning time, with interactions lasting 30 s on average. Moreover, Bayesian multilevel analyses revealed that students with special educational needs received less constructive teacher support than their peers. Bayesian mediation analyses indicated that this association was partly explained by students with special educational needs requesting support less often. The findings on interindividual differences in dyadic teacher-student interactions provide insights into how teachers' constructive support is differentially distributed across students in dyadic interactions.

AB Although the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools has facilitated AI-enhanced and informal digital learning of English, traditional classroom ecology remains a central context for adolescent English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) learners' language learning and development. TI Reversing the Decline: Evidence From a Quasiexperimental Study on How
   Classroom Practices Support Adolescents' Reading Motivation and Amount
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN READING
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescence; book access; Chile; reading amount; reading motivation
ID INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; ENGAGEMENT; ACHIEVEMENT; STUDENTS; COMPREHENSION
AB Background Reading for pleasure has been declining worldwide, with significant drops in reading motivation and frequency among adolescents. In Chile, national assessments indicate that students' reading motivation and frequency decrease as they progress through school. This study examines the effects of a school-based reading intervention aimed at increasing intrinsic reading motivation and reading amount among Chilean eighth-grade students.Methods A quasiexperimental design was implemented with 574 eighth-grade students (45% female), aged 13-14 years, from schools with a predominantly medium-low socioeconomic status. The intervention included three groups: full intervention, books only and control. The full intervention included initial teacher training in motivationally oriented practices: self-selected independent reading of popular books, peer recommendations and discussions, absence of summative grading for reading activities, teacher-kept reading records and monthly teacher support meetings. The books-only condition provided book access without additional motivational components. Intrinsic reading motivation and reading amount were the outcomes. Print exposure, language arts grades and home literacy environment were included as covariates.Results The full intervention produced significant gains in intrinsic reading motivation relative to control; gains in reading amount relative to control were positive but did not reach significance. The books-only condition did not differ from control on either outcome. The full intervention produced significantly greater gains in reading amount than books only; the difference in motivation between intervention groups was not significant.Conclusions Combining book access with motivationally oriented classroom practices can effectively increase students' intrinsic reading motivation and reading amount. Book access alone was insufficient to produce significant gains, highlighting the importance of comprehensive, motivation-focused strategies to promote leisure reading among adolescents.

TI Academic Self-Efficacy and Learning Engagement Among Law-English Dual
   Degree Students: The Mediating Role of Professional Identity Under the
   Foreign-Related Rule of Law Orientation
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic self-efficacy; foreign-related rule of law; Law-English dual
   degree programme; learning engagement; professional identity
ID EDUCATION
AB While interdisciplinary professional education is increasingly vital for complex contexts, little is known about how academic self-efficacy, professional identity, and learning engagement are related in Law-English dual degree programmes under a foreign-related rule-of-law orientation. Drawing on social cognitive theory and perspectives on professional identity development, this study examined these relationships among undergraduates in such a programme at an eastern Chinese university using an explanatory mixed-methods design. A total of 230 questionnaires were collected (215 valid for quantitative analysis) and 16 semi-structured interviews were conducted to elaborate the statistical findings. The study contributes to research on interdisciplinary professional education by identifying professional identity as an identity-related link between academic confidence and learning engagement in an emerging legal-language pathway. It also offers practical implications for curriculum integration, professional orientation, and practice-based learning in such programmes.

TI Beyond Using AI: Self-Regulated Pathways to Engagement in AI-Assisted
   Language Learning
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted language learning; human-AI trust; learner engagement;
   metacognitive strategies; self-regulated learning theory
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly reshaped language learning, yet how learners become engaged in AI-assisted language learning remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on self-regulated learning theory, this study examined the relationships among AI literacy, human-AI trust, metacognitive strategies, critical thinking and engagement. A questionnaire survey was conducted with 768 undergraduate students who had experience with AI-assisted language learning. Data were analyzed using structural equation modelling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The structural equation modelling results showed that AI literacy and human-AI trust were positively associated with both metacognitive strategies and critical thinking, which were further related to learner engagement. The mediation results indicated that metacognitive strategies and critical thinking served as significant linking mechanisms between AI-related antecedents and engagement. The configurational analysis revealed that no single condition was necessary for high engagement, while five sufficient configurations were identified, highlighting multiple pathways to engagement. These findings suggest that engagement in AI-assisted language learning is associated with learners' AI-related readiness, self-regulatory processes and critical evaluation. The study provides theoretical and pedagogical insights into self-regulated AI-supported language learning.

TI Emotions in engineering education: state of the art and future
   directions
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotions; engineering education; engineering culture; emotional labour;
   engineering identity; sociotechnical responsibility
AB This editorial synthesizes the special issue Emotions in engineering education: Widening perspectives in a rapidly growing field of research. It shows how the included studies reposition emotions from peripheral outcomes to central mechanisms shaping engineering cultures, indentities, responsibilities, and professional practice, while also broadening the field's topical, methodological, and theoretical scope. TI The melancholic engineer: emotional intelligibility and the costs of
   persistence in engineering education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Engineering education; discrimination and exclusion; persistence;
   qualitative longitudinal research; emotions
ID FEMINIST; WOMEN; IDENTITIES; STUDENTS; CRITIQUE; GENDER; SENSE; VIEW
AB Engineering education increasingly asks how participation can become more equitable and sustainable. Yet efforts to broaden participation often focus on access and persistence, paying less attention to what participation demands from those already committed to engineering. Drawing on a longitudinal, phenomenologically informed qualitative study across multiple engineering education contexts (2019-2025), this article examines how emotional experiences become intelligible in relation to discrimination, belonging, and exclusion. The findings show that feelings can shape orientations, actions, and possibilities before participants can interpret them in relation to unequal conditions of participation. I develop emotional intelligibility to conceptualise this relation between the efficacy of emotional experience and its social interpretability, and critical reflexivity to describe how the conditions through which experiences become meaningful can themselves become questionable. Melancholic attachment, developed through Butler, explains why recognising exclusion need not dissolve disciplinary commitment. Persistence can therefore coexist with substantial emotional, social, and existential costs. The article argues that equitable and sustainable engineering education requires moving beyond retention towards conditions for dwelling in which unequal costs can become intelligible, contestable, and open to transformation.

   Interpretable Evidence
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

   learning analytics; formative assessment; assessment infrastructure
AB The digital transformation of higher education requires assessment approaches capable of capturing complex learning processes. This methodological pilot study examines Mission Control-Didascalias VC, an analytics infrastructure for classroom-management simulations. Of 626 sessions, 595 were retained in the cleaned analytical corpus. Data sources comprised session metadata, verbal interactions, programmed challenging events, vocal and movement signals, dashboard exports and, for 17 focal cases, video recordings and transcripts. The analysis examined data quality, traceability and interpretability, developed and refined a multimodal coding framework, and included a worked example of sequence-based coding. Results show that simulation records do not constitute assessment evidence in themselves. Their formative value emerges through cleaning, temporal alignment, multimodal triangulation and contextual interpretation, which transform isolated technical traces into pedagogically meaningful interactional sequences. Critical verbal interactions, participant responses, emergent classroom situations, and vocal and movement patterns provided complementary evidence, including in sessions without programmed challenging events. The study concludes that VR analytics can support sustainable formative assessment when technical records are transformed into pedagogically interpretable interactional evidence for debriefing, feedback and evidence reuse over time.

TI From College to Homeownership: How Undergraduate Major, Salary, and
   Student Loan Debt Are Associated with Housing Outcomes in the United
   States
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; educational outcomes; economics of education; finance;
   alumni; human capital; status attainment; homeownership; United States;
   quantitative
ID LOW-INCOME; TRANSITION; EDUCATION; RETURNS; WEALTH; YOUNG; DISPARITIES;
   ATTAINMENT; MARKET; BLACK
AB Homeownership has become increasingly difficult for many college graduates in the United States. This quantitative study examines the conditional associations among undergraduate major, post-college income, student loan debt, and homeownership using restricted data from the 2021 College and Beyond II Alumni Survey. Grounded in Human Capital Theory and informed by Status Attainment Theory as a secondary interpretive perspective, the study analyzes a sample of 2513 college graduates approximately a decade after degree completion. The findings highlight the complex relationships among educational pathways, post-college economic circumstances, student loan experiences, and homeownership and underscore the need for further research on the long-term financial outcomes associated with higher education.

TI Artificial Intelligence in Contemporary Education: Teachers'
   Competencies, Challenges, and Pedagogical Implications
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; teachers; AI competencies; teaching practice;
   primary and secondary education
AB The increasing integration of AI in education imposes the need to examine the competencies of teachers for its pedagogically meaningful, safe, and responsible application. The goal of this research was to examine the self-assessments of teachers' AI-related competencies, as well as to determine whether there were statistically significant differences regarding the subject area and years of teaching experience. The research was conducted on a sample of 165 primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic of Serbia. Data were collected using the Serbian-language version of the original Teacher Artificial Intelligence Competence Self-Efficacy (TAICS) Scale. The reliability and factor structure of the instrument were checked using Cronbach's alpha coefficient, Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) indicator, Bartlett's test of sphericity, and exploratory factor analysis using principal axis factoring with Varimax rotation, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to examine differences. The results showed high internal consistency of the scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.972) and an interpretable three-factor solution explaining 71.202% of the total variance. The following factors were extracted: pedagogical-evaluative AI competencies, ethical-safety AI competencies, and operational-technical AI competencies. No statistically significant differences in pedagogical-evaluative or ethical-safety AI competencies were found according to subject area or years of teaching experience. For operational-technical AI competencies, an unadjusted difference was observed according to teaching experience; however, this finding did not remain statistically significant after the Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary and require replication in larger and more representative samples. The findings indicate that the competencies of teachers for artificial intelligence should be viewed as a multidimensional basis for further research, improvement of teaching practice, and planning of professional development in the field of application of AI in education.

TI Learning Gains in Research Proposal Writing with a Project-Based
   Interactive E-Book: A Quasi-Experimental Study in Two Indonesian
   Undergraduate Programmes
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE scientific writing skills; research proposal writing; project-based
   learning; interactive e-book; academic literacy; higher education
ID ACADEMIC LITERACIES; METAANALYSIS
AB Scientific writing remains a persistent difficulty for Indonesian undergraduates, and the Indonesian language teaching materials currently in use neither embed project-based learning (PjBL) nor exploit interactive digital formats. This study examined whether students receiving a combined PjBL-interactive e-book intervention demonstrated greater gains in research proposal writing than students receiving conventional instruction. The e-book, developed through the ADDIE model and organized as five weekly project cycles culminating in a mini research proposal, was first evaluated by content, media, and language experts and then by lecturers and students in a limited pilot. Learning outcomes were compared using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group design with 138 students taking the compulsory Indonesian language course in two study programmes at two universities. Writing performance was scored with an analytic rubric comprising five aspects and twelve weighted sub-indicators derived from an established framework for proposal construction. Students who learned with the e-book outperformed their peers in conventional instruction on the posttest and on normalized gain. The between-group difference was large, remained similar after adjustment for pretest scores and in sensitivity analyses accounting for class clustering, and was of comparable magnitude in both disciplinary contexts. Because the intervention combines a project syntax with an interactive digital format, the design evaluates the combined instructional package; the independent contribution of the pedagogy and the medium cannot be separated and is not claimed here.

TI Comparing the Predictive Importance of Mathematics Self-Efficacy,
   Socioeconomic Status and ICT Access: A SHAP Analysis of PISA 2022 Across
   19 Education Systems
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE mathematics achievement; PISA 2022; large-scale assessment; mathematics
   self-efficacy; mathematics anxiety; socioeconomic status; ICT access;
   predictive modelling; interpretable machine learning; SHAP; gradient
   boosting; educational data science
ID ACADEMIC RESILIENCE
AB Digital access occupies a prominent place in educational policy debates, yet its predictive contribution to mathematics achievement, relative to psychological and socioeconomic factors, remains insufficiently quantified. Existing evidence often relies on linear models, examines predictor blocks separately, or considers technological resources without placing them alongside psychological constructs within a common framework. This study compares the predictive importance of psychological, socioeconomic, demographic and ICT-access indicators for mathematics achievement in PISA 2022. The analysis used data from 141,563 students across 19 education systems and included seven predictors: mathematics self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, sense of school belonging, economic, social and cultural status (ESCS), gender, ICT resources at home and ICT resources at school. Weighted gradient boosting models were fitted separately to each of the ten plausible mathematics values and interpreted using TreeSHAP; a weighted random forest with permutation importance was used as a robustness check. The full model explained 39.2% of the weighted test-set variance in the plausible-value outcomes (R2 = 0.3922, SEtotal=0.0066 , and RMSE = 77.95 score points). Mathematics self-efficacy ranked first under both criteria (42.3% of SHAP importance; 57.8% of permutation importance), ahead of socioeconomic status (30.9%; 32.0%), while the ICT-access block contributed 6.9% and 2.1%, respectively and added 0.0122 to test-set R2. The two importance rankings were identical (Spearman's rho = 1.000). The SHAP ranking was unchanged across all 800 plausible-value & times; replicate-weight runs, matched XGBoost permutation importance, and was reproduced under a school-grouped train-test split. The model also detected a non-monotonic association between school belonging and predicted achievement, together with a MATHEFF & times; ESCS interaction pattern, supported by a direct-outcome interaction model, in which the modelled association between self-efficacy and achievement was stronger at higher ESCS levels. Because PISA 2022 is cross-sectional and plausible values are designed for population-level inference, these findings should be interpreted as predictive and associational rather than causal. The results suggest that, in systems where ICT access is already widespread, reported access to technological resources contributes comparatively little to prediction once psychological and socioeconomic indicators are considered, although sensitivity analyses indicate that home ICT access is partly affected by missingness patterns.

TI Aligning Undergraduate Residential Construction Education with Workforce
   Needs: A Mixed-Method Study
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE construction education; residential construction; higher education;
   workforce competencies; curriculum design
ID SYSTEMATIC COURSE DEVELOPMENT; STUDENTS
AB Undergraduate residential construction programs face growing pressure to prepare graduates with competencies that reflect evolving workforce expectations. This study develops a preliminary evidence-informed framework for aligning undergraduate residential construction education with workforce expectations identified from selected U.S. residential construction markets and practitioner perspectives. Two complementary evidence streams were integrated. First, a systematic screening process informed by PRISMA reporting yielded 156 residential construction job postings collected from selected markets in the U.S. Southeast and Southwest (2024: 70; 2025: 86), which were analyzed using thematic coding to identify labor-market competency requirements. Second, a three-hour focus group involving 14 senior residential construction professionals representing 10 NAHB-affiliated firms provided practitioner perspectives on workforce competency expectations and educational preparation. Findings were integrated using Patton's convergence model to examine convergence, complementarity, divergence, and source-specific signals across the two evidence streams. Five competency areas received cross-source support from labor-market evidence and practitioner perspectives. These findings were subsequently organized for educational interpretation within the following four domains: Technical; Professional; Management; and Safety, Quality, and Regulatory Compliance. Digital construction capability emerged as a cross-cutting practitioner-anticipated signal. The integrated findings informed six proposed educational modules and associated indicative learning outcomes. The study contributes a mixed-method approach for integrating labor-market and practitioner evidence and demonstrates how such evidence can inform preliminary curriculum design.

TI Instructional scaffolding and critical literary analysis among EFL
   undergraduates: a brief research report
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE critical literary analysis; EFL literature education; instructional
   scaffolding; quasi-experimental design; undergraduate education
AB This study examined whether instructional scaffolding improves critical-analytical abilities among non-native English literature undergraduates relative to traditional lecture-based teaching. In a within-subjects quasi-experimental design, 101 undergraduates across four sections were taught a poetry unit using scaffolding (Unit 1) and a drama unit using traditional instruction (Unit 2). Students scored significantly higher on the Unit 2 exam than the Unit 1 exam (n = 89; M = 11.88 vs. 10.83/15; t(88) = -3.78, p < .001, d = 0.40), and forced-choice comparisons showed a small, consistent preference for the traditional method; however, because unit order and literary genre were not counterbalanced across sections, this difference cannot be attributed to teaching method alone. Scaffolding activities were rated positively at the activity level despite this pattern. A secondary finding - that group-based scaffolding carried a real implementation cost from uneven group participation - offers actionable guidance independent of this limitation. These results should be read as evidence about scaffolding's implementation under authentic classroom conditions rather than as a causal test of its effectiveness; they motivate a counterbalanced follow-up study and identify specific logistical factors to manage in EFL literature classrooms.

TI Effects of Gagné's instructional model on performance and retention in
   Algebra among secondary school students in Nigeria
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Algebra; Gagne's instructional strategy; performance; Quade's ANCOVA;
   retention
AB Background Algebra remains a challenging aspect of the secondary school mathematics curriculum in Nigeria, contributing to persistent learning difficulties and poor achievement. Objectives This study examined the effect of Gagn & eacute;'s instructional strategy on students' performance and retention in Algebra, as well as its impact across gender. Methods A quasi-experimental design was employed involving 382 students selected through multi-stage sampling. An Algebra Performance Test with a reliability coefficient of.69 was used for data collection. Descriptive statistics and Quade's non-parametric ANCOVA were used to analyse the data. Results Results showed that students taught using Gagne's instructional strategy performed significantly better than those taught through the conventional approach, F(1, 380) = 518.11, p < .001, partial eta(2) = .577, indicating a large practical effect. Conclusion The findings demonstrate that Gagn & eacute;'s instructional strategy effectively enhances both immediate and sustained Algebra learning. It is recommended that Gagn & eacute;'s instructional strategy be integrated into mathematics instruction and teacher training programmes to improve learning outcomes in secondary schools. Implications of these findings and recommendations for practice are discussed.

TI Effect of laboratory-based pedagogy on junior secondary students' basic
   science achievement: a pilot randomised pretest-posttest study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; basic science achievement; experimental study;
   laboratory-based pedagogy; science education
ID PRACTICAL WORK
AB Laboratory-Based Pedagogy (LBP) is widely advocated for promoting active, inquiry-based science learning. Yet, evidence of its effectiveness at the junior secondary school level remains underexplored in developing educational contexts. Guided by Piaget's constructivist theory, this pilot randomised pretest-posttest study examined the effect of LBP on Basic Science achievement among 30 junior secondary students from a single school, randomly assigned to experimental (n = 15) and control (n = 15) groups. The experimental group engaged in structured hands-on laboratory activities integrated into classroom instruction, whereas the control group received teacher-centred instruction covering the same content. Data was collected using the Basic Science Achievement Test (BSAT), adapted from National Examination Council (NECO) examination items. Mean scores, standard deviations, and Analysis of Covariance were employed to analyse the data, while controlling for pretest scores. Result revealed a significant effect of instructional method on posttest achievement, F(1, 27) = 19.44, p < .001, partial eta(2) = 0.419, with the laboratory-based group outperforming the control group. Pretest achievement also significantly predicted posttest performance. These findings suggest that LBP can improve Basic Science achievement by promoting active learning. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted with caution because the study was conducted at a single school, involved a small sample, and the groups exhibited substantial baseline differences in pretest performance. The study provides preliminary evidence to support larger, well-powered randomised trials in diverse educational settings.

AB The increasing digitalization of education and the growing emphasis on twenty-first-century competencies have expanded expectations for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers' continuous professional development. However, limited evidence exists on how teachers' self-regulated professional learning and perceived digital educational opportunities are associated with their readiness to integrate Critical Thinking, Communication, Collaboration, and Creativity (4Cs) into teaching. A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted with 225 in-service EFL teachers from secondary schools and universities in Shymkent, Kazakhstan. Data were collected using measures of Self-Regulated Professional Learning (SRL), Perceived Digital Educational Opportunities (DEO), and an eight-vignette scenario-based assessment of readiness for 4Cs integration. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, multiple linear regression, Welch's independent-samples t-tests, and adjusted regression analysis were applied. The mean overall scenario-based readiness score was 21.43 (SD = 4.42; theoretical range = 8-32), with Critical Thinking showing the highest mean and Creativity the lowest. Overall readiness was strongly associated with SRL (r = .809, p < .001) and perceived DEO (r = .761, p < .001). In the multiple regression model, SRL (beta = .553, p < .001) and perceived DEO (beta = .375, p < .001) were independently associated with readiness, with the model explaining 72.3% of its variance (R-2 = .723). Creativity showed the strongest dimension-specific relationships with SRL and perceived DEO and the largest proportion of explained variance (R-2 = .593). University instructors demonstrated higher unadjusted readiness than secondary-school teachers; however, the institutional association was substantially reduced after adjustment for teaching experience and gender (beta = .111, p = .003). EFL teachers' scenario-based readiness for 4Cs integration is closely associated with both self-regulated professional learning and perceived digital educational opportunities, although the strength of these relationships differs across individual 4Cs dimensions and institutional contexts. The findings highlight the potential value of CPD approaches that combine access to digitally mediated professional-learning opportunities with support for teachers' planning, reflection, self-monitoring, and pedagogical adaptation. Because the study was cross-sectional and scenario-based, the findings represent statistical associations and stated pedagogical preparedness rather than causal effects or directly observed classroom competence.

TI From effectiveness to sustainable use: understanding university
   students' adoption of generative AI for academic writing through an
   extended UTAUT mixed-methods study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic writing; GenAI; sustainable education; university students;
   UTAUT model
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; TECHNOLOGY; CHALLENGES; ACCEPTANCE; FACULTY
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education and students' academic writing practices. However, existing research has largely focused on technology acceptance and usage intention, with less attention to whether and how GenAI use can be sustained. This study investigates the determinants and dimensions of sustainable GenAI use among university students through a mixed-methods approach, combining an online survey of 1,084 Chinese university students with semi-structured interviews. An extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model was employed to examine the quantitative relationships. The results indicated that performance expectancy (beta = 0.195, p < 0.001), effort expectancy (beta = 0.094, p = 0.030), social influence (beta = 0.147, p < 0.001), perceived enjoyment (beta = 0.224, p < 0.001), and perceived creativity support (beta = 0.211, p < 0.001) positively affected behavioral intention, whereas perceived risk had a negative effect (beta = -0.044, p = 0.019). Facilitating conditions (beta = 0.355, p < 0.001) and behavioral intention (beta = 0.531, p < 0.001) were positively associated with actual usage behavior. Additionally, gender, educational level, usage experience, and disciplinary background exerted significant moderating effects. Qualitative findings identified three interconnected dimensions of sustainable GenAI use: long-term continuance, balanced and moderate use, and responsible and ethical use. By extending UTAUT beyond technology acceptance toward a multidimensional conceptualization of sustainable use, this study showed that sustainable GenAI use depended not only on technology acceptance but also on students' ability to engage with GenAI critically, responsibly, and autonomously. The findings provide practical insights for fostering AI literacy and the appropriate integration of GenAI in higher education.

AB Introduction Higher education institutions often rely on STEM viewbooks that display a diverse student body to recruit ethnic-racial minoritized students (ERMs) into STEM. SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Professional brand position; Pharmacy/pharmacists; Image gap analysis;
   Brand image of nursing; Conceptual framework
ID PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY
AB Objective: To explore pharmacist perceptions of their profession's current versus desired brand image. Methods: Data were collected through 50 facilitated discussion groups (n = 423) at a national pharmacy conference. TI Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and
   generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI misconduct; Human-AI separation; Item-response theory;
   Person-fit statistics
ID ACADEMIC DISHONESTY; PARAMETER-ESTIMATION; PERSON-FIT; ITEM; LIKELIHOOD;
   PATTERNS; BEHAVIOR
AB The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT raises serious concerns about academic integrity, especially in the context of assessments. While detection efforts have focused on open-ended responses, multiplechoice questions (MCQs), which are common in high-stakes testing, remain largely overlooked, partly due to their perceived detection difficulty. The present work establishes a theoretical and empirical foundation for ap plications of psychometric theory to separate GenAI and human responses. Specifically, it investigates whether person-fit statistics (PFS), a class of methods within Item Response Theory (IRT) used to evaluate how well an ex aminee's response pattern fits the expectations of the IRT model, can distinguish between GenAI and human responses to MCQ assessments. To study this, we use data from two authentic assessment contexts: a highschool level chemistry test and the national university entrance exam, each with approximately 1000 human respondents. Our results demonstrate that PFS reveal significant differences between human responses and those generated by advanced chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), which appear as 'aberrant' respondents. We also demonstrate that different chatbots present significantly different response patterns, suggesting that they should be treated as a heterogeneous group of 'intelligences' rather than as a single one. Using the PFS measures, we also demonstrate, however, that newer GenAI versions not only improve in performance but also become more 'human-like' in their response patterns. Together, these results position IRT as a robust framework for character izing and separating human and GenAI response patterns in MCQ assessments, providing a theoretical foundation and empirical evidence.

TI Skill formation and policy transfer in Vietnam's TVET reform:
   Implications for educational development in emerging economies
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE TVET; Skill formation; Policy transfer; Vietnam; Educational
   development; Emerging economies
ID UNIVERSITY; EMPLOYMENT
AB Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) is widely promoted as a policy instrument for human capital development, industrial upgrading and inclusive growth in emerging economies. Vietnam provides an important case for examining this assumption because its TVET system has been repeatedly reformed in response to foreign direct investment, global value chain integration and persistent concerns about skills mismatch. This article analyzes Vietnam's TVET reform through the integrated lenses of skill formation systems and policy transfer theory. Based on a theory-informed integrative literature review and qualitative synthesis of academic publications, it examines how existing research has addressed the historical development, externally transferred models, uneven skill demand and institutional coordination challenges shaping Vietnam's TVET reform. The synthesis suggests that Vietnam's TVET system is historically layered and institutionally hybrid; that supply-side reforms have been unevenly implemented and weakly connected to skill demand, workplace skill use and institutional coordination; that reform implementation is constrained by weak coordination among education, industry and local governance; and that externally transferred TVET models often lack sufficient institutional embedding. The article argues that TVET reform in emerging economies should be understood not merely as the improvement of training provision, but as a system-building process linking skill supply, skill demand, workplace skill use and institutional coordination. The Vietnamese case suggests that transnational educational development cooperation should move beyond one-way model transfer towards context-sensitive institutional codevelopment.

TI "Slow Is Smooth, Smooth Is Fast": Artificial Intelligence-Driven
   Suturing Simulation for Cardiothoracic Surgical Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgical education; simulation; suturing; artificial intelligence;
   cardiothoracic surgery
ID SKILL
AB OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate a suturing simulator using Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven computer vision for objective, high-resolution assessment of technical performance in cardiothoracic surgery, applied to a novel 3D-printed simulator across different levels of surgical expertise. DESIGN: Prospective study using a novel 3D-printed suturing simulator with targets positioned at multiple depths and angles relevant to cardiothoracic surgery. Participants performed standardized running baseball sutures on 2 planes while procedural videos and post-completion images were recorded. Supervised machine learning-based video tracking (MediaPipe) and classical image processing were used to derive temporal metrics, hand path length, acceleration variability, movement irregularity, and suture uniformity. These metrics were then compared between attending surgeons and trainees. SETTING: Brigham and Women's Hospital, an academic tertiary care center in Boston, Massachusetts. PARTICIPANTS: Ten attending cardiac surgeons and 10 surgical trainees. RESULTS: AI-assisted video analysis differentiated experts from trainees with high precision. Attending cardiac surgeons performed significantly faster than trainees in needle loading (1.9 seconds vs.2.5 seconds, p < 0.01) and stitch execution (4.6 seconds vs. 6.4 seconds, p < 0.01), resulting in shorter ring completion times (252 seconds vs. 312 seconds, p < 0.02). Attending surgeons also demonstrated superior motion efficiency and less irregular movements during key maneuvers, characterized by reduced overall path length (6,714 vs. 10,154 mm, p = 0.01), lower average acceleration (20 vs. 25 mm/ s(2), p = 0.01) and reduced vibrational motion patterns (26,786,414 vs. 56,008,703 mm(2)/s(4), p = 0.01). Image analysis confirmed that attending surgeons produced significantly more uniform sutures with lower variability in inter-stitch distances (standard deviation [SD] 1.72 vs. 2.14 mm, p = 0.02; uniformity 68.9% vs. 63.1%, p = 0.03). CONCLUSIONS: AI-based assessment on an anatomically relevant simulator distinguished experts from novices using granular and mechanistic metrics of suturing skill across AI-segmented motion phases. Experts demonstrated more deliberate, controlled, and smoother movements while completing tasks in less time.

TI Understanding positive affect in Angelman syndrome: Smiling and laughter
   across comparison groups
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Angelman syndrome; Positive affect; Smiling; Laughter; Facial action
   coding system; Autism spectrum disorder
ID PATHOLOGICAL LAUGHTER; INFANT IMITATION; CHILDREN; AUTISM;
   COMMUNICATION; BEHAVIOR; PHENOTYPE; EVOLUTION; SMILES
AB Angelman syndrome (AS) is a neurogenetic condition marked by frequent smiling and laughter. Early descriptions portrayed these expressions as inappropriate or disconnected from context, but recent work has questioned this view. This study examined the emotional responses of children with AS to auditory, tactile, visual, and social stimuli and compared them to typically developing (TD) children and children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Using Bayesian mixed-effects models, we analyzed behavioral ratings and Facial Action Coding System (FACS) data. Children with AS showed more frequent positive-expression behavior, but these elevations were selective rather than indiscriminate. All groups relied on a shared repertoire of smile- and laughter-related facial actions, with AS differing primarily in the intensity and frequency of these shared actions. These findings indicate that emotional expressions in AS are context-sensitive and grounded in meaningful environmental cues, challenging the notion that their positive affect is reflexive or aberrant.

   Questioning strategies; Skilled conversation
ID SCIENCE CLASSROOMS; INSTRUCTION; STUDENTS
AB Productive teacher questioning is key to effective teaching and learning, and acquiring such questioning skills is a holy grail of teacher professional development. TI Cognitive-linguistic orchestration in Bangladeshi tertiary EFL
   education: A translanguaging perspective
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive-linguistic orchestration; EFL learners; Language ideologies;
   Learner agency; Translanguaging
ID LANGUAGE IDEOLOGIES; ENGLISH; L1
AB Despite increasing support for translanguaging in second language pedagogy, English-only ideologies remain dominant in many EFL higher education contexts. In Bangladesh, limited empirical research has examined how tertiary learners systematically use translanguaging for cognitive and pedagogical purposes. This study investigates the functional distribution and ideological orientations of translanguaging practices among Bangladeshi university EFL learners and their relationship with English proficiency. A mixed-methods design was employed, using a structured questionnaire (n = 222), semi-structured interviews, and focus group discussions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were thematically interpreted. The findings demonstrate that translanguaging is a normative, cognitively-driven learning strategy, not a deficit. Statistical analysis confirmed its high prevalence and a significant preference for metalinguistic and knowledge-construction functions over social ones. Crucially, as students' English proficiency grew, their adherence to monolingual ideology weakened, and their reliance on strategic Bangla-English integration for cognitive clarity and emotional grounding intensified. Qualitatively, learners exhibited a sophisticated spectrum of agency, from covert "linguistic rebellion" to overt advocacy for a "bilingual cognitive model", using Bangla as a "rehearsal space" to deconstruct complex concepts before formal English output. Theoretically, this study advances translanguaging scholarship by introducing Cognitive-Linguistic Orchestration (CLO), a framework demonstrating how learners strategically deploy languages for specific cognitive functions while developing L2 proficiency. Nevertheless, to address the limitations of this study, future study can employ longitudinal classroom observations to trace the developmental trajectory of orchestration competence across proficiency levels.

TI The influence of cognitive tools on the quality of coach-teacher
   professional learning conversations
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive tool; Literacy coaching; Professional learning conversation;
   Dialogic teaching
ID CLASSROOM; INSTRUCTION; SECONDARY
AB This study explores how literacy coaches use cognitive tools to foster productive professional learning conversations around teachers' videoed classroom text discussions. The use of cognitive tools increased the evidencebased specificity of these exchanges and was also associated with a greater likelihood that coaches and teachers connected specific instructional interactions in video-recorded lessons to dialogic goals and principles. Tool use, however, was not consistent. Specifically, coaches were more likely to use tools in planning reflection questions prior to the post-conference, rather than in 'real time' to support problematizing processes and interpretations of classroom discussions during the post-conference conversation. Even when tools were used, connections between specific evidence from class discussions to dialogic goals and principles rarely occurred. Implications are discussed for professional development that supports coaches in using cognitive tools more strategically and consistently to facilitate professional learning conversations that can advance teachers' adaptive expertise for dialogic teaching.

TI Bridging the gap in integrative STEM teaching competence: Framework
   construction and needs assessment for teacher professional development
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Integrative STEM teaching competence; Needs assessment; STEM teacher
   professional development; Importance-performance analysis
ID ATTITUDES; PERCEPTIONS; CHALLENGES; SCIENCE; VALUES
AB This study aimed to develop and validate an integrative STEM (i-STEM) competence framework for secondary educators and to investigate their professional development needs in the context of Vietnam's ongoing STEM reforms. A two-stage design was applied. First, an i-STEM teaching competence framework with 17 items was constructed using the Fuzzy Delphi method with 20 experts, followed by a pilot survey of 116 teachers.
