TI National Impact of Virtual Residency Interview Format on the Integrated
   Vascular Surgery Match
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE residency; recruitment; virtual interviews
ID PERSPECTIVES
AB OBJECTIVE: Due to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) required that residency interviews be conducted virtually, instead of the traditional in-person format. Previous survey studies have indicated that vascular surgery (VS) residency applicants favor remote interviews, noting sufficient exposure to the program, location and residents, with minimal travel-related cost and time burden. However, the overall impact of the virtual interview on objective measures of VS residency match have not been examined. DESIGN: Residency application and match-related data were collected from National Resident Matching Program (NRMP) Main Residency Match reports. In-person interview cycles (2010-2019) were compared with virtual interview cycles (2020-2024). Metrics of VS specialty popularity included total applicants per position and position fill rate. Metrics of VS competitiveness included overall match rate, first-choice match rate, and proportion of unmatched applicants. SETTING: NRMP interview cycles from 2010 to 2024. PARTICIPANTS: All VS residency applicants from 2010 to 2024. RESULTS: The total number of VS programs (68.8 +/- 7.9 vs 42.3 +/- 11.2), positions (86.2 +/- 10.2 vs 48.8 +/- 14.3), and applicants (164.8 +/- 10.6 vs 96.3 +/- 18.3) were significantly higher during the virtual interview cycles (p < 0.001 each). Similar increases were noted in total ACGMEaccredited programs, positions, and applicants (p < 0.001 each). Measures of VS specialty popularity, including applicants per position (1.9 +/- 0.3 vs 2.1 +/- 0.5, p = 0.54) and position fill rate (99.1% +/- 1.1% vs 97.2% +/- 2.9%, p = 0.20), remained unchanged when comparing in-person and virtual interview cycles. In comparison, the proportion of applicants per position (1.8 +/- 0.0 vs 1.9 +/- 0.1) and position fill rate (93.9% +/- 0.8% vs 95.9% +/- 0.5%) across all ACGME-accredited programs were both significantly lower during the virtual interview years (p < 0.001 each). At the same time, the percentage of overall applicants applying into VS increased from 0.18% (+/- 0.03%) to 0.26% (+/- 0.02%) in the virtual era (p < 0.001). Three metrics for specialty competitiveness were also examined. For VS residency programs, overall match rate (52.0% +/- 7.1% vs 48.7% +/- 10.2%, p = 0.53) and percentage of unmatched applicants (48.0% +/- 7.1% vs 51.3% +/- 10.2%, p = 0.53) remained unchanged, whereas the proportion of applicants matching at their first choice (41.5% +/- 2.9% vs 59.2% +/- 13.5%, p = 0.01) was lower during the virtual interview cycles. In comparison, overall match rate was greater (53.2% +/- 0.8% vs 49.3 +/- 2.1%) and the proportion of unmatched applicants were lower (46.8% +/- 0.8% vs 50.7% +/- 2.1%, p = 0.001) across all ACGME-accredited programs during the virtual interview years. CONCLUSIONS: The study period of virtual recruitment saw no change in VS popularity, suggesting that this approach does not detract interested applicants. However, VS did become a more competitive residency, with fewer applicants matching at their first choice. Potential hybrid approaches, such as the protocol described within the VISIT trial, may offer viable alternatives that capitalize on the strengths of both virtual recruitment and face-toface engagement. TI Professional Grief and the Second Victim Experience in Neurosurgery: An
   International Cross-sectional Study on Professional Sustainability and
   Educational Implications
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE neurosurgical education; peer support; professional grief; professional
   sustainability; second victim phenomenon; support systems
ID MEDICAL ERROR; PATIENT; COMPLICATIONS; PHYSICIANS; IMPACT; DEATH
AB beta OBJECTIVE: Adverse events are inevitable in neurosurgical practice and may have significant emotional and professional implications for surgeons. While second victim experiences have been increasingly recognized, the role of professional grief remains insufficiently characterized within the field of neurosurgery. This study aimed to examine professional grief as a component of the second victim experience and its associations with distress, support dimensions, educational needs, and professional sustainability. METHODS: We conducted an international, cross-sectional, anonymous web-based survey among neurosurgeons and neurosurgical trainees. Professional grief related to a personally impactful adverse event was assessed retrospectively using the Professional Bereavement Scale-Short-term Bereavement Reactions Subscale (PBS-Acute); scores therefore reflect retrospectively recalled acute grief responses rather than contemporaneously measured reactions. Second victim dimensions were evaluated with the Second Victim Experience and Support Tool-Revised (SVEST-R). Associations among grief severity, second victim dimensions, and professional sustainability indicators were analyzed using correlation and multivariable regression. RESULTS: Of 465 respondents from 49 countries, 314 completed the survey and were included in the analysis. A total of 240 participants (76.4%) reported a personally impactful adverse event. Professional grief severity was substantial among respondents (PBS-Acute mean 37.9 +/- 13.8) and was strongly correlated with psychological distress (r = 0.71, p < 0.001). Higher grief severity was independently associated with increased turnover intention ( = 0.026, p < 0.001). Perceived preventability and primary surgeon role were associated with higher grief severity, while event timing and seniority were not. Supervisor support was inversely associated with grief severity. Participants reported substantial unmet educational needs related to medicolegal processes, communication with patient families, and grief coping skills. CONCLUSIONS: Among surveyed neurosurgeons who described a personally impactful adverse event, professional grief was frequently reported. Professional grief in this sample was associated with second victim experiences, psychological distress, and indicators of professional vulnerability. These cross-sectional associations suggest that professional grief may warrant consideration in structured educational models and tiered support systems within neurosurgical training and institutional practice. Prospective work is needed to clarify the direction and durability of these relationships and their implications for professional sustainability.

TI Development of a Data-Driven, Noninflationary Author-Credit Allocation
   Model in Multiauthor Publications in Pharmacy Practice
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Authorship; Publications; Pharmacy practice; Faculty; Bibliometrics
ID CONSEQUENCES; ORDER
AB Objective: To derive and validate a noninflationary author-credit allocation model (schema) from empirical author-credit allocation data provided by primary authors of multiauthor pharmacy practice publications. Methods: Primary authors of pharmacy practice faculty publications were surveyed in 2 studies (derivation and validation), and respondents' demographic information and their allocation of nonzero percentage credits to authors based on each author's contributions to the publication were collected for documents with 2 to 5 (derivation), and 2 to 6 authors (validation). Lack-of-fit index and other error metrics were used to assess the fit of existing noninflationary schemas (fractional-equal, arithmetic, geometric, golden share, and harmonic) with the empirical data; empirical data patterns were used to derive variants of the schema with the lowest error metrics (best fit); and the fit of the derived schema was validated in the validation study. Results: Unique respondents (155 and 99) reported 232 and 152 documents in the derivation and validation studies, respectively. The credit-allocation pattern showed a decrease from the first author to the penultimate author, with the last author receiving the second-highest credit. A novel schema consistent with the harmonic pattern, with a unique "last-author-bump," was derived, and it showed the best fit in the validation study. Conclusion: Author-credit allocation in pharmacy practice is inconsistent with the whole-count method that inflates publication credits and unfairly allocates equal credits to all coauthors. The harmonic with "last-authorbump" schema is an evidence-based alternative to authors' statement of percentage contributions. It is included in AuthormetriX (https://sadeosun-a-uthormetrix-v1.streamlit.app/) to facilitate adoption and use in evaluating faculty scholarly output.

TI Three-Option Multiple-Choice Questions Retain Discrimination and
   Reliability: A Prospective Randomized Crossover Study in Pharmacy
   Education
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessment; Psychometrics; Multiple-choice questions
ID OPTIONS
AB Objective: To prospectively compare the psychometric performance of 3-option versus 4-option multiple-choice question (MCQ) examinations and evaluate differences in item difficulty, item discrimination, examination reliability, examination performance, and elapsed testing time. Methods: This randomized crossover study was conducted in 2 required Doctor of Pharmacy courses at a single school of pharmacy, including a first-year pharmacokinetics course and a third-year pharmacotherapy course. Students were assigned to alternating sequences of 3-option and 4-option MCQ examinations throughout the study period. Four-option examinations were developed first, after which 1 distractor was removed from each item to create the corresponding 3option version. Item-level psychometric measures, examination-level outcomes, and elapsed testing time were compared between formats using paired analyses and linear mixed-effects modeling. Results: Three-option MCQs were associated with students answering approximately 1 additional question correctly on a 50-item MCQ test compared with 4-option MCQs. No differences were observed in point-biserial discrimination or Kuder-Richardson 20 reliability estimates between examination formats. Course-specific analyses demonstrated differences in item difficulty within pharmacokinetics examinations but not pharmacotherapy examinations. Examinations containing 4-option MCQs also required longer testing times for students. Conclusion: Reducing MCQs from 4 to 3 answer options did not meaningfully compromise examination reliability or item discrimination in 2 required pharmacy courses. Although 4-option MCQs produced slightly greater difficulty and longer testing times, the practical educational benefit of routinely requiring a fourth answer option may be limited when distractors are not consistently plausible or functioning effectively.

TI Impact of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots on Student Confidence and
   Perceptions in a Communication Course
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Simulated patient; ChatGPT; Chatbot; Communication; Patient counseling
AB Objective: To (1) improve pharmacy students' perceived confidence in communication skills and (2) identify perceptions of counseling a text-based artificial intelligence (AI)-simulated patient using ChatGPT 4o.<br /> Methods: This study involved first-year pharmacy students in a required communications course at the University of Georgia. Four AI-simulated patients with unique characteristics and medication-related problems were developed in ChatGPT 4o (OpenAI). After didactic instruction, students completed a pre-survey, practiced counseling with the text-based AI patients to prepare for 2 separate graded standardized patient counsling (GSPC) assessments and completed identical post-surveys after each GSPC to assess changes in confidence and overall perceptions. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed rank test, and thematic analysis was used for open-ended responses.<br /> Results: Of 146 students, 117 (80.1%) completed all 3 surveys, with significant improvements in perceived confidence observed across all 7 communication domains. The greatest gains were noted in initiating counseling sessions, applying prime questions, and using probing techniques in the first post-survey. While significant in the first post-survey, no significant changes were noted in nonverbal communication skills (body language, active listening) in the second post-survey. Thematic analysis of 386 comments identified 5 benefit themes (eg, realistic practice, accessibility, structured counseling), 4 limitation themes (eg, lack of human-like interaction, response limits), and 4 improvement areas (eg, expanded scenarios, enhanced feedback).<br /> Conclusion: ChatGPT 4o text-based chatbot patients improved student perceived confidence in verbal counseling skills and were valued as a convenient, low-pressure, and accessible training tool. While limitations in realism and nonverbal skill development were noted, text-based AI-simulated patients represent a scalable supplement to traditional communication training in pharmacy education.

TI VR scuba diving with harbor seals increases ocean connectedness, and the
   effect of conversational AI on pro-environmental engagement depends on
   prior experience with seals
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
ID BEHAVIOR
AB This study presents an empirical investigation of OceanSpeak-a unique combination of virtual reality (VR) scuba diving and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) designed to educate about how ocean acidification and overfishing impact marine life. This pre-registered study examined the effect of interacting with an AI-powered harbor seal on ocean connectedness, empathy with seals, pro-ocean behaviors, and knowledge. The participants were 106 adults affiliated with a university in California, the United States. Participants in the experimental group (N = 53) engaged with the complete version of OceanSpeak, including AI-powered conversation with a virtual harbor seal. We implemented a yoked control design such that participants in the control group (N = 53) were exposed to identical content but experienced another participant's AI-enabled conversation. In addition, we measured a number of individual differences related to their views on the environment and specific experience with seals. All participants experienced a significant increase in ocean connectedness as a result of the intervention. The control condition outperformed the AI condition regarding knowledge of pro-environmental actions, whereas a small subset of AI participants demonstrated better understanding of seal-specific issues. Without accounting for individual differences, there were no significant differences between conditions in terms of ocean connectedness, empathy, and protective behaviors. However, post hoc analyses indicated that after accounting for baseline ocean connectedness and nature connectedness and their interactions with condition, AI-powered conversation led to significantly more empathy with seals. Moreover, AI-powered conversation with a virtual seal increased protective ocean behaviors among participants with prior seal exposure, suggesting previous experiences with the actor who is speaking in conversational AI may improve the outcome of those interactions.

TI Modular dissertation pathways in undergraduate economics: A case study
   of curriculum innovation
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Dissertations; Supervision; Employability; Scaffolding; Inclusivity;
   Curriculum
ID EXPERIENCES; IMPACT
AB This paper presents a case study of curriculum innovation in undergraduate economics education at a UK Russell Group university. A modular dissertation structure was introduced to address uneven econometric preparation, rising supervision pressures, and increasingly diverse student interests. The redesigned framework separated dissertation activity into three interconnected modules: a shared research design module, a traditional empirical dissertation route, and a policy-oriented dissertation pathway with structured support. The initiative integrated thematic topic allocation, Stata training, digital scaffolding, drop-in support sessions, and oversight by a dedicated Director of Dissertations. Drawing on institutional data, student feedback, and reflective curriculum evaluation, the paper examines how the redesign was perceived to support student engagement, reduce supervision pressures, and strengthen the alignment between dissertation provision, inclusivity and employability. The study contributes to economics education literature by demonstrating how modular curriculum design and collaborative leadership can support sustainable dissertation delivery while preserving research-led learning in large undergraduate cohorts.

TI Examination of the Social Experience in a Virtual Culinary Nutrition
   Program for Dementia Risk Reduction
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE culinary nutrition; virtual program; risk reduction; socialization;
   dementia
ID OLDER-ADULTS; MIND DIET; COOKING; INTERVENTIONS; INTENTIONS; MANAGEMENT;
   BEHAVIOR; OUTCOMES; IMPACT
AB Objective: Examine the social experience of participants in a pilot virtual nutrition education program for dementia risk reduction. Design: Observational fieldnotes, digital journal entries, semistructured interviews (n=15), and focus groups (n = 13) were used to collect qualitative data. Setting: Two separate but identical Cognitive Kitchen (CK) programs were delivered via Zoom from November to December 2022. Participants: Participants (n = 21) were adults aged 55 years or over living in Saskatchewan, Canada. Intervention: The CK consisted of a preprogram orientation and 6 60-90-minute sessions that incorporated nutrition education and interactive food demonstrations. Main Outcome Measures: The functions of social interactions in the program; facilitators and barriers to social engagement within the virtual setting. Analysis: The interpretive description approach guided inductive coding and the construction of themes. Results: Four themes were developed. Two themes captured the functions of social interactions in supporting learning and encouraging application. Another theme identified inherent trade-offs: advantages and missed connections with virtual delivery. The last theme described strategies to maximize socialization, ingredients for engagement. Conclusions and Implications: Social interactions facilitated perceived outcomes of enhanced knowledge and implementation of health-promoting strategies among adults in the CK. Careful planning is required to overcome inherent barriers to socialization with web-based program delivery.

TI The Role of Dietary Diversity in Mitigating Pregnancy Distress: A
   Randomized Clinical Trial
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE dietary patterns; pregnancy; psychological distress; randomized
   controlled trial
ID PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; FOOD
AB Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a dietary diversity intervention in reducing pregnancy distress. Design: A single-blind randomized clinical trial with 2 parallel groups. Setting: Health centers in Birjand city. Participants: Pregnant women between 12 and 16 weeks of gestation were recruited for this study and randomly assigned to either the intervention group (n = 42) or the control group (n = 42). Intervention: The intervention contained dietary diversity education for 8 weeks. The control group received standard antenatal care (monthly check-ups) and general nutritional guidance for pregnancy. Main Outcome Measure: Data were collected at baseline and end line using the Tilburg Pregnancy Distress Scale (TPDS) and Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women. Analysis: Comparing the 2 groups at baseline (independent t test and chi-square test of independence), and at the end line (paired sample t test and analysis of covariance were conducted). P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: We found significant differences between the 2 groups regarding adjusted mean values of dietary diversity score (DDS) and TPDS, controlled for baseline values (P < 0.001). Changes in DDS were significantly correlated with changes in TPDS (r =-0.41; P < 0.01). Conclusions and Implications: The results of this study demonstrated a significant reduction in pregnancy distress and an enhanced DDS within the intervention group. These findings indicate that such educational programs could be essential to comprehensive health initiatives for pregnant women in underdeveloped contexts.

AB Objective: Examined convergent validity of reflection spectroscopy-assessed skin carotenoid scores (SCS) by examining associations between SCS and (1) self-reported fruit and vegetable (F&V) intake, (2) Healthy Eating Index scores derived from 24-hour recalls, (3) food security, (4) self-efficacy for F&V intake, and (5) barriers to F&V intake.    Elementary School Teachers' Experiences and Perceptions

LA English
DT Article
DE universal free school meals; teachers; qualitative research; school
   meals policy
ID FOOD INSECURITY; LUNCH; ASSOCIATION
AB Objective: To explore teachers' perceptions of student hunger and behavior, school meal participation, food waste, family stress, supervision, and meal locations during a federal universal free school meals (UFSM) policy, comparing the 2021-2022 school year to the 2022-2023 school year. Methods: Twenty-five kindergarten through sixth-grade teachers participated in online interviews in 6 elementary schools in Anchorage, Alaska. DT Article

   readiness; Head start

   EDUCATION; MODELS; CARE
AB Children's positive task engagement in preschool demonstrates their readiness to get the most out of a classroom learning environment. Self-regulation skills, such as emotion regulation, provide a foundation for children to engage positively with tasks, yet children growing up in poverty face an increased risk for difficulties with emotion regulation. Teachers' use of high-quality instructional practices can support children's task engagement and may act as a protective factor. These findings further lead us to advocate for a broader focus toward creating a high-quality instructional environment that naturally motivates children to be positively, and actively, engaged during learning.

TI Bridging autism spectrum disorder and otolaryngology: A bibliometric
   analysis of research trends and clinical implications
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Otolaryngology; Bibliometric analysis;
   Pediatric otolaryngology; Communication disorders; Hearing loss
ID INDIVIDUALS; CHILDREN
AB Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition often accompanied by comorbid ear, nose, and throat (ENT) disorders, including hearing loss, otitis media, auditory processing deficits, and sleep-disordered breathing. These conditions can further impair communication and behavior, yet research at the ASD-ENT intersection remains scattered. This study presents the first bibliometric analysis of ASD-related ENT research to map trends, identify influential contributions, and guide future clinical integration. A systematic PubMed search identified 107 peer-reviewed articles addressing ENT conditions in ASD populations. Citation data and metadata were extracted from Web of Science and analyzed using descriptive statistics and visualization tools. Otology and audiology comprised 40% of publications, followed by cochlear implantation (15%) and speech or communication-focused studies (14%). The United States led in volume and citations, though contributions from China, Egypt, and Europe highlighted growing global interest. Institutional collaboration was common, with 75% of studies involving multiple centers. Thematic growth was observed in areas such as auditory hypersensitivity, vestibular dysfunction, and ENT-related sleep disorders. However, research remains primarily pediatric and observational, with limited focus on adolescent or adult populations. Our findings support routine ENT screening in individuals with ASD, especially for hearing and sleeprelated concerns. Interdisciplinary approaches involving audiology, speech therapy, and neurodevelopmental care are essential for improving outcomes. This bibliometric analysis highlights the evolution of ASD-ENT research and underscores the need for expanded lifespan-inclusive studies to address these clinically significant comorbidities.

TI Generative artificial intelligence for language learning and teaching:
   Opportunities, challenges, and ethical considerations
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI); L2 education; L2 learning
   and teaching; GenAI literacy; Ethics
AB This special issue explores the opportunities, challenges, and ethical considerations arising from the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into foreign/second language (L2) education. Drawing on fifteen articles published in this collection, we synthesize the field's evolving landscape across three interconnected dimensions: opportunities, challenges, and ethical considerations. We argue that GenAI holds great potential for scaffolding L2 learning and teaching processes, fostering learner engagement and positive emotions, supporting teacher development, and reshaping language assessment and educational innovation. At the same time, this collection foregrounds important tensions surrounding the reliability and contextual appropriateness of GenAI output, learner over-reliance, weakened agency, uneven access, and varying levels of teacher preparedness. Crucially, the ethical use of GenAI in L2 education demands attention not only to individual responsibility, but also to teacher mediation, institutional policy, assessment governance, data privacy, and educational equity. This editorial concludes by charting a research agenda that advocates theoretically grounded, empirically rigorous, and contextually sensitive inquiry into GenAI's role in transforming L2 education.

   educators

AB Teacher leadership has grown as a significant area of emphasis in the field of world languages (WLs) in the United States. TI Fostering teachers' interpretations of formative assessment results
   using clustered heatmaps
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Formative assessment; Clustered heatmaps; Dashboards; Teachers;
   Data-based decision making
ID METAANALYSIS; PSYCHOLOGY; MODELS
AB Teachers can use formative assessment results to inform their instruction to each student's current level of understanding. In practice, this is a complex task. Thus, we investigated in two preregistered online experiments whether clustered heatmaps can support teachers in reading and interpreting assessment results accurately and efficiently for adaptive teaching according to their students' strengths and weaknesses. N = 202 pre-service and N = 262 in-service teachers for primary and secondary education interpreted formative assessment results from the subjects German and mathematics. The findings indicate that clustered heatmaps are sufficiently intuitive and can improve the accuracy and efficiency with which teachers group students according to their strengths and weaknesses. Novice teachers, in particular, appear to benefit from the algorithm-based visual cues provided by clustered heatmaps. If future research corroborates this evidence, clustered heatmaps could be implemented in dashboards to promote beneficial teacher-technology interactions with the aim of enhancing student learning.

TI Scholarly Productivity of Emergency Ultrasound Fellowship Directors: A
   National Cross-Sectional Analysis
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Background The updated 2026 American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM) approved Advanced Emergency Medicine Ultrasonography requirements specify that fellowship directors must demonstrate scholarly activity through >= 5 first-, second-, or last-author publications. Contemporary data describing scholarly productivity among emergency ultrasound fellowship directors (EUSFDs) is limited.Methods We performed a cross-sectional study of U.S. emergency ultrasound fellowship programs listed by the Society of Clinical Ultrasound Fellowships (SCUF). Publication histories were identified through PubMed, the SCUF website, MedEdPORTAL, and ACEP (American College of Emergency Physicians) Sonoguide. Qualifying publications included original research, reviews, editorials, educational scholarship, and other PubMed-indexed work. The primary outcome was the proportion of EUSFDs meeting the 2026 publication benchmark of >= 5 first-, second-, or last-author emergency ultrasound publications. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated factors associated with meeting this threshold.Results Among 134 eligible programs, EUSFDs had a median of 3 years in their role (IQR 1-6) and 1 qualifying publication (IQR 0-4). Twenty-six directors (19.4%) met the 2026 publication benchmark based on identified publications. Fifty-seven (42.5%) had at least one first-author publication, and 70 (52.2%) had at least one first- or last-author publication. Under the 2011 requirements, 56 directors (41.8%) met publication criteria. Interrater agreement was high (kappa = 0.895). Each additional year as a fellowship director was associated with 12% greater odds of meeting the publication threshold (aOR 1.12, 95% CI 1.02-1.24).Conclusions Among U.S. EUS fellowship programs, one in five EUSFDs met the 2026 publication benchmark based on identified publications. Longer-serving directors were more likely to meet the publication benchmark, although this association may reflect career duration or prior scholarly productivity. As expectations for fellowship leadership evolve, national efforts focused on mentorship, support, collaboration, and protected time may help support scholarly development and facilitate attainment of these standards.

TI Modelling the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC)
   on Critical Thinking and Emotional Learning: The Moderating Role of
   Intrinsic Motivation in Higher Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AIGC; critical thinking; generative AI-supported learning; higher
   education; intrinsic motivation
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY
AB This study investigated the impact of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC) tools, such as ChatGPT, on higher education students' intrinsic motivation, emotional learning, development of critical thinking and transformation of emotional learning. By designing a conceptual framework grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the study explored how the use of AIGC tools shapes learning outcomes through both direct and moderating effects of intrinsic motivation. A survey was administered to 475 university-level students across several disciplines in the Punjab province of Pakistan. Data analysis was conducted using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to measure the relationships between AIGC usage, intrinsic motivation and learning outcomes. The results revealed that AIGC tools have positive effects on intrinsic motivation, which significantly influences the development of critical thinking and the transformation of emotional learning. Intrinsic motivation demonstrated a limited moderating role. A significant interaction was observed only between AIGC Impact and intrinsic motivation in predicting Emotional Learning Transformation (p = 0.044), whereas the moderation effect for Critical Thinking Development was non-significant (p = 0.405), and interactions involving AIGC Tools for Learning were not significant. These findings suggest that the moderating role of intrinsic motivation is pathway-specific rather than general. Furthermore, high-frequency usage of AIGC tools was found to negatively predict ELT when controlling for motivation (beta = -0.069), highlighting risks of over-dependency. The findings emphasize the importance of fostering intrinsic motivation to maximize the pedagogical benefits of AI-powered tools. The study suggests that educational institutions must prioritize AI literacy and ethical guidelines to prevent cognitive passivity and ensure responsible AI integration in the digital era.

TI When 'is' is ought: A dynamic, relational developmental systems-based
   model of moral development-The Kohlberg memorial lecture of 2026
SO JOURNAL OF MORAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Moral development; dynamic, relational developmental systems;
   metatheory; developmentally nurturant relationships; theological
   anthropology
ID SCIENCE
AB Human beings are fundamentally relational organisms. From the very beginning of life, the survival of a human being and, across life, human well-being depend on mutually influential and mutually beneficial relationships between individuals and their interpersonal, sociocultural, and physical ecological contexts. Using concepts derived from dynamic, relational developmental systems metatheory, I present a model wherein moral development emerges through and is constituted by increasingly complex dynamic relationships that sustain and enrich human life. In this model, mutually beneficial individual double left right arrow individual coactions are the foundation of human survival, development, and flourishing, and their promotion, maintenance, and growth among individuals, social groups (such as families), communities, nations, and the physical ecology of the planet are the essence of moral behavior and development. There are profound convergences between this conception of morality and moral development and theological anthropology, and these convergences open new pathways for dialogue between developmental science and religion and collaborations aimed at saving our world from the actions of individuals and groups who possess absences in positive moral development.

TI Learning Teach-Back in clinical practice: a qualitative study of
   healthcare professionals
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Workplace learning; Feedback; Health communication; Health literacy;
   Stroke prevention; Organizational learning; Practice-based learning;
   Qualitative method
ID COMMUNICATION; LITERACY; NURSES
AB Background Teach-Back is a widely recommended communication method to support patient understanding, yet little is known about how healthcare professionals learn Teach-Back in everyday clinical practice. The study aimed to explore how healthcare professionals learn Teach Back within an acute hospital setting, and how this learning is experienced and enacted in everyday clinical practice.Methods This qualitative study invited staff in two healthcare settings that had partaken in a Teach-Back method training program. Participants included 18 healthcare professionals and four first-line managers. Data were generated through interviews conducted in the beginning and after the training program, and through observations of clinical encounters when applying the Teach-Back method. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.Results Learning Teach-Back was identified as a multilevel workplace learning process that developed through interactions between individual experiences, interpersonal learning processes, organizational engagement, and workplace conditions. This was reflected in four interrelated themes: (1) Individual level: Learning by doing and experiencing Teach-Back: authentic Teach-Back encounters with patients were critical for skill development but could trigger insecurity when Teach-Back was experienced as unnatural. Emotional responses, discouragement and "aha" moments, shaped whether healthcare professionals used Teach-Back or not; (2) Interpersonal level: Learning through feedback and shared meaning: recurring peer reflection and supportive feedback were crucial for learning Teach-Back, yet often lacking; (3) Organizational level: Engaging the organization to promote learning: early adopters, ambassadors, leadership support, and interprofessional communication were decisive for learning Teach-Back; and (4) Workplace conditions: Making space for learning in a pressured work environment: staff shortages, turnover, and high workload constrained opportunities for doing and engaging in reflection and feedback about Teach-Back.Conclusions Learning Teach-Back can be understood as a multilevel workplace learning process that develops through opportunities for practice, reflection, and collegial feedback in everyday clinical work. Supporting Teach-Back learning requires workplace learning approaches that foster shared meaning across professional teams, organizational engagement, and protected space for learning.Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT02925871. Registration date: first submitted 8 April 2016; first posted 6 October 2016.

TI Socially Shared Metacognition in De-Streamed Secondary Mathematics:
   Making Barriers and Strategies Visible
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; SRL; Group-level self-regulated learning;
   G-SRL; Metacognition; Mathematics education; De-streaming; Secondary
   education; Classroom culture; Barriers and Strategies Protocol; BSP
ID TEACHERS; SEEKING; GOALS; HELP
AB This participatory mixed-methods study followed two rural grade 9 mathematics classes for 4 months as they explored an approach for group-level self-regulated learning support (G-SRL). Interviews, diaries, surveys, and structured observations were used to track the ways teachers adapted the intervention, as well as its perceived influence on the learning processes and experience of both teachers and students. Findings suggested that many participating students and teachers perceived value in integrating G-SRL in high school mathematics lessons, including participant-reported improvements in student focus and emotional well-being, a normalization of strategic talk and action, and increased student agency and voice. Challenges included a slow adjustment to public reflection and self-disclosure for both teachers and students, uneven student uptake, and a lag in student application of strategies. The study suggests that opportunities for G-SRL naturally arise during typical mathematics instruction, but that successful implementation requires sustained trust-building and structured encouragement for teachers as well as students. Overall, the study highlights the potential for G-SRL routines to offer feasible, context-sensitive support for shared metacognition in de-streamed secondary mathematics classrooms.

TI Citizenship Education-Based Political Thinking Skills: Thinking About
   the Refugee Issue
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE citizenship education; political literacy; political thinking; refugee
   issue; social studies teacher education
ID LITERACY
AB This study employs action research, a qualitative research design, to enhance political thinking skills (PTS) of social studies teacher candidates studying at Ege University in T & uuml;rkiye. In this context, a needs analysis was conducted, leading to the redesign of the political literacy course. Data were collected through 2N form, interviews, observations, and student reflective diaries and were analyzed in a cyclical manner. Teacher candidates believe that the designed activities help them become citizens who use better their political thinking (PT), empathy, and questioning skills and help them raise politically thinking students while practicing their teaching profession. Modifying analogous studies for other teacher training programs could contribute to the cultivation of 21st-century teachers and citizens capable of effectively addressing and resolving current political issues.

TI How the American College of Surgeons Quality In-Training Initiative
   helps quality improvement education focusing on safety: a national
   review of 1,412,068 surgeon trainee cases
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Quality improvement; Quality in-training initiative; Outcomes; Risk
   adjustment; Surgical education; Surgical training
ID RESIDENT INVOLVEMENT; AUTONOMY; OUTCOMES; COMPLICATIONS; COMPLEXITY;
   IMPACT; ISSUES
AB Purpose The American College of Surgeons (ACS) developed the Quality In-Training Initiative (QITI) to link surgeon trainee participation with patient outcomes within ACS National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP). As surgical education shifts toward competency-based and outcomes-informed training, QITI may offer a platform not only for data collection, but also for resident learning and preparation for practice. We evaluated QITI as a system for collecting resident-linked clinical outcomes, supporting meaningful clinical education, and preparing trainees for data-driven surgical practice. Methods This is a retrospective study of NSQIP cases with completed QITI fields from July 2013 through July 2025. Descriptive analyses evaluated case volume, participation across institutions, operative case mix, and postoperative outcomes by PGY level. Multivariable regression models were used to assess the association between PGY level and postoperative outcomes after adjustment for standard NSQIP preoperative risk factors. Results From 190 participating institutions, 1,412,068 cases met inclusion criteria, including 1,098,264 PGY1-5 cases. While operative case mix increased in complexity across PGY levels, some procedures such as laparoscopic appendectomy and cholecystectomy remained common at all levels. Unadjusted complication rates increased stepwise with PGY level (all p < 0.001). After risk adjustment, most differences attenuated, although cases involving PGY5 residents remained significantly associated with higher odds of select outcomes, including intubation, prolonged ventilation, renal complications, cardiac complications, readmission, morbidity, and mortality. Sensitivity analysis performed for years 2022-2024 showed fewer significant associations. Conclusions These findings suggest that QITI is a feasible and sustainable system for collecting resident-linked clinical outcomes at national scale. The data provide meaningful educational value by characterizing progression in operative complexity and linking cases with outcomes. In addition, risk-adjusted comparisons and benchmarking reflect the types of outcome reports surgeons encounter in practice, creating an opportunity to expose residents to the types of data-driven quality reports they may encounter in independent practice. QITI may therefore serve as a valuable platform for competency-based surgical education and future trainee feedback systems.

TI Metacomprehension accuracy with multiple texts: a comprehensive approach
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacomprehension; Multiple document comprehension; Monitoring accuracy;
   Perceived difficulty; Self-concept; Self-regulation
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; KNOWLEDGE; PERFORMANCE; JUDGMENTS; ABSOLUTE;
   UNAWARE
AB This study investigated metacomprehension accuracy for university students reading multiple texts about the same topic, using a Dutch translation of a German multiple document comprehension instrument. Based on research with single texts, we expected students' performance estimates to have relatively low accuracy, as well as being associated with several student-related and task-related variables. Moreover, we expected metacomprehension accuracy to be related to students' ability and confidence. We conducted our study with 401 psychology students from one Dutch university, asking for their exam grades, multiple document comprehension habits, self-concept, and a prediction of their performance. Next, students completed two tasks from the multiple document comprehension instrument and after each task provided performance estimates and confidence ratings, rated perceived difficulty, mental effort, interest, text cohesion and ease of comprehension. Finally, students gave a postdiction of their overall performance. Results showed a significant association between task performance and performance estimates of .33, comparable to what has been found with other tasks. Beyond the variance explained by task performance, students' estimates were predicted by exam grade, self-concept, and perceived task difficulty, but not by any of the other variables. Postdictions were more accurate than predictions, suggesting that task experience allows students to use more valid cues in their performance estimates. Other than with single texts however, metacomprehension accuracy was unrelated to students' ability and confidence. These findings can inform efforts to improve university students' metacomprehension accuracy with multiple texts, benefitting their self-regulation.

TI Development and Application of a Virtual Experiment Software for Chaotic
   Circuits Based on Unity3D
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational value; teaching software; virtual laboratory; virtual
   reality; virtual simulation
AB To address the core pain points of abstract theories, high equipment costs, significant experimental risks and insufficient immersion of traditional simulation tools in chaotic circuit experimental teaching for electronic information and control engineering majors, this study focuses on chaotic circuit experiments in nonlinear systems. By integrating virtual reality (VR) technology and the Unity3D engine, a virtual simulation teaching software for chaotic circuits (VSTS-CC) for higher education is developed. VSTS-CC is modeled with 3dsMax. The interactive logic is implemented using the Elegant Target (ET) framework and C# to construct an immersive experimental environment. It supports core functions such as theoretical learning, experimental operation, and assessment feedback, and is released in both. exe and WebGL versions. In this study, a multi-dimensional evaluation was conducted on 60 undergraduate students. The average score of the System Usability Scale (SUS) reached 86.2, and users provided positive feedback on functionality, reliability, and experience satisfaction. Controlled experiments show that the experimental group using this software achieved significantly better final scores than the control group with traditional teaching, effectively improving knowledge mastery and learning efficiency. Finally, the improvement directions including performance optimization, experience upgrading and teaching function enhancement are proposed. The VSTS-CC software overcomes the limitations of time, space, cost and safety in traditional experimental operations, providing a generalizable digital practical teaching solution for abstract engineering courses such as nonlinear systems.

TI Research on the Evaluation Framework of International Business Master's
   Degree Education in Applied Universities Based on Six-Dimensional
   Integration
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
LA English
DT Article
DE six-dimensional integration; applied universities; international
   business; master's degree education; evaluation framework;
   programme-level evaluation
AB China has actively promoted the transformation of selected local universities into applied universities, with the aim of strengthening practice-oriented, innovative, and internationally competent talent cultivation. Against this background, the evaluation of international business master's (MIB) education in applied universities should move beyond examination results and should capture program-level evidence of employability, practical competence, international business capability, innovation, and value formation. Based on a review of international and domestic MIB education practices, Chinese policy context, and relevant teaching and learning literature, this paper develops a conceptual evaluation framework based on six-dimensional integration. The framework comprises six mutually connected dimensions: employability and work-integrated learning, curriculum coherence and industry alignment, experiential and competition-based learning, professional credentials and external recognition, innovation and entrepreneurship integration, and ethics, civic responsibility, and value formation. Rather than claiming empirical validation, this study clarifies the conceptual logic, scope of application, indicator structure, and implementation conditions of the framework. It aims to provide a structured reference for improving the quality assurance and program evaluation of MIB education in applied universities, especially in contexts where international business education is expected to serve local economic development, enterprise internationalization, and responsible global engagement.

TI Coding Robots for Empathy: Teacher Candidates Learning to Teach STEAM
   Integration in Communities of Practice
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE elementary teacher candidates; coding and robotics; STEAM integration;
   computational thinking; engineering design practice; empathy;
   interdisciplinary; communities of practice; critical friends
ID COMPUTATIONAL THINKING
AB Despite growing curricular emphasis on computational thinking (CT) and engineering design practice (EDP), preparing elementary teacher candidates (ETCs) for integrated, practice-based instruction remains challenging. Grounded in Communities of Practice (CoP) and design-based implementation research (DBIR) frameworks, this study examines how ETCs (pre-survey: n = 23, post-survey: n = 13) develop learning-to-teach practices for integrating coding and robotics into PreK-5 STEAM learning (STEM with Arts integration) to foster these competencies. The study is situated within an interdisciplinary, community-partnered course, Toying with Technology (TwT), where ETCs collaborate in Critical Friends teams to design, facilitate, and reflect on community partners' need-oriented, empathy-centered STEAM experiences. Utilizing PreK-5 learning technologies and field-based insights from STEM/STEAM professionals, ETCs developed 5E lesson plans integrating science, literacy, mathematics, and robotics, culminating in both an in-person and a virtual STEAM Family Night. Data sources include pre- and post-surveys measuring ETCs' technology integration perceptions, post-field exit tickets, family feedback, community partner reflections, and course artifacts. Pre-survey results indicated limited prior experience and neutral confidence regarding technology integration. In contrary, post-survey findings demonstrated significant increases in self-reported confidence, conceptual understanding of CT and EDP, and readiness to facilitate empathy-centered, technology-rich learning. Qualitative analysis further revealed growth in collaboration, problem-solving, and pedagogical reasoning, while parent and partner feedback highlighted high levels of engagement and increased STEAM interest. Overall, this study provides initial empirical evidence, within a community-partnered, empathy-oriented course design, showing how community-engaged teacher education, informed by CoP and DBIR frameworks, prepares ETCs to teach CT, EDP, and critical problem-solving through integrated, authentic STEAM integration.

TI Vocational STEM Teachers' Teaching Autonomy Attitude: A Structural Model
   of Perceived Past Behavior, Subjective Norms, and Perceived Teaching
   Autonomy Support
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teaching autonomy attitudes; stem teachers; subjective norms; perceived
   past behavior; China
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; EDUCATION; PERCEPTIONS; INTENTION; EFFICACY;
   CHINA
AB Research on teacher autonomy in STEM has been a popular topic in the field. In order to explore the factors influencing STEM teachers' attitudes toward teaching autonomy in vocational education and its structure, this study constructed a conceptual model of influencing teachers' attitudes toward teaching autonomy. By analyzing 590 valid questionnaires, this study used SEM (structural equation modeling) to verify the validity of the model. It was found that the effects of perceived past behavior (PPB) and subjective norms (SN) on teaching autonomy attitudes (TA) were both significant and positively correlated, and perceived teaching autonomy support (PTS) can significantly and positively influence PPB and SN. Additionally, PPB significantly and positively influenced SN. This study fills the gap of vocational education teachers in the STEM teacher research population, and the findings are useful for teachers and school organizations to improve teacher autonomy attitudes.

TI Enhancing Young EFL Learners' Grammar Development Through Oral
   Corrective Feedback in Focus-on-Form Instruction
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE oral corrective feedback; Focus-on-Form instruction; grammar
   development; young learners; foreign language learning
ID WORKING-MEMORY; ACQUISITION; IMPLICIT; TEACHERS; EXPLICIT; RECASTS;
   PROMPTS; AGE
AB Despite the ongoing debate surrounding oral corrective feedback (CF), recent studies emphasize CF's pedagogical value in foreign/second language teaching, as it informs learners about the accuracy of their utterances and helps increase their awareness of language forms. Viewing CF as a classroom-based instructional strategy for supporting language development, this study examined the effects of different types of oral CF (recasts, explicit correction, and metalinguistic feedback) on young learners' grammar acquisition within Focus-on-Form (FonF) instruction in an EFL context. The study involved 88 fifth-grade students, aged 11-12, who were assigned to three experimental groups, each receiving one type of oral CF during FonF instruction, and a control group that received FonF instruction without feedback. Data were collected through oral production and scenario description tasks administered as pre-tests, immediate post-tests, and delayed post-tests. The instructional phase included approximately 10.7 h of treatment, and the assessment phase included approximately 15 h of testing. All classroom interactions and test recordings were transcribed and quantitatively analyzed. The results showed that oral CF statistically significantly enhanced young learners' grammar acquisition compared to no oral feedback. Among the feedback types, explicit correction showed a significant advantage over the other feedback conditions in both immediate and delayed-test performance; however, this advantage was not consistent across all assessment tasks. These findings also highlight the pedagogical value of integrating oral CF into FonF instruction as an evidence-based classroom practice for promoting grammar acquisition and language development in young learner EFL classrooms.

TI Gamification, Peer Networks, and the Reconstruction of Sociograms: A
   Social Network Analysis in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gamification; higher education; social network analysis; sociometry;
   sociogram; research methodology; peer relationships; reproducibility;
   case study
AB Background: Gamification is widely used in higher education, yet its consequences for the relational structure of a class are rarely measured, and sociometric data are often analyzed without attention to how the underlying matrix is built. Methods: We report an exploratory, single-case, pre-post study of a gamified master's course in Didactics and Media Education (N = 19), with a dual aim: to demonstrate a transparent procedure for reconstructing directed, weighted sociograms from raw questionnaire responses, and to explore how the peer-preference network changed over one semester of cooperative group work; inference used permutation methods suited to a small single network. Results: A pre-existing matrix contained roughly one-third of ties with no basis in the data, doubling the apparent centralization and mischaracterizing the least-chosen, most-rejected student as the most popular hub; reconstruction reversed these conclusions. On the reconstructed network, cohesion increased and previously isolated students were integrated, while centralization stayed stable-integration without hierarchy-with a reciprocal, transitive, and highly stable structure and no demographic homophily. Conclusions: Social network analysis (SNA) is a sensitive instrument for the relational evaluation of gamified courses, but the construction of the sociomatrix is itself a substantive analytic decision that must be reported transparently.

TI Training Biomedical PhD Students in Applied Biostatistics with R:
   Lessons from a Three-Year Intensive Program
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE biostatistics education; R programming; doctoral training; programme
   evaluation; active learning; biomedical research
AB Statistical literacy is essential for biomedical researchers, yet doctoral training in applied biostatistics and reproducible data analysis remains limited despite the growing accessibility of open-source tools such as R. This retrospective observational programme evaluation examined three consecutive editions (2021-2023) of an intensive three-day doctoral course in applied biostatistics with R, delivered at the Instituto Maim & oacute;nides de Investigaci & oacute;n Biom & eacute;dica de C & oacute;rdoba (IMIBIC) and the Universidad de C & oacute;rdoba (UCO). Each edition enrolled 15 doctoral students with a 5:1 student-to-instructor ratio and used a problem-based curriculum of nine modules supported by a purpose-written open-access textbook. End-of-course examination performance was described using a ten-item multiple-choice examination; because the examination was not psychometrically equated across editions, score distributions are reported descriptively by cohort rather than used to infer cross-edition differences in learning or competence. Satisfaction was evaluated across four ACSA-aligned domains and was descriptively high in all editions; in the combined within-participant analysis, the Teaching Team domain was rated higher than the other domains. Self-reported theoretical and practical knowledge ratings increased descriptively from pre- to post-course within each edition. The 2021 ratings were reconstructed retrospectively from qualitative responses and were therefore not pooled or directly compared with the directly scaled 2022-2023 ratings. Qualitative feedback highlighted the theory-practice balance and low student-to-instructor ratio, with longer duration as the principal suggestion. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of this intensive R-based training model, but the uncontrolled design, non-equated examination, small samples, and self-reported outcomes preclude claims about learning improvement, causal effectiveness, or durable competence.

TI Formation of technical competencies in future electrical power engineers
   through professionally oriented physics education: a practice-based
   approach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency-based approach; engineering education; future electrical
   power engineers; practice-based learning; professionally oriented
   physics education; technical competencies; technical thinking
AB This study examines the development of technical competencies among future electrical power engineers through professionally oriented physics education. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test design with experimental and control groups was used. The study involved 60 undergraduate students enrolled in an Electrical Power Engineering programme at Almaty University of Power Engineering and Telecommunications named after G. Daukeyev, with 30 students in each group. The experimental group received physics instruction enriched with professionally oriented problems, laboratory activities, and engineering interpretation tasks, whereas the control group studied the same physics content through traditional instruction. The assessment included professionally oriented practical tasks, a questionnaire, and calculation- and graph-based assignments, with a maximum composite score of 100 points. The methodological framework combined systemic, competency-based, synergistic, and practice-based approaches. At baseline, the experimental and control groups demonstrated comparable results, with mean scores of 43.8 +/- 8.6 and 44.2 +/- 9.3, respectively; the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.852). After the intervention, the mean score increased to 75.7 +/- 10.8 in the experimental group and to 52.5 +/- 8.1 in the control group. The mean gain was 32.0 +/- 15.0 percentage points in the experimental group and 8.3 +/- 7.9 percentage points in the control group. The between-group difference in gain scores was statistically significant (p < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.98). These findings provide evidence that professionally oriented physics education can contribute to the development of technical competencies among future electrical power engineers. The proposed approach may be applied in the design of physics courses, laboratory activities, and assessment materials aligned with the professional tasks of electrical power engineering.

TI Behavioral effectiveness: a conceptual framework for explaining the
   relationship between behavioral potential and actual performance
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE actual performance; behavioral effectiveness; behavioral gap; behavioral
   potential; educational performance; motivation; self-regulation
ID MOTIVATION
AB Understanding why individuals with similar resources often achieve different levels of performance remains an important challenge in psychology, education, and the behavioral sciences. Existing theories have provided valuable explanations for factors such as motivation, self-efficacy, self-regulation, and behavioral intentions. However, less attention has been given to the relationship between what individuals possess and what they ultimately accomplish. This paper introduces the concept of behavioral effectiveness as a framework for explaining the relationship between behavioral potential and actual performance. Behavioral effectiveness is provisionally defined as the context-bound process through which individuals mobilize, coordinate, and adapt available behavioral resources-knowledge, desire, and ability-into observable performance. The framework proposes that performance differences are not determined solely by variations in these resources but may also reflect differences in how they are translated into action. The paper further introduces the behavioral gap as the discrepancy between behavioral potential and actual performance. Behavioral effectiveness is proposed as a conversion process, whereas the behavioral gap is a descriptive outcome indicator; the two concepts are related but are not interchangeable. Theoretical distinctions between behavioral effectiveness and related constructs, including motivation, self-efficacy, self-regulation, executive functions, grit, learning transfer, and the intention-behavior gap, are discussed. The paper also specifies preliminary conversion mechanisms and testable propositions, considers measurement implications, and outlines educational applications and directions for empirical research. Behavioral effectiveness is proposed as a preliminary, complementary perspective that shifts attention from the possession of resources to their utilization under specified task and contextual conditions. Whether it provides explanatory value beyond established constructs remains an empirical question.

TI Sedentary behaviour and psychosocial and sleep-related outcomes in
   primary school children: a cross-sectional study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic motivation; emotional regulation; primary school children;
   sedentary behaviour; self-esteem; sleep disorders; well-being
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; ADOLESCENTS; HEALTH; FITNESS; YOUTH
AB Background Physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour have become major public health concerns among children and adolescents due to their potential associations with physical, psychological, and educational outcomes. This study aimed to examine the associations between sedentary behaviour and self-esteem, emotional regulation, academic motivation, and sleep disorders among primary school students.Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 185 students aged 9-12 years from two primary schools in Ja & eacute;n, Spain. Sedentary behaviour was assessed using the Sedentary Behavior Questionnaire, while self-esteem, emotional regulation, academic motivation, and sleep disorders were evaluated using validated instruments. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify the direction of these associations and determine whether reducing sedentary behaviour may contribute to improved well-being in school-aged children.

TI Comparability of student evaluations of teaching across Arabic- and
   English-medium higher education tracks: measurement invariance evidence
   from the UAE

LA English
DT Article
DE course evaluation; EMI; measurement invariance; multilingual higher
   education; quality assurance; teaching evaluation
ID FIT INDEXES; R PACKAGE; EQUIVALENCE; INSTRUCTION
AB Introduction Universities increasingly use student evaluations of teaching across parallel language tracks, but meaningful interpretation requires evidence that the survey functions comparably across groups.Methods This study examined the measurement comparability of the 49-item Course Evaluation Survey (CES) across Arabic-medium and English-medium tracks in a parallel monolingual teacher-preparation program in the United Arab Emirates. The CES was administered to 528 students (229 Arabic-track and 299 English-track). The tracks followed equivalent learning outcomes, content, assignments, assessments, and objectives, while differing in language of instruction and survey administration. TI Teachers' and learners' perspectives on disciplinary approaches in a
   South African special school through an inclusive education Lens
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE behaviour support; disciplinary practices; inclusion-exclusion
   continuum; inclusive education; learner belonging; learner voice;
   special schools
AB Background Inclusive education seeks to promote learner participation, belonging, and responsiveness to diversity. However, despite growing scholarship on inclusive education and behaviour support, limited research has examined how disciplinary approaches in special schools align with or contradict the principles of inclusive education.Objective This study addresses this gap by exploring disciplinary approaches employed in a South African special school through an inclusive education lens.Methods Within an interpretivist paradigm, the study adopted a single-case qualitative design. Data were originally generated through semi-structured interviews with four teachers and a focus group discussion with six learners. The existing dataset underwent a secondary, theory-informed thematic analysis that combined deductive and inductive coding.Results The findings showed that disciplinary practices could not be understood as inherently inclusive or exclusionary. The findings suggest that the implications of disciplinary practices depend on their purpose, enactment, context, and learners' experiences. Inclusive disciplinary practice, therefore, requires balancing accountability with learner voice, responsiveness, fairness, dignity, support, and a sense of belonging.

TI Development and initial psychometric validation of a multidimensional
   scale for assessing entrepreneurial competence in primary education
   teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE entrepreneurial competence; entrepreneurship education; primary
   education; psychometric validation; teacher competence; teacher training
ID BEHAVIOR
AB Introduction Entrepreneurial competence has become a key competence for addressing the social, economic, and educational challenges of the 21st century. Despite the growing recognition of teachers as central agents in entrepreneurship education, available instruments have primarily focused on entrepreneurial behaviour or related constructs, while validated measures specifically designed to assess entrepreneurial competence among primary education teachers remain limited. This study aimed to develop and obtain initial evidence of validity and reliability for a scale designed to assess teachers' entrepreneurial competence.Method An instrumental, cross-sectional, non-experimental study was conducted with a convenience sample of 477 primary education teachers from Castilla-La Mancha (Spain). Content validity was assessed through expert judgment. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and Exploratory Structural Equation Modeling (ESEM) were conducted to examine the internal structure of the instrument. Internal consistency was estimated using ordinal alpha and McDonald's omega, while convergent and discriminant validity were assessed using the average variance extracted (AVE), the Fornell-Larcker criterion, and the Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT), and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for the HTMT coefficients.Results The analyses supported a multidimensional structure composed of 16 items distributed across five related dimensions: Skills, Traits, Values/Self-image, Knowledge, and Motives. The scale showed excellent content validity, acceptable internal consistency for most dimensions, and favorable evidence of convergent and discriminant validity. Although the CFA provided mixed evidence regarding model fit, the ESEM solution showed substantially better fit indices and provided complementary evidence supporting the representation of entrepreneurial competence as a system of related but distinguishable dimensions.Conclusions The findings provide initial evidence supporting the use of the Teacher Entrepreneurial Competence Scale as a multidimensional instrument for assessing entrepreneurial competence among primary education teachers. The results further suggest that entrepreneurial competence is more appropriately represented through an ESEM framework than by a traditional independent-cluster CFA model. The scale may be useful for educational research, teacher professional development, and the evaluation of entrepreneurship education initiatives, although additional validation studies in independent samples and diverse educational contexts are warranted.

TI Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in
   higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; critical thinking; ethics; generative artificial
   intelligence; higher education
ID ACADEMIC INTEGRITY; AI
AB Introduction Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into higher education; however, its adoption raises challenges related to authorship, transparency, content verification, privacy, and student responsibility. The objective of this study was to identify the factors associated with and structurally contributing to the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence among students at the State University of Milagro. Methods A quantitative, applied, non-experimental, cross-sectional, correlational, explanatory-predictive, and confirmatory study was conducted. The sample comprised 980 students selected through non-probability purposive sampling. Data were collected using a 44-item questionnaire. Results The proposed model demonstrated an excellent fit (CFI = 0.998; SRMR = 0.021; RMSEA = 0.008). The six predictor constructs jointly explained 44.0% of the variance in ethical GenAI use (R2 = 0.440), and all structural paths were positive and statistically significant. Academic integrity and transparency exhibited the strongest effect (beta = 0.231), followed by ethical and technical literacy (beta = 0.181), critical thinking and content verification (beta = 0.177), institutional guidance and ethical education (beta = 0.159), self-regulation and academic responsibility (beta = 0.119), and data protection, privacy, and risk management (beta = 0.114). Bivariate correlations between the six predictor constructs and the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence ranged from r = 0.370 to r = 0.507 (all p < 0.001). Conclusion The ethical use of generative artificial intelligence was associated with the interaction of individual competencies, academic principles, and institutional conditions. These findings highlight the need to strengthen clear institutional policies, integrate ethics education across the curriculum, promote critical verification of AI-generated content, encourage transparent disclosure of AI use, and reinforce data protection practices. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than evidence of causal relationships.

   and alignment with adaptive assignments
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; SELF-EFFICACY; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION;
   EXAMPLES; OUTCOMES; DESIGN
AB Introduction Smart learning environments (SLEs) increasingly integrate adaptive technologies to personalize instruction. A central design question concerns the balance between adaptivity (system-controlled adaptation) and adaptability (learner-controlled modification). Hybrid approaches, such as adaptive recommendations that learners may override, aim to combine instructional optimization with learner autonomy. Information about the choices from students in these hybrid approaches can further inform future design of SLEs.Methods This study investigates learners' task difficulty selections in a web-based SLE using worked examples for quantitative physics problem solving. A total of 530 secondary students were randomly assigned to either a fully adaptive condition, or an adaptable condition with adaptive recommendations. Log data and survey responses were analyzed to examine alignment with recommendations and underlying rationales. Learning gains were analyzed using an atomized problem-solving test.Results The adaptability condition shows adherence rates of approximately 84% resulting in similar learning paths for both conditions. Learning gains show no significant differences between both conditions. Students' rationales revealed reasons like trust in the system, effort avoidance, and self-challenging. Several appreciated the possibility to make choices.Discussion These findings suggest that adaptive recommendations can effectively nudge learner decisions in an adaptable SLE while the possibility for choice is appreciated, yielding learning outcomes comparable to a fully adaptive system. The study contributes empirical evidence on learner-system interaction in adaptable SLEs with adaptive recommendations and thus informs future designs of personalized learning environments. Limitations arise from many students that did not provide rationales and future research could focus more precisely on concepts like perceived autonomy.

TI National Survey of Pharmacy Program Self-Study Processes, Strategies,
   and Stakeholders
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Accreditation; Self-study; Doctor of Pharmacy program
AB Objective: To describe current approaches and perceptions in preparing self-study reports for an Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE) site visit at United States schools/colleges of pharmacy.<br /> Methods: A 28-item survey was administered to programs completing a full ACPE site visit between spring 2021 and spring 2025. Questions developed by the research team assessed self-study planning and preparation processes (10 items plus 2 items based on responses), site visit preparation approaches (1 item), stakeholder involvement (6 items), perceptions of the process (5 items), and open-ended questions (4 items: challenges, what respondents would do differently, strategies that led to success, and additional comments). Frequencies were used to report quantitative results and themes were identified for open-ended questions.<br /> Results: A total of 32 programs (out of 62) completed the survey (response rate = 51.6%). Among the 32 respondents, most programs (93.8%) conducted "kick-off" meetings and provided preparatory materials; 59.4% started the self-study process 12 to 18 months before submission. Self-study leadership was typically assigned to deans or administrators with assessment roles (62.5%), with most using newly created committees (68.7%). Administrators, faculty, and staff were involved in both writing (>90%) and reviewing drafts (>80%). Leadership, organization, and clear timelines emerged as key success strategies. Conclusion: Despite varying institutional contexts, programs employed similar structural approaches to managing the self-study process. This project contributes to limited research analyzing how academic programs manage the self-study process. Future research should examine how implementation of the new accreditation requirements has influenced practices.

TI Inclusion of topics related to climate and health in U.S. Doctor of
   Pharmacy Didactic Curricula
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Climate change; Education, pharmacy; Students, pharmacy
ID CARE
AB Introduction: Among growing calls to incorporate topics related to climate change and health in U. S. Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) curricula, a cross-sectional survey was developed and administered to collect baseline information for monitoring, comparison, and benchmarking. Methods: An electronic survey was sent to each fully-accredited U.S. PharmD program (n = 138) in summer 2025. Questions assessed whether selected content related to the impact of climate change on health across 5 domains (Knowledge and Analytic Skills; Communication and Collaboration; Policy; Public Health Practice; Clinical Practice) was included in required or elective didactic courses. Teaching modalities utilized and future plans for such content were also collected. Results: Sixty-eight schools (49%) completed the survey. Concepts most often identified as being taught in either required or elective didactic courses fell into the domains of Knowledge and Analytic Skills or Clinical Practice. No concept included in the survey was taught at more than 40% of respondent schools, and for many concepts 10% or fewer reported inclusion in the didactic curricula. The most common teaching modalities utilized was lectures (53%), labs (16%), and case studies (13%). Four percent of respondent schools indicated a plan to incorporate more topics related to climate change and health in the curricula, while 49% indicated "no" and 47% "didn't know". Conclusion: While some PharmD programs currently include topics related to climate change and health in their didactic curricula, gaps remain. More programs need to integrate these topics into their curricula to better prepare student pharmacists regarding the impact of climate change on health.
