TI Digital health competencies among pharmacy students and practitioners: A
   post-intervention evaluation for participant perceived knowledge,
   attitudes, and confidence
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital health; Wearable technology; Technology-based teaching;
   Continuing professional development; Clinical pharmacist
ID SELF-ASSESSMENT; ACCURACY
AB Introduction: As digital health tool use accelerates, clinicians are expected to make data-informed decisions despite limited formal training. This study aimed to address the training gap by assessing a digital health fair's potential to facilitate digital health tool integration into clinical practice and by evaluating digital health competencies of student pharmacists and pharmacists following participation in an innovative digital health fair. Methods: Participants attended a brief introductory lecture then rotated through five interactive stations featuring 10 digital health products and visual displays of their data outputs. Each station demonstrated the device, presented an example patient case, and provided practical tips to improve patient outcomes. Immediately following the fair, participants completed a survey evaluating their pre- and post-intervention knowledge, attitude, skills, and confidence surrounding digital health. Survey responses were evaluated using descriptive statistics. Results: Thirty-four student pharmacists and sixteen pharmacists completed the survey. Across all measures, there was a significant increase in both knowledge and confidence mean scores (p < .001) from pre- to post-intervention. Participants indicated greater confidence in discussing digital health tools with patients, recommending appropriate solutions, addressing data privacy concerns, and higher confidence integrating biometric outputs from digital health tools. Student pharmacists and practicing clinicians expressed similar knowledge gains, while practicing pharmacists responded with greater confidence gains for integrating and applying digital health technology into their practice settings (all items p < .05). Conclusions: An innovative digital health fair improved both student pharmacists' and pharmacists' reported knowledge, attitudes, and confidence, integrating digital health tools and services into patient care environments.

TI Community health education led by faculty pharmacists and pharmacy
   students: A pilot study of feasibility and effects on health-seeking
   attitudes and self-medication literacy
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article; Proceedings Paper
CT 10th Annual Meeting of the Japanese-Society-of-Pharmacy-Education
CY AUG, 2025
CL Tokyo, JAPAN
SP Japanese Soc Pharm Educ
DE Pharmacy education; Community engagement; Student facilitation;
   Self-medication; Health literacy; Pharmacy practice
ID OUTCOMES; CLINICS
AB Background Community pharmacist utilisation in Japan remains low despite the Health Support Pharmacy (HSP) framework: approximately 7.6% of residents have a regular pharmacist and only 8.6% are aware of the HSP framework. In this context, connecting residents with pharmacists is worthwhile, and community health education can make pharmacists more visible and approachable. The Health Cafe program pursues this while also serving as an experiential-learning model, positioning faculty pharmacists as content providers and pharmacy students as dialogue facilitators. Objective To assess the feasibility of the Health Cafe & eacute; model and its effects on residents' consultation sources, health-seeking attitudes, and self-medication literacy. Methods Feasibility (participation, questionnaire completion, as-planned conduct) was summarized descriptively. Two sessions with independent samples used single-arm pre-post designs (N = 49 and N = 22), analysed at the participant level. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Teikyo Heisei University (No. 2025-080). Findings Feasibility was demonstrated: enough residents participated (49 and 22), questionnaire completion was near-complete (100% and 95.5%), and it was held as planned without problems. In the first, pharmacist selection rose from 2.0% to 40.8% (p < 0.001). In the second, the largest improvement was in anxiety about health and medicines (p = 0.070); this and the other four - self-care, pharmacist-consultation decisions, trust in the pharmacist, and intention to consult one - were non-significant (all p > 0.05). Implications The Health Cafe proved feasible and promising for its three aims - connecting residents with pharmacists, making them visible and approachable, and an experiential-learning model. A larger controlled study with student-outcome measures is warranted.

AB Objective: To develop a group of "Junior Key Indicator Procedures" (JKIPs) for junior residents to facilitate tracking and development of basic skills necessary for success in more advanced procedures. Design: ACGME case logs for Oto-HNS residents at the University of Wisconsin were reviewed between 6/24/2016 and 6/23/2023. Conclusions: Oto-HNS residents complete most KIPs in PGY 4-5. A subset of procedures that are commonly completed by junior residents (PGY 1-3) has been identified for use as JKIPs. A set of models were developed to evaluate junior resident experience with the JKIPs.

TI The long-term cost of short-term economic incentives: Evidence from
   China's political turnover
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Official turnover; Human capital; Promotion incentives; Uncertainty;
   Opportunity cost
ID SCHOOL ENROLLMENT; SKILL ACQUISITION; INVESTMENT; UNCERTAINTY;
   INEQUALITY; EDUCATION; OPPORTUNITY; ADJUSTMENT
AB Using data from the 2010 China Population Census and a dataset on official turnover, this paper employs a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to examine the impact of local official turnover on human capital investment. The results show that official turnover reduces the probability that junior high school graduates enroll in high school. This paper extends the literature on local governance, human capital accumulation and educational development.

TI From Data to Dialogue: A Mixed-Methods Study of Resident Confidence and
   Knowledge Gaps in Adrenal Surgery
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adrenalectomy; endocrine surgery; resi-dency; graduate medical
   education; autonomy
ID EXPERIENCE
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate general surgery resident competence in adrenalectomy using national case log data and qualitative resident feedback to identify actionable training gaps. DESIGN: A mixed-methods analysis of Society for Improving Medical and Professional Learning (SIMPL) national case evaluations and semistructured interviews with general surgery residents. SIMPL data included faculty-and resident-reported assessments of performance, autonomy, and case complexity for laparoscopic and open adrenalectomies. Logistic regression modeled predictors of competent performance and meaningful autonomy. Interview transcripts were coded using content analysis to identify themes related to perioperative knowledge and skill gaps. SETTING: SIMPL data for quantitative analysis came from a national database, and semistructured interviews took place at a single academic center. PARTICIPANTS: For quantitative analysis of SIMPL evaluations, participants included general surgery residents across all residency programs participating in the SIMPL system from 2015 to 2023. For qualitative analysis of semistructured interviews, participants included postgraduate year (PGY)-3 to PGY5 residents. RESULTS: A total of 317 adrenalectomy cases (265 laparoscopic, 52 open) were analyzed, including 225 residents who completed an average of 1.4 adrenalectomies each (SD = 0.84). Competent performance was observed in 41.7% of laparoscopic and 32.6% of open cases, while meaningful autonomy occurred in 37.4% and 13.5%, respectively. PGY5 residents demonstrated a 47.2% predicted probability of competent performance and 45.9% probability of meaningful autonomy. Agreement between resident and faculty ratings occurred in 45.9% of competency and 58.2% of autonomy assessments, with residents underestimating their performance in 44.1% of cases. Fourteen resident interviews revealed limited exposure to adrenal surgery, variability in intraoperative autonomy, and persistent knowledge gaps in postoperative management- particularly steroid replacement and long-term surveillance. CONCLUSIONS: General surgery residents infrequently achieve competence or autonomy in adrenalectomy by graduation and often underestimate their abilities relative to faculty assessments. Resident-reported data highlight insufficient longitudinal exposure and perioperative management knowledge gaps. These findings underscore the need for resident-informed training interventions and support the role of fellowship training for surgeons intending to perform adrenal surgery independently. TI Fear, shame, and the multilingual repertoire: What students' language
   maps reveal about the lived experience of language
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multimodal social semiotics; Language mapping; Fear and shame;
   Multilingual repertoire; EAL/D; Affect; Arts-based research
ID CLASSROOM
AB Research on the affective dimensions of multilingual experience has focused predominantly on language anxiety as a measurable individual trait located in the target language and studied through self-report surveys and interviews. These verbal methods capture what students can articulate but not how they materialise emotion through semiotic design, and the embodied, socially produced character of fear and shame across the wider repertoire has received comparatively little attention. This paper addresses both gaps through a multimodal social semiotic analysis of eight language mapping artefacts produced by Year 11 EAL/D students with refugee and migrant backgrounds in a Melbourne secondary school. Drawing on Kress and van Leeuwen's (2006) visual grammar, Busch's (2017, 2018) lived experience of language, and Ahmed's (2004) affect theory, it examines how design choices, colour, spatial composition, drawn bodies, and textual-visual orchestration, materialise fear and shame across students' repertoires. Fear and shame circulate across the whole repertoire, produced wherever linguistic norms are enforced by interlocutors with evaluative authority, and students construct them as spatially distributed, embodied, and repertoirewide in ways verbal data alone rarely makes visible. The paper extends multimodal social semiotics into the affective domain and demonstrates the value of language mapping for accessing the lived experience of language in education. TI Dissertation Topic Selection Priorities Among Pharmaceutical Outcomes
   Research Students and Alumni
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmaceutical outcomes research and health; economics; Dissertation
   topic selection; Doctoral training; Preference elicitation; Doctoral
   decision-making
AB Objective: Dissertation topic selection is a central decision in doctoral training, yet little empirical evidence describes how trainees in pharmaceutical outcomes research (POR) approach this choice. This study describes how POR students and alumni prioritize dissertation topic selection criteria and how these perceptions evolve over time. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional, web-based survey of current and former POR doctoral trainees in the United States. Participants completed a ranking task and a point-allocation prioritization exercise to assess the relative importance of predefined selection criteria. Open-text responses were analyzed thematically to capture differences in perspectives across stages of training. Results: Thirty-eight respondents completed the ranking task and 32 completed the prioritization exercise. Personal interest, real-world impact, and policy relevance were each selected among the top 5 criteria by 76.3% of respondents and received the highest relative weights (0.178, 0.179, and 0.163, respectively), whereas career alignment, originality, and flexibility received moderate relative weights (0.116, 0.104, and 0.086, respectively). Funding availability received a lower relative weight on average (0.036), whereas faculty expertise received a moderate relative weight (0.093); qualitative responses indicated that feasibility constraints, such as data access, mentorship alignment, and funding pathways, often became more salient with experience and reshaped early topic preferences. Conclusion: POR trainees and alumni in this exploratory sample described dissertation topic selection as an evolving process shaped by both personal motivation and practical constraints. The findings highlight how trainees weigh common trade-offs when choosing a topic and may support clearer discussions between trainees and mentors.

TI Examining the relationship between secondary students' ICT engagement
   and computational thinking achievement: Does gender make a difference?
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational thinking; ICT engagement; Gender differences; Path
   analysis; ICILS 2018
ID SELF-EFFICACY; VALUE BELIEFS; COMPUTER; TECHNOLOGY; SCIENCE;
   MATHEMATICS; ACCEPTANCE; EXPECTANCY; GIRLS; STEM
AB Computational thinking is increasingly recognized as an essential outcome of digital education. Although information and communication technology (ICT) use is often assumed to support such development, greater ICT use does not necessarily translate into more advanced computational thinking. Using the Korean Grade 8 sample from the International Computer and Information Literacy Study 2018, this study examined how four behavioral and cognitive-motivational facets of ICT engagement were related to computational thinking achievement and whether the modeled associations differed by gender. The analytic sample comprised 2851 students (1479 boys and 1372 girls) in 150 schools. These findings argue against a simple moreICT-is-better account of computational thinking and support a facet- and task-sensitive account of ICT engagement.

TI Work-family conflict and teacher turnover intention: A chain mediation
   model of workload and relative deprivation in Chinese junior high
   schools
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Work-family conflict; Turnover intention; Workload; Relative
   deprivation; Chain mediation; Junior high school teachers; Double
   reduction policy
ID RESOURCES; CONSERVATION; ATTRITION; OUTCOMES; CONTEXT; BIAS
AB Teacher attrition is a growing global concern, largely linked to workload, stress, and work-family conflict (WFC). In China, the Double Reduction Policy-intended to ease student burden-has unintentionally intensified teachers' demands, heightening WFC. We examined how WFC predicts turnover intention among 409 junior high school teachers, focusing on the sequential mediating roles of workload and relative deprivation (RD). Drawing on the Work/Family Border Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Cognitive-Affective Personality System, we used structural equation modeling to test aggregate and bidirectional pathways. WFC significantly predicted turnover intention, with RD as the primary mediator. However, workload alone did not significantly mediate turnover intention, challenging the assumption that high job demands are directly associated with attrition. A small supplementary chain effect (WFC -* workload -* RD -* turnover intention) emerged, whereas RD remained the dominant mediator. Work-interference-with-family affected both workload and RD; familyinterference-with-work affected only RD. RD is the critical psychological link between WFC and turnover; interventions addressing perceived unfairness in policy-driven contexts are needed.

TI Evaluation of the new Egyptian undergraduate medical program from
   students' perspectives: a nationwide cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate medical program; Students' experiences; Students'
   perspectives; Competency-based education; Program evaluation
AB Background The global emphasis on medical education reform highlights the need for essential competencies to meet evolving healthcare demands. In Egypt, significant reforms in 2018 introduced a competency-based, integrated undergraduate medical curriculum-a five-year program followed by a two-year internship aligned with the National Academic Reference Standards for Medicine. This study assesses graduates' perceptions and experiences with the newly implemented reformed national medical program. Methods This descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted between December 2023 and December 2024. Using a convenience sampling, it included 7,264 recent graduates from 27 Egyptian medical schools. Data was collected via an online survey comprising 45 Likert-scale items assessing various aspects of the program. Additionally, three open-ended questions explored graduates' most and least favorable aspects of the program and improvement suggestions. The survey underwent validity testing through exploratory factor analysis and expert review, as well as reliability testing through Cronbach's test. Data analysis included descriptive and inferential statistics, such as independent samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA, with significance set at p < 0.05. Effect sizes (Cohen's d and eta & sup2;) were calculated for all significant group comparisons to assess practical significance. Responses to open-ended questions were categorized and analyzed using quantitative content analysis (thematic categorization with frequency counts). Ethical approval, informed consent, and participant anonymity were ensured. Results The study received responses from 7,264 graduates (40.7%). Validity and reliability tests confirmed the survey's robustness, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.98 and exploratory factor analysis identifying four factors, accounting for 64.53% of total variance. Survey responses indicated moderate overall satisfaction across program dimensions, with mean scores ranging from 2.71 to 3.41. Key strengths included integration of basic and clinical sciences, diverse learning opportunities, early clinical exposure, emphasis on critical thinking, self-directed learning, and faculty support. Male students, high achievers, and those with strong English proficiency or university housing reported slightly higher satisfaction, though effect sizes were small. Challenges such as heavy workload, difficulty adapting to the new curriculum, and frequent assessments were noted. Quantitative content analysis of open-ended responses reinforced the quantitative findings, offering additional descriptive insights into students' experiences. Conclusion The shift to Competency-Based Medical Education in Egypt marks a significant reform to better prepare graduates for modern medical practice. Key strengths include subject integration, diverse learning opportunities, early clinical exposure, emphasis on critical thinking and self-directed learning. However, challenges like increased workload, frequent assessments, and difficulties adapting to the new curriculum were noted.

TI Visualizing the future: impact of holographic visualization on teaching
   minimally invasive veneer preparation: a randomized controlled trial
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Holographic visualization; Immersive technologies; Hologram; Spatial
   ability; Dental education; Prosthodontic education; Veneer preparation;
   Preclinical training
AB Background Minimally invasive veneer preparation in prosthodontic education requires advanced spatial understanding and psychomotor precision. Although immersive technologies are increasingly used in dental education, evidence regarding the educational effectiveness of holographic visualization in prosthodontics remains limited. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the impact of holographic visualization on preparation quality and student-reported educational outcomes during preclinical training in minimally invasive veneer preparation. Methods Sixty undergraduate dental students were randomly assigned to receive either conventional two-dimensional photographic visualization (n = 30) or holographic three-dimensional visualization (n = 30). Following a standardized calibration session and baseline preparation, participants performed a second veneer preparation after exposure to the assigned visualization modality. Preparations were independently assessed by two blinded evaluators using a predefined scoring rubric. Within-group changes were analysed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and between-group differences were assessed using analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline performance. Student-reported outcomes were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests with false discovery rate correction. Results Both groups showed significant improvements in preparation quality from baseline to post-intervention (both p < 0.001). However, no significant between-group differences were observed (adjusted mean difference: 0.60 points; 95% confidence interval: -0.48 to 1.67; p = 0.269). Overall student-reported outcomes were comparable between groups. Spatial understanding showed the largest between-group effect in favour of holographic visualization, although this difference was not significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Holographic visualization was highly accepted by students, and 70% supported its future integration into dental education. Conclusions Although holographic visualization did not significantly improve immediate preparation quality compared with conventional two-dimensional photographs, it was highly accepted by students and showed the largest observed effect for perceived spatial understanding. These findings suggest that holographic visualization may primarily support spatial understanding and represent a valuable adjunct for teaching complex three-dimensional concepts in preclinical prosthodontic education.

AB Purpose: Understanding professionals' attitudes towards evidence-based practices (EBPs) is critical for improving service quality for autistic children. This study investigated these attitudes among Chinese autism service professionals, identifying core dimensions as well as individual and multi-level contextual factors associated with them. Methods: 505 autism service professionals completed the Chinese version of the Evidence-Based Practice Attitude Scale-50 along with questionnaires on individual (e.g., education level, professional certification) and contextual factors (e.g., EBPs learning experience, supervisory support, organizational culture). Network analysis was used to identify core dimensions, and multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine associations between these factors and attitudes towards EBPs. Principal results: Overall EBPs attitude scores were mildly right-skewed, with the majority falling between 150 and 175. Appeal, Organizational Support, and Feedback emerged as the key dimensions through network analysis. Higher education level, autism-related professional certification, EBPs learning experiences, supervisory support, and organizational culture were significantly associated with more favorable attitudes towards EBPs. Notably, professional certification moderated the associations of EBPs learning experiences and supervisory support with attitudes towards EBPs, with both associations being stronger among certified professionals. Major conclusion: As the first study to systematically examine attitudes towards evidence-based practices (EBPs) among autism professionals in China, this research identified core attitudinal dimensions, key associated factors, and the moderating role of professional certification. Findings suggest that to foster positive attitudes towards EBPs, training programs should go beyond knowledge dissemination, strengthen supervisory support, and offer individualized professional development pathways.

TI "Four Integrations and Four Forces" for Emerging Engineering Course
   Groups: A Case Study of Industrial Software Talent Development
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital twin; emerging engineering; historical-cohort comparison;
   industrial software; interdisciplinary engineering education;
   manufacturing execution system; project-based learning
ID EDUCATION
AB This study examines how interdisciplinary industrial-software education was implemented at an application-oriented university through a longitudinal institutional case study with an embedded historical-cohort comparison. Evidence collected from 2014 to the end of the 2025-2026 spring semester included curriculum documents, platform and project records, competition and collaboration records, institutional surveys, and de-identified course-attainment and semester-1 baseline-grade data. The proposed Four Integrations and Four Forces framework was operationalized through a Foundation-Empowerment-Scenario curriculum architecture, an Engineering-Engineering Integration mechanism connecting operational and information technologies in authentic tasks, and a Four-Party and Six-Sharing university-industry collaboration mechanism. To provide course-level evidence, Fundamentals of Low-Code Technology was examined as a representative implementation case. A 2024-entry cohort (n = 41) was compared with a 2025-entry cohort (n = 40), while the instructor, platform, contact hours, course objectives, and assessment procedures remained unchanged. The later cohort experienced enterprise-linked scenarios, project-based teaching, and a smart-course environment. Because the cohorts were non-randomized and adjustment was limited to observed baseline grades, the results remain associational. The case nevertheless demonstrates a feasible task-level approach to connecting industrial mechanisms with computational technologies in interdisciplinary curricula.

TI Student perspectives on the value of university mobility programmes
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE aspirational capital; cultural capital; employability; global
   citizenship; international student mobility; undergraduate students;
   widening participation
ID NURSING-STUDENTS; PLACEMENTS; EDUCATION; ABROAD; PERFORMANCE; CRITIQUE;
   BOURDIEU; THINKING; CONTEXT; IMPACT
AB The purpose of this study was to examine the benefits of university-organised international experience for full-time undergraduate students at a single English post-1992 university with a high proportion of widening participation entrants. Using a mixed-methods design, data were collected from 91 undergraduates through a questionnaire and a focus group with semi-structured questions. Findings show that participation in international experience is associated with increased cultural capital and a marked development of aspirational capital, evidenced by shifts in students' confidence, career awareness and perceptions of international opportunity. These benefits were most pronounced among students from socio-economic disadvantaged backgrounds and were strongly mediated by institutional support. The study's key contribution is the extension of cultural and aspirational capital into the context of undergraduate international experience at a post-1992 university, demonstrating how structured institutional support can enable transformative outcomes for students who would not otherwise engage in outward mobility. This research can aid UK Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) by informing enhancements to outward student mobility programmes. These improved practices may contribute to understanding the pre-requisites of enabling a high-quality, meaningful and sustainable approach to international experience programmes.Context and implications Rationale for the study: This study provides insight into the benefits of a university-organised international experience for undergraduates at a post-1992 university in the UK, focusing on those from widening participation backgrounds where outward mobility has historically been low. Why the new findings matter: The findings demonstrate that international experience can build cultural and aspirational capital, enhance employability and broaden global outlooks for students from socio-economic disadvantaged backgrounds. This highlights its transformative value beyond traditional academic outcomes. Implications for relevant audiences: For practitioners, the study underscores the importance of targeted promotion, structured support and accessible short-term mobility options. Policymakers and funders can use the findings to strengthen schemes such as the Turing Scheme and Erasmus+, to better support widening participation and social mobility agendas. Researchers and practitioners gain an extended application of cultural and aspirational capital theories within international student mobility education. Institutions and senior leaders can apply the insights to inform the design of inclusive, sustainable international programmes that enhance student engagement, employability and global citizenship.

TI Event-Related Potential Components and the Lexical Decision Task in
   Greek-Speaking Children With and Without Reading Difficulties
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
ID DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA; REMEDIATION; SPEED; ERPS
AB The present study examined neurocognitive differences in visual word processing between children with reading difficulties (RD) and chronological-age-matched controls (CA) using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a lexical decision task. Participants were Grade 3 and Grade 6 children (ages 7.6-12.1 years) who were required to discriminate real words from orthographically similar pseudowords. ERP analyses focused on the N200 and N400 components, which are thought to reflect early stages of visual word processing and later processes involved in lexical access and stimulus evaluation. The results showed that the Grade 3 RD group exhibited significantly higher Nu 200 amplitudes than their CA controls, suggesting less efficient early processing of the presented stimuli. However, no differences in the N200 were observed between the Grade 6 groups. Children with RD in both grades exhibited reduced N400 amplitudes compared to their counterparts, suggesting differences in the neural processes supporting word recognition. These findings contribute to a clearer understanding of the temporal dynamics of written word processing in children with RD in transparent orthographies and highlight the value of ERP measures for examining neurocognitive mechanisms underlying reading development.

TI When Professional Development Fails: EFL Academics Becoming Researchers
   Under Conditions of Institutional Stratification in Chinese Higher
   Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE doctoral education; epistemic access; institutional stratification;
   professional development; research competence
ID KNOWLEDGE; TEACHERS; CURRICULUM; SOCIOLOGY
AB Professional development is widely promoted as a strategy for enhancing the research capacity of EFL academics in higher education. However, existing research has paid less attention to the disciplinary knowledge and research practices through which research competence is developed. This study examines professional learning under conditions of institutional stratification in Chinese higher education. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 12 Chinese EFL academics from two universities, the study uses Bernstein's concepts of recognition rules, realisation rules, and recontextualisation to examine how access to research knowledge varies across institutional contexts. The findings show that doctoral education provides sustained access to research practice through supervision, feedback, and participation in disciplinary communities. The study reconceptualises professional development as a form of differential epistemic access. It shows that institutional stratification can produce unequal research development through differences in access to doctoral education, mentoring, and other pedagogic conditions for learning disciplinary knowledge and participating in knowledge production.

TI From insight to intervention: learning analytics and generative AI
   support for learning design and educational decision-making
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning analytics; Generative artificial intelligence; Learning design;
   Educational decision-making; Educational interventions; Trustworthy AI
ID FRAMEWORK
AB Recent advances in learning design tools, learning analytics, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have created new possibilities for educators to design, monitor, and adapt learning experiences. Yet evidence that these possibilities routinely translate into student-centred, inclusive, personalised, and effective practice remains limited. This editorial synthesises four contributions to the special issue on learning analytics and AI support for learning design and educational decision-making. Across student, teacher, disciplinary, and institutional levels, the studies show that technology does not become educationally valuable through technical capability alone. Its value is mediated by learning design, community and interaction, digital literacy, educator and learner agency, ethical fitness, organisational strategy, resources, and wide stakeholder engagement. At the same time, the evidence base remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-report, discourse-based, and expert-judgement studies. We argue that the field must now move from demonstrating associations and proposing frameworks towards intervention research that tests causal mechanisms, implementation conditions, longer-term outcomes, and distributional effects. A future agenda should connect learning analytics and GenAI tightly to educational visions, pedagogical intentions, preserve human and epistemic agency, and build trustworthy socio-technical infrastructures that enable educators and learners to act on evidence.

TI Exploring neuro-inclusivity by design in assessment: A scoping review
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment design; fairness; inclusion; neurodivergence; neurodiversity;
   neuro-inclusive assessment; validity
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; STUDENTS
AB Understanding of neurodivergent characteristics remains limited in educational assessment, which hinders inclusive design approaches. Consequently, assessment design processes can fail to prevent unintended barriers being introduced in assessment, which can negatively impact neurodivergent learners' academic performance and emotional wellbeing. Guided by PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a scoping review was conducted to examine neurodivergent learners' assessment challenges and neuro-inclusive assessment design strategies. Overall, 23 studies were reviewed. Autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and dyslexia were most frequently examined in the literature, with neurodevelopmental differences such as dyspraxia and dyscalculia underrepresented. Following a grounded theory approach to qualitative data analysis, three broad themes emerged from the review: (1) pedagogical considerations, (2) understanding neurodivergent learners and (3) approaches to assessment. Pedagogical considerations include a need for greater awareness amongst educators and improved institutional infrastructures to foster inclusive learning environments. Understanding neurodivergent learners involves recognising specific neurodivergent characteristics that pose challenges in assessments, such as difficulties with sensory sensitivity and distorted time perception in formal, timed exams. Finally, approaches to assessment prioritise inclusion-by-design, such as participatory design methods, rather than relying exclusively on post hoc accommodations. Such approaches can support fairer, more valid assessments that more accurately capture the strengths and abilities of neurodivergent learners.

TI Lessons Learned About the Implementation and Sustainability of a

LA English
DT Article
DE access to care; asthma; community health workers; implementation;
   sustainability
ID DISPARITIES
AB Background Racially minoritized and economically disadvantaged children are disproportionately affected by asthma and often receive less or lower quality care. This paper describes the implementation of a community health worker (CHW)-delivered program in the School District of Philadelphia, asthma management challenges in under-resourced schools, and provides potential solutions. TI Academic resilience in 75 education systems: how operationalization and
   threshold choices shape findings on protective factors
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic resilience; PISA; Operationalization; Student motivation;
   Expectancy-value theory; Educational assessment
ID EXPECTANCY-VALUE; ACHIEVEMENT; MATHEMATICS; PREDICTORS; VARIABLES
AB Background Academic resilience-students' capacity to succeed despite socioeconomic disadvantage-is widely studied, but little consensus exists on how it should be operationalized. Inconsistent definitions make it difficult to compare findings across studies and to draw conclusions about what promotes resilience. The present study asks whether different operationalizations and thresholds lead to different estimates of resilience and different conclusions about its predictors.Methods Using PISA 2018 data from 75 education systems and based on an existing measurement framework, we compared three ways of operationalizing academic resilience: identifying high-achieving disadvantaged students, identifying students who outperform expectations given their socioeconomic status, and predicting achievement within a disadvantaged sample. We applied each at three relative threshold levels of disadvantage and/or high achievement, and assessed the consequences for the estimated prevalence of resilient students and for the associations of four factors (gender, self-perceived reading competence, reading enjoyment, attitude toward learning) with resilience.Results Prevalence estimates varied nearly fivefold across operationalizations, and rankings of education systems differed substantially. When associations were pooled meta-analytically, they were broadly consistent across operationalizations and threshold levels. When education systems were analyzed separately, however-as is standard in PISA-based research-findings were consistent in only 20-72% of systems, depending on the factor, and threshold level alone altered conclusions in 3-37%. A complementary interaction analysis of risk and protective factors, which requires no threshold, further showed that some motivational factors were associated with a flatter socioeconomic gradient in achievement and others with a steeper one-a pattern that threshold-based definitions cannot detect.Conclusions Operationalization and threshold levels can meaningfully affect the conclusions studies reach about academic resilience and its predictors. While part of this dependence is mechanical, given how the operationalizations are constructed, the magnitude of this dependence across education systems suggests that findings should not be interpreted independently of the operationalization used to produce them. We provide recommendations for matching operationalization choices to research questions.

TI A self-regulated learning perspective on L2 learners' engagement with
   peer feedback in writing
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 writing; Peer feedback; Self-regulated learning; Student engagement
ID WRITTEN-CORRECTIVE-FEEDBACK; STUDENTS
AB Considering the crucial role of self-regulated learning (SRL) in L2 learners' use of feedback, our study explored how SRL influences students' engagement with peer feedback in writing in the Chinese EFL contexts. To this end, we employed a mixed-methods design and collected data from questionnaires, students' writing samples, peer feedback, and semi-structured interviews. The quantitative results from the questionnaires (N = 293) revealed that SRL was correlated to and positively predicted L2 learners' affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement with peer feedback in writing. Specifically, skilled self-regulators managed and regulated their negative emotions in revision more effectively, used AI instruments to refine their revisions, and deployed various cognitive/metacognitive operations to derive learning opportunities from peer feedback. These results demonstrated that SRL played an important role in L2 learners' engagement with peer feedback in writing.

TI Bridging teacher noticing and metacognition: introducing the concept of
   metanoticing
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacognition; Metacognition and teaching; Teacher noticing; Mathematics
   teacher education; Professional development
ID MATHEMATICS EDUCATION; DECISION-MAKING; PRESERVICE TEACHERS; KNOWLEDGE;
   PERCEPTION; FRAMEWORK; COGNITION; THINKING
AB This study proposes metanoticing as a concept that reframes teacher cognition. Teacher noticing has generally been examined through the processes of attending, interpreting, and deciding. However, how teachers monitor, evaluate, and regulate their own noticing processes has not been sufficiently addressed in the literature. Drawing on metacognitive theory, this study suggests that noticing itself can become the object of metacognitive regulation. Within this framework, metanoticing is conceptualized as the process by which the teacher becomes aware of and regulates their own noticing. Integrating key literature from both domains (metacognition and noticing), we argue that teacher noticing can fundamentally become the object of metacognition. By framing metanoticing as a core dimension of professional expertise, we provide a theoretical architecture that explains how noticing processes are actively monitored, evaluated, and regulated. We articulate how metacognitive functions operate within the core phases of noticing and discuss their implications for teacher learning, professional development, and future research. Metanoticing, we contend, provides a promising lens for investigating the development of teacher expertise and designing teacher education programs that promote reflective instructional practice.

TI School burnout during the transition from primary to secondary school in
   Switzerland. Changes over time and the role of educational tracking
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School burnout; Educational transition; Risk factors; Longitudinal;
   Primary to secondary school
ID ACADEMIC SELF-CONCEPT; SOCIAL SUPPORT; MIDDLE SCHOOL; ADOLESCENTS;
   ACHIEVEMENT; ENGAGEMENT; STUDENTS; MODEL; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; TRAJECTORIES
AB The transition from primary to secondary school represents a developmentally sensitive period characterized by increased academic demands and major social and institutional changes. This longitudinal study examined the development of school burnout and its predictors during this transition in the Swiss educational system. The study was grounded in three complementary perspectives: Multiple and Multi-dimensional Transitions theory, Neuenschwander's multilevel model, and the life course perspective. We hypothesized (H1) an overall increase in burnout after the transition, (H2) a greater increase in burnout among students on the most demanding academic track, and (H3-H8) associations between burnout and factors operating at three levels: individual, family and educational-system. The participants were 162 Swiss students (87 boys, 75 girls; Mage = 11.91 years), followed from the final year of primary school (T1) to the first year of secondary school (T2). Linear mixed-effects and multilevel longitudinal models were estimated. The results showed a significant increase in overall burnout after the transition, mainly reflected in higher emotional exhaustion and cynicism. Feelings of inadequacy decreased among students on less demanding tracks. Burnout increased more strongly among students placed in the most demanding academic track. Before the transition, lower mathematics achievement predicted higher burnout, but this association disappeared after the transition. Across both time points, somatic symptoms and workload-related stress were consistent risk factors, whereas teacher support was a protective factor. Longitudinal analyses further showed that somatic symptoms, teacher support, and future-related stress at T1 predicted burnout at T2. These findings highlight the significance of academic demands and adult support during the transition to secondary school. They also suggest that tracking placement influences students' burnout trajectories during early adolescence.

TI The vocabulary learning strategy use of international students in the
   academic context in EMI programmes at Hungarian universities: a
   questionnaire study
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English as a medium of instruction (EMI); International students;
   Academic context; Vocabulary learning strategies (VLSs); Instruction
ID INSTRUCTION
AB The acquisition of English vocabulary items related to the academic context, which involve both the so-called academic vocabulary and the field-specific technical vocabulary, is crucial for university students in programmes with English as a medium of instruction (EMI). The use of vocabulary learning strategies (VLSs), especially the types that require active information manipulation, is an individual difference factor in language learning that was found to characterize proficient learners with high vocabulary size. This finding indicates the importance of VLS use in the academic context as well and provides relevance to conduct research about the VLS preferences of international students with diverse backgrounds in EMI programmes at Hungarian universities. The study consisted of an initial piloting phase with 5 participants and a main data collection with 390 participants with diverse educational and geographical-cultural backgrounds, who were administered the adapted questionnaire that was modified after the initial piloting. The adapted questionnaire demonstrated acceptable to good reliability (most scales alpha >= 0.70; lowest subscale alpha = 0.588); and the participants were found to apply dictionary use and inferencing/guessing with the highest frequency. Few differences were found; however, the results indicate that previous VLS instruction in EAP and ESP courses has a slightly stronger impact on VLS use than the other variables. These findings call the attention of stakeholders to the need for more EAP and ESP learning opportunities for international students in programmes with EMI, with explicit instruction in VLSs that could contribute to success in their studies.

TI Academic Peer Network Effects of Doctoral Students: An Empirical
   Research Based on Response-Driven Sampling in China
SO HIGHER EDUCATION QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE academic network; doctoral education; peer effects; research competence;
   respondent-driven sampling
ID WORK; CREATIVITY; SKILLS
AB This study used Response-Driven Sampling (RDS) to construct an academic peer network for PhD students in China and conducted a questionnaire survey. After testing 639 valid samples that met the random recruitment assumption, empirical analysis was conducted on academic peer network effects on the research competence of PhD candidates (RCPC). The results show that RCPC is significantly influenced by academic peer network size, homogeneity, and peer competence. (1) Peer competence demonstrates the strongest positive effect on RCPC, particularly for those with low initial research competence. (3) The network size of weak ties does not significantly affect RCPC. However, among strong ties, the number of peers from other departments and universities exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with self-assessed competence, with the optimal network size being 16 peers. This study not only suggests PhD students strengthen their social connections with peers from different disciplines and institutions, aiming to maintain a moderate-sized network within strong ties, thereby enhancing their own abilities and achieving long-term development, but also indicates the applicability and generalizability of applying RDS to peer network surveys.

TI Career Competencies and Job Market Readiness: The Role of Career
   Self-Management and Labor Market Uncertainty
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE sustainable graduate employability; career competencies; career
   self-management; job market readiness; labor market uncertainty; higher
   education; education-to-work transition
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; EMPLOYABILITY; CONSERVATION; RESOURCES; BEHAVIOR;
   CULTURE; WORK
AB Preparing graduates to navigate increasingly uncertain labor markets is an important challenge for higher education and the broader pursuit of sustainable graduate employability. Although higher education institutions invest substantially in developing Career Competencies (CC), comparatively less is known about how these competencies are associated with graduates' Job Market Readiness (JMR), the role of Career Self-Management (CSM) in this relationship, and whether perceived Labor Market Uncertainty (LMU) conditions the strength of this association. Drawing on Human Capital Theory, Career Construction Theory, and Conservation of Resources Theory, this study develops and empirically examines an integrated framework linking developmental resources, self-regulatory career behavior, employment readiness, and perceived labor market conditions. Data were collected from 398 final-year university students and recent graduates in Saudi Arabia using a non-probability, multi-institutional purposive sampling approach and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27, AMOS 27, and Hayes' PROCESS macro. The findings show that CC was positively associated with both CSM and JMR, while CSM was also positively associated with JMR. The analysis further identified a significant indirect statistical association between CC and JMR through CSM, along with a remaining significant direct association. In addition, perceived LMU significantly moderated the CC-JMR relationship, such that the positive association was stronger at higher levels of perceived uncertainty. These findings contribute to graduate employability research by showing that the employment relevance of Career Competencies is associated not only with the resources graduates possess but also with their Career Self-Management and the labor market conditions they perceive. Therefore, sustainable graduate employability is treated as a broader theoretical implication of these relationships rather than an outcome directly measured by this study. These findings provide a basis for future longitudinal research examining whether these associations contribute to more sustainable education-to-work transitions over time.

TI Between Co-Intelligence and Cognitive Offloading: Educators'
   Perspectives from Dutch Academic Medical Settings on Generative AI,
   Critical Thinking, and Adult Professional Learning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; adult learning; medical education;
   critical thinking; cognitive offloading; AI literacy; assessment design;
   technology acceptance
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming embedded in adult professional education, yet its capacity to accelerate academic work may also remove cognitive processes that underpin professional judgement. This qualitative study explored how educators working in Dutch academic medical settings perceive GenAI's implications for students' critical thinking and how they believe it should be integrated into medical curricula. Seventeen educators from Dutch academic medical settings participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically using a mixed inductive-deductive approach informed by the Technology Acceptance Model and the Paul-Elder critical thinking framework. Three themes were identified: educational value and efficiency; threats to independent critical thinking; and conditions for responsible integration. Educators valued GenAI for personalised learning, writing support, research assistance, accessibility, simulation, and administrative efficiency. However, they associated low-friction use with cognitive offloading, weaker source appraisal, reduced information filtering, possible erosion of foundational knowledge, and difficulties verifying authentic student understanding. Participants proposed AI literacy, transparent use, institutionally governed models, comparative human-AI tasks, simulation, staged access, and AI-free oral or in-class assessment. The findings suggest that adult professional education should design GenAI as co-intelligence rather than cognitive substitution, preserving productive friction while verifying unassisted competence.

TI Intergenerational Teacher Learning in Schools: A Situated Explanatory
   Model of Professional Collaboration
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE intergenerational learning; teacher professional development;
   collaborative work; intergenerational relationships
AB Teacher professional learning increasingly depends on situated collaborative practices that emerge in the everyday work of schools. In educational contexts characterized by diverse career paths and the coexistence of different generations of teachers, it is important to understand how professional knowledge circulates and is reinterpreted among teachers with varying levels of experience. From this perspective, Intergenerational Teacher Learning (ITL) is understood as a process of reciprocal knowledge and practice exchange among teachers from different generations. This study analyzes how ITL takes shape through the everyday working relationships among teachers of different generations in Chilean schools, adopting a qualitative paradigm grounded in constructivist grounded theory. To this end, fifteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with practicing teachers at different career stages. Based on the initial, focused, and theoretical coding of the data, an inductive, situated explanatory model of ITL was constructed, organized into five dimensions. The results show that age and professional experience are associated with teachers' assessments of their peers' competencies, and that ITL manifests primarily through traditional mentoring, reverse mentoring, and peer learning. Furthermore, novice teachers in particular contribute to knowledge related to the use of technology and innovation, while experienced teachers contribute knowledge related to school culture and pedagogical management, which is especially relevant to the professional integration of novice teachers.

TI Unmasking the Impact of Teaching Workload on Learning Outcome Attainment
   in Outcome-Based Engineering Education: A Multi-Level Analysis of CLO
   and PLO Achievement
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE objective-based education implementation; educational challenges;
   workload; course learning outcome; continuous quality improvement;
   program learning outcome
AB Outcome-Based Education (OBE) has been widely adopted in engineering education as a systematic framework for curriculum design, teaching, assessment, and Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) through clearly defined learning outcomes. Effective implementation of OBE requires continuous monitoring of Course Learning Outcome (CLO) and Program Learning Outcome (PLO) attainment to support evidence-based educational improvement. The purpose of this study is to examine the relationship between teaching conditions and learning outcome attainment by analyzing CLO and PLO achievement under different workload categories. CLO and PLO attainment data commonly used in higher education were analyzed using a 50% attainment benchmark across four workload levels: minimal, low, medium, and high. The results show that average CLO attainment ranged from 60% to 95% across different workload levels, indicating variations in course-level achievement under different teaching conditions. Program-level analysis showed that overall PLO attainment remained above the benchmark, demonstrating that OBE effectively supports the achievement of program outcomes while highlighting variations in course-level performance that provide valuable evidence for Continuous Quality Improvement. The findings demonstrate that systematic analysis of CLO and PLO attainment can support informed assessment practices, academic planning, and evidence-based decision-making, thereby strengthening the effective implementation of Outcome-Based Engineering Education.

TI Evidence of Content Validity for Essential Teaching Practices in
   Physical Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE physical education; teaching practices; teacher education; content
   validity; expert judgment
AB The quality of instruction in physical education depends, in part, on the identification and systematization of essential pedagogical practices that guide teachers' professional performance. The objectives of this study were to obtain evidence of content validity for a matrix of essential pedagogical practices for initial teacher education in physical education and to analyze the degree of consensus among experts regarding their clarity and practical and theoretical relevance. A quantitative, instrumental, descriptive, and cross-sectional study was conducted. Ten experts in education and subject-specific pedagogy participated, evaluating 20 pedagogical practices. Content validity was estimated using Aiken's V coefficient and its confidence intervals, supplemented by analyses of internal consistency and inter-rater agreement. The results showed that most practices achieved high or very high scores, particularly in planning, assessment, monitoring, and feedback. In contrast, practices related to families, context, and reflection on teaching practice received less consensus. It is concluded that the matrix provides favorable evidence of content validity and serves as a useful framework for guiding initial teacher education, pedagogical supervision, and future research aimed at its application with practicing teachers.

TI How Student Engagement Shapes Perceived Academic Achievement: Distinct
   Competence- and Well-Being-Based Pathways
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE student engagement; perceived academic achievement; perceived
   competence; life satisfaction; mediation; higher education
AB Student engagement is widely recognized as a key determinant of academic success; however, its underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Existing measures frequently conflate engagement in learning activities (SELA) with engagement in the academic community (SEAC), which obscures their distinct contributions to students' perceived academic achievement (PAA). To address these limitations, the present study proposes and empirically tests a theoretically grounded dual-pathway model based on the Dual Component Framework of Student Engagement. This framework differentiates between competence-based and well-being-based mechanisms that link engagement to PAA. Specifically, SELA is hypothesized to influence PAA through perceived competence, whereas SEAC is expected to operate through life satisfaction. Additionally, gender and academic year are examined as potential moderators of these indirect relationships. Two studies were conducted with university students from different academic programs and year levels (Study 1: N = 404; Study 2: N = 396). The findings indicate that perceived competence fully mediates the relationship between SELA and PAA. Life satisfaction also fully mediates the effect of SEAC on PAA, even after controlling for gender and academic year. Neither SELA nor SEAC exhibited direct effects on academic achievement, emphasizing the central role of psychological mediators. Furthermore, gender and academic year did not moderate these relationships. Collectively, these findings provide strong evidence for distinct psychological pathways linking specific forms of engagement to academic self-evaluations and highlight the need for mechanism-based models of student engagement in higher education.

TI Faculty Perceptions of Teacher Education Curriculum Responsiveness and
   Pre-Service Teachers' Acquisition of 21st Century Skills: A Case Study
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE 21st century skills; perceptions; pre-service teachers; teacher
   educators; teacher education curriculum; curriculum responsiveness
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB The curriculum is the vehicle that drives teaching and learning processes. Regarding the South African teacher education curriculum (SATEC), scholars and researchers are negatively disposed and have contrasting views about its responsiveness to learners' diverse learning needs and skill development. This study, therefore, explored the perceptions of teacher educators at a public university in South Africa with regard to the teacher education curriculum's responsiveness (TECR) and potential in developing pre-service teachers' 21st century skills (PT21Cs). Underpinned by the constructivist theory (CT), via the interpretivist paradigm, this study utilised a phenomenological case study design of the qualitative research approach. This study's population consisted of lecturers in the education faculty at the sampled university. The purposive sampling technique was used in selecting seven participants (five females and two males). A semi-structured interview guide was used to collect data for this study, and analysed using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA) via ATLAS.ti software version 24. The findings reveal that SATEC is somewhat culturally and disciplinarily responsive but highly structured and is not adequately developing pre-service teachers' 21st century skills as it should. The challenges in implementing a responsive curriculum and the development of pre-service teachers' 21st century skills, as well as strategies for addressing these, were discussed. This study recommends that further teacher education curriculum reviews and evaluations, as Education 5.0 dictates and per the Sustainable Development Goals 2030 and 2063, as well as teacher educators' professional development and training, be pursued and actualised.

TI A machine learning-based adaptive platform is associated with cognitive
   improvements in Peruvian secondary school students: a quasi-experimental
   study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive teaching; cognitive learning; machine learning; personalized
   educational platform; secondary education
ID EDUCATION
AB This study determined the impact of a personalized educational platform based on machine learning (ML) on the cognitive learning of secondary education students at a public institution in Piura, Peru. The research followed an applied, quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental design. A sample of 56 fourth-grade students was distributed into a control group (n = 26, traditional teaching) and an experimental group (n = 30, platform-assisted teaching), using two pre-existing classrooms randomly assigned to each condition. Cognitive learning was assessed across four dimensions (attention, memory, reasoning, and comprehension) with pretest and posttest exams administered at the start and end of the same two-hour session per topic, over three consecutive weeks. The platform combined an unsupervised clustering model for cognitive profiling with a supervised classifier that predicted, in real time, the optimal content level for each student. Analyses were based on improvement scores (posttest - pretest); intergroup comparisons used the Mann-Whitney U test with rank-biserial effect sizes, and the relationship between platform metrics and the posttest score was examined through Spearman correlations. Results showed significant differences favoring the experimental group across the three topics (p < .001), with increasing effect sizes (r = 0.527, 0.610, 0.738), confirmed through a sensitivity analysis that controlled for the pretest. The experimental group achieved an average improvement of 8.29 points out of 20, versus 4.90 for the control group. Requested adaptations showed a moderate association on average with the posttest score (rho = 0.485, p < .001), strengthening over the course of the intervention (up to rho = 0.588), while the predictive weight of the initial micro-diagnostic declined progressively. The platform was associated with a significant, progressive, and dimension-differentiated improvement, although the single-classroom-per-condition design and the within-session measurement warrant interpretive caution. This work contributes to inclusive education in resource-limited contexts and aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 4 and 10.

TI Communicative competence development through indigenous folklore in
   primary EFL classrooms: evidence from Kazakhstan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE communicative competence; culturally responsive pedagogy; indigenous
   folklore; Kazakhstan; primary EFL education
AB Introduction Culturally responsive language education seeks to connect English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction with learners' cultural identities and local knowledge. However, classroom-based quantitative research on the integration of indigenous folklore into primary EFL education remains limited, particularly in Central Asia. This study examined changes in fourth-grade learners' linguistic, speech, and sociocultural competence following the integration of Kazakh indigenous folklore into primary EFL instruction. Methods A quasi-experimental one-group pre-test-post-test design was employed with 100 fourth-grade students aged 9-10 years at a public primary school in Kazakhstan. The 12-week intervention comprised two 45-minute lessons per week and was delivered by the regular classroom teacher. Adapted Kazakh folk narratives, cultural traditions, traditional games, storytelling, role-play, retelling, discussion, and productive language tasks were incorporated into English lessons. Learners' communicative competence was assessed using parallel pre- and post-test forms of a 25-item lexical-grammatical test, three composite speech performance tasks, and a 25-item sociocultural competence test. Paired-samples t-tests were used to examine within-group changes, and Cohen's dz and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results Post-test scores were significantly higher than pre-test scores across all three competence domains (all p < .001). Linguistic competence increased from M = 12.84 (SD = 4.63) to M = 17.92 (SD = 4.41), with a mean gain of 5.08 points and a large effect size (dz = 0.84). Speech competence increased from M = 16.27 (SD = 5.18) to M = 22.68 (SD = 4.95), with a mean gain of 6.41 points and a large effect size (dz = 0.98). Sociocultural competence increased from M = 11.96 (SD = 4.88) to M = 18.74 (SD = 4.37), producing the largest mean gain (6.78 points) and effect size (dz = 1.10). All 95% confidence intervals for the mean differences excluded zero. Discussion The findings indicate substantial within-group development in linguistic, speech, and sociocultural competence during the folklore-based instructional period, with the strongest improvement occurring in the sociocultural domain. These results suggest that culturally familiar materials may help learners connect English language use with their existing cultural knowledge and experiences. However, because the study involved a non-randomized one-group design without a control group and was conducted in a single school with one teacher, the observed improvements cannot be attributed exclusively to the intervention. The study contributes classroom-based quantitative evidence from an underrepresented Central Asian context and highlights the potential value of culturally meaningful resources in multilingual primary EFL education.

TI From talk to networked reasoning: bridging inquiry discourse and
   epistemic patterns of investigation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE contextual inquiry; contextual scientific literacy; discourse analysis;
   epistemic development of students; epistemic network analysis; local
   wisdom
ID ARGUMENT; MODEL
AB Science learning in elementary school ideally fosters scientific thinking through meaningful experiences, but learning practices are still often oriented to memorization so that inquiry dialogues that record students' reasoning questions have not been optimally utilized to map the development of scientific thinking. A research gap exists: most studies either describe "science talk" or focus on individual elements of scientific thinking, but few model how these elements such as questioning, explanation, and reasoning are interconnected as a dynamic, visualizable epistemic structure. This study aims to address this gap by analyzing the dynamics of inquiry dialogue among elementary students in science learning based on local wisdom at Rumah Tuan Kadi, Pekanbaru. The method used is qualitative descriptive design; Participants totaled 20 students who were divided into four groups (5 students each) with different inquiry focuses (stairs, ventilation, structure, lighting); The main data is in the form of audio video recordings of inquiry discussions (after context exploration through virtual media), transcribed verbatim, segmented into utterance, then encoded (Q, E, R, I, S, D, Rf, Ev) and analyzed using ENA to map the strength of connections between codes. The findings show a gradual development pattern from reasoning centered networks to inquiry driven, reflective synthesis, to evidence based reflective networks, with Explanation-Reasoning-Investigation-Reflection connections as markers of the maturity of scientific thinking. These results contribute to a model of students' epistemic development in contextual inquiry as well as provide pedagogical implications for a more dialogical and reflective design of local culture based science learning. Furthermore, the epistemic network analysis approach demonstrated here provides an analytical framework for understanding students' reasoning development in nanoscience and nanotechnology education, where complex, multi step investigations similarly demand the integration of questioning, explanation, investigation, and evidence based reflection.

TI Proteus-based circuit simulation and differentiated learning in
   vocational electronics education: a quasi-experimental study to overcome
   laboratory infrastructure limitations in vocational high schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE circuit simulation; differentiated instruction; electronics learning;
   equal access; Proteus; vocational education; vocational high school
ID SCIENCE; STYLES
AB Electronics education at vocational high schools (SMK) in Indonesia often faces a gap between curriculum requirements and limited laboratory infrastructure. This situation makes it difficult for students to develop an understanding of abstract electrical concepts. This study evaluates the effectiveness of integrating the Proteus circuit simulation software with a differentiated learning process strategy on students' cognitive achievement in the subject of Fundamentals of Electricity and Electronics. The research design used was quasi-experimental with a nonequivalent control-group pretest-posttest design, involving 62 students in the Electronics Engineering Program at a vocational high school in Central Java. The experimental group (n = 31) received Proteus simulation-based learning with process differentiation through three types of activities (hands-on manipulation, visual demonstration, and guided verbal explanation), while the control group (n = 31) received conventional instruction. Students' learning style preferences were measured using the Index of Learning Styles descriptively to explain the variety of activities, not as a basis for instruction matching. Data collection was conducted through a cognitive achievement test (30 items; KMO = 0.87; alpha = 0.84), the Index of Learning Styles questionnaire (44 items; alpha = 0.79), and a structured observation sheet (kappa = 0.82). The Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney U, N-Gain, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were applied for data analysis. The results showed a substantial improvement in the experimental group (Z = -4.852; p < 0.001), with a mean N-Gain of 0.93 (high category), compared to the control group's 0.38 (moderate category). Because the Proteus simulation and process differentiation were delivered simultaneously as a single intervention package, the findings are interpreted as the effect of the combined intervention rather than of either component in isolation. These results indicate that circuit simulations combined with various learning activities can serve as an ICT-based alternative to bridge the limitations of laboratory infrastructure in vocational education. This study also critically discusses the hypothesis of matching instruction to learning styles and offers a process differentiation framework as a more valid alternative interpretation

TI Psychometric evidence for the universal design for learning 3.0 teacher
   implementation questionnaire (CID-DUA3): development and preliminary
   validation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE factor structure; inclusive education; psychometric evidence; teacher
   implementation; universal design for learning
AB Introduction: Universal Design for Learning (UDL 3.0) provides a framework for designing educational environments that anticipate barriers, broaden participation, and promote student progress. Despite its increasing incorporation into educational policy and practice, there remains a need for robust instruments capable of assessing its implementation through the self-reported frequency of specific and potentially observable teaching practices. The aim of this study was to develop the Universal Design for Learning 3.0 Teacher Implementation Questionnaire (CID-DUA3) and obtain preliminary evidence of its validity and reliability. Methods: An instrumental, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted in two phases. In the first phase, an initial 20-item version was reviewed by a panel of 10 experts. Following the content validation process, a refined 12-item version was obtained. This version was subsequently administered to 91 practicing teachers. Descriptive and internal consistency analyses were conducted, together with an exploratory factor analysis based on polychoric correlations and a confirmatory factor analysis in R using the lavaan package and the mean-and variance-adjusted weighted least squares estimator. Results: The CID-DUA3 showed high internal consistency (alpha = 0.876; standardized alpha = 0.879). The ordinal EFA supported the retention of a single factor, and the preliminary CFA evaluation showed fit indices consistent with this structure (CFI = 0.975; TLI = 0.969; RMSEA = 0.068). In addition, teachers who reported greater knowledge of UDL obtained significantly higher questionnaire scores than those with lower levels of knowledge (p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings provide preliminary evidence of the content validity, reliability, and initial unidimensional structure of the CID-DUA3, suggesting that it is a useful instrument for assessing the implementation of UDL 3.0 in teaching practice.

TI Play as the meaningful work of childhood: views from evolutionary
   science, Indigenous cultures, and Montessori pedagogy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE evolutionary psychology; Indigenous communities; Montessori education;
   play; playful learning
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; YOUNG-CHILDREN; GUIDED PLAY; MEMORY
AB Young children learn best when they can explore, experiment, and engage-activities that comprise play. Yet play is often contrasted with work, which includes learning in school (we call it schoolwork!). Here we consider three complementary perspectives (evolutionary developmental psychology, Indigenous ethnography, and Montessori pedagogy) indicating that play, characterized by choice, movement, and active engagement, is the meaningful work of childhood. Drawing on evolutionary theory, we present evidence that children have evolved to learn most effectively through self-directed play, hands-on exploration, and social participation, not direct instruction. Ethnographic accounts from Indigenous communities worldwide illustrate how children learn through genuine participation in the real work of daily life, where the line between play and work is largely absent. We then examine Montessori education as a modern pedagogical model that closely reflects these ancestral learning conditions, centering child-directed activity, embodied learning, and purposeful engagement with real materials. By bridging evolutionary developmental psychology with cross-cultural perspectives on early childhood learning, this essay challenges educational models that separate play from productive learning and highlights how evolutionarily aligned environments support development and wellbeing.

TI Nuances on algebra teaching knowledge: preservice mathematics teachers'
   understandings of simultaneous equations
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE algebra; knowledge of algebra for teaching (KAT); mathematical knowledge
   for teaching (MKT); preservice mathematics teachers; simultaneous
   equations
ID CONNECTIONS
AB High-quality algebra teaching can be significantly influenced by algebra-specific knowledge, but broad teacher mathematical knowledge frameworks may not fully capture the nuances of this knowledge. The present study examined these nuances in the case of preservice secondary mathematics teachers (PMTs) by employing the Knowledge of Algebra for Teaching (KAT) framework. The study analysed the solutions and explanations of fifteen PMTs from a metropolitan university in Australia to three worded problems involving simultaneous equations. The findings revealed strengths in PMTs' proficiency with basic algebraic problem-solving procedures and their ability to recognise the efficiency of algebraic approaches for solving simultaneous equations. Limitations in KAT included, first, a lack of firm understanding of simultaneous equations and algebraic generalisation; and second, gaps in the use of graphical methods, in recognising the strengths and weaknesses of relevant solution methods (e.g., algebraic, numerical), and in articulating the mathematical content of the problems. These findings contribute to the ongoing work on mathematics teacher preparation by providing actionable insights for the content and delivery of teacher education. Additionally, the study offers a methodological approach for assessing teachers' KAT that can inform research and practice in this area.
