TI Effects of declarative language and an indirect reward system on
   participation in adult-selected activities in an autistic child with
   features of pathological demand avoidance
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Pathological demand avoidance; Declarative
   language; Indirect reward; Single-case research methodology
ID EXTREME; EXPERIENCES
AB Pathological Demand Avoidance (PDA) is a behavioral profile that is often associated with autism spectrum disorder and has received increased attention in the field of child psychiatry, child neurology, and pediatrics. Despite its prevalence, autistic children with a PDA profile often do not respond to many evidence-based interventions recommended for individuals on the autism spectrum. Scarce but available research, coupled by practical guidelines from the PDA Society and PDA North America, suggests the use of low or indirect demands and prioritizing the individual's autonomy. Using an experimental, single-case, concurrent multiple baseline across activities design, we examined the effects of declarative language and an indirect reward system on participation in adult-selected activities in an autistic child with PDA. Results showed a robust functional relation between the intervention package and the child's participation in adultselected activities. Interventionists and the participant's caregiver positively reported the social importance, appropriateness, and effectiveness of the intervention package. Contributions, limitations, and implications for research and practice are discussed.

TI Executive functions in Cantonese-English bilingual autistic and
   neurotypical children: The role of first and second language exposure
   across different communicative contexts
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Executive functions; Bilingual autistic children; Communicative
   contexts; First language exposure; Second language exposure
ID SPATIAL WORKING-MEMORY; SPECTRUM DISORDERS; LANGUAGE CONTROL;
   ADVANTAGES; CHILDHOOD; TASK; INTERFERENCE; EXPERIENCES; PERFORMANCE;
   SCHOOL
AB This study investigated the impact of first language (L1) and second language (L2) exposure on working memory and inhibitory control in 6- to 10-year-old Cantonese-English bilingual autistic children (N = 36, mean age = 8;05, SD = 1.02) and bilingual neurotypical children (N = 40, mean age = 8;02, SD = 1.02), with a particular focus on how different communicative contexts influence executive functions (EFs). In contrast, no significant associations were observed between L1 or L2 exposure and EF performance in neurotypical children across communicative contexts. These findings provide new evidence that L2 exposure in general does not harm working memory or inhibitory control in autistic children, and highlight the critical role of specific communicative contexts in shaping EF outcomes in bilingual autistic children.

TI Efficiency of technical and technological education in Colombia
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational evaluation; Institutional efficiency; Technical and
   vocational education; Nonparametric frontiers; Higher education;
   Colombia
ID NONPARAMETRIC FRONTIER ESTIMATION; VOCATIONAL-EDUCATION; INFERENCE;
   MODELS
AB Evaluating technical and vocational education institutions in a context-sensitive way requires instruments that approximate institutional contribution conditional on students' pre-entry conditions. This study estimates the teaching efficiency of Colombian public and private Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) offering Technical and Technological programs using the order-alpha partial frontier, drawing on Saber TyT (2023) and Saber 11 (2018-2021) data. Outputs are institution-level scores in critical reading and quantitative reasoning; inputs are students' socioeconomic stratum and prior competency performance. Nonparametric tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, a second-stage OLS regression with robust standard errors, and two Random Forest models complement the analysis. TI Information-seeking behavior in second language acquisition:
   Conceptualization and operationalization
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Proactive language learning; Second language learning; Explicit L2
   knowledge; Implicit L2 knowledge
ID INSTRUCTION; LEARNER
AB Drawing on Proactive Language Learning Theory (Papi & Hiver, 2025), this study is the first to formally operationalize the construct of information-seeking behavior, which is defined as proactive engagement in seeking and using explicit linguistic and metalinguistic information to enhance one's L2 knowledge and skills. Questionnaire scales were developed and validated in two studies: Study 1 administered the scales to 207 Spanish learners in the US, and Study 2 administered them to 294 English learners in Iran. Exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor solution: Information Gathering, referring to learners' efforts to gather explicit L2 information, and Information Use, representing learners' incorporation of the information in their L2 use. Confirmatory factor analysis, correlational analyses, and reliability analyses confirmed the discriminant and convergent validity of the scales. Hierarchical regression analyses supported the predictive validity of the scales: Information Gathering significantly predicted proficiency when entered before Information Use, while Information Use made a significant unique contribution to proficiency in the final models. Together, these findings support Information-Seeking Behavior as a multidimensional construct and provide a theoretically grounded instrument for investigating learners' proactive engagement with explicit L2 information.

TI "I hope to change" vs. "I have to follow": Tensions and positioning in
   novice teacher identity construction
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher identity; Novice teachers; Tensions; Positioning theory;
   Comparative case study
ID WORK; VULNERABILITY; AGENCY
AB This comparative case study, grounded in positioning theory, examines the identity construction of two novice teachers in a Chinese middle school. Utilizing ethnographic fieldwork and interview data, the study reveals that when encountering analogous tensions between student-centered teaching beliefs and exam-oriented environments, one teacher became an agent of change, while the other complied with the dominant school culture. To illustrate these divergent trajectories, we propose the positioning seesaw that conceptualizes identity construction as a dynamic equilibrium-seeking process between rights and duties. We demonstrate that disciplinary subject status activates specific moral orders which shape this equilibrium. The (re)configuration of rights and duties then conditions teacher agency, thereby shaping different functions of tensions. Our analysis indicates that the school structure is stratified; agency is constrained yet can counter-shape structure under favorable leverage, and tensions may become productive for identity development.

AB The role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in different aspects of English as a foreign language (EFL) education has recently gained increasing attention. TI "That Sounds Like ChatGPT!": Youth Civic Literacies and Unhumanizing
   Generative AI
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; civic literacy; design-based research; generative
   artificial intelligence; human-centered; youth participation
AB This design-based study explored how youth civic literacies manifested as young people demystified GenAI-tinkering and playing with the tool in an informal setting. Students "unhumanized" GenAI, using its tools for civic and humanistic purposes. Analysis of ChatGPT logs, video/audio recordings, and artifacts indicated that students: (1) dissected, mimicked, and resisted GenAI; (2) employed an agentic, "robots-in-the-loop" approach in considering their civic and personal futures; and (3) realized a techno-optimism characterized by a lack of fear, sense of possibility, and joy. These activities paved the way for personal, social, and political explorations using GenAI. This article offers insight into the praxes of AI and civic literacy, providing opportunities for educators and researchers to support learners as they engage with (and critique) these technologies.

TI Resource Protection and Motivation: A Dual-Path Moderated Mediation
   Model of the Impact of Perceived Organizational Change on Teachers' Work
   Engagement
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE career resilience; emotion regulation; event system theory; perceived
   organizational change; psychological contract violation; teachers' work
   engagement
ID JOB DEMANDS; CONSERVATION
AB Although previous studies have established a positive correlation between perceived organizational change and teachers' work engagement, the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions governing this relationship remain insufficiently explored. Integrating Event System Theory with Conservation of Resources Theory, this study develops a dual-path moderated mediation model to examine how perceived organizational change influences teachers' work engagement through psychological contract violation and career resilience. Survey data were collected from 513 teachers across 15 vocational colleges in China using a two-stage cluster convenience sampling approach. The empirical results indicate that rather than acting as a disruptive stressor, perceived organizational change functions as a positive structural event that significantly reduces psychological contract violation, thereby exerting a protective effect on work engagement. Simultaneously, this change perception actively stimulates work engagement by enhancing teachers' career resilience. Furthermore, emotion regulation capacity plays a critical moderating role within the model. Specifically, higher levels of emotion regulation significantly catalyse the motivational pathway driven by career resilience but demonstrate no significant moderating effect on the protective pathway concerning psychological contract violation. These findings provide a novel event-resource perspective for organizational change theory in educational contexts and offer essential implications for management practices in vocational education.

TI Learners' and Teachers' Trust, Emotions, and Agency in AI-Mediated
   Language Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated EFL learning; foreign language enjoyment; learner autonomy;
   perceived control; trust in AI feedback
AB The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms has reshaped feedback, assessment, and interactional practices. However, limited research has examined how learners' trust in AI systems relates to their emotional experiences and agency in AI-mediated instruction. This study investigated the structural relationships among EFL translation learners' trust in AI-assisted language feedback and assessment, foreign language enjoyment, foreign language classroom anxiety, learner autonomy, and perceived control. A cross-sectional survey design was employed with 732 university EFL translation learners who had prior experience using AI-supported language learning tools. Trust also showed indirect effects on learner autonomy and perceived control through emotional pathways. The findings indicate that learners' trust in AI-assisted feedback is associated with both their emotional experiences and agency-related outcomes in AI-mediated EFL learning. These findings provide empirical evidence for understanding the relationships among trust in AI, achievement emotions, learner autonomy, and perceived control in AI-supported language learning environments.

Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory, this 8-month longitudinal case study of a Senior-One English PLC in western Inner Mongolia, China, draws on 51 meeting recordings, reflective journals from one early-career teacher, and interviews with eight PLC members to enable robust analysis of evolving interactions and agency over time. Teacher agency was shaped by multiple contradictions within the PLC, which were experienced differently across career stages. Teachers responded with varied strategies, including covert resistance, active coordination, rational adjustment, passive coping and silent compliance. The study proposes two exploratory constructs: efficacy compensation, where an early-career teacher sought professional worth from self-directed practice when collective recognition was unavailable; and institutional aphasia, the structural silencing of teacher voice under material scarcity, age hierarchy and top-down administration. TI The Impact of GenAI-Integrated Instruction on EFL Learners' Willingness
   to Communicate, Motivation, and Well-Being in Tertiary Education: A
   Mixed-Effects Modelling Approach
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL learners; GenAI-integrated instruction; motivation;
   self-determination theory; tertiary education; well-being; willingness
   to communicate
AB Willingness to communicate (WTC) is recognised as a vital element in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning; however, developing students' WTC in tertiary education is usually a constant challenge. Likewise, improving students' well-being and motivation is equally significant as these constructs support better engagement and successful language achievement among undergraduate students. Despite the quick incorporation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in education, there remains a critical research gap concerning the effect of GenAI-supported instruction on the intersection of learners' well-being, motivational states, and communicative behaviours. Based on Self-determination Theory (SDT), which underscores the significance of meeting students' primary psychological needs, the current research investigates the way GenAI-based teaching can affect EFL students' well-being, motivation, and WTC. The participants were 78 Chinese EFL learners who were assigned to either an experimental group (EXPG) that received GenAI-supported instruction through ChatGPT or a control group (CG) that received conventional instruction. Three assessment points were used to collect data, namely, a pre-test, an instant post-test given at the final stage of intervention, and a delayed post-test done after 10 weeks. Using Mixed-Effects Modelling (MEM), the data were analysed to investigate variations over time and variations between groups. The strongest effect was observed for WTC (d = 1.89), followed by motivation (d = 1.34) and well-being (d = 1.16). The results indicated a significant enhancement in well-being, motivation, and WTC among students within the EXPG in comparison to those within the CG. By offering empirical evidence of its effect on students' emotional, motivational, and communicative experiences in class settings, the present research can contribute to the increasing body of studies on the usage of GenAI in teaching.

TI Intersections of Equitable Sensemaking and Equitable
   Relationship-Building: A Study of Two Elementary Teachers' Science
   Teaching
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE elementary; equity; relationship-building; sensemaking
ID EDUCATION; RELIGION; PEDAGOGY
AB Young students are naturally curious about the world around them. The increasing diversity of elementary classrooms necessitates elementary teachers equitably engage culturally and linguistically diverse students' curiosities through sensemaking and to build relationships with students. However, scientific sensemaking and relationship-building are often treated separately in research and teacher education. Given their close proximity to one another in the work of teaching, we ask, How do equitable relationship-building and equitable scientific sensemaking manifest in two elementary teachers' science teaching? And When a teacher foregrounds opportunities for equitable sensemaking, what effect (if any) does this have on relationship-building? And When a teacher foregrounds equitable relationship-building, what effect (if any) does this have on opportunities for sensemaking? We conducted a comparative case study of two early career elementary teachers who engaged their multilingual learners in making sense of local phenomena. Drawing on video recordings and interviews from two larger qualitative research studies, we conducted a secondary analysis to explore how these two teachers engaged in equitable relationship-building and scientific sensemaking opportunities. We found that opportunities for sensemaking and relationship-building co-occurred, for example when opening up space to hear students' stories. In contrast, at times there were trade-offs when the teachers foregrounded either sensemaking or relationship-building. The teachers also discussed challenges related to district mandates that conflicted with their beliefs about best practices for teaching multilingual learners, as well as uncertainty about how to respond to students' religious beliefs in science, both of which complicated their efforts to build relationships with students and support their sensemaking. We theorize that equitable sensemaking and relationship-building can and do co-occur in spite of being typically studied separately in the literature. As well, we articulate practical implications for how teacher educators can help teachers engage students in equitable scientific sensemaking and relationship-building, while also attending to organizational challenges.

TI A systematic integrative review methodology using phenomenographic
   analysis: bridging empirical and theoretical literature in educational
   research, with an exemplar protocol on educational purpose
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Complexity; Wicked problems; Purpose; Review methodology; Integrative
   review; Phenomenography
ID WICKED PROBLEMS; KNOWLEDGE; TYPOLOGY
AB Educational researchers and policymakers require robust literature review and analysis methodologies capable of engaging with complexity. This paper presents a novel systematic integrative review methodology in tandem with phenomenographic analysis methods to explore diverse concepts, and wicked problems. Traditional approaches to literature reviews may fail to integrate diverse literature types, especially when addressing complex educational phenomena. In addition, the 'difficult to define' aspect of complex concepts that often lie at the heart of wicked problems require appropriate analytic methods. This methodological duo is illustrated in a protocol examining recent literature on the purposes of school-based education (2000-2025). The protocol may support first principles exploration of other wicked problems by mapping diverse bodies of literature and conceptions. The methodology integrates diverse types of literature and uniquely treats research papers as primary data for phenomenographic analysis. It adopts a five-stage framework: problem identification, literature search, data evaluation, analysis, and presentation, and utilises phenomenography as its analytical lens. This research provides effective methods for reviewing diverse literature types while examining phenomenographical dimensions within them. This approach integrates empirical and philosophical insights, recognising that the theoretical frameworks, methodological choices, and contextual factors that shape each study are integral to its contribution to understanding, rather than variables to be controlled or standardised. This methodology significantly informs educational discourse by revealing nuanced complexities through its focus on the qualitatively different ways a phenomenon is experienced, understood and conceptualised, thereby providing researchers and policymakers with a valuable tool for investigating complex educational phenomena.

TI When Attention Fails but Grades Do Not: Attentional Vulnerability, AI
   Compensation, and Resilience in College Students with ADHD
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ADHD; attentional vulnerability; resilience; artificial intelligence;
   compensatory strategies; mind wandering; academic achievement; higher
   education; self-efficacy
ID SELF-EFFICACY; DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; READING-COMPREHENSION;
   BOREDOM PRONENESS; META-AWARENESS; MIND; SCALE; INTELLIGENCE; ANXIETY;
   IMPACT
AB Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) presents substantial challenges in higher education, including elevated mind wandering, difficulties sustaining attention during academic reading, and diminished self-regulatory capacity. Yet, many students with ADHD achieve academic outcomes comparable to their neurotypical (NT) peers, suggesting that protective and compensatory mechanisms may help decouple attentional vulnerability from distal academic achievement. This study examined whether artificial intelligence (AI) tools may function as compensatory support for college students with ADHD and whether resilience is differentially associated with academic success in this population. A sample of 195 engineering students (ADHD = 84, NT = 111) completed self-report measures of trait mind wandering, boredom proneness, self-efficacy, resilience, return-to-focus ability, AI usage and motivation, alongside Raven's Progressive Matrices, an academic reading task with attention probes and comprehension questions, and end-of-semester course grades. Students with ADHD reported significantly greater AI usage than NT students (d = 0.32), despite no significant group differences in cognitive ability or course grades. Hierarchical regression showed that once attentional traits were included, diagnostic group membership no longer accounted for AI usage, indicating that attentional vulnerability, particularly elevated mind wandering, rather than diagnosis per se, may better explain AI usage. Self-efficacy was positively associated with AI usage among students with ADHD but not among NT students, though this group difference was not statistically significant; the pattern is therefore reported as tentative rather than as an established compensatory mechanism. Resilience was lower among students with ADHD than among NT students but was not associated with course grade in either group, and neither resilience nor AI usage was independently associated with course grade once cognitive ability and attentional traits were accounted for. These findings suggest that AI use may reflect compensatory academic adaptation to attentional vulnerability in ADHD. More broadly, the results highlight how attentional vulnerability, self-efficacy, AI-based compensatory strategies, and resilience jointly shape academic outcomes in ADHD and raise questions about how equitable, AI-supported learning environments might be designed in higher education. Because the design is cross-sectional, the present data do not establish that AI use improves academic achievement.

TI Counting on Genre: Exploring Mother-Child Math Talk During Shared
   Reading of Narrative and Information Picturebooks
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE book genre; early numeracy; math talk; preschoolers; mothers
ID MATHEMATICAL LANGUAGE; BOOKS; TEXT; HOME
AB Research shows that parent-child shared reading may create opportunities for early math learning, yet less is known about how reading different picturebook genres, such as narratives and information books, may promote math learning opportunities. Understanding how book genre influences mother-child math talk can help identify additional ways to leverage shared reading to support math development. Therefore, the present mixed-methods study investigated how the shared reading of narrative and information genre picturebooks related to the frequency and nature of mother-child math talk. This study utilized transcripts from 45 mother-child (M = 60.4 months; SD = 6.84) shared reading sessions among English-speaking families in Israel. Each mother-child dyad read two sets of narrative and information books characterized by genre-specific features, which were matched by theme-apples, ice cream, seasons, and animals in winter. Qualitative coding was conducted iteratively with ChatGPT Codex used as an analytic support tool; suggestions for codes including references to counting, numbers, measurement, size, and comparison were proposed and evaluated by the authors. The qualitative analysis yielded four main themes: (1) Math talk prompted by math content that appears in books; (2) Genre-specific characteristics that promote different kinds of math talk; (3) The function of math talk, comprising noticing, explaining, and scaffolding; and (4) The child-led co-construction of math learning. These findings suggest that everyday picturebooks can support mother-child math talk, with genre influencing the mathematical opportunities available and mother-child interactions surrounding these opportunities.

TI Fostering Situated Ethical Awareness in First-Year Engineering Students
   Through Board-Game-Based Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study at Two
   Colombian Universities

DT Article
DE game-based learning; engineering ethics; situated ethical awareness;
   ethical decision-making; Introduction to Engineering; first-year

ID ENGAGEMENT
AB Engineering ethics education faces the challenge of moving students from abstract principles toward context-sensitive decision-making. TI The Role of Communication in Upper Primary Education: A Mixed-Methods
   Study of School Relationships
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE school communication; teacher-student relationship; parent-teacher
   communication; digital; upper primary education; mixed methods
ID CLIMATE
AB This study examined communication practices in an upper primary school, focusing on interactions among students, teachers, and parents, as well as the role of digital communication in shaping these relationships. The study used a mixed-methods design, integrating quantitative questionnaire data with qualitative, semi-structured teacher interviews. The sample comprised 50 students, 50 parents, and 25 teachers. The questionnaires explored the frequency, forms, and perceived quality of communication, while the interviews provided deeper insights into the relational and emotional dimensions of communication. The findings indicate that communication is generally perceived as functional and supportive, although its quality and reciprocity vary across stakeholder groups. Students emphasized the importance of teacher support but noted a need for more frequent, meaningful personal interactions. Parents regarded communication as essential but reported only moderate satisfaction with its quality. Teachers identified limited time and the increasing demands of digital communication as the primary barriers to effective interaction. Based on these findings, despite well-established communication structures, schools should strengthen opportunities for reciprocal engagement and interpersonal interaction while maintaining an appropriate balance between digital and face-to-face communication. The findings contribute to a better understanding of school communication dynamics and offer practical implications for developing more effective, relationship-oriented communication practices in upper primary education.

   Students with ADHD
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gifted education; ADHD; special education
ID SECONDARY-SCHOOL STUDENTS; TALENT DEVELOPMENT; ENRICHMENT; GIFTEDNESS;

AB Twice-exceptional students with ADHD may experience educational challenges related to both their giftedness and their ADHD diagnosis. This article presents a case study with two twice-exceptional students (7. Grade and 10. Grade) and explores their experiences within the educational systems of the United States and Norway. TI Between Participation and Disturbance: Multilingual Repertoires of
   Students in Special Schools for SEBD
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE multilingual repertoires; institutional language orders; social,
   emotional and behavioral development (SEBD); multi-sited ethnography
AB Multilingual students' repertoires are often framed either as resources for participation or as possible sources of difficulty, yet their situated use in special education remains underexamined. This study investigated how students in German special schools for social, emotional and behavioral development (SEBD) mobilized migration-related multilingual repertoires to address practical interactional problems and how situational conditions shaped the functions and consequences of these practices. A multi-sited ethnography was conducted in six SEBD special schools in the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region (North Rhine-Westphalia) between April 2024 and March 2025. Data comprised participant observation, written and talking fieldnotes, and informal ethnographic conversations. They were analyzed through a constant-comparative approach informed by reflexive grounded theory. Six recurring practice types were grouped into four result domains: Participation and Meaning-Making, Relational Positioning and Communicative Accessibility, Affective Mobilization and Counter-Positioning, and Navigation of Institutional Language Orders. Repertoire use had no fixed inclusive, disruptive, or resistant function. Its meaning emerged within interaction and changed with participation structures, public visibility, adult comprehension, and peer responses. In SEBD settings, migration-related linguistic marking and behavioral interpretation could reinforce one another. Multilingual practices should therefore be analyzed sequentially and situationally rather than treated as direct indicators of competence or disturbance.

TI From Stagnation to Renewal: How Principal Leadership Catalyzed Teacher
   Leadership in Early Childhood Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE principal leadership; teacher leadership; teachers' agency;
   instructional practices; professional collaboration
ID SCHOOL LEADERSHIP
AB In increasingly complex and uncertain educational contexts, school leadership is expected to foster improvement while responding to both external pressures and internal organizational challenges. This study examines how principal leadership promoted changes in instructional practice and enabled the emergence of teacher leadership and professional engagement in early childhood education. An instrumental qualitative case study was conducted at an early childhood level of a school in Spain, drawing on semi-structured interviews, a focus group, non-participant observations, and document analysis. The findings show that principal leadership played a catalytic role not through prescriptive actions, but by creating organizational and relational conditions, such as trust, protected time and space, professional learning opportunities, and curricular prioritization, that enabled teachers to redesign practice collaboratively. The establishment of expert groups fostered pedagogical experimentation, professional learning, and knowledge sharing, thereby expanding teachers' agency and leading to the emergence of informal teacher leadership. These processes strengthened professional confidence, ownership, and alignment with the school's educational project. The study concludes that sustainable improvement in complex times depends on integrating principal and teacher leadership by creating a supportive school climate as interdependent, mutually reinforcing forms of influence that build organizational capacity for continuous learning and change.

TI Leading for Improvement: Reimagining School Leadership in Kenya's Public
   Schools
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE communal transformational leadership; decolonized hybridity; agentic
   continuous professional development; collaboration; competency-based
   education
ID EDUCATION; CHALLENGES
AB The transition to Competency-Based Education in Kenya-operationalized through the Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC)-has intensified operational demands on school heads, revealing a systemic misalignment between legacy postcolonial governance structures and 21st-century pedagogical mandates. Drawing on a qualitative, multilevel case design and thematic analysis, this study explores how a purposive sample of participants ( n=8 , comprising classroom teachers, school heads, and Ministry officials) perceive and navigate school leadership practices, teacher agency, and collaborative cultures within their specific institutional contexts. In-depth, semi-structured interviews were conducted to investigate how frontline Continuous Professional Development (CPD) and team-teaching initiatives are negotiated under rigid administrative constraints. The analysis yielded three interconnected themes: contextual leadership efficacy, agentic CPD, and collaborative teaching and learning. The findings illustrate that while macro-policies mandate relational, context-sensitive leadership, inherited bureaucratic architectures frequently default to rigid, top-down compliance models. This clash creates profound structural friction with localized, communal principles such as Harambee (collective pooling) and Ubuntu (shared humanity). To reconcile this tension, this study proposes a theoretical framework of decolonized hybridity-operationalized through a Communal Transformational Leadership (CTL) model. Crucially, however, the study cautions against uncritically institutionalizing Harambee-Ubuntu within hierarchical school structures. Without structural financial backing, operationalizing these frameworks risks turning communal self-reliance into state cost-shifting-forcing teachers to absorb systemic deficits and converting authentic collaboration into coercive labor extraction.

TI Does Laboratory-Theory Assessment Correspondence Differ Across
   First-Year Engineering Degree Cohorts?
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; curricular alignment; entry profiles; laboratory
   learning; academic performance; physics course
AB Laboratory practices in engineering education, and particularly first-year Physics laboratories, are traditionally considered a cornerstone for acquiring technical competencies. However, this study examines whether the correspondence between laboratory and theoretical-exam performance is uniform across student cohorts. We present a quantitative analysis of 477 student performance observations from the Universitat Polit & egrave;cnica de Val & egrave;ncia across three degree programs with different aggregate admission profiles: Telecommunications Engineering (GITST), Agricultural Engineering (GIAMR), and Forestry Engineering (GIFMN). The methodology focuses on thematic course units designed under the established framework of constructive alignment, with GIAMR and GIFMN providing the closest within-study comparison because the same course is taught in both programs by the same teaching staff, with shared laboratory activities and procedures and jointly administered assessments. For GITST, only the laboratory and written partial-exam outcomes corresponding to the Magnetism and Induction thematic unit were analyzed, whereas GIAMR and GIFMN contributed separate assessment pairs for the two thematic units. GIAMR Partial 1 showed a positive association that reached the significance threshold under both Pearson's chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests (OR = 2.53; Pearson p=0.039 ; Fisher p=0.046 ). GIAMR Partial 2, the GITST pairing, and GIFMN Partial 1 showed positive but non-significant associations, whereas GIFMN Partial 2 showed a pronounced inverse descriptive pattern that did not reach the significance threshold under Fisher's exact test ( p=0.062 ). In this study, "curricular decoupling" denotes a weakening or loss of correspondence between laboratory and theoretical-exam outcomes; the observational design does not establish that aggregate entry profiles caused the observed differences.

TI Extending individual language policy of bilingual youths: integrating
   proactive and reactive language management through insights from family
   language policy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE family language policy; heritage language maintenance; individual
   language policy; proactive management; Spolsky's tripartite model
ID IDENTITY; IDEOLOGIES; EDUCATION; SPACES
AB Based on the tripartite model of language policy developed by Spolsky, Nguyen formally introduced the concept of Individual Language Policy (ILP) in 2022 to highlight individual agency. While this framework advanced understanding of how ethnic minority bilingual youths negotiate heritage language maintenance in dominant-language environments, ILP studies have mainly emphasized reactive management-responses to external pressures-while overlooking proactive management theorized in Family Language Policy (FLP) research. Drawing on FLP insights, this paper redefines "management" in ILP to distinguish between reactive management and proactive management-self-initiated construction of linguistic environments. By foregrounding proactive management and clarifying the dynamic relationships among ideology, proactive management, and practice, the framework provides a refined analytical tool for ILP research and offers new directions for multilingual policy research.

Far less is known about whether learners' broader sense of meaning is related to classroom WTC. Drawing mainly on research on meaning in life, enjoyment, and engagement, and treating self-concordance theory only as an exploratory lens, this study examined whether meaning in life was related to L2 classroom WTC among Thai undergraduates, both directly and indirectly through enjoyment and engagement. This cross-sectional study included 301 Thai-speaking undergraduate L2 learners at a public university in Thailand. Hayes' PROCESS Model 6 with 5,000 bootstrap samples showed that meaning in life was positively associated with WTC. Enjoyment and engagement each accounted for part of this association, and the indirect association through both variables in the theory-specified order was significant. Accordingly, the specified ordering should be read as theory-driven rather than temporal. Overall, meaning in life was associated with classroom WTC, with significant indirect associations through enjoyment and engagement. Longitudinal or intervention studies are still needed before causal, temporal, or pedagogical conclusions can be drawn.

TI Place, performance and teacher policy: an exploratory comparative
   institutional analysis of territorial disparities in Portugal
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE comparative institutional analysis; educational equity; PISA 2022;
   Portugal; school context; student achievement; teacher policy;
   territorial disparities
ID PISA; EDUCATION; REGIONS
AB Educational outcomes in Portugal vary across regions, reflecting territorial and socioeconomic disparities. This paper examines how geographic location, regional socioeconomic conditions and school factors are associated with student achievement, using published evidence from PISA and TIMSS, Portuguese empirical studies, regional indicators and policy documents. The analysis combines a targeted narrative review, descriptive analysis of published international-assessment estimates and an exploratory comparative institutional analysis of Madeira and the Azores. PISA 2022 reported that Portugal scored 472 in mathematics, 477 in reading and 484 in science; Madeira recorded 474, 487 and 492, respectively, whereas the Azores recorded 408, 413 and 417. Previous Portuguese research indicates that socioeconomic composition and observable school characteristics account for an important share of regional differences. The Madeira-Azores comparison is interpreted as an exploratory institutional comparison, not as a causal or quasi-experimental test. The study does not estimate the effects of teacher-policy arrangements on student achievement; rather, it identifies hypotheses about how teacher education, professional learning, institutional capacity and wider territorial conditions may interact with regional inequalities. These findings support future research and policy development on context-sensitive approaches to educational equity in geographically peripheral regions.

TI Global and adaptive split conformal prediction for capacity-constrained
   Top-K screening: a methodological evaluation using synthetic
   student performance data
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE auditable decision support; capacity-constrained Top-<italic>K</italic>
   screening; conformal prediction; learning analytics; normalized adaptive
   calibration; postselection validity; synthetic benchmark
AB Introduction Learning analytics models commonly produce predictive scores without specifying how uncertainty should inform prioritization when review capacity is limited.Methods This study developed a reproducible methodological workflow integrating predictive benchmarking, global and normalized adaptive split conformal calibration, hypothetical capacity-constrained Top-K screening, threshold-relative analytical routing, and deterministic audit recording. The workflow was evaluated on a public synthetic student performance benchmark containing 6,607 records, 19 mixed-type predictors, and one numerical examination score outcome. Seven regression models were compared over five repeated 60%/20%/20% train-calibration-test partitions.Results Regularized linear regression produced the most favorable observed mean performance, with a mean absolute error of 0.502 +/- 0.016, a root mean squared error of 2.104 +/- 0.149, a coefficient of determination of 0.713 +/- 0.030, and a Spearman correlation of 0.976 +/- 0.003. Global and adaptive conformal procedures both achieved complete-test empirical marginal coverage close to the nominal 90% level. Across all seven models, adaptive calibration generated record-varying intervals, reduced mean interval width and interval score, increased the mean split-wise minimum coverage across the examined encoded categories, and reduced mean coverage disparity, although several category-level estimates remained below 0.90. The common radius used by global calibration preserved the point-prediction rankings, whereas adaptive scores changed Top-K membership. However, the resulting changes in Precision@K, Capture@K, and FN@K were numerically small at the reported precision and showed no consistent screening advantage. Training-quantile-derived robustness analyses supported the same interpretation.Discussion Within this synthetic benchmark, adaptive calibration contributed primarily through uncertainty differentiation and interval efficiency rather than improved retrospective screening utility. The study demonstrated computational reproducibility and record-level traceability; it did not validate real student screening, establish category- or selection-conditional coverage, or support automated or causal intervention decisions.

TI Between moral panic and moral resilience: professional perceptions of
   value enactment among young adolescents in Malta
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ethics; moral courage; moral panic; moral resilience; values education;
   youth values
AB Public concern about young people's values is frequently framed through narratives of moral decline. This study explores how professionals working with young adolescents in Malta perceive the values and ethical behaviour of young people aged 11-14 and considers the implications for values education. Using an interpretivist qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 19 professionals, including subject education officers, school leaders, psychosocial practitioners and youth organisation representatives. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, generating six interconnected themes. Participants generally perceived young people as recognising ethical principles such as respect, fairness, honesty, responsibility and inclusion, while also reporting considerable inconsistency in their enactment, particularly under pressures associated with belonging, digital environments, consumer culture and fragmented social influences. At the same time, professional accounts contained concrete examples of behaviour interpreted as caring, responsible, inclusive or courageous. The findings therefore suggest a perceived gap between moral recognition and consistent enactment rather than straightforward evidence of moral decline. Moral resilience is proposed tentatively as an interpretive framework for considering the capacities and conditions that may support ethical action under social, emotional and digital pressure. The study argues that values education should complement moral understanding with dialogic, experiential and relational opportunities through which young people can practise ethical judgement and action.

TI Bullying victimization, support networks, and perceived school
   preparedness in Spain: a multi-stakeholder survey study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescence; bullying; childhood; family; teacher-education
ID EXCLUSION; BEHAVIORS
AB Bullying is a significant problem in education, affecting students' academic performance and socio-emotional development. Between 10% and 30% of young people worldwide have experienced it, and the variability of the types of bullying and places where it occurs make it a highly complex educational and social challenge, requiring knowledge of the training available to the entire educational community. The aim of this study was to describe self-reported bullying victimization among surveyed children and adolescents aged 5-18 years, the types and places where it occurs, and the training and perceptions of families and teachers. A descriptive study was conducted, based on quota-based online survey datasets collected between 2019 and 2024. The sample consisted of 6,896 students aged 5-18, 9,181 parents aged 18-65, and 1,334 teachers. Twenty-three percent of surveyed students reported having experienced bullying at some point in their lives. The most common type of bullying was psychological (13.3%), followed by verbal (13.1%), while the most frequent location was the school (57.3%). The main sources of support for victims were family (88.6%) and friends (62.5%). 59.3% of families considered that schools were not sufficiently prepared, while teachers' self-assessments showed a mixed pattern: 39.8% felt quite or very prepared, and 24.2% reported being not prepared or only slightly prepared. The findings indicate a substantial proportion of lifetime self-reported bullying victimization among the surveyed students, with school settings being the most frequently reported context. Despite the important role of teachers as key agents in the prevention and resolution of bullying, perceived preparedness to address these situations could be further strengthened, highlighting the need for comprehensive interventions within teacher training programmes.

AB OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated differences in conference goals and preferred learning modalities across demographic groups at a national surgical conference. TI Awareness and perceptions of career domains among pharmacy students: The
   TECVP (tasks, expertise, compensation, valuation, and prospects)
   framework
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Career awareness; Career perceptions; Pharmacy students; Nonclinical
   career fields; Career information sufficiency
AB Objective: Despite the expansion of pharmacists' roles beyond clinical practice, the career paths of pharmacy graduates remain concentrated in clinical fields. This study aimed to examine awareness and perceptions of career domains among pharmacy students in South Korea and to identify factors associated with their career awareness. Methods: A nationwide cross-sectional online survey among pharmacy students was conducted from September to November 2025. Seven career fields, classified into clinical and nonclinical domains, were evaluated using the Tasks, Expertise, Compensation, Valuation, and Prospects (TECVP) framework, which comprises 10 items across 5 career-attribute categories. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors influencing career awareness. Results: A total of 825 students were included in the final analysis. "Don't know" responses were more frequent in the nonclinical domain than in the clinical domain, particularly for research pharmacists and public service pharmacists. Regarding career perceptions, the clinical domain was rated higher for financial compensation and job security, whereas the nonclinical domain was rated higher for professional expertise and growth opportunity. In regression analysis, students who reported sufficient career information and those with higher family economic status were less likely to demonstrate limited career awareness in both domains. In the nonclinical domain, transfer students were more likely to demonstrate limited career awareness compared to students admitted through early admission. Conclusion: Career awareness among pharmacy students in South Korea showed a marked imbalance between clinical and nonclinical domains. Balanced provision of career information and systematic strengthening of career education for nonclinical fields are needed.

Methods: Students from 2 campuses and each professional year at 1 pharmacy school participated in focus groups exploring factors that influenced their choice of pharmacy school and campus. A consensual qualitative research approach was used for semistructured focus groups and data analysis. A total of 38 students participated in 1 of 7 focus groups. Results: Student choices were influenced by characteristics of the program, such as program prestige, curricular strengths, unique educational opportunities, types of learning communities, faculty accessibility, graduate outcomes, and positive admissions and recruitment experiences. Financial considerations also played an important role in decision-making and included tuition and other costs, the availability of scholarships, and reciprocity agreements with other states. Finally, geographic location contributed to decisions on school and campus choice, including proximity to home and family, familiarity with the schools, geographic ties and pharmacy opportunities in the state, the desire to experience a new area in which to live, and characteristics of the local community. Conclusion: Attributes of geography, financial considerations, and curricular offerings are significant contributors to choice. Conducting focus groups is one way to determine the factors that are most important to pharmacy students and to develop more effective recruiting efforts and tailored investments building on their strengths. In a competitive landscape for enrollment and admissions, understanding the drivers of school and campus choice is critical for schools seeking to attract and retain students.

TI Discrimination in grading? Evidence on teachers' evaluation bias toward
   minority students
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Immigration; Discrimination; Grading bias
ID IMPACT; GIRLS; ME
AB We analyze whether teachers discriminate against ethnic minority students with regard to grading. Using comprehensive data on students in German primary and secondary schools, we compare students' scores on standardized, anonymously graded achievement tests with non-anonymous teacher ratings within a difference-in-differences framework. Although minority students tend to score lower on the standardized test than majority students, this achievement gap is significantly reduced when graded by the teacher. This finding cannot be fully explained by differences in socioeconomic background, language-related differences in standardized test performance, or the sorting of students into educational contexts with different grading standards. Overall, our findings suggest that teachers have a positive evaluation bias toward ethnic minority students.

TI Seeing Eye to Eye During Robotic Training: Do Residents and Faculty
   Agree on Operative Time and Performance Evaluations?
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy; competency; robotic surgery; urology
ID EDUCATION
AB OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize the robotic experience of residents and how their self-reported level of competency and active robotic console time (ARCT) aligned with that of faculty. DESIGN: Survey data were prospectively gathered from index robotic urology cases within a single institution during the 2024 to 2025 academic year from both residents and faculty. Case-related data (perceived difficulty, procedure, etc.), including an estimation of resident ARCT, were recorded. The Zwisch scale of surgical autonomy was used to assess experienced and potential competency for each surgical step (defined a priori). Statistical analysis was performed using chi-squared, two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), Wilcox on rank sum, and Kruskal-Wallis tests as appropriate. SETTING: The University of Kentucky, a tertiary care academic medical center in Lexington, KY. PARTICIPANTS: All residents and faculty within the Urology Department who perform robotic surgery. RESULTS: A total of 64 paired surveys were completed from 10 residents and 6 faculty for robotic radical nephrectomy (n = 10), partial nephrectomy (n = 13), cystectomy with intracorporeal ileal conduit (n = 3), radical prostatectomy (n = 22), and pyeloplasty Funding: None. (n = 16). Junior residents (PGY-2&3) reported overall lower ARCT (20% vs 53%, p < 0.001) and Zwisch scores (2.22 vs 2.73, p = 0.004) than senior residents (PGY-4&5), and those differences were consistent with faculty reported ARCT (30% vs 50%, p < 0.001) and Zwisch scores (2.36 vs 2.75, p < 0.001) for both groups. Across all cases and PGY levels, Zwisch scores and ARCT were similar, regardless of if reported by resident or faculty. Resident reported ARCT was moderately associated with both resident (R = 0.52, p <0.001) and faculty (R = 0.56, p < 0.001) reported Zwisch scores. Resident and faculty reported Zwisch scores were strongly associated with each other (R = 0.71, p < 0.001). However, gaps still exist between resident reported Zwisch scores and where they believe their potential Zwisch score could have been. CONCLUSIONS: Residents and faculty agree on perceived ARCT and resident performance, and these 2 metrics are positively correlated. However, gaps still exist in experienced and potential autonomy of residents demonstrating continued work can be done to optimize the robotic experience to improve competency and ultimately enhance resident's ability to operate independently.

TI Perceptions and Impact of Grief Among Surgical Trainees
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE resident; surgery; trainee; neurosurgery; grief; burnout
ID PHYSICIANS; DEPRESSION
AB INTRODUCTION: Grief is an underrecognized yet pervasive occupational exposure in surgical training. Surgical residents routinely encounter patient death, devastating complications, and ethically complex decisions, often without adequate time or institutional structures to process the emotional consequences. Neurosurgery, in particular, may place trainees at heightened risk given the frequency of catastrophic neurological injury and end-of-life care. This study sought to quantify the prevalence, intensity, and correlates of professional grief among surgical trainees. METHODS: An anonymous, cross-sectional survey was distributed to residents across multiple surgical specialties at a tertiary academic medical center. Participants reflected on experiences from the prior three months. Professional grief was defined as grief occurring in the setting of patient care. Responses were measured using 5-point Likert scales and analyzed across specialties and training levels. RESULTS: Fifty-nine of 194 eligible surgical residents (30%) completed the survey. Overall, 76% of respondents reported experiencing professional grief at least sometimes, often, or daily. Grief-provoking events included traumatic injury, death of long-term patients, and perceived clinical or intraoperative mistakes. Over 75% of residents reported that grief had affected their work at some point, and 40% acknowledged that patient loss had contributed to thoughts of leaving residency. Most residents preferred to discuss grief with co-residents or trusted attendings and 41% had participated in a debrief, nearly all of whom found it helpful. Neurosurgery residents reported significantly higher grief frequency than most other surgical subspecialties and trended toward greater functional impact. CONCLUSIONS: Professional grief is a common and consequential feature of surgical training, with neurosurgery residents bearing a disproportionate burden. Without structured support, unresolved grief may undermine well-being, professional identity, and workforce retention. Culturally embedded, peer-supported debriefing represents a promising strategy to normalize emotional processing and mitigate the cumulative toll of professional grief. ( J Surg Ed 83:104153. LA English
DT Article
DE robotic surgery; general surgery education; curriculum development;
   resident education
AB INTRODUCTION: Robotic-assisted surgery has expanded rapidly in recent years and has become a core component of general surgery resident education and training. A standardized curriculum is needed to guide residency programs and trainees in achieving proficiency and preparedness for independent practice. METHODS: Our program performed an analysis of learners and faculty to create a robotic-assisted surgery curriculum to adopt during general surgery residency training. RESULTS: The curriculum incorporates core tenets of robotic-assisted surgical training including comprehension of the robotic surgery platform, preoperative planning, bedside assistance, and technical proficiency on the console. TI What Works Against Peer Bullying? A Meta-Analysis of School-Based
   Interventions in Türkiye
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer bullying; Victimization; Interventions; Meta-analysis; T &
   uuml;rkiye
ID CYBERBULLYING EVALUATION; AGGRESSIVE-BEHAVIOR; PROGRAM; PREVENTION;
   CHILDREN; STUDENTS; VICTIMS; BIAS
AB Peer bullying remains a persistent global concern with far-reaching implications for students' psychological, social, and academic development. While numerous interventions have been developed to address this issue, their effectiveness within culturally specific contexts warrants further investigation. This meta-analysis synthesizes 35 empirical studies conducted in T & uuml;rkiye, encompassing 1,534 participants aged 4 to 17. Using a random-effects model, the findings indicate that intervention programs are associated with reductions in bullying (ES = 0.78) and victimization (ES = 0.74) and improvements in social skills (ES = 0.62) and well-being (ES = 0.83), although effects varied across studies and should be interpreted in light of between-study heterogeneity. Exploratory moderator analyses suggested that effects were associated with educational level and participant type for bullying, and with theoretical background for victimization; however, these subgroup patterns should be interpreted cautiously given the limited number of studies in some categories and the fact that moderators were examined in separate models. In exploratory univariable meta-regression analyses, session duration was associated with bullying effect sizes, whereas the number of sessions was not. These results underscore the importance of developing comprehensive, theoretically informed, and culturally responsive anti-bullying strategies, while also suggesting potential mechanisms and boundary conditions that may inform the adaptation of such interventions beyond the Turkish context.

TI Changes in students' well-being over time: a longitudinal approach
   spanning from lower to upper secondary education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Well-being; Mental health; Compulsory education; Upper secondary
   education; Gender; Academic achievement
ID HEALTH COMPLAINTS; SOCIAL ORIGINS; FIT INDEXES; ADOLESCENCE;
   ACHIEVEMENT; SCHOOL; DETERMINANTS; ATTAINMENT
AB The study aimed to investigate how students' social well-being and mental health developed from the age of 12 to 19. Reports from Swedish authorities and research have shown that students' self-reported well-being has decreased during the last decade, but few studies have examined longitudinal changes during primary and upper secondary school. Longitudinal questionnaire data from the Swedish project Evaluation Through Follow-up was analysed with growth modelling within the structural equation modelling environment. The sample was drawn from the cohort of students born in 2004 (N = 9,437). By using data from three time-points (Grades 6, 9, and 12), the development in well-being within individuals over time could be investigated. Besides, grade point average (GPA) from sixth grade, parental education, and gender were included as covariates. Social well-being at school declined over time, while emotional distress and psychosomatic symptoms increased, including sadness, irritation, stomach aches, headaches, and sleeping difficulties. Girls reported lower social contentment than boys and consistently experienced more emotional and physical health problems, with some differences widening over time. Students from families with lower parental education also reported higher levels of emotional distress and psychosomatic ill-being than those from more highly educated families. Overall, girls and students from lower-education backgrounds appear especially vulnerable to declining well-being.

TI From Compliance to Co-Production: Developing a Sector-Informed Equality
   Impact Analysis Framework for Inclusive Governance in Higher Education
SO HIGHER EDUCATION QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE co-production; equality; governance; impact assessment; inclusivity
AB Equality Impact Assessments (EqIAs) in higher education are often perceived as bureaucratic exercises rather than tools for transformative change. This paper presents research on the existing use of EqIAs across Britain, including key challenges, and an exploration of the value of the coproduction of EqIAs. It utilises the findings to inform the contribution of an evidence-based, holistic and context-driven framework. Research underpinning this paper explores how participatory approaches can reposition EqIAs from compliance-driven processes towards inclusive governance. This paper draws on multi-phase qualitative research with marginalised voices and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) leads across England, Scotland and Wales. Findings reveal widespread inconsistency in EqIA application, limited integration into institutional strategy and perceptions of disproportionate burden. Core barriers to effective use include insufficient resources, poor understanding among decision-makers and tokenistic consultation with marginalised communities. Conversely, the evidence highlights the potential of co-production to embed lived experience, foster accountability and strengthen meaningful impact analysis. The consequent Equality Analysis Framework, underpinned by the research, calls for simplified, proportionate and context-sensitive approaches that seek to mainstream EqIAs into institutional decision-making and risk assessment. The Framework emphasises the need for institutional capacity building, early engagement, and power sharing with staff, students and community stakeholders to ensure EqIAs are cultural enablers rather than procedural hurdles. While developed primarily for the English HE sector, the Framework offers wider applicability across sectors and nations as a means of moving beyond performative equality towards authentic values-driven transformation. The success of this reimagined approach will depend on sustained leadership commitment, adequate resourcing, and willingness to embed co-production as a catalyst for systemic change.

TI 'We're cannibalising each other': a case study of teacher turnover in
   hard-to-staff schools
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Hard-to-staff; Turnover; Teachers' work; Retention; Recruitment
ID MATHEMATICS; SHORTAGES
AB In this paper, we present a case study of hard-to-staff secondary schools to examine teacher turnover in Australia. The paper draws on interviews with teachers and school leaders to explore issues related to turnover, an aspect of workforce instability that is less recognised in discussions of the Australian teaching workforce. We situate this analysis within the broader context of education marketisation to consider the implications for disadvantaged schools in the context of widespread teacher shortages. We map the dynamics of localised experiences of turnover, highlighting the impacts of marketisation on the teaching workforce through increasing competition between schools for teachers, the ongoing process of continuous recruitment, and the complexities of teacher retention in hard-to-staff schools. We demonstrate how this cycle of constant staff replacement not only disrupts school stability and social relationships but also places additional strain on remaining teachers and leaders, creating unsustainable working environments that further drive turnover contributing to increasingly stratified working conditions for teachers across different school contexts.

TI Integrating Machine Learning Into Environmental Engineering Education:
   Design, Implementation, and Outcomes of an Interdisciplinary Course
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE environmental engineering; interdisciplinary course; machine learning
ID SOFT SKILLS; THINKING
AB As global environmental challenges intensify, engineering education increasingly requires approaches that integrate computational methods with interdisciplinary collaboration. This paper presents the design, implementation, and outcomes of a 5-day intensive machine learning course tailored to civil and environmental engineering students and professionals with diverse backgrounds. The course integrated foundational machine learning concepts with hands-on applications using real-world environmental datasets from Uruguay. It was designed to support competencies relevant to interdisciplinary engineering practice, including the integration of environmental reasoning with data-driven modeling and collaboration across diverse disciplinary backgrounds. Using Google Colab notebooks, students explored data preprocessing, supervised and unsupervised learning, and data analysis in an interactive, collaborative environment. Interdisciplinary teamwork was a core feature, enabling diverse perspectives to be brought to bear on solving environmental problems. The course outcomes were examined through three complementary perspectives: the instructors' assessment of how the design functioned in practice, the academic results from the final projects, and the students' perceptions gathered through a post-course survey. Particular attention was given to how collaborative projects and practice-oriented activities supported the integration of computational tools into environmental reasoning, while fostering interdisciplinary interaction among students with different academic backgrounds. These perspectives suggest that carefully designed, practice-oriented sessions can help students engage with computational thinking, create conditions for meaningful cross-disciplinary collaboration, and raise awareness of sustainability challenges. Beyond assessing a single course, the analysis identifies key strengths, such as improved collaboration and contextualized learning, as well as challenges, including disparities in prior knowledge and technical preparedness. These findings offer concrete lessons for future implementations and provide a replicable framework for embedding machine learning in engineering curricula, better preparing students for complex environmental challenges.

TI Teacher Agency: Finding Spaces to Transform ELA Classrooms
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
AB Amid ongoing attacks on teachers and their professionalism, we studied three middle school ELA teachers who exercised their agency to transform their classrooms and curricula through social justice pedagogy (SJP). Using Panti & cacute;'s (2017) model, we examined their sense of purpose, competence, autonomy, and reflexivity in confronting barriers. TI When inclusion meets the curriculum: How students with and without SEN
   in Croatia see their teachers' inclusive practices
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Croatia; inclusive education; inclusive teaching practices; special
   educational needs; student perceptions
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; EFFICACY; DIFFERENTIATION; EDUCATION; INSTRUCTION;
   CLASSROOMS; IMPACT
AB This study examines lower secondary students' perceptions of inclusive teaching practices in Croatia, with a focus on personalisation and differentiation. It also evaluates the psychometric properties and measurement invariance of the Croatian version of the Inclusive Teaching Practices Scale-Students' version (ITPS-S). The sample comprised 1317 sixth- and seventh-grade students, including students with and without special educational needs (SEN). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the expected two-factor structure of the ITPS-S, and the scale demonstrated strong reliability and full measurement invariance across SEN status, gender, grade level and partial invariance across subject domain (Croatian language & Mathematics). Overall, students reported moderate use of inclusive practices, indicating that personalisation and differentiation are present but not yet implemented intensively. No differences were found between students with SEN and their peers or between genders. However, younger students perceived higher levels of inclusive practices than older students. Additionally, Croatian language teachers were rated as using inclusive practices more frequently than Mathematics teachers, particularly in differentiation. Results highlight the need for strengthening the implementation of inclusive teaching strategies across subjects. Implications for teacher education and professional support are discussed, emphasising the importance of enhancing teachers' competencies in differentiation and personalisation to address diverse student needs.

TI Understanding teacher recruitment and retention across the UK: A 'home
   international' comparison
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE home international comparison; recruitment; retention; teacher supply
ID SOCIAL-CLASS; ENGLAND; WALES
AB A persistent and pressing issue for education policymakers is the need to ensure a reliable supply of high-quality staff within schools. Teacher shortages are a well-documented phenomenon in England, with clear indications of some issues in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too. The extent to which the teacher recruitment and retention landscape is similar or different across each of the UK nations though is an under-researched area, and one which has clear implications for how these issues are addressed in policy. This study presents a novel and significant contribution to the teacher supply literature by sharing findings from a large-scale comparative analysis of policy, secondary data, and interviews with key stakeholders from across the four countries. Theoretically, it also highlights the value of adopting a 'home-international' comparison approach, drawing from the work of Raffe et al. (Comparative Education, 1999, 35, 9) and extending this to contemporary contexts and challenges. Our findings particularly point to the complex and often uneven teacher supply situation across and within nations. They also foreground the diverse policy approaches that we see across the UK, including strategies for improving recruitment, varying teacher training routes, and approaches to early career support and development. A key commonality, however, is the limited evidence base for determining and implementing policy interventions and reforms. Our study concludes by calling for a more joined-up approach to tackling teacher supply issues across the UK, one that recognises country-specific contexts and challenges where relevant but is also characterised by shared expertise, evidence, and collaboration across the four nations.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Ensuring an adequate supply of effective teachers in schools is a persistent global issue. The United Kingdom (UK) has faced challenges with teacher shortages for many years, despite some policy interventions designed to improve the situation. Why the new findings matter: This four nations, mixed-methods analysis highlights the uneven situation for teacher supply across the UK and the diversity of policy interventions used to tackle teacher shortages. The findings also signal the urgent need for improved data accessibility in some jurisdictions in order to better understand the recruitment and retention challenges faced and the reforms needed to address these. Implications for policymakers and researchers: Addressing teacher shortages requires strategies that are responsive to issues found within each nation. Further though, we also argue that there is a rationale for a more UK-wide 'joined-up' approach, identifying where effective approaches could be adopted and adapted to tackle common recruitment and retention issues. The study highlights the importance of evaluating the effectiveness of existing policy interventions and strengthening collaboration across jurisdictions to share evidence and best practice. Improved access to high-quality, comparable workforce data are also essential to support informed decision-making, monitor trends, and assess policy impact.

TI The criticality of effective teacher-student relationships when working
   with students with dyslexia
SO SUPPORT FOR LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE dyslexia; mathematics; maths anxiety; mindset; self-efficacy theory
ID SELF-EFFICACY; MATHEMATICS; CHILDREN; VOICE
AB This paper explores the critical role of teacher-student relationships in supporting learners with dyslexia, with a particular focus on mathematics. Through a mixed-methods approach, the research included 10 participants aged 10 to 50+, each engaged in 35 one-to-one mathematics lessons. The research investigated how relational dynamics influence self-belief, mindset and academic engagement. Data from pre/post exam papers, Q-sort, interviews, drawings and reflective journals showed the damaging impact of negative teacher interactions. Ridicule, indifference or denial of dyslexia can reinforce fixed mindsets, heightened maths anxiety and reduced self-efficacy. Conversely, positive relationships built on empathy, encouragement and trust enabled learners to reframe their self-perceptions, develop resilience and achieve measurable gains in mathematical understanding. The findings showed that effective teaching for students with dyslexia extends far beyond content delivery. It relies on relationships that build emotional safety, show belief in students' potential and challenge negative viewpoints. It also demonstrated how the most powerful driver of success was not a specialist intervention or resource, but the quality of the teacher-student relationship. When teachers combine strong subject knowledge with empathy and belief in the student, they enable students to reframe dyslexia. This changes dyslexia from a perceived weakness into a source of resilience and strength.

TI A two-part hybrid session for teaching cardiac and venous function
   curves
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cardiac and venous curves; cardiovascular physiology; case-based
   scaffolding; graphical reasoning; hybrid session
ID MISCONCEPTIONS; LEARN
AB Cardiac and venous function curves can be challenging for first-year medical students, especially when abstract concepts are presented without opportunities to apply them. To address this, we implemented a simple two-part hybrid session combining a brief conceptual foundation with guided clinical case discussions. In the first 30 min, students reviewed core curve relationships through instructor-led questioning and visual representations. The remaining time focused on small-group and whole class analysis of a small set of clinical scenarios, where students predicted curve shifts and explained their reasoning. The cases were sequenced from simple to more complex situations to scaffold students' understanding and support progressive integration of concepts. The structure promoted active participation, frequent check-ins for understanding, and clearer links between physiology and clinical findings. The approach was easy to deliver, required minimal resources, and generated strong engagement. This Illumination article shares the session format so others may adapt it.
