TI Universal Access by Design: Archetypal Inquiry & Reflexive Approaches
   for Enriched Learner Experiences
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Universal Design for Learning; inclusive education; design-based
   research; reflexive practice; narrative identity; learner variability;
   teacher education; professional learning
AB Universal Design for Learning (UDL) has advanced inclusive education by positioning learner variability as an anticipated condition of instructional design and emphasizing the proactive reduction of barriers. Yet, structural accessibility alone does not fully explain how learners and educators experience belonging, construct identity, exercise agency, or translate lived experience into pedagogical decision-making. This study examines how these interpretive dimensions of learning may extend existing approaches to inclusive educational design. Using a Phase I exploratory Design-Based Research methodology, the study investigated the reflexive and pedagogical experiences of 20 leaders of learning working across educator preparation, professional learning, and school-based instructional contexts in the United States. Participants included 12 faculty leaders facilitating graduate-level or professional learning experiences and 8 teacher leaders engaged in school-based instructional practice. The inquiry was designed for conceptual development rather than intervention validation, examining how authentic professional experiences could inform the emergence of an identity-responsive framework for inclusive educational design. Prototypical Narration Surfacing and Synthesis served as the interpretive methodology through which lived experience was surfaced, interpreted, and synthesized across participant narratives, instructional artifacts, observation records, coaching documentation, and portfolio evidence. Narrative inquiry, thematic analysis, iterative coding, and cross-context interpretation supported the identification of recurring developmental patterns. Findings indicated that professional growth extended beyond the acquisition of discrete instructional competencies and was experienced as an interconnected process of identity development, belonging, self-efficacy, professional agency, and pedagogical reasoning. Across faculty leaders and teacher leaders, reflexive interpretation increasingly informed intentional instructional decision-making and more responsive approaches to learner variability. Cross-context synthesis further revealed recurring developmental orientations related to challenge, agency, belonging, identity, and transformation. These patterns contributed to the emergence of Archetypal Inquiry as a provisional, anti-reductionist interpretive lens rather than a predetermined participant classification system. The iterative synthesis of: (a) structural accessibility, (b) lived experience, (c) reflexive interpretation, (d) pedagogical reasoning, and (e) contextual responsiveness, subsequently informed Universal Access by Design, an emerging Phase I conceptual framework for identity-responsive inclusive education. The study suggests that inclusive educational design may be strengthened when UDL's structural commitments are complemented by attention to how learners and leaders interpret experience, construct identity, and continually redesign educational environments in response to emerging evidence. Universal Access by Design is therefore offered not as a replacement for UDL or as a validated intervention, but as a provisional framework and foundation for continued Design-Based Research, implementation, and empirical refinement across diverse educational settings.

TI Academic Well-Being as Transition Work: First-Semester Students'
   Navigation in a Problem-Based Learning University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE academic well-being; transition to higher education; problem-based
   learning; first-semester students; teamwork; student belonging
AB Academic well-being is often examined as an individual condition or support need, but less is known about how students construct well-being during transition into demanding pedagogical environments. This qualitative study explores how first-semester students in a Danish Problem-Based Learning (PBL) university understood and sustained academic well-being. Semi-structured interviews with 17 students from health-related and engineering/technology-related programs were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings show that academic well-being was experienced as transition work: students made academic demands meaningful through relevance and purpose, developed confidence through emerging competence, negotiated support and vulnerability in teamwork, and managed autonomy within pedagogical and institutional structures. The study contributes to higher education research by showing how academic well-being emerges through interactions among intrapersonal resources, peer collaboration, and learning environments. It argues that transition support in PBL contexts should scaffold autonomy, collaboration, belonging, and academic meaning-making rather than treating well-being as an individual student responsibility alone.

TI Assessing Learning Progression in a Vehicle Dynamics Course Using a
   Rubric-Based, GenAI-Assisted Open-Ended Approach
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative Artificial Intelligence; learning assessment; experiential
   learning; simulation-based learning; cognitive level
ID EDUCATION; SIMULATOR; PLATFORM
AB This study introduces a formative assessment approach for examining changes in cognitive demand across student responses using open-ended questions and rubric-based evaluation. The method is designed for small cohorts and emphasizes instructional refinement across predefined cognitive levels. It integrates Generative AI to support rubric application, scoring consistency, and identification of response patterns without replacing instructor judgment or established assessment practices. The approach addresses challenges in specialized programs with low enrollment, where large-scale statistical designs may be impractical, particularly in rapidly evolving fields such as automotive engineering. The methodology was applied in a vehicle dynamics course with 19 students, self-assigned to 6 teams of similar size by selecting an available slot; teams were then allocated to one of two learning paths by team number, in which the same activities were delivered in reversed order in a crossover design combining simulation-based and experiential activities. Assessments were aligned with Bloom's taxonomy and ABET outcomes. Four Generative AI models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT o4-mini, DeepSeek, and GPT-4o-mini) were used to support scoring under rubric and prompting procedures defined by an experienced instructor. Overall, inter-model agreement was moderate (Krippendorff's alpha=0.666 ). This value did not meet the reference criterion of 0.7 adopted in the study and indicates meaningful model-dependent variation in rubric application. Within this limitation, task-level performance indicators showed a shift toward higher cognitive demand, particularly at the application level, with responses moving from conceptual definition toward early analysis. The approach also surfaced learning gaps that informed instructional adjustments, supporting its potential as a diagnostic tool for continuous improvement in engineering education.

TI Ethical principles and cybersecurity dimensions shaping cybersecurity
   behavior in the metaverse
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Metaverse; Cybersecurity behavior; Higher education institutions;
   PLS-SEM; Ethical principles; Cybersecurity dimensions
ID SECURITY CHALLENGES
AB This study aims to examine how ethical principles and cybersecurity dimensions shape cybersecurity behavior in the Metaverse among university students in Oman. A conceptual framework was proposed that integrate ethical principles constructs (Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Autonomy) with cybersecurity dimensions (Availability, Authenticity, Confidentiality, and Integrity). Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey from 477 metaverse users in Omani higher educational institutions (HEI) using an online survey. Data analysis was conducted using PLS-SEM to examine and validate the proposed model. The results shows that cybersecurity behavior was signifyingly influenced by Autonomy, Accountability, Authenticity, Transparency and Availability, in their order of influencing the power and explained 62.7% of the variance in cybersecurity behavior. Contrary to expectations, Confidentiality, Fairness and Integrity did not have an influence on cybersecurity behavior. The findings are expected to inform policy development, institutional cybersecurity strategies, and aid in developing digital literacy skills to guide the ethical and secure adoption of immersive platforms in Omani higher education.

TI Remote parent coaching in preschool mathematics: Evidence from Peru
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Preschool learning; Education technologies; Interactive radio
   instruction; Parent engagement
AB We evaluate a 10-week intervention in Peru that randomly offered remote coaching to parents of preschool children during the 2021 summer break, complementing publicly available mathematics lessons delivered by broadcast media. Coaches provided guidance and encouragement through phone calls, SMS, and printed materials designed to increase mathematics-related parent-child interactions. We find positive effects on mathematics achievement of approximately 0.10 standard deviations, although statistical significance is sensitive to conservative adjustments for multiple hypothesis testing, particularly when mathematics and oral comprehension are jointly evaluated. We do not find clear evidence of improvements in oral comprehension. By contrast, we document important and precisely estimated increases in mathematics-related parental engagement, including more time spent on targeted activities, greater participation in mathematics games, and more mathematicsfocused tutoring. These findings suggest that light-touch remote coaching can shift parental inputs and may translate into gains in early numeracy.

TI Information for vision: Experimental evidence on nudging low-income
   students to wear eyeglasses
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Information nudge; Vision health; Behavioral mechanism; Decision-making
ID EDUCATION; CHILDREN; SPECTACLES; BARRIERS; PROGRESS; HEALTH; POLICY; HIV
AB Inaccurate information and biased beliefs about myopia and glasses-wearing can lead to low take-up of eyeglasses among myopic students. This paper provides experimental evidence on behavioral barriers affecting students' belief updating and stated preferences regarding glasses-wearing. We conducted a lab-in-the-field experiment with 8262 middle school students in a remote, underdeveloped county in China to test four targeted information nudges. Among myopic students without glasses, information on glasses prices and the short-term academic benefits of wearing glasses was most effective. The nudges worked by updating beliefs or increasing the salience of myopia and glasses-wearing, with substantial heterogeneity by myopia duration, academic performance, and peer groups. Cost-benefit analysis shows that targeted nudges remain cost-effective even under conservative take-up assumptions. Our results provide evidence of the importance of precise, personalized information nudges in improving students' educational input and academic achievement.

TI Childhood spatial skills and adolescent STEM achievement in maths and
   science: The role of visuospatial working memory
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic achievement; Longitudinal cohort study; Spatial skills; STEM;
   Visuospatial working memory
ID MISSING-DATA; MATHEMATICS ACHIEVEMENT; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; MENTAL
   ROTATION; SCHOOL-CHILDREN; ABILITY; METAANALYSIS; PERFORMANCE;
   PREDICTORS; KNOWLEDGE
AB Background: Existing evidence suggests that there are robust associations between spatial skills and achievement in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Maths) subjects and occupations. However, there are knowledge gaps regarding underlying processes: the role of visuospatial working memory (VSWM), whether associations observed in childhood extend to adolescence and whether findings regarding maths extend to sciences. Aims: Drawing on the developmental cascades framework, this study extends the existing literature by examining the connections between childhood spatial skills and adolescent STEM achievement in maths and science and whether VSWM mediates them. Sample: The Millennium Cohort Study was linked to the National Pupil Database to create a longitudinal dataset spanning nearly a decade of cognitive skills and STEM achievement measurements for a sample broadly representative of England's population (N = 8814). Method: Age 16 Maths and Science achievement were adapted from English national examination (GCSEs) results and were included in path analyses with Age 7 Spatial Skills and Age 11 VSWM as predictors. Results: Direct effect analyses demonstrated that participants with stronger spatial skills at age 7 also had higher academic achievement in both maths and science at age 16. Indirect analyses suggested this effect was mediated by VSWM at age 11. Models accounted for early maths skills. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the long-term associations between early childhood spatial skills and VSWM and their links to adolescent STEM achievement in a large-scale, nationally representative sample. These findings can inform the design of interventions and educational practices that foster positive STEM outcomes with benefits that extend across the lifespan.

TI At the intersection of policy and digital tools: Boundary work and
   professional identity among Chinese schoolteachers and shadow-education
   tutors under the double reduction policy
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher professional identity; Boundary work; Shadow education; Double
   reduction policy; Digital tools; China
ID TEACHER IDENTITY
AB China's Double Reduction Policy (DRP) restricts private tutoring and expands school-based after-school services. At the same time, digital and AI-supported tools are changing how teachers organise, monitor, and justify their work. These forces are usually studied separately. Based on semi-structured interviews with 24 educators in Sichuan (12 schoolteachers and 12 shadow-education tutors), this reflexive thematic analysis examines how policy and tool-mediated work jointly reshape professional identity through boundary work. The findings show three linked processes. First, DRP makes legitimacy more visibly graded across tenured teachers, non-tenured teachers, and tutors. Second, AI-supported systems and broader digital tools generate different forms of checking, monitoring, and replaceability anxiety. Third, participants use policy language and tool talk to claim legitimacy, compliance, and human judgement under unequal risk exposure. The study contributes to international debates on regulation, digitalisation, and teacher identity.

TI Associations of emotional intelligence and job crafting with EFL teacher
   work engagement: The statistical mediating role of mindfulness
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Job crafting; Emotional intelligence; Mindfulness; Work engagement; EFL
   teachers
ID VARIANCE; AWARENESS
AB This study examined how job crafting, emotional intelligence (EI), and mindfulness relate to English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' work engagement. Structural equation modeling (SEM) results showed that job crafting and EI were positively associated with work engagement, and mindfulness was positively associated with it while also mediating both associations in the primary model. However, a common-latent-factor sensitivity analysis controlling for common-method variance indicated that this support was asymmetric: whereas the indirect pathway through job crafting remained significant, the indirect pathway through EI did not. These findings suggest that job crafting relates to higher engagement partly through an indirect pathway involving mindfulness. Conversely, the corresponding pathway for EI is more sensitive to shared method variance, warranting cautious interpretation. The study advances current theorization on teacher engagement by integrating behavioral, emotional, and attentional resources within a unified structural model, though its cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation. Tentative implications are discussed.

TI AI-Enhanced Economic Simulations for International Business Education:
   Impact on Learning Outcomes in Colombian Universities
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
LA English
DT Article
DE Economic literacy; international business education; ChatGPT; AI
   simulations; business education
AB This study examines whether generative-AI-supported economic role simulations improve conceptual understanding in undergraduate International Business education. The manuscript was revised to clarify the educational problem: International Business students must use economic literacy to reason about market entry, pricing, investment risk, supply chains, and competitive structure, yet many struggle to connect abstract economic concepts to realistic cross-border business decisions. A quasi-experimental longitudinal design compared 79 Colombian International Business students in intact class sections over two academic semesters. The experimental group completed structured ChatGPT-supported simulations, while the comparison group completed the same scenarios through instructor-led discussion and peer role-play. Outcomes included economic concept assessment scores, coded argumentation quality, and computational indicators of interaction quality. Mixed linear models indicated larger learning gains in the AI-supported group than in the comparison group. Mediation analysis suggested that improvements in economic argumentation partly explained the intervention effect, while dialogue turns, TF-IDF-weighted lexical diversity, and LDA C_v topic coherence were associated with stronger posttest performance among students using ChatGPT. Because the sample was modest and assignment occurred at class-section level, the findings are interpreted as promising but not definitive.

   its elements and dimensions
SO ASSESSMENT IN EDUCATION-PRINCIPLES POLICY & PRACTICE

ID TEACHER ASSESSMENT LITERACY; HIGHER-EDUCATION; SELF-ASSESSMENT;
   FEEDBACK; TENSIONS; LEARNER; BELIEFS; AGENCY
AB With the shift towards learner-centred assessment, students are increasingly positioned as active participants in assessment as learning. TI A missing player: the absence of Indigenous video games in schools
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous video games; Indigenous perspectives; Digital classrooms;
   Educational games; Scoping review
ID EDUCATION; IMPACT
AB Whilst the use of video games in education is not an innovative field of study, the use of Indigenous video games is. Understanding how, and if, Indigenous developed video games are used in classrooms can aid in the identification of support for teachers and the benefits for students, particularly regarding colonial and decolonial discourse. Research in this space is limited, highlighting a significant gap in the literature. A two-stage scoping review of research regarding the application of Indigenous video games in schools was undertaken which also identified communities leading the way in this space. The analysis of captured literature identified North America, Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Australia yielded the most results in the use of Indigenous video games in education. A common theme amongst the research demonstrated the prevalence of settler colonial narratives within video games, and how Indigenous-made video games were pushing back against this rhetoric. These findings highlight the need for Indigenous-made video games to be used more widely within education to prompt critical thinking in students, especially in reference to colonial discourse in digital spaces. Additionally, due to curriculum priorities within settler colonies, Indigenous video games provide a way to incorporate Indigenous voices in classrooms.

LA English
DT Article

ID SOCIAL INTERDEPENDENCE THEORY; CHATGPT
AB This study investigates the impact of teacher-facilitated generative artificial intelligence (AI) lesson plans on students' collaborative learning, attitudes towards science and academic performance in a sixth-grade science course. TI Distinct or similar? Career choice motivation in preservice special
   education and secondary school teachers
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE career choice motivation; latent mean analysis; preservice special
   education teachers; special education; teacher education
ID MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE; STUDENTS; ASPIRATIONS; ACHIEVEMENT; COMMITMENT
AB Career choice motives play a central role in teacher development, professional commitment and retention. Although special education is often assumed to attract individuals with strong pedagogical and altruistic motives and lower extrinsic orientations, empirical evidence is inconsistent. This study examines whether preservice special education teachers in Germany differ systematically in their career choice motives from preservice secondary school teachers. Data were drawn from two samples in Baden-W & uuml;rttemberg, Germany: 703 preservice special education teachers and 1012 preservice secondary school teachers. Career choice motives were assessed using self-reports. After establishing the factorial validity and partial scalar invariance, latent mean analyses were conducted controlling for age and gender. Preservice special education teachers reported higher self-efficacy and lower instrumental motives than preservice secondary school teachers. No group differences emerged for pedagogical interest. Unexpectedly, preservice special education teachers reported higher subject-related interest. Social influences did not differ between groups. Findings suggest that preservice special education teachers do not exhibit a uniform motivational pattern but rather a hybrid configuration of motivational orientations that combines theoretically expected and unexpected elements. The results highlight the need for refined motivational models and further longitudinal research.

TI Reclaiming Critical Consciousness: Literacy for Digital Oppression
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
ID MULTILITERACIES; EDUCATION; RETHINKING; TEACHERS
AB Digital information landscapes and communication platforms are controlled by algorithmic curation and polarized content that serve larger societal systems. The need for a reimagined approach to literacy education has never been more urgent. Drawing on Freire's foundational concepts of critical consciousness, dialogic pedagogy, and the rejection of the banking model, this paper defines and sustains digital oppression or the ways digital platforms reproduce prescriptive, extractive relationships between institutions and users and offers key instructional strategies organized around resisting it. This analysis examines how youth engagement with digital texts requires pedagogies that are experiential, dialogic, and attuned to power, identity, and meaning-making. By situating literacy as a tool for empowerment, resistance, and transformation, this paper calls for a renewed commitment to critical pedagogy as both the "word" and the "world" are increasingly mediated by digital infrastructures. It concludes with a call to educators and researchers to co-construct emancipatory practices that support young people in becoming critically literate agents capable of remaking their social realities.

TI "I learned a lot, but…": preservice elementary teachers' integrated STEM
   teaching self-efficacy and perceived challenges
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Integrated STEM; Self-efficacy; Preservice teacher education; STEM
   challenges
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; SCIENCE; BELIEFS; TECHNOLOGY; CONFIDENCE;
   EDUCATION; ATTITUDES; IMPLEMENTATION; MATHEMATICS; STANDARDS
AB Background Recent K-12 education reforms emphasize integrated STEM (iSTEM) instruction to prepare young learners for interdisciplinary careers. However, elementary teachers often find iSTEM teaching challenging, partly due to limited emphasis on iSTEM training in teacher preparation programs. As a relatively new and evolving field, there remains a limited understanding of the challenges that preservice elementary teachers (PSTs) perceive and how these influence their iSTEM teaching self-efficacy. This mixed-methods exploratory concurrent research addresses this gap in the literature by investigating changes in PSTs' self-efficacy and perceived challenges at the beginning and end of their science or STEM methods coursework. Data were collected from 465 PSTs across five institutions in the United States using the Self-Efficacy for Teaching Integrated STEM instrument (SETIS) and an open-ended questionnaire.Results Multivariate analysis of variance and paired t-tests revealed significant positive gains in iSTEM teaching self-efficacy, while McNemar tests indicated a significant decrease in overall perceived challenges by the end of the semester. Qualitative content analysis identified six major categories of perceived challenges: (1) teacher affect and experience, (2) student-related concerns, (3) content and curricular challenges, (4) pedagogical challenges, (5) support from others, and (6) time and resources. Structural equation modeling results showed a significant negative effect for the challenge related to lack of science or STEM content knowledge, with lower SETIS scores among those reporting this concern on the post-survey. In contrast, the challenge of technology access had a significant positive effect, suggesting that PSTs with higher SETIS scores were more likely to identify this concern.Conclusions The overall gains in PSTs' iSTEM teaching self-efficacy highlight the potential benefits of methods coursework, whether these experiences are situated within science methods coursework or a designated STEM semester with multiple STEM-themed methods courses. PSTs reported fewer challenges at the end compared to the beginning of the semester, suggesting that participation in science or STEM methods coursework alleviated, though did not entirely eliminate, some concerns. Recognizing perceived challenges can better prepare PSTs for iSTEM instruction and help reduce future surprises. Accordingly, these findings offer valuable implications for PST preparation in iSTEM coursework and future research.

TI Emotion and Writing in Primary School-Aged Children: Writing Attitudes,
   Writing Ability and Wellbeing
SO LITERACY
LA English
DT Article

   wellbeing; writing

AB Previous research has shown that the 'will' to write (children's motivations and feelings about writing) is associated with the 'skill' or ability to write; although, the nature of this relationship across primary schooling remains unclear. There is also a paucity of research into how children's general emotional wellbeing relates to writing attitudes and ability. This study examined differences in wellbeing, writing attitudes and writing ability across Years 3-6 and the associations between these variables. Educational implications and theoretical underpinnings are discussed.

TI Engaging the powerhouse: mitochondrial biology learning through
   Minecraft
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biology; education; Minecraft; mitochondria; technology
AB Gaining a comprehensive understanding of mitochondrial biology and applying it effectively require adequate content knowledge, critical thinking skills, and evaluative judgment. Minecraft Education Edition (MEE), a versatile educational platform, facilitates the creation of immersive learning environments that help address these challenges. This article outlines a comprehensive, structured learning pathway, built in MEE, aimed at teaching mitochondrial function to second-year biology university students. The Minecraft Mitochondrial World (MMW), the first of its kind, was created to provide a comprehensive immersive learning experience that fosters critical thinking, deeper understanding, and meaningful engagement with mitochondrial biology. The learning pathway begins with students assuming the persona of an electron as they "dive" through representations of the electron transport chain (ETC), learning about ETC carriers, potential energy, and mitochondrial function. This is followed by scaffolded three-dimensional (3-D) modules that simulate key mitochondrial processes, including electron flow, reduction potential, proton pumping, ATP synthesis, and reactive oxygen species production. The third element of the learning pathway engages students in a gravity-inspired "electron carrier" role-play serious game. In the fourth activity, students explore gigantic 3-D models of ETC complexes I and IV to examine electron flow through large-scale representations that metaphorically depict molecular processes. The fifth activity explores mitochondrial dynamics, whereas the final activity engages students with an innovative cellular respiration simulator, where they control inputs while diagnosing an array of visually dynamic outputs to apply higher-order thinking skills. Innovative "in-world" learning support approaches are outlined, as are reflections regarding deployment of such resources in tertiary-level biology education.NEW & NOTEWORTHY The Minecraft Mitochondrial World (MMW) is the first comprehensive tertiary-level cell biology learning environment developed in Minecraft Education Edition (MEE). We describe an innovative approach to designing and deploying a dynamic, interactive, and experiential mitochondrial learning experience in MEE. The approach includes sophisticated simulations to model cellular respiration. We further describe how the MMW's design principles make complex mitochondrial biology engaging, understandable, and enjoyable for learners of diverse educational backgrounds and learning preferences.

TI A flipped physiology course positively impacted student success and
   perceptions of learning
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE flipped classroom; higher education; science education
ID CLASSROOM; PERFORMANCE
AB The flipped classroom model is an approach that contrasts with the traditional model for higher education by moving curated lecture material to independent study time, expected to be completed before lectures. With this switch, lectures can focus on "active" modalities to consolidate knowledge via group activities, problem solving, and discussions, thereby increasing student engagement. In this study, we sought to understand students' views of the flipped classroom model in a university human physiology class on actual and perceived academic performance. Data from 41 participants were collected in spring 2024 using surveys, classroom observations, focus groups, and final course grades. Results revealed that the flipped classroom model maintained student engagement and participation, while allowing the instructor to gauge student progress on a given subject, from background knowledge to new applications. In addition, students consistently displayed the ability to incorporate previously held information into new contexts, an opportunity facilitated by the activities that took place during class time. Finally, student responses demonstrate deeper levels of cognition assessed through Bloom's Taxonomy in regard to their learning and methods of learning, building foundational skills to support new and more complicated concepts as they come.

TI Using "you" as a subject in biology assessment questions: examining
   student preferences for second-person framing
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment questions; subject framing; undergraduate biology
ID DATA SATURATION; SELF-REFERENCE; PERSONALIZATION; ACHIEVEMENT;
   INSTRUCTION; INTERVIEWS; ATTITUDES; CONTEXT; WORDS; LEARN
AB In college biology courses, exams and quizzes are often used to assess students' knowledge and performance. Since assessments are a crucial part of biology classes, there has been a wide range of work examining how assessment questions are written, revealing that small changes in how such questions are worded may have large impacts on students' reading comprehension and performance. One aspect that instructors consider when writing a question is subject framing, i.e., which individual, if any, is being placed as the focal point of the question. In this study, we focus on the following subject framings, an authentic scientist, a classmate name, or the second-person "you," referring to the reader. Past work suggests variable subject framing can impact students' preferences, perceptions, and how well they can see themselves in the questions. In this study, we utilize semistructured interviews with 11 students from an introductory molecular biology class to elucidate why students prefer a certain subject framing over another and how variable subject framing can impact students' ability to relate to and visualize the question. Our results suggest that the second person is preferred because it is the most straightforward and easy to understand and that many students do not prefer when a scientist's name and date of the study are included in the question potentially due to multiple cognitive and affective factors.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Small changes in how biology assessment questions are worded, such as who is placed in the subject, may greatly impact how students relate to and visualize the subject or subject matter. In this study, we focus on students' preferences for the following subject framings: an authentic scientist, a classmate name, or the second-person "you." Our results suggest that students prefer the second-person framing because it is straightforward and easy to understand.

TI Assessment of Clinical Empathy by an LLM-as-a-Judge: Bias Patterns in
   ATENA and a Replicable Audit Protocol for Medical Simulation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE virtual patient; medical simulation; LLM-as-a-judge; empathic
   communication; algorithmic bias; educational assessment
ID COMMUNICATION
AB Background: Automated assessment of relational competencies by large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction in medical education, yet its empirical reliability remains poorly documented. Methods: We evaluated ATENA, a GPT-3.5-Turbo virtual-patient simulator deployed at the Faculty of Medicine of Nice (France), in two sequential components. First, 21 university hospital professors rated seven dimensions of realism on 7-point Likert scales. Second, across 129 student simulations of a single diagnostic disclosure scenario, expert human scores based on the empathic communication coding system (ECCS) were compared with ATENA's automated scores using agreement metrics, Bland-Altman analysis, confusion matrix, and qualitative subcorpus analysis. Results: Realism was rated high on six of seven dimensions. Evaluative agreement was poor (ICC = 0.146), with a systematic overscoring bias (+0.80 points) and wide limits of agreement [-1.57; +3.16]. Three bias patterns emerged-score compression (76% of scores within 4.2-4.3), overscoring of weak performance, and underscoring of exemplary performance-indicating that ATENA responds to formal markers of empathy present in nearly every transcript. Conclusions: In this first-generation version of ATENA, the system distinguishes stronger from weaker interviews without being able to place them at the level assigned by expert human raters. These patterns preclude any certificatory use and support a critical, formative-only deployment grounded in instructor algorithmic literacy. The audit protocol applies to any LLM evaluator scored against human coding on a validated instrument.

AB The development of teachers' digital competence has become a key issue in contemporary education systems, particularly in contexts where technology integration remains uneven. This study aims to profile teachers' digital competence through a cluster analysis based on pedagogical digital competence, digital integration, and contextual conditions, and to examine its relationship with selected professional and demographic variables. AB Slovene-medium schools in Italy are public schools in which Slovene is the language of instruction and the protected language of the Slovene national community, yet many pupils encounter Slovene mainly through schooling. This creates a didactic situation that cannot be adequately described as first-, second-, foreign- or heritage-language education. This article analyses how a minority-language didactic model was developed through a six-year collaborative action research process in Slovene-medium schools in Italy (2019-2025). Using retrospective documentary analysis, the study reconstructs four accredited professional development programmes (2019-2022) and subsequent phases of consultation, curriculum refinement, teaching-material development, documented practice-based revision and extension into assessment development. The article contributes an analytically transferable model for supporting multilingual students in minority-language-medium education where the language of schooling is socially less dominant outside school.

TI From Academic Integrity to Institutional Stewardship: A Reflexive and
   Responsible Innovation Paradigm for Generative AI in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; higher education; AI governance; responsible innovation;
   epistemic stewardship; assessment redesign; AI policy
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has diffused through higher education faster than institutions have been able to govern it, reshaping the conditions under which universities produce knowledge, judgement, credentials, and public trust. Current responses (prohibition, detection, and accommodation) fall short of a settled governance posture, and existing frameworks, from AI ethics principles to standard Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) models, are not calibrated to higher education's distinctive epistemic, formative, and public-good missions. This article addresses that gap through a disciplined conceptual synthesis drawing on RRI, reflexive governance, and higher education theory. The synthesis develops a Reflexive and Responsible Innovation Paradigm (RRIP): a six-dimensional framework that re-specifies RRI's canonical dimensions (anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, responsiveness) for the university context and adds two higher-education-specific dimensions: epistemic stewardship and distributive justice. Epistemic stewardship, the article's central theoretical contribution, names the institutional obligation to protect the conditions under which knowledge claims are formed, warranted, assessed, and trusted under AI mediation. RRIP is operationalized through a multi-level architecture of institutional mechanisms (deliberative AI councils, transparency registers, and reflexive assessment redesign) with a tiered implementation pathway calibrated to institutions of varying capacity. Institutional leaders, program directors, policymakers, and accreditation bodies will find in RRIP a theoretically grounded and practically applicable guide for assessment redesign, curriculum decisions, procurement governance, and sectoral coordination.

TI Teaching Practices for Scientific Argumentation in K-12 Classrooms
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE argumentation; science teaching; core practices; teacher education;
   equity; styles of reasoning
ID HIGH-SCHOOL-STUDENTS; MODEL-BASED INQUIRY; DRIVEN INQUIRY;
   PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; SCIENCE TEACHERS; SUPPORT STUDENTS; LEARNING
   SCIENCE; CORE PRACTICES; SENSE-MAKING; KNOWLEDGE
AB Frameworks of core practice in science teaching name practices either generally enough to span the disciplinary practices of the field or specifically toward explanation and modeling, leaving open what teaching requires when the practice at hand is argument. I elaborate those frameworks by specifying seven foundational teaching practices for argumentation that are scientific in nature. The practices are creating and leveraging instances of uncertainty, framing joint enterprise, making argumentation public, introducing and mediating argumentation tools, establishing and refining shared criteria for what counts as an acceptable argument, developing and maintaining norms for critique and disagreement, and noticing and responding to student reasoning and needs. What distinguishes them is the shift from building an account of a phenomenon to adjudicating among competing accounts, which asks a class to work out what counts as adequate reasoning rather than only to apply standards it has been given. Because the sciences reason in more than one style, and each carries its own epistemic criteria, the criteria a class develops are style-dependent rather than general. Equity is constitutive of the practices rather than a parallel commitment. I close by considering enactment under institutional constraint and implications for teacher educators, researchers, and curriculum designers.

DT Article
DE inclusive education; early childhood; curriculum comparison; inclusion
AB This study examines inclusive early childhood education in China and T & uuml;rkiye through a comparative qualitative analysis of policy, curriculum, and teacher perspectives. TI Determinants of the Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence in
   Academic Research: A Structural Equation Model from Colombian
   Universities
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; technology adoption; academic
   research; PLS-SEM; university faculty; Colombia
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; FIT INDEXES
AB This study examined the determinants of both the intention to use and the self-reported use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in academic research by means of a partial least squares structural equation model (PLS-SEM), collecting data from 167 research-active faculty members at three higher education institutions in southwestern Colombia. The findings show that perceived ease of use is the strongest predictor of usage intention, followed by social influence and perceived benefits, whereas social influence emerges as the primary predictor of perceived benefits. Contrary to the conventional reading that associates resource deficits with non-adoption, individual resource barriers are positively associated with perceived benefits, supporting a compensatory logic: the greater the constraints of time and knowledge, the higher the value attributed to a tool capable of mitigating them. Concerns about AI output quality exhibit an asymmetric pattern, as they are unrelated to perceived benefits yet are associated with lower usage intention, suggesting that these concerns operate as a behavioral brake without eroding the recognized utility. The main contribution lies in identifying this dissociation between the recognition of utility and the willingness to act accordingly. It is concluded that GAI is valued as a useful tool for compensating research-related deficits, yet it coexists with concerns about the quality of its outputs that must be addressed by institutions through training, communities of practice, and clear guidelines on verification and responsible use.

TI Undergraduate students' engagement with MOOCs in Kazakhstan: variations
   by gender, year of study, and discipline
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital learning; Kazakhstan; massive open online courses; MOOCs; online
   learning
AB Higher education (HE) has undergone a significant digital transformation, supported by Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), which offer more flexible interactive learning opportunities, but their use and perceived value vary across institutional and national contexts. Given the importance of understanding students' engagement in using these platforms to develop effective digital learning, this study examined patterns of MOOCs engagement among students (n = 682) through a survey at a regional university in Kazakhstan. Independent samples t-tests, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's HSD post hoc test, and Pearson's chi-square tests were used to examine differences by gender, year of study, and discipline. Preference for Kazakh language MOOCs is dominant among respondents (68.8%). Statistically significant differences in MOOCs use, purposes, and perceptions were observed across gender and year of study (p < 0.05), with more limited differences by discipline, while gender emerged as the most consistent differentiating factor. The study concludes that the effective integration of MOOCs into the HE system requires not only technical access but also stronger instructional support, greater interactivity, and availability of local-language content.

   Qatar Semi-Annual Survey
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education governance; higher education policy; academic
   credential fraud; academic integrity; credentialism Qatar
AB Academic credential fraud threatens trust in higher education, labour-market fairness, and professional standards. This study examines self-reported familiarity with forged higher-education certificates and public perceptions of credential fraud in Qatar using data from the May 2022 Qatar Semi-Annual Survey. The model examines associations between reported familiarity and respondents' age, gender, education, employment status, interview language, and marital status, including an exploratory gender-by-age interaction. Higher educational attainment is positively associated with reported familiarity, while gender and the gender-by-age interaction are not statistically significant. Married respondents report lower familiarity than never-married respondents. A separate Qatari-expatriate comparison indicates a statistically significant but small difference in the distribution of familiarity. The findings should be interpreted as broad patterns of self-reported familiarity rather than objective measures of knowledge, involvement, or fraud prevalence. The study highlights the importance of transparent credential-verification procedures, employer due diligence, and public education while acknowledging limitations concerning measurement sensitivity, sampling documentation, and generalization beyond Qatar. Additionally, the study offers policy implications and recommendations aimed at improving governance within the system.

TI Development of a virtual reality model for STEM education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive processing; electromagnetism education; learning motivation;
   learning retention; stem education; structural equation modelling;
   virtual reality; visualisation quality
AB Immersive virtual reality (VR) enables interactive three-dimensional representations of abstract scientific phenomena, but its educational value depends on how it is integrated into instructional practice. This study developed and longitudinally evaluated a VR-supported instructional model for undergraduate electromagnetism. The baseline cohort comprised 193 students from two physics-related programmes; 187 completed the immediate post-test (T2), and 181 completed the two-month follow-up (T3). The intervention consisted of four 40-50-minute instructional sessions delivered over two weeks, with approximately 5-10 min of active VR interaction per participant during each session. The instructional sequence combined guided exploration, manipulation of a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field, prediction tasks, instructor-facilitated discussion, and structured reflection. Repeated-measures analyses based on 181 complete cases showed significant changes over time in electromagnetism achievement, cognitive processing, learning motivation, and perceived learning outcomes (all p < .001; partial eta p(2) = .385-.465<bold>)</bold>. Cognitive processing, learning motivation, and perceived learning outcomes remained relatively stable from T2 to T3, whereas electromagnetism achievement showed a small descriptive decline while remaining above its baseline mean. Structural equation modelling using T2 data (n = 187) showed positive associations between perceived visualisation quality and cognitive processing (beta = .61), cognitive processing and learning motivation (beta = .57), and learning motivation and perceived learning outcomes (beta = .63). The sequential indirect association between perceived visualisation quality and perceived learning outcomes through cognitive processing and learning motivation was also significant [beta = .22, 95% CI (.142,.319), p < .001]. Given the single-group design and concurrent measurement of the SEM constructs, the findings indicate within-cohort temporal changes and theoretically consistent associations rather than causal effects of VR.

TI Analysis of learning in Moroccan secondary education: computer model and
   data-driven pedagogy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE data-driven pedagogy; digital education transformation; educational
   artificial intelligence; learning analytics; pedagogical visualization
ID ANALYTICS
AB In an educational context characterized by rapid digital transformation, learning analytics offers strong potential to personalize instruction and enhance teaching practices. However, in Moroccan pioneer colleges, this potential remains largely underexploited. This study aims to design a computational model that transforms students' digital traces into interpretable and actionable insights to support data-driven pedagogy accessible to non-technical teachers. Grounded in Learning Analytics, pedagogical visualization, and educational artificial intelligence, the proposed model is organized into five interconnected modules. These modules process learner interaction data from educational platforms to generate key indicators such as engagement, persistence, and academic achievement. This study contributes a context-sensitive framework that facilitates the integration of learning analytics in classroom practice. By providing simple indicators and visual feedback, it promotes evidence-based decision-making and pedagogical differentiation. As a theoretical and exploratory model, it still requires empirical validation and teacher training for effective implementation.

TI "Los niños tienen derecho de jugar": exploring Latina mothers'
   experiences as co-researchers and advocates for playful learning in
   community spaces
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE community-based participatory research; co-researchers; informal
   learning; Latine families; playful learning
ID PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; LOW-INCOME; CHILDREN; HEALTH; YOUTH; FAMILIES;
   PARENTS; SCIENCE
AB Playful learning in public spaces can expand children's access to enriching learning opportunities beyond formal educational settings, yet these opportunities remain unequally distributed across communities. The Playful Learning Landscapes initiative integrates community engagement with the science of learning to create playful learning opportunities in everyday public spaces. Although community engagement is central to this work, less is known about how parents experience sustained involvement as co-researchers. This study explored how Latine parents understood and experienced their participation as co-researchers in a Playful Learning Landscapes project. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 Latina mothers in Southern California who participated as parent co-researchers and conducted site intercept surveys before and after the implementation of playful learning installations in community spaces. Using a codebook thematic analysis approach, we found that parents engaged in relational, community-centered research practices grounded in care, trust, responsibility, and lived expertise. Parents drew on their knowledge of their communities to engage families, share information about the installations, and advocate for playful learning opportunities in everyday public spaces. Parents also described the installations as creating more welcoming, culturally meaningful environments, while recognizing ongoing structural barriers that continue to limit families' access to safe public spaces. Participation as co-researchers contributed to parents' confidence, sense of agency, and expanding roles as advocates for children, families, and community well-being. These findings suggest that community-based participatory approaches can position parents as community experts and advocates while supporting more equitable, justice-oriented access to playful learning opportunities.

TI Dimensions of mathematics teachers' pedagogical knowledge and their
   association with mathematics teaching: a structural equation modelling
   approach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment strategies; classroom management; instructional strategies;
   lesson planning; mathematics teaching; teachers
ID PROFESSIONAL KNOWLEDGE; SCIENCE; PERCEPTIONS; MANAGEMENT; SKILLS; KEY
AB Despite growing attention to teachers' Pedagogical Knowledge (PK) in mathematics education, limited empirical evidence exists on how its key dimensions jointly relate to mathematics teaching among practising mathematics teachers enrolled in an undergraduate mathematics education programme while on study leave. In particular, the combined role of classroom management, assessment strategies, lesson planning, and instructional strategies remains underexplored. Accordingly, this study examined the relationships between these four sub-dimensions of PK and mathematics teaching. The study adopted a descriptive correlational design. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire from 330 participants selected through stratified and simple random sampling. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was conducted using IBM SPSS and AMOS (v.23). The results indicated that all four dimensions were positively and significantly associated with mathematics teaching. Assessment strategies demonstrated the strongest direct association with mathematics teaching, followed by instructional strategies, lesson planning, and classroom management. The findings suggest that multiple dimensions of PK represent distinct but complementary domains that are individually associated with mathematics teaching, highlighting the importance of developing classroom management, assessment strategies, lesson planning, and instructional strategies within teacher professional development programmes.

   enhance knowledge and emotional support based on scaffolding theory
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Video-based learning; Learning support; Generative AI; Scaffolding
   theory; Experimental data analysis
ID STUDENT PERCEPTIONS; ONLINE; AI
AB With the rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), tools such as ChatGPT have shown great potential in enhancing online learning. However, existing applications in video-based learning remain limited, as they typi cally require learners to pause or switch interfaces to access AI support, disrupting learning continuity. To address this challenge, this study proposes a framework that utilizes ChatGPT to generate comments for an individual learner (i-Comments), displayed as scrolling text over educational videos, providing both knowledge and emo tional support based on scaffolding theory. The present study evaluates the framework's generation capabilities to gain empirical insight that will inform future individualization based on learner profiles. The proposed frame work integrates multimodal video information analysis, individual information and comment attribute settings, generation of i-Comments, and customized display, through which pedagogical principles such as cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, and scaffolding theory are systematically translated into technical components, including few-shot learning, prompt engineering, and entropy-based density control. A validation experiment compared ChatGPT-generated and human-generated comments across linguistic and pedagogical di mensions, including part-of-speech composition, 3-gram diversity, Zipf's law conformity, readability, and topical relevance. Results indicate that ChatGPT-generated comments are more complex and descriptive, whereas human comments show stronger topic relevance and natural language norms, leading to higher perceived helpfulness under the GPT-3.5 condition used in the main comparison; a supplementary ablation with a newer model (GPT-5.4) suggests that this gap narrows substantially. This research provides foundational knowledge for developing Agentic AI supported educational systems by empirically evaluating and exploring key capabilities required for autonomous instructional support, offering insights into the feasibility of applying generative AIto enhance learner engagement in video-based learning.

TI A meta-analysis of English proficiency and academic achievement in
   English-medium instruction
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE EAP; EMI; Proficiency; Achievement; Meta-analysis; Heterogeneity
ID BIAS; STUDENTS; SUCCESS
AB English-medium instruction (EMI) has expanded on the assumption that students' English proficiency underpins their academic success, yet primary evidence is strikingly inconsistent. This study reports a random-effects correlational meta-analysis of the zero-order association between English proficiency and academic achievement across 29 studies (N = 8396) in EMI higher education in six country/context groupings, with every effect size verified against its primary report and the evidence base current to 2026. The pooled correlation was moderate and positive, r = 0.34 (95% CI [0.26, 0.42]), and robust to publication bias, study quality, and dependencies among overlapping research teams. Heterogeneity, however, was substantial (I2 = 88.6%), and the 95% prediction interval (-0.07 to 0.65) indicates that the true association ranges from negligible to strong across settings. Academic discipline was the only significant moderator: the correlation was moderate in mixed-discipline samples (r = 0.38) but weak in engineering samples (r = 0.12), though this subgroup comprised only two studies, while neither proficiency-measure type nor outcome type moderated the effect. The findings position English proficiency as a modest, context-dependent correlate of EMI success that is positive on average, and they carry a direct message for English for Academic Purposes (EAP) practice. Because proficiency at entry accounts for only a modest, uneven share of the variance in achievement, admission thresholds cannot substitute for sustained, discipline-sensitive academic-language support during study. EAP provision calibrated to the language demands of specific disciplines is likely to serve EMI students better than uniform proficiency requirements.

TI When the scaffold is withdrawn: Motivational trajectories and
   differences in AI-supported inquiry learning
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-supported learning; Scaffolding withdrawal; Intrinsic motivation;
   Self-determination; Science education
ID SCIENCE; TECHNOLOGY; ORIENTATION; ACHIEVEMENT; ENGAGEMENT; EFFICACY;
   CAREER
AB Sustaining motivation is central to science education. Whether AI-supported inquiry produces durable motivational gains remains unclear, as few studies examine what happens after scaffolding ends. This longitudinal mixed-methods study (N = 131) compared traditional inquiry, technology-supported inquiry, and AI-augmented inquiry (ATSI) across intervention and withdrawal phases, assessing four motivation dimensions at four time points. Open-ended attributions and contrastive case analysis provided explanatory depth. Both technology-supported conditions outperformed traditional inquiry in intrinsic motivation during intervention, with ATSI producing the largest growth but also the sharpest post-withdrawal decline. Self-determination declined most in ATSI after scaffolding removal, while self-efficacy and grade motivation did not differ significantly across conditions. ATSI students continued to attribute their motivational changes to technological support even after withdrawal. Case analyses suggested that motivational sustainability depended on how students positioned AI-augmented support within their own practices. These findings indicate that AI-supported motivational gains are dimension-specific and withdrawal-vulnerable, suggesting that durable benefits require scaffolding designs that gradually shift regulatory ownership from tool to learner. Educational relevance statement: Although artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for science education, its impact on student motivation after technology removal remains underexplored. Our findings reveal that while AI-supported inquiry boosts motivation during use, dimension-specific declines follow once students return to traditional classrooms, accompanied by students attributing their motivation to technological support. To counteract this dependency, pedagogical designers should guide learners to recognize AI as a collaborative partner while progressively assuming ownership of the regulatory functions the scaffold provides. By building this transfer into scaffold design, educators can support the persistence of self-directed motivation after the scaffold is withdrawn.

TI Perceptions of School-Based Health-Preserving Practices and
   Health-Related Learning Engagement Among Primary School Students in
   Kazakhstan
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE health-preserving practices; primary school; safe lifestyle; school
   health; students
ID PROMOTING SCHOOLS; PERFORMANCE; FRAMEWORK
AB The school period is critical for developing health-related knowledge, attitudes and behaviours. However, evidence on primary school students' perceptions of school-based health-preserving practices and engagement with health-related educational content remains limited in Kazakhstan. This cross-sectional survey of 1750 primary school students aged 6-12 years in Kazakhstan assessed perceived health awareness, attitudes, perceived cognitive impact and health-related learning engagement. Psychometric properties were evaluated using reliability and factor analyses, and associations were examined using correlation, regression and cross-sectional path analyses. The hypothesized four-factor model showed strong incremental and residual fit (CFI = 0.972, TLI = 0.964, SRMR = 0.034), although RMSEA was elevated (0.087) and discriminant separation was incomplete for selected domains. Health-related learning engagement was positively associated with perceived health awareness, attitudes and perceived cognitive impact, with the multivariable model explaining 60.6% of its variance (R 2 = 0.606, p < 0.001). Language of instruction and grade level were also associated with engagement through direct and indirect statistical pathways. Overall, the findings support a four-dimensional framework of closely related health-related perceptions and educational engagement among primary school students. The instrument assesses self-reported perceptions and engagement rather than objective health knowledge or actual health behaviours, warranting cautious interpretation and further validation.

TI Conditional Standard Errors, Posterior Standard Deviations, and
   Conditional Standard Errors of Prediction in IRT Scoring
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID ACCURACY; ABILITY
AB Operational testing programs often rely on different uncertainty summaries to answer different inferential questions. This article distinguishes three such quantities in item response theory (IRT) scoring: the conditional standard error (CSE), which summarizes variability of a reported estimate under repeated measurement at fixed proficiency; the posterior standard deviation (PSD), which summarizes uncertainty about proficiency conditional on observed responses; and the conditional standard error of prediction (CSEP), which summarizes uncertainty in a future reported estimate under specified future administration, scoring, and reporting conditions. The central argument is that uncertainty summaries should be defined by their random quantities, conditioning, and intended uses, with estimation guided by those definitions. CSEP receives particular attention because it is less commonly discussed in operational IRT scoring. Building on classical test theory's standard error of prediction and Bayesian posterior predictive ideas, CSEP is defined as the standard deviation of the posterior predictive distribution of a future reported estimate produced by the operational reporting rule. A posterior predictive Monte Carlo/parametric bootstrap procedure is described for estimating CSEP under arbitrary scoring and reporting rules, with a nested law-of-total-variance extension for decomposing predictive uncertainty into future measurement variability and propagated proficiency uncertainty. An appendix illustrates CSEP estimation and decomposition.

TI Beyond the binary definition of "Stupid" and "Smart" education: towards
   "Smupid" education?
SO SMART LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
LA English
DT Article
DE Smart education; Stupid education; Smupid education; Technology; Edtech;
   Pedagogy
ID INDUSTRY
AB This study examines the conceptual relationship between "smart" and "stupid" education binaries by moving beyond this simplistic opposition, tracing how broad scholarship constructs "smart education" and its antithetical complement. An analysis of smart education definitions reveals that the discourse is heavily weighted toward technological integration and personalization, while more recent formulations emphasize education as an overall ecosystem of values, policies, and practices. In contrast, definitions of stupid education reveal a complex and multifaceted critique of educational failure - encompassing systemic rigidity and uncritical techno-optimism. Notably, the same actors and stakeholders are identified as primary agents in both smart and stupid education, yet their roles and attributions are opposed. Such a perspective suggests that the smart/stupid binary is not a fixed attribute of actors but a dynamic outcome of their configuration in relation to all other actors in the system - how they are positioned, how they exercise agency, and how systems enable or constrain their contributions. Therefore, we argue and consider existing educational systems as smupid with four states (inept, benign, pernicious, and wise), depending on the degree of smart and stupid at the same time. We conclude by calling for more systematic thinking to increase smartness and reduce stupidity within these systems.

TI Teacher well-being and coping strategies: a two-wave qualitative study
   with secondary school teachers in Switzerland
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher well-being; Coping strategies; Teacher challenges; Secondary
   school; Qualitative research
ID EXPLORING RELATIONS; JOB RESOURCES; STRESS; MODEL; RESILIENCE;
   MOTIVATION; EDUCATORS; EMOTIONS
AB This qualitative study examines the role of coping strategies in shaping teacher well-being within secondary school environments while considering different levels of professional expertise. Focus groups with 23 secondary school teachers over two waves revealed the dynamic nature of well-being and coping mechanisms throughout a school year. Utilizing Zuckerman and Gagne's () framework, our analysis confirmed five key coping strategies: self-help, approach, accommodation, avoidance, and self-punishment. Self-help, mainly instrumental support-seeking, emerged as the most frequently used strategy, especially among novice teachers who relied on the experiences of their more experienced colleagues. Approach strategies, including active problem-solving, were prevalent among more experienced teachers, while accommodation strategies involved accepting unchangeable aspects of their roles. While less frequently reported, some teachers described using avoidance and self-punishment as coping mechanisms, indicating ongoing challenges in their professional experiences. The findings underscore the importance of fostering a supportive work environment where teachers can use effective coping strategies to navigate professional challenges. This study contributes to understanding how coping strategies relate to teacher well-being, providing insights into the specific strategies that support or hinder well-being in challenging contexts. The results emphasize the need for targeted interventions to enhance teacher well-being, considering teachers' professional expertise, and particularly for those employing maladaptive coping strategies.

TI The relationship between social support and academic engagement in
   junior high school students: a longitudinal study
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Social support; Academic engagement; Grit; Ambition
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; GRIT; ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION; NUMBER; TRUE;
   LIFE
AB One primary objective of adolescent education is to foster students' academic progress and deep learning. Grounded in Bandura's social cognitive theory, it is generally held that academic performance results from the interaction of individual internal factors and external social environments. Building on this foundation, this present study examines how social support from school, family and peers promotes academic engagement among junior high school students. The study further explores the mediating role of grit, the moderating role of ambition, as well as the dynamic patterns underlying different types of academic engagement, aiming to provide evidence-based insights for educational practice. This study conducted a two-wave longitudinal design over a four-month period among 559 junior high school students. The findings revealed that social support significantly and positively predicted academic engagement, with grit functioning as a mediator. Ambition exhibited a negative moderating effect that high ambition weakens the positive effect of social support on academic engagement, suggesting a partially compensatory mechanism whereby adolescents with high ambition maintain academic engagement even when external support is lacking. Latent profile analysis (LPA) and latent transition analysis (LTA) further identified three profiles of academic adaptive-high, moderate and low, and demonstrated social support significantly promotes individual's transition to more high profile. Overall, the findings highlight the value of integrating social support from family, school and peers to enhance academic engagement. Moreover, when social support is insufficient, fostering students' ambition through motivational education may serve as a compensatory strategy, which offer both theoretical and practical implications for personalized educational support.

AB Children's beliefs about abilities shape their learning. TI Small stories, big impacts on children; a quasi-experimental mixed
   methods study on gender roles
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Children's picturebook; Counter-stereotypic intervention; Early
   childhood; Gender inclusion; Mosaic approach; Gender stereotypes; T &
   uuml;rkiye
ID PICTURE BOOKS; SEX; REPRESENTATION
AB Early childhood is a critical period for the formation of gender perceptions, making children's exposure to symbolic and narrative content highly influential. In this context an interactive reading activity titled "Gender-Inclusive Reading Circle" consisting of 25 children's picturebooks presenting gender-inclusive content was developed and implemented over five-week period. The aim of this study is to examine the effect of this reading activity on five-year-old children's perceptions of gender stereotypes. Conducted as a counter-stereotypic intervention, this study employed a complementary mixed-methods approach and followed a partially mixed concurrent equal status design using a single-group pretest-posttest experimental model. The participants were 15 (five-year-old children). Data collection was inspired by the Mosaic approach and included quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative data were gathered through the Social Gender Stereotypes Assessment Instrument while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews and a storybook drawing activity. Findings indicated that after the intervention children developed more flexible and inclusive gender perceptions across domains including toys, occupations, household roles, colors and emotions. Visual thematic analysis also showed greater diversity in character choices, story themes and emotional expressions. TI Fostering the Creative Process Using the Wallas Model: A Case Study

SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; creative process; cognitive activities; creative process
   report diary; creative teaching
AB Following on from the modeling of the creative process developed by Wallas in the early 20th century, this study examines the creative processes of pupils aged 10-12 and focuses on the sequence of various cognitive activities involved in school-based object projects. Drawing on theoretical models of the creative process and the multivariate approach, the aim of this study is to understand the relationship between the activities observed and the stages of Wallas' model, as well as how the type of task influences the outcome. Forty-one pupils attending school in French-speaking Switzerland were divided into two groups and carried out two separate projects over 6 weeks (a stop-motion film and a school box). However, we observe certain specific features, such as dynamic and iterative sequences between stages. Furthermore, the analyzes highlight the influence of the nature of the task on the density (quantity) and variety (alignment) of transitions. These observations confirm the sustainability of the model proposed by Wallas and encourage future research on the development of the creative process in compulsory school education.

AB Autonomy-supportive environments are vital in fostering learning motivation, a core feature of the Guided-Autonomy Syllabus (GAS) implemented in Japanese university EFL classrooms. Based on the self-determination theory framework, learning motivation is maintained by satisfying the basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Previous research has shown the GAS to satisfy students' needs for autonomy and relatedness. However, the need for competence remains underexamined. This study explored, within a Japanese university EFL context, (a) the extent to which lectures on how languages are learned, delivered prior to autonomous study in a Guided-Autonomy Syllabus (GAS), were associated with changes in students' perceived competence in language learning, (b) whether the use of student response systems (clickers) facilitated retention of lecture content, and (c) whether such retention was associated with maintaining perceived competence over the semester. TI Reorganising the conditions of participation: Effects of differentiated
   instruction on the social dimension of inclusive education
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE differentiated instruction; mild intellectual disability; social
   acceptance; social dimension of inclusive education; social interaction
ID HIGH-SCHOOL-STUDENTS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; INTERVENTION; PUPILS;
   EXPERIENCES; ADOLESCENTS; SUPPORT; PEERS; NEEDS
AB This study examines the effectiveness of a structured Differentiated Instruction (DI) programme, implemented as a universal practice for learning "Differentiation for All", in enhancing the social dimension of inclusive education for students with mild intellectual disabilities in second and third-grade inclusive primary classrooms. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, using a pre-post design with an intervention and a comparison group. The study included 32 students with mild intellectual disabilities, 202 typically developing peers, and 30 general-education teachers. Data were collected through systematic observations, sociometric techniques, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative findings showed that after the intervention, the intervention group demonstrated a statistically significant increase in social interaction with typically developing peers and an improvement in social acceptance, whereas the comparison group showed no comparable changes. Qualitative data indicated a trend toward increased perceived peer support, particularly in terms of invitations to participate, positive attention, and greater participation in school activities. Students' and teachers' narratives linked these changes to flexible grouping strategies, collaborative roles, shared outputs, accessible materials, and clear and cooperative routines. Overall, the findings suggest that the implementation of DI as a systematic and non-stigmatising universal practice within the context of environmental studies may contribute to enhancing social participation and school inclusion for students with mild intellectual disabilities in inclusive primary classrooms.
