TI The significance of Indigenous chemistry knowledge in Western chemistry
   education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous chemistry knowledge; Western chemistry knowledge;
   contextualization; chemistry prior knowledge; academic performance
ID SCIENCE
AB Introduction This study explored the potential role of indigenous chemistry knowledge (ICK) within Western chemistry education frameworks from the learner's perspective. This research offers distinct novelty by shifting the focus from passive curriculum consumption in primary or secondary schools to active pedagogical translation within an initial teacher education framework. By examining preservice teachers-who act as both daily practitioners of indigenous chemistry and future Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics educators-this study bypasses broad decolonial theory to target the exact pipeline, where cultural knowledge transforms into actionable classroom pedagogy. Furthermore, it provides a reproducible mapping strategy using concrete, localized biochemical entry points, such as the thermal regulation of enzymes in the Mahewu fermentation and agricultural fruit oxidation.Methods Guided by a social constructivist theoretical framework, this study employed a qualitative research methodology with a descriptive design. Data were collected from 29 purposively sampled pre-service science teachers through focus group interviews, observations, and document analysis. The constant comparative method, categorical coding, the rule of literal presence, and the four-part verification framework were applied as data analysis techniques.Results The findings reveal a distinct tripartite dynamic in how learners navigate these knowledge frameworks. First, regarding practical convergence, the results suggest that certain ICK practices and Western chemistry share complementary empirical features, with both frameworks addressing similar practical chemical phenomena. Second, on an epistemological level, this study distinguishes functional convergence from epistemological equivalence, noting that learners navigate the differing foundational worldviews and validation systems of each framework rather than treating them as identical systems of knowledge. Third, regarding pedagogical value, the results demonstrate that ICK offers relevant contextual connections and leverages prior knowledge for learners. Integrating these localized practices into chemistry education was found to support learner engagement, facilitate meaningful learning experiences, and enhance contextualization.Discussion This study contributes to science education by exploring potential pedagogical linkages between indigenous and Western chemical perspectives without conflating their epistemic roots. These findings suggest that incorporating ICK concepts can foster a more culturally responsive, contextualized curriculum that supports student engagement, comprehension, and sustainability.

TI Integrating virtual reality into spoken English instruction: a
   mixed-method study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE immersive learning; language education; mixed-methods research; spoken
   English; virtual reality
AB This study addresses the challenge of providing scalable and immersive environments for spoken English training in foreign language education. To this end, we designed and implemented a virtual reality (VR)-based instructional system that integrates immersive scenarios, avatar-based interaction, and task-based learning activities to support oral communication practice. A convergent parallel mixed-method design was employed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed instructional framework. Using convenience sampling, 60 university students from two intact English classes voluntarily participated in the study. One class (n = 30) received VR-supported instruction, whereas the other class (n = 30) received traditional instruction. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-intervention IELTS speaking assessments, while qualitative data were obtained from questionnaires and interviews to examine learners' perceptions and experiences. Quantitative analyses, including independent-samples t-tests and ANCOVA, revealed no statistically significant difference in speaking proficiency between the two groups. However, a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.2085) suggested a modest advantage for the VR group. Qualitative findings indicated high levels of learner engagement and perceived improvement, with over 90% of participants reporting increased confidence, vocabulary use, and opportunities for authentic communication. Learners particularly valued the immersive environments, avatar-based interaction, and immediate feedback provided through the VR platform. Rather than developing a new VR engine, this study contributed a structured instructional framework that demonstrates how existing immersive technologies can be systematically integrated into spoken English instruction. The findings provide practical insights into the pedagogical design, implementation, and classroom integration of VR technologies for language learning.

TI Measuring bilingual input and output in early childhood education:
   English and Vietnamese speech within a language exposure program
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE additional language; automatic speech measurement; heritage language;
   preschool children; Vietnamese and English speech; Vietnamese exposure
   program
ID SPANISH; KINDERGARTEN; VOCABULARY; FAMILY
AB In Australia, languages other than English are not included in the educational curriculum of most preschools and primary schools, with exceptions for some high prestige languages, such as French, Italian, Mandarin or Spanish. Languages such as Vietnamese are rarely supported, accentuating the substantial challenge in transmitting the Vietnamese language to younger generations in Australia. In this study, we examined the quantity of Vietnamese language input and output in a program designed to provide Vietnamese language exposure in an Australian preschool. The Vietnamese language exposure program was delivered by an adult facilitator trained in the Little Multilingual Minds method, featuring 176 language sessions delivered across 29 weeks of the year. We measured the amount of speech in English and Vietnamese during the program sessions following the annotation method used in previous research, selecting 48 of the total 176 audio recordings. For each selected recording, the start and end of the facilitator (input) and preschoolers' (output) speech in either English or Vietnamese was manually annotated, with an automatic script measuring the duration of each segment. Children's output doubled the output reported by a similar previous study, indicating that structured sessions offered higher opportunities for children's speech. Crucially, children's speech increased as the Vietnamese language exposure program progressed, demonstrating greater engagement and interest from the preschool children. Although the facilitator was encouraged to use Vietnamese, her use of English increased from first to second term, remaining high thereafter due to the constraints in starting a Vietnamese exposure program in a preschool where only English was previously used. Nevertheless, Vietnamese played an important role in the facilitator's input, with children's Vietnamese output showing signs of increase. We conclude by highlighting that children's overall speech increase aligned with the engagement and interest reported in the language exposure program evaluation, laying a good foundation for program continuation the following year.

ID PREPARING TEACHERS; RETHINKING; KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK; FIELD; WORK
AB Preparing teachers for increasingly diverse classrooms is a central responsibility of initial teacher education. This qualitative study explores how preservice teachers in Norwegian initial teacher education experience learning to interpret and respond to learner variability, with attention to the relationship between campus-based coursework and school-based supervised professional training. Diversity is conceptualised as a relational and contextual feature of classroom life rather than as an attribute of particular pupils. The study therefore examines how preservice teachers learn to interpret learner variability, participation patterns, and support needs as pedagogically meaningful. The study draws on two focus group interviews with eight third- and fourth-year preservice teachers in Norwegian primary and lower secondary teacher education programmes. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with attention to participants' accounts and meanings constructed through focus group interaction. The findings suggest that participants valued diversity-related coursework and school-based experience, but often struggled to connect diversity-related principles with pedagogical action. Short and fragmented placements constrained opportunities to develop contextual knowledge of pupils and interpret how learner variability and classroom arrangements shaped participation and learning. Mentoring supported pedagogical reflection and professional judgement when feedback was timely and connected to classroom events, but such opportunities were uneven. Participants also reported varying opportunities to connect coursework with observation, lesson planning, teaching, feedback, and reflection. The findings concern participants' reported experiences and do not demonstrate actual classroom noticing or teaching practices. The study argues that preparation for diversity-responsive teaching requires coherent, practice-oriented opportunities to develop contextual knowledge, professional noticing, reflective judgement, and pedagogical decision-making across university and school settings. Enactment coherence is proposed as a tentative heuristic for examining whether diversity-related principles become connected to pedagogical analysis and action in initial teacher education.

TI Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers'
   acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short
   professional development training session
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive teaching; artificial intelligence in education; inclusive
   education; large language models; teacher professional development;
   technology acceptance model
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; STUDENTS; INSTRUCTION; EDUCATION; PROGRAM;
   TAM
AB In increasingly diverse classrooms, artificial intelligence (AI)-based technologies, including large language models (LLMs), are widely discussed as tools to support teachers in implementing differentiation. However, the successful integration of such technologies largely depends on teachers' social acceptance of these systems. The present study reports findings from a pilot pre-post evaluation of INSIGHT (Information on Schooling with Generative and Helpful AI Tools), a short teacher professional development (TPD) training session on AI-based technologies in schools, with a particular focus on LLMs. Pre- to post changes in teachers' social acceptance of AI-based technologies for supporting differentiation were examined. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), social acceptance was conceptualised as Perceived Usefulness (PU), Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), and Behavioural Intention (BI). Data were collected from N = 100 teachers from primary and secondary education in Germany. Results of paired-samples t-tests indicated significant pre-post increases in PU and PEOU, whereas no significant change was found for BI. While teachers perceived AI-based technologies as more useful and easier to use after the training, these changes did not translate into a stronger behavioural intention to use these technologies in practice. The discussion therefore considers potential barriers that may influence teachers' intentions to use AI-based technologies for differentiation.

TI From general academic to disciplinary literacy: A collaborative
   autoethnography of GenAI-enhanced EAP materials development

LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; EAP materials development; Disciplinary literacy; Teacher
   governance; Collaborative autoethnography
AB A persistent challenge in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) is how to support undergraduate students' progression from general academic literacy to the discipline-specific literacy practices required for academic participation. This challenge is compounded by the limited availability of pedagogical materials capable of mediating this transition in scalable and pedagogically principled ways. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offer new possibilities for addressing this gap through the development of context-sensitive EAP materials. This study reports a collaborative autoethnographic investigation of how two EAP practitioners engaged with GenAI during the development of an integrated two-volume textbook series for undergraduates. The findings highlight both the pedagogical affordances and constraints of GenAI, underscoring the central role of teacher judgement in GenAI-enhanced materials development.

TI Educators' experiences and perspectives on teaching pharmacy law
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy; Law; Educators; Teaching
ID COMMUNITY PHARMACY; ETHICS
AB Introduction: Laws regulate many aspects of pharmacy practice, helping ensure safe and appropriate care is provided. It is important, therefore, to teach pharmacy law effectively to students so they can practise legally (i.e. practice within the framework that pharmacy laws and regulations provide). However, the experiences, perspectives and content-related teaching practice (i.e. delivery of pharmacy law education) of pharmacy law educators has not been reported. Such information is pertinent to design learning experiences for pre-registration pharmacy students to gain knowledge around contemporary legal concepts relevant to pharmacy practice. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate educators' experiences and perspectives to inform future teaching of pharmacy law. Methods: A qualitative approach was utilised. Participants were recruited via purposive and convenience sampling, and one-on-one semi-structured interviews examining educators' professional backgrounds and teaching experiences were conducted. Zoom (R) was used to generate audio recordings and transcripts. Data analysis was conducted using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis process and NVivo (R) was used to identify codes in an inductive paradigm. Results: Five themes were identified within the data: philosophies around teaching, alignment of pedagogical approaches with learning goals, perceptions of students regarding pharmacy law, factors restricting pedagogical approaches, and experience in practice as a qualification. Participants outlined two distinct philosophies-one focused on law and one which additionally incorporated ethics along with law. Educators explained how they aligned pedagogical approaches with learning goals. Pharmacy law was reported to be viewed as dry, complex, unfamiliar and unimportant by students warranting strategies including case scenarios and content integration. University and faculty requirements and lack of time and staff affected teaching. Educators relied on practising as pharmacists to guide their teaching. Conclusions: Various considerations and experiences specific to pharmacy law education were identified, including the need to teach it in a way tailored for pharmacy students. Pharmacy law appeared to be insufficiently prioritised in pharmacy programs.

TI Renewing the chemical engineering curriculum: A topic-level analysis of
   current provision, future priorities, and disciplinary identity
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Chemical engineering education; Curriculum mapping; Curriculum renewal;
   Accreditation; Bachelor degree; Digitalisation
ID EMPLOYABILITY
AB Chemical engineering curricula must respond to digitalisation, sustainability, artificial intelligence and changing professional expectations while retaining the disciplinary core of the field. This study examines future curriculum priorities through a topic-level comparison of stakeholder views, curriculum design proposals, current international syllabus content and accreditation expectations. Topic priorities were identified through a survey and a structured workshop involving academic and industrial participants. Current provision was mapped using publicly available syllabus information from 40 leading international chemical engineering programmes, with topics coded by year, compulsory or optional status and frequency of appearance. The findings show strong agreement that mathematics, engineering fundamentals, unit operations and process design remain central to chemical engineering education. However, applied process design and safety topics were less consistently explicit in current syllabuses than their perceived importance would suggest, while broader digital, sustainability and sector-specific capabilities remain unevenly represented. These findings indicate that the future chemical engineering curriculum should evolve by making applied design, safety, digital and sustainability capabilities more visible, coherent and assessable across the programme, while allowing specialisation in emerging sectors. Curriculum renewal should therefore augment rather than replace the established chemical engineering core. Whilst transferable skills are noted, they are outside the scope of this paper.

TI Researching racial covenants: Integrating archival research and a
   marginal approach to antiracism in introductory US economic history

LA English

ID STUDENTS; RACE
AB This paper describes an introductory U.S. economic history project that engages students in original archival research while examining the historical legacy of racial discrimination in local housing markets. Students identify racially restrictive covenants in county property records (legal agreements within property deeds prohibiting non-White residents), analyze contemporary neighborhood demographic data, and reflect on the relationship between housing, wealth accumulation, and systemic inequality. We provide details on how the project and its essential elements can be applied in different locations, courses, and assignments.

TI Tool or tutor? A dynamic assessment-informed comparison of pedagogical
   AI agents and general-purpose GenAI for EFL speaking development and
   anxiety
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Dynamic assessment; Pedagogical AI agent; Generative AI; EFL speaking
   performance; Speaking anxiety
AB English speaking is often the most anxiety-provoking skill for low-achieving EFL undergraduates, and recent research suggests that AI chat tools and pedagogical AI agents (PAIA) can expand opportunities for speaking practice. However, empirical evidence remains limited regarding whether DA-informed pedagogical AI agents differ from general-purpose generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) in supporting speaking development and regulating speaking anxiety over a full semester. This study therefore examined how the two different AI modalities, conceptualized through dynamic assessment (DA), influences low-achieving learners' English speaking performance and speaking anxiety. Using a 16-week quasi-experimental design with intact classes (n = 59), students engaged in identical task-based speaking activities supported by either a DA-oriented pedagogical AI agent (n = 30) or general-purpose GenAI (n = 29). Speaking performance, operationalized as fluency, accuracy, complexity, and task completion, was evaluated using preand post-test recordings, and speaking anxiety was assessed through a questionnaire. English speaking performance was analyzed using MANCOVA and moderated ANCOVA with pretest scores as covariates. Results revealed a significant multivariate effect of AI modality on speaking performance. Follow-up analyses showed that learners supported by the pedagogical AI agent demonstrated significantly higher post-test complexity and task completion, whereas no significant group differences were found for fluency or accuracy. For speaking anxiety, results indicated a significant interaction between AI modality and learners' initial anxiety levels. These findings suggest that the pedagogical value of AI-mediated speaking practice is design-dependent, and that DA-informed mediation may be particularly effective for supporting the developmental and affective needs of low-achieving EFL speakers.

TI Establishment of Core Entrustable Professional Activities for Advanced
   Emergency Medicine Ultrasonography Fellowship Using a Nominal Group
   Technique
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID OBSERVABLE PRACTICE ACTIVITIES; COMPETENCE; ENTRUSTMENT; SCALES
AB Background Advanced Emergency Medicine Ultrasonography (AEMUS) has become a recognized subspecialty within Emergency Medicine, yet no unified national curriculum or assessment framework exists for fellowship training. As competency-based medical education develops, entrustable professional activities (EPAs) offer a structured approach to defining essential tasks, guiding curriculum design, and standardizing assessment. To support high-quality, equitable AEMUS fellowship training, the Education Committee of the Society of Clinical Ultrasound Fellowships (SCUF) convened a diverse expert panel to develop core EPAs for AEMUS fellows.Methods We employed a modified virtual nominal group technique (vNGT) to achieve expert consensus. Eleven AEMUS education leaders participated between July 2024 and June 2025. Prior to the initial session, panelists reviewed curated literature and independently generated EPA ideas. During structured virtual meetings, participants engaged in round-robin idea sharing, clarification, and discussion, guided by existing national AEMUS standards of certification and program accreditation. Ideas were subsequently subjected to iterative voting, with >= 80% agreement required for acceptance. Three vNGT rounds were conducted. Accepted EPAs were further refined by assigned primary editors.Results The expert panel produced 15 core EPAs spanning four established domains: Administration, education, sonography skills, and scholarship. Professionalism was designated as its own domain. Panel deliberations focused on feasibility within a one-year fellowship, post-graduation scope of practice, and variability in program resources. The group endorsed a modified entrustment scale tailored to AEMUS to guide assessment across EPAs.Conclusion Using a structured consensus process, we developed the first EPA-based framework for AEMUS fellowship training. These EPAs provide a foundational curriculum and assessment structure intended to support program rigor, promote national consistency, and prepare fellows for independent advanced practice and leadership in clinical ultrasound.

TI Feasibility and implementation of a final year Objective Structured
   Clinical Examination (OSCE) in a medical model curriculum
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE); Final Year OSCE;
   Development and evaluation of OSCE
AB Background Practical clinical skills cannot be adequately assessed through written examinations. This article describes the development and implementation of a summative Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) prior to the Practical Year (PJ) at Hannover Medical School.Methods An interdisciplinary team, medical experts and students developed 34 OSCE stations based on Entrustable Professional Activities. Stations were piloted in 2022 with voluntary student participants and focus group feedback. The PJ-OSCE was curricularly integrated in 2023/24 and linked to five core clinical clerkships/modules. Pass-fail cut scores were established using the modified Angoff method.Results The pilot OSCEs proved high staffing demands but overall feasible and favorable for student learning. In June 2024, 278 students completed the mandatory PJ-OSCE across 15 circuits of eight stations (8 min each). Mean score was 603.08 (SD 67.57)/800 points (75.2%); pass rate was 97.1%. Examination reliability averaged 0.84 (Cronbach's alpha, SD 0.06). Students rated the examination 10.90/15 points, with 41.0% reporting substantial learning gains. Examiners rated the format as appropriate (86.3%).Conclusions This feasibility and implementation study demonstrates that a large-scale summative PJ-OSCE can be successfully developed and delivered within a German model curriculum context. The structured development process may serve as a model for other medical faculties implementing similar examination formats.

TI Using a Translanguaging Lens to Analyze Students' Meaning-Making in
   Mathematics
SO COGNITION AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE DRT; linear functions; translanguaging; academic discourse; emergent
   bilingual; meaning-making
ID MULTIPLE REPRESENTATIONS; ACADEMIC LITERACY; KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK;
   GESTURES; LANGUAGE; SLOPE; TALK
AB An epistemological shift toward heteroglossia in research on language diversity in mathematics classrooms transcends the dualities (e.g., home/new language; everyday/academic language) and hierarchies (e.g., valuing academic above everyday language or school over home language) that have traditionally shaped our understanding of language diversity and language learning. In this article, we propose translanguaging theory as a transformative framework for expanding our awareness of the complex and dynamic nature of emergent bilingual students' mathematical meaning-making. Translanguaging theory shifts the focus from identifying the distinct resources that EB students use in their meaning-making (e.g., languages, gestures) to understanding how mathematical meaning emerges from the blending of the resources present in a particular learning activity. This blending of resources is a collective process that emerges, flows, and changes moment-by-moment as participants engage in meaning-making together. Using data from the DMELL project, we use translanguaging theory to analyze how two Spanish-English EB students in middle school in the US use their communicative repertoires and their interactions with each other, the facilitator, and the dynamic representational technology (DRT) to engage in the mathematical practice of modeling. Microethnography provided an analytic framework compatible with translanguaging theory to conduct a moment-by-moment analysis of how the mathematical activity unfolded. The results show how the students flexibly used their communicative repertoires and the affordances of the learning environment to construct their model of the problem situation and find a solution. Furthermore, they made sense of the problem situation collectively, building on each other's ideas and the facilitator's suggestions, making stepwise progress toward creating their model. This analysis provided a holistic depiction of the students' meaning-making, allowing us to recognize their modeling process without labeling any of their contributions as "less" than mathematical. Implications for how translanguaging theory may guide future research and practice on EB students' mathematical learning are provided.

TI Explainable AI for predicting and interpreting mathematics achievement:
   a cross-national analysis of PISA 2018
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE PISA 2018; Mathematics achievement; Explainable machine learning; SHAP;
   Plausible values; Survey weights
AB This study applies a survey-weighted, plausible-value-aware explainable machine-learning workflow to PISA 2018 mathematics data from 74,235 students in ten purposively selected education systems. The analysis examines cross-national stability and country-specific variation in prediction and interpretation within a comparative, non-representative sample. A primary pool of 33 student questionnaire predictors and OECD-derived indices was constructed, followed by country-specific train-only stability feature selection. Four weighted models were compared using school-level holdout test sets: weighted linear regression, weighted linear regression with pairwise interactions, random forest, and CatBoost. Model performance was evaluated across all ten mathematics plausible values using final student weights and replicate-weight variance estimation. CatBoost achieved the strongest performance across all systems, with an average weighted of 0.358 and an average MAE of 57.29 score points. PV-robust SHAP summaries showed that books at home, highest parental occupational status, grade placement, mathematics learning time, socioeconomic status, test effort, directed instruction, and disciplinary climate were among the most stable predictors. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the SHAP pattern was not driven by PV1MATH or by grade placement alone. The study contributes a reproducible framework for explainable machine learning in comparative large-scale assessment research.

TI "Some highly effective strategies can have a negative impact on
   enjoyable things" - considerations of university students about
   motivation regulation strategies
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Motivation regulation; Qualitative; University students; Effectiveness;
   Costs
ID GOAL-GRADIENT HYPOTHESIS; SELF-CONTROL; PROCRASTINATION; DISTRACTIONS;
   PERFORMANCE; PROGRESS; BELIEFS
AB By applying motivational regulation, university students can sustain persistence in study tasks they find boring, irrelevant, or difficult. However, students often do not apply motivation regulation effectively. With a qualitative study, the considerations university students make concerning distinct motivation regulation strategies were investigated, aiming to shed light on the discrepancies between knowledge about and implementation of motivation regulation strategies. Moreover, individual resources and barriers that help or hinder effective motivational regulation were explored. Twenty-one semi-structured interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results indicated that university students make considerations concerning the effectiveness of a strategy and doubts about its effectiveness. Moreover, the situational nature of motivational regulation, associated enjoyment, and costs of putting a strategy into action may matter. Having higher self-regulation skills (especially self-discipline) was the most mentioned individual resource by students. Regarding barriers, procrastination tendencies, and a fixed mindset (especially negativity) seemed to be prominent issues according to students. Overall, students seem to weigh the value of regulating motivation against their other goals and decide whether or not to invest in motivation regulation because they juggle academic responsibilities with multiple other goals.

TI Design and Evaluation of an AI-Supported Automated Programming
   Assessment Environment for Concept-Aligned Reinforcement in Engineering
   and Computing Education
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE automated programming assessment; concept-aligned micro-assessment;
   generative AI; learning analytics; programming education
AB Automated programming assessment systems are widely used in engineering and computing education to support scalable programming practice, but correctness-based verdicts often provide limited concept-level reinforcement for novice learners. This study designed and evaluated an AI-supported automated programming assessment environment that transforms verified incorrect submissions into governed, concept-aligned micro-assessments. Rather than using generative AI as an open-ended tutor or grading agent, the proposed environment used AI as a constrained orchestration layer within a deterministic assessment workflow. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design was implemented in an introductory Python programming course with 90 first-year undergraduate students, including 45 students in the experimental group and 45 students in the control group. Both groups completed the same macro-level programming tasks through the same automated assessment system, whereas the experimental group additionally received assessment-triggered, learner-initiated micro-assessment opportunities through a mobile chatbot after verified incorrect submissions. Results indicated that learners in the experimental group demonstrated higher post-intervention concept-level mastery across all five programming components and reported greater gains in programming self-efficacy and higher post-intervention learning motivation. Log-based analyses further showed sustained engagement with the reinforcement environment, with learners completing an average of 51.3 micro-assessment interactions and 46% of these interactions occurring outside class sessions. These findings suggest that a governed, evidence-anchored reinforcement workflow can extend automated programming assessment systems from correctness evaluation toward scalable, concept-aligned support, although the observed advantages should be interpreted as outcomes associated with the integrated environment rather than as isolated effects of generative AI or additional practice alone.

TI Idea Evaluation: Can Training Facilitate the Recognition of Creative
   Ideas?
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; idea evaluation; originality; quality; training;
   verification
ID PERFORMANCE-APPRAISAL; SELECTION; SKILLS; WORK; IMPLEMENTATION;
   GENERATION; INNOVATION; RATINGS; SCALES; MODEL
AB Wallas suggests a number of cognitive processes associated with creativity, including the process of verification. Accurately evaluating creative ideas is a complex skill that often requires deep domain expertise or extensive training. This study examined whether better training methods can effectively enhance the accuracy of creativity ratings. Using a 2 (training: with practice and feedback vs. no practice) & times; 3 (rating rubric quality: low, moderate, high) between-subjects design, novice raters (N = 216) evaluated solutions to an ill-defined problem previously scored by expert judges. Rating accuracy was defined as the correspondence between participant and expert ratings on dimensions of originality and quality. Results indicated that participants who received practice and feedback during training, and those provided with more descriptive rating rubrics, demonstrated significantly greater accuracy in judging solution quality. However, these effects did not extend to originality ratings. Findings suggest that better rater training can improve aspects of creativity assessment, particularly when it includes opportunities for guided practice and detailed evaluation criteria. Implications for creativity assessment and scalable training methods are discussed.

TI A Creative Experimental Design Using Multiple Tools in Graduate
   Engineering Education Course in China
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; lane-change behavior; multi-tool experimental
   design; traffic flow theory; unmanned aerial vehicle
AB Experimental engineering education in transportation increasingly requires students to integrate field data acquisition, data processing, programming, and engineering interpretation. This study describes and evaluates a multi-tool experimental workflow implemented in a graduate Traffic Flow Theory course in China. Centered on vehicle lane-change analysis, the activity combined UAV-based traffic-video acquisition, video processing and trajectory extraction using Adobe Premiere Pro and Tracker, Python-based lane assignment and lane-change identification, and MATLAB-based visualization and interpretation. Educational outcomes were evaluated using a historical cohort comparison involving 30 pre-reform students in 2021 and 100 post-reform students from 2022 to 2024. An 18-item course-specific questionnaire and course-performance data were analyzed using Welch's independent-samples t-tests, Fisher's exact tests, and Hedges' g effect sizes. The post-reform cohorts reported a higher overall self-reported ability score than the pre-reform cohort (87.77 vs. 76.83; mean difference 10.94, 95% CI 8.70-13.17; p < 0.001; g = 2.65). Mean total course scores were also higher (82.96 vs. 74.95; mean difference 8.01, 95% CI 3.57-12.43; p < 0.001; g = 0.83), while overall satisfaction increased from 46.7% to 89.0% (p < 0.001). These findings indicate that the integrated workflow was practically implementable and was associated with higher student-reported competencies and course performance. The proposed workflow provides a reproducible framework for integrating field observation, computational tools, and traffic-flow interpretation in graduate transportation education.

TI A cross-group study of relationships among university students' online
   academic emotions, motivation, and engagement
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online learning; Academic emotions; Motivation and engagement wheel;
   Multi-group analysis
ID SELF-REGULATION; ACHIEVEMENT; PROCRASTINATION; BEHAVIOR; SCHOOL; NEEDS
AB Academic emotions, learning motivation, and engagement are critical factors influencing the quality of online education. Drawing on the motivation and engagement wheel (MEW) and control-value theory (CVT), this study aims to explore the mechanisms underlying effects of students' online academic emotions on their engagement through motivation and examine whether the relationships vary by gender. The final sample consisted of 402 graduate students from a university in central China. Results from structural equation modeling (SEM) showed that positive academic emotions were positively associated with adaptive motivation but were not significantly associated with maladaptive motivation, whereas negative academic emotions were positively associated with maladaptive motivation and negatively associated with adaptive motivation. Adaptive motivation was positively associated with adaptive engagement and negatively associated with maladaptive engagement, whereas maladaptive motivation was positively associated with maladaptive engagement but was not significantly associated with adaptive engagement. Furthermore, the multi-group analysis showed that the positive associations between adaptive motivation and adaptive engagement and between maladaptive motivation and maladaptive engagement were stronger among males, whereas the negative association between adaptive motivation and maladaptive engagement was stronger among females. This study suggested that instructors should consider the influence of both positive and negative aspects of students' emotions, motivation, and engagement to design and implement targeted teaching methods and strategies based on gender differences.

TI Implementation-Relevant Components of Digitally Mediated Teacher
   Activity Groups in Multilingual Vietnam
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE digital professional development; teacher activity groups; facilitation;
   online professional learning; implementation-relevant components;
   situated teacher agency; multilingual English language teaching; Vietnam
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; COMMUNITIES; INFORMATION
AB In geographically dispersed and multilingual Vietnamese lower-secondary English language teaching contexts, digitally mediated professional development can widen access to peer learning, yet less is known about how dialogue, facilitation, and practical resources are configured under curriculum, workload, and infrastructure constraints. This bounded qualitative case study examined the implementation-relevant components of digitally mediated Teacher Activity Groups and the contextual conditions shaping their operation. The primary dataset comprised eight semi-structured facilitator interviews, supplemented by 24 documentary sources: 18 facilitator-authored reports and six structured observation forms. Interviews were analysed through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic approach, while documents were analysed abductively to corroborate, qualify, and complicate interview interpretations. Three interrelated components were identified: structured peer dialogue across dispersed professional contexts; facilitation routines as human infrastructure; and modelling with adaptable digital resources. Their reported operation was shaped by workload and time scarcity, curriculum and textbook pressures, infrastructure instability, uneven participation, conceptual uncertainty, and institutional support. The findings illuminate digitally mediated teacher professional learning as a socio-technical arrangement in which professional exchange, facilitation, resources, and context are relationally configured. Instead of quantifying theme prevalence, we present these findings as a contextually grounded interpretation, deliberately avoiding claims regarding programme effectiveness, causal mechanisms, or generalisable outcomes.

TI Co-Constructing Rubrics with Multilingual Writers: Inclusive Approaches
   to Formative Assessment in L2 Classrooms
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE rubric co-construction; assessment as learning; L2 writing; multilingual
   learners; qualitative case study
ID SCORING RUBRICS; STUDENTS
AB Although rubric co-construction has been associated with positive outcomes in L2 writing classrooms, relatively little is known about how multilingual learners experience participation in rubric development or how collaborative interactions contribute to learning. This qualitative case study examined rubric co-construction in an undergraduate ESL writing course to investigate (1) students' perceptions of participating in rubric development and (2) the interactional processes through which assessment criteria were negotiated. Data included classroom recordings, collaborative worksheets, rubric drafts, student reflections, semi-structured interviews, and researcher field notes, and were analyzed thematically through the lenses of democratic assessment, assessment for learning, and sociocultural theory. Findings indicate that rubric co-construction clarified expectations, strengthened students' engagement with assessment, and increased confidence in evaluating both their own writing and that of their peers. Collaborative dialogue, negotiation of meaning, consensus building, instructor scaffolding, and the development of shared assessment criteria emerged as key mechanisms supporting assessment literacy. The findings suggest that the educational value of rubric co-construction lies not only in the resulting rubric but also in the participatory processes through which multilingual learners develop shared understandings of writing quality.

TI Epilepsy, Participation, and Belonging in South African Secondary
   Schools: Learners' Accounts Through a Capability Approach
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE epilepsy; Capability Approach; inclusive education; educational
   participation; secondary schooling
ID STIGMA
AB Learners with epilepsy experience persistent educational challenges that remain underexplored within inclusive education discourse, particularly in secondary school contexts. Guided by the Capability Approach, this study examines how epilepsy shapes learners' opportunities to participate meaningfully in schooling and achieve valued educational outcomes. Situated within an interpretivist paradigm, this interpretive qualitative research employed semi-structured interviews with 12 learners diagnosed with epilepsy, recruited from four secondary schools in South Africa. Grounded in learners lived experiences, the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that seizure episodes disrupt classroom participation and continuity of learning, while stigma and fear of embarrassment constrain learners' confidence and social inclusion. Recurrent absenteeism, linked to both medical and psychosocial factors, further limits academic engagement and progression. These interconnected challenges restrict learners' capabilities not only to learn, but also to participate fully and develop a sense of belonging within the school environment. The findings suggest that participants experienced educational disadvantage through the interaction between health-related challenges and contextual barriers rather than through epilepsy alone. It highlights the potential value of inclusive and responsive educational practices that may expand learners' opportunities for participation and belonging, including enhanced teacher awareness, flexible pedagogical approaches, and psychosocial support. By foregrounding learners' voices, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how chronic health conditions intersect with inclusive education and calls for systemic efforts to promote meaningful participation and well-being.

TI Fostering AI Literacy in Teacher Education: A Case Study of Pre-Service
   and In-Service Teachers' Perceptions
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; AIEd; AI literacy; teacher
   training; educational perceptions; anthropocentric approach
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB This case study examines changes in participants' educational perceptions and technology acceptance following a targeted, short-term training intervention based on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. Utilizing a quasi-experimental longitudinal pre-test/post-test design, the study examined the perceptions of 476 pre-service and in-service teachers at a major public university in Italy before and after a 10 h training course covering AI architecture, Large Language Models (LLMs), and practical pedagogical applications. TI Structured Freedom: How AI, Teacher Support, and Periodic Testing Shape
   Engagement in Informal Vocabulary Learning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-supported informal vocabulary learning; teacher support; periodic
   testing; self-determination theory; Chinese EFL context
ID MOTIVATION; RETENTION
AB The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed informal language learning, providing learners with flexible, self-directed opportunities for vocabulary acquisition outside formal classroom instruction. This study examined how AI use, teacher support, and periodic testing influence Chinese EFL learners' engagement in informal English vocabulary learning. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed, combining a three-group pretest-posttest quantitative intervention over three months with follow-up qualitative interviews involving 15 participants. Quantitative results showed significant increases in all three engagement dimensions across conditions. At posttest, the teacher-guided AI with testing condition produced the highest behavioral and cognitive engagement, whereas the teacher-guided AI condition produced the highest emotional engagement; the AI-only condition showed the lowest levels across all dimensions. Qualitative accounts suggested that teacher support facilitated goal-setting, strategic scaffolding, and emotional reassurance, helping learners use AI more purposefully, while participants described testing as providing structured feedback for strategic adjustment and self-monitoring. The AI tool supported deep lexical processing and personalized learning, while learners appeared to use these affordances more strategically when combined with teacher guidance and structured feedback. These findings are broadly consistent with Self-Determination Theory and provide practical guidance for designing learner-centered vocabulary programs that balance autonomy, guidance, and accountability while sustaining strategic and emotional engagement.

TI Australian Educators' Use of Children's Heritage Language in Early
   Childhood Services: Facilitators and Barriers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood education; heritage language; multilingualism;
   multilingual family
ID FAMILIES; PARTNERSHIP; CARE; TEACHERS; PARENTS; PROFESSIONALS; ATTITUDES
AB Educators' use of multilingual children's heritage languages (HLs) in Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) settings can support their sense of belonging and wellbeing. Although multilingual educators are increasingly recognised as important in supporting multilingual families, the relationship between educators' multilingual competence and their use of HL with children and parents remains underexplored. This study employed a mixed-methods design, combining an online survey with interviews, to examine factors contributing to educators' HL use with multilingual children and parents in Australian ECEC settings. Quantitative findings showed significant associations between educators' self-reported multilingual fluency and their use of HL with both children and parents. These findings suggest that supporting HL use in ECEC requires not only individual educators' multilingual competence but also broader organisational support. A whole-centre approach involving educators, leaders, and management may therefore help create more supportive environments for multilingual practices and strengthen support for multilingual children and families.

TI Analysis of a Structural Thinking Task Solved by Pre-Service Mathematics
   Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher education; theory of mathematics education; structural
   understanding; structural thinking; pattern generalization; structuring
   representations
AB Structural thinking is widely recognized as an important aspect of mathematical thinking, yet the role of structuring representations in supporting generalization has received relatively little attention. This study examined how pre-service mathematics teachers construct mathematical structure when solving a pattern generalization task. Written solutions produced by 62 pre-service mathematics teachers at different stages of their teacher education program were analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis informed by theoretical perspectives on emergent and mathematical structure. Six distinct solution strategies were identified, differing primarily in the structuring representations participants used to reorganize the mathematical situation. The findings indicate that participants differed not only in their solution procedures but also in the mathematical relationships highlighted by their representations. These differences were reflected in the general rules participants formulated and in the mathematical reasoning they used to support their conclusions. The study highlights the importance of structuring representations as a component of structural thinking and suggests that developing pre-service teachers' ability to construct and interpret mathematically productive representations may support the transition from recognizing local relationships to formulating general mathematical relationships and supporting them through mathematical reasoning.

TI Digital Technology Use During Teaching Internship: Profiles and
   Predictors Among Preservice Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE technology infusion; preservice teachers; teaching internship;
   educational technology; technology use profiles; cluster analysis;
   initial teacher education
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; SELF-EFFICACY; KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK; INFORMATION;
   COMPETENCE; BARRIERS; BELIEFS; ICT
AB The use of technology is a central component of initial teacher education; yet how preservice teachers use technological resources during teaching internship remains poorly understood, particularly when assessed through actual deployment frequencies rather than self-perceived competence. This study aimed to analyze material technology use among student teachers (N = 705) at a Spanish university during teaching internship, to examine differences by personal, academic and contextual variables and to identify technology use profiles. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was employed. Exploratory factor analysis, cross-validated through confirmatory factor analysis in an independent subsample, revealed four dimensions of technology use: mobile, emerging and innovative technology; printing, digitization and storage equipment; audiovisual equipment and connectivity; and interactive presentation technologies. Multivariate analyses of variance, multiple linear regression and cluster analysis were conducted. Results showed differentiated patterns of technology use, with greater reliance on conventional tools and more limited adoption of mobile and emerging technologies. Among academic variables, year of study showed the most consistent associations with technology use dimensions, while educational stage was significantly related to the use of specific resources. Cluster analysis identified differentiated levels of technology use (low, moderate and high). The high-use profile was concentrated among fourth-year Primary Education students completing teaching internship in upper primary grades, a pattern that should be interpreted alongside the longer duration and greater autonomy of the final-year practicum. This study offers a more granular account of technology infusion than other competence-based approaches due to combined variable and person-centered analyses of technology use during real school-based internships. These findings indicate that technology infusion during teaching internship is shaped by both training and contextual factors, underscoring the need to strengthen technology-related learning opportunities in teaching internship and to foster closer university-educational centers coordination to support effective technology integration in teaching and learning.

TI Helpful or harmful? generative AI dependence, self-reported critical
   thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business
   students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI dependence; business education; CB-SEM; generative AI; PLS-SEM;
   self-perceived employability; self-reported critical thinking
   disposition
ID PLS-SEM; VALIDATION; INTERVENTIONS; VALIDITY; SCALE
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by offering new forms of learning support while also raising concerns about over-reliance, reduced verification, and the weakening of independent cognitive engagement. Drawing on cognitive load theory, cognitive offloading, habit formation, and the augmentation-automation distinction, this study examines the associations between GenAI use, GenAI dependence, self-reported critical-thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among undergraduate business students in Oman. Cross-sectional survey data from 412 students were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, with covariance-based SEM used as a robustness check. The findings show that GenAI use is positively associated with GenAI dependence and self-perceived employability. Its positive association with self-reported critical-thinking disposition emerges in the adjusted structural model after accounting for GenAI dependence and the interaction between GenAI use and GenAI dependence, rather than as a strong zero-order relationship. GenAI dependence is negatively associated with both student outcomes and reduces the strength of the positive associations between GenAI use and both outcomes. The results suggest that GenAI use may support students' perceived learning and career readiness when it functions as a reflective augmentation tool involving verification, comparison, and independent judgement, while higher dependence is associated with weaker perceived learning and employability-related outcomes.

TI Scientific Competence in Undergraduate Medical Education: Professional
   Orientations of Physiology Educators
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE scientific competence; medical education; physiology; documentary
   method; competency-based medical education; scientific literacy
ID EPISTEMIC AGENCY; IMPLEMENTATION
AB Introduction: Scientific Competence (SC) is a central objective in medical education, but its conceptualization remains insufficiently differentiated, particularly regarding the relationship between evidence use and participation in scientific knowledge generation. Objective: This study reconstructs how physiology educators conceptualized SC and related different forms of scientific engagement within their professional orientation frameworks. Methods: Three group discussions were conducted in 2015-2016 with physiology educators from two German medical faculties and a didactic workshop of the German Physiological Society (n = 30). Conclusions: This historically situated reconstruction suggests that the central curricular question is not simply whether SC should be developed, but which forms of scientific participation should be expected of all physicians and which remain more closely associated with research-oriented trajectories. The findings offer conceptual hypotheses for examining this distinction in contemporary medical education.

TI From the classroom to the page: a decade of engaging pharmacy students
   in publishable research in a Small Island Developing Nation
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH; BENEFITS; SCIENCE
AB Purpose: To describe the implementation and evolution of a faculty-led undergraduate research program integrating publishable research into the pharmacy curriculum at the University of Belize, a Small Island Developing State in Central and South America and the Caribbean, and to offer practical insights for educators in resource-limited settings. Description: Beginning in 2017, the pharmacy program shifted from teaching research as abstract content to actively engaging second-year students in mentored research that led to co-authorship on peer-reviewed publications. Course assignments were converted into research experiences aligned with course learning objectives. Students worked in small groups, received longitudinal mentorship, and contributed to all stages of the research process. Analysis: The model succeeded because early introduction (year two) allowed skill development over time, assignment conversion created purpose and accountability, group-based peer learning distributed cognitive load, and the expectation of publication motivated quality. Challenges included faculty time demands, student writing proficiency, and post-graduation engagement for manuscript revisions. Conclusions: Pharmacy students in resource-limited settings can produce publishable research when curricula are intentionally designed to scaffold research skills progressively and when faculty commit to sustained mentorship. Implications: This model is replicable in other developing nation contexts and offers a pathway for building research capacity while enhancing student learning outcomes. Institutions should consider curricular restructuring to embed research experiences rather than treating research as an isolated exercise.

TI Understanding student attrition in pharmacy education: Personal,
   academic, and environmental factors and their interrelationships
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Attrition; Students; pharmacy; Education; Student dropouts; Academic
   performance; Mental health; Educational measurement; Cross-sectional

AB Background: Student attrition remains a challenge in pharmacy education. This study examined the perceived influence of personal, academic, and environmental factors associated with student attrition, differences across selected student characteristics, and the interrelationships among attrition domains. Methods: A descriptive-comparative study with an exploratory correlational component was conducted among 100 former pharmacy students who discontinued enrollment in a Bachelor of Science in Pharmacy program. Responses to a validated attrition questionnaire were analyzed using descriptive statistics, group comparison tests, and exploratory multiple linear regression analyses of inter-domain associations. Differences across senior high school academic strands were observed for Personal (epsilon 2 = 0.090), Academic (epsilon 2 = 0.102), and Environmental Factors (epsilon 2 = 0.062), with the largest group effect observed for Academic Factors. Male respondents also reported greater perceived influence of Academic Factors than female respondents (|r(r)(| = 0.249). Exploratory regression analyses showed positive associations between Academic and Personal Factors ((3 = 0.585 and 0.519) and between Academic and Environmental Factors ((3 = 0.446 and 0.322), with the model for Academic Factors accounting for the greatest proportion of explained variance (R2 = 0.543). Conclusions: Student attrition in pharmacy appears to be associated primarily with academic and personal experiences. Academic factors showed the strongest and most consistent associations with the other attrition domains, highlighting their importance within the broader attrition experience and in understanding student persistence in pharmacy programs.

SO GEOSCIENCE COMMUNICATION

DT Article

   EXTRACTIVISM
AB The Geosciences are amongst the least diverse research fields, where women and other underrepresented groups face systemic biases. This paper presents the state of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in the cloud-physics community, by combining a metadata analysis of 6987 cloud-physics peer-reviewed journal articles published between 1970 and 2020 with responses from a survey of 198 participants from the cloud-physics community. Although the survey data shows the general experiences of cloud physicists globally, the perspectives from this work can aid the cloud-physics community to develop strategies to improve DEI in institutions beyond a business case for a diverse science community. Rather we should consider an equity-centered approach by understanding our ethical responsibilities to benefit research of the climate system, as it is promoted by the International Association for Promoting Geoethics (IAPG) in Geosciences.

   problems: A longitudinal study of Arab-speaking children with speech and
   language conditions
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Expressive language delay; Stuttering; Behavior problems; Maternal
   sensitivity; Arabic
ID TYPICALLY DEVELOPING-CHILDREN; PARENT-CHILD; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY;
   EMOTIONAL AVAILABILITY; SOCIAL COMPETENCE; MOTHERS; IMPACT; IMPAIRMENT;
   PREVALENCE; ATTACHMENT
AB Children with expressive language delay or stuttering conditions have an increased risk of behavior problems. However, the mechanism underlying this association is poorly understood. Studies show maternal sensitivity shapes the socioemotional development of typically developing children, yet little is known about this association in the context of children with speech and language conditions. To address this gap, we examined whether maternal sensitivity would be concurrently associated with children's behavior problems and prospectively predict changes in these problems over time. TI An evaluation of didactic oncology curriculum coverage in U.S. schools
   of pharmacy
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING

DT Article
DE Oncology; Didactic; Curriculum; Cancer pharmacotherapy; Oncology
   education; ACCP Toolkit; Oncology pharmacy
AB Objective: As oncology pharmacotherapy continues to expand in complexity and scope, characterization of oncology-related didactic instruction is needed. This study sought to determine the breadth and depth of oncology topics taught in U.S. schools of pharmacy using the 2019 American College of Clinical Pharmacy (ACCP) Pharmacotherapy Didactic Curriculum Toolkit. Methods: An 18-item survey instrument was electronically distributed to faculty involved in didactic oncology instruction across 139 U.S. schools of pharmacy. Conclusion: Although faculty-reported oncology curriculum coverage generally aligns with the 2019 ACCP Toolkit, potential gaps remain in select tier one topics and notable variability exists between programs. These findings provide a contemporary description of oncology curriculum coverage and may inform ongoing curricular review and discussion across pharmacy programs.

TI Removing barriers to college credits: Where and for whom AP exam fee
   waivers work
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Advanced placement; AP exam; Fee waiver; College credit
ID ADVANCED PLACEMENT
AB We study the effects of North Carolina's Advanced Placement (AP) exam fee-waiver policy on exam participation and potential college-credit attainment conditional on AP enrollment. Using student-course level administrative data, we first exploit within-student variation among students enrolled in multiple AP courses during both pre-and post-waiver periods. We find that fee waivers increased exam participation by 2.1 percentage points but did not significantly increase the share of AP enrollments yielding an exam score of 3 or higher, a common threshold for college-credit eligibility. This average null, however, masks a 3percentage-point increase in the share of low-SES AP enrollments yielding a score of 3 or higher, narrowing the baseline attainment gap by 15 percent. Using the full sample of AP enrollments and a difference-in-differences framework, we then show that enrollments with the lowest predicted exam-taking propensity absent the waiver experienced the largest gains in both exam participation and potential college-credit attainment, suggesting that universal fee waivers generate larger benefits where barriers to AP exam participation are most likely to bind. Under illustrative assumptions, our welfare calculations indicate that the policy's benefits far exceed its costs.

TI Not just loss: Multi-level structural changes in the L2 lexical-semantic
   network after formal instruction
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 lexical-semantic network; Lexical attrition; Network analysis;
   Lexical attrition foundation framework
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE ATTRITION; SAVINGS; MEMORY; VOCABULARY
AB Despite growing interest in second-language (L2) lexical attrition, little is known about how the structure of the L2 lexical-semantic network evolves after formal instruction ends. Drawing on a complex network perspective, this longitudinal study examined the dynamic reorganization of L2 lexical-semantic networks over a 12-month post-instruction period. Semantic fluency data were collected from Chinese EFL learners at five time points and analyzed at the macro, meso, and micro levels of network organization. The results revealed that the lexical-semantic network retained its small-world properties throughout the observation period, while undergoing a nonlinear process of structural adaptation. At the macro level, centralization increased during the initial post-instruction period, indicating a temporary concentration of connectivity around relatively highly connected lexical nodes. At the meso level, modularity gradually declined, indicating weaker differentiation between lexical communities, whereas within-community semantic similarity remained stable. At the micro level, peripheral lexical items exhibited substantial turnover, and lexical stability was jointly shaped by lexical properties and local neighborhood structure. These findings suggest that L2 lexical attrition is not a simple process of lexical loss but a dynamic process of network reorganization characterized by core stabilization, peripheral fluctuation, and structural reconfiguration. The study extends current Lexical Attrition Foundation (LeAF) framework by demonstrating how cognitive economy and local network ecology jointly shape the development of the L2 mental lexicon under conditions of reduced language use.

TI Exploring the role of need for cognition in daily cognitive activity
   engagement among elementary students: A mixed-methods study
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Need for cognition; Cognitive engagement; Elementary school;
   Mixed-method; Daily diary
ID MOTIVATION; UNIVERSITY; ADOLESCENCE; PERFORMANCE; PREDICTORS; CHILDHOOD;
   REWARD; HARD
AB To date, little is known about how elementary students' Need for Cognition (NFC) manifests in their everyday engagement with cognitive activities. This mixed-methods study examined cognitive engagement (activity types, frequency, and enjoyment) in home and school settings in a sample of 391 fourth-and fifth-grade students (51.8% boys, Mage = 10.03), using a seven-day online diary. Educational relevance statement: This study provides initial insights into the relation between late-elementary students' Need for Cognition (NFC) and their everyday engagement in cognitive activities. Across both settings, high-NFC students engaged in these activities more often and reported greater enjoyment, with NFC-related differences in enjoyment being more pronounced at school and differences in engagement frequency being larger at home. These patterns suggest that similar dispositional tendencies may be expressed differently depending on contextual structures and may thus require different supports. Overall, the findings highlight the important and complementary roles of both home and school settings in students' cognitive engagement.

TI Operationalizing Carrying Capacity Through Rationing Mechanisms in
   Northeast Asia's Protected Areas: Applying the Recreation Rationing
   Spectrum to Yushan National Park, Taiwan
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE recreation rationing spectrum; distributive justice; carrying capacity;
   lottery system; protected areas
ID LAND-USE; MANAGEMENT
AB The rapid growth of nature-based tourism has intensified pressure on natural protected areas (PA), especially on the capability of PAs to balance conservation and recreational use. In this context, the Recreation Rationing Spectrum (RRS) by Rice and Phillips offers a way to understand how limited access to high-demand natural areas is allocated among visitors. While carrying capacity has long been used to define acceptable levels of use, less attention has been given to how access is distributed once those limits are established, as the RRS has not yet been applied as a systematic analytical tool in empirical research. This study addressed both gaps by examining how carrying capacity is operationalized through rationing mechanisms in Yushan National Park, Taiwan, while testing an empirical application of RRS as an analytical lens. A nested case study design was adopted, drawing on multiple rounds of fieldwork and semi-structured interviews with park management staff conducted between 2023 and 2026. The findings indicate that carrying capacity management in Yushan National Park is primarily operationalized through infrastructure constraints and operational visitor limits, and rationing, with the lottery system playing a central role in regulating access to high-demand areas. In addition, quantitative evidence indicates that accommodation capacity is closely associated with access outcomes, particularly in determining access competitiveness under the lottery-based rationing system. By examining how rationing mechanisms function under carrying capacity constraints, the study highlights how different allocation arrangements reflect trade-offs between equality, equity, and efficiency in the distribution of recreational opportunities. This study contributes to bridging the gap between theoretical allocation frameworks and their practical implementation, particularly in the context of Northeast Asia's PA, and offers insights for park managers seeking to balance conservation, recreation, and administrative feasibility.

AB The application of GenAI in science education research has sparked debates on how students perceive themselves as science persons when they use GenAI to engage in scientific activities. In this study, we explored how students self-reported their science identity in relation to their use of GenAI in scientific activities. TI Interactional Patterns of Adolescent Health Education: A Roter
   Interaction Analysis System-Based Study in Moroccan Secondary Schools
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescent health; classroom interaction; health communication; health
   literacy; mixed-methods research; school health education
ID STRATEGIES; LITERACY; FUTURE
AB Background Adolescence is a critical developmental period during which health-related behaviors consolidate. In Moroccan secondary schools, health education remains largely educator-guided, with limited evidence of classroom communication. This study analyzes how verbal interaction patterns structure health education delivery at middle and high school levels. Methods An exploratory mixed-methods study was conducted in five Moroccan secondary institutions (N = 169 students). Verbal interactions (1024 utterances) were coded using the Roter Interaction Analysis System (RIAS), adapted to the Moroccan educational context. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires assessed short-term knowledge acquisition. Qualitative and quantitative analyses examined speech distribution, functional communication categories, and developmental differences. Results Educators produced 57.5% of utterances. Instrumental communication predominated (62%-67%), while affective exchanges represented approximately one-third of interactions. Middle school sessions combined directive guidance with experiential anchoring, whereas high school sessions demonstrated increased dialogic debate and argumentative engagement. Knowledge scores improved significantly across all sessions (p < 0.001), with improvements evident in both middle and high school interventions. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Findings highlight interactional competence as a measurable pedagogical skill and support the integration of structured communication training modules and developmentally adapted dialogic strategies within secondary educator preparation programs. Conclusion The findings suggest that secondary health education operates as a negotiated communicative process in which language shapes participation, learning, and emerging health literacy.

TI A polycentric regime of linguistic legitimacy: language policy from
   below in Kazakhstan
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Kazakhstan; Language policy and planning; Practiced language policy;
   Multilingualism; Narrative analysis
AB This article examines how language policy in Kazakhstan is understood and enacted in everyday life. Since independence, state initiatives have aimed to strengthen Kazakh while maintaining multilingual stability, yet most research has focused on top-down policy. This study adopts a bottom-up perspective, combining survey data from 6,260 respondents with 1,775 written narratives to explore language use, beliefs, and lived experiences. The findings show a domain-based distribution of languages rather than a linear shift from Russian to Kazakh. Kazakh is primarily associated with identity and private life, while Russian remains central in professional and urban contexts, and English gains importance in global and digital domains. At the same time, respondents express hierarchical and moralized language ideologies, often linking Kazakh proficiency to ethnic authenticity and civic duty. These dynamics are reflected in lived experiences of linguistic discrimination, including both institutional barriers and everyday forms of shaming and exclusion. The study argues that Kazakhstan's linguistic order is best understood as a polycentric multilingual configuration, in which different languages carry distinct symbolic, practical, and aspirational value. Rather than a simple case of language replacement, the findings highlight ongoing tensions between policy goals, social practices, and competing forms of linguistic legitimacy.

TI Whose voices count? Multilingualism, AI policy, and equity at
   Hispanic-Serving institutions
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Language policy; AI governance; Higher education; Hispanic-serving
   institutions (HSIs); Multilingualism; Institutional identity; Critical
   discourse analysis
ID DIVERSITY
AB Universities have been rapidly developing generative AI policies to govern teaching, learning, research, and administration. Although these policies are typically framed around innovation, academic integrity, and risk management, they also shape language practices and participation in multilingual institutional contexts. Drawing on language policy scholarship that conceptualizes policy as discourse-in-action, this study examines AI policy discourse at two Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs) in the United States. Using critical discourse analysis of AI guidance documents, syllabus templates, faculty guidelines, task force materials, and administrative communications, we identify two interrelated patterns across both institutions. First, AI governance constructs an implicitly English-dominant user while leaving multilingual practices and perspectives largely unaddressed. Second, responsible AI use is framed through procedural compliance and individualized responsibility, creating uneven terrain for multilingual users to navigate. Together, these patterns suggest that institutional AI policies function as de facto language policies that reproduce monolingual assumptions through both what they explicitly address and what they leave unsaid. Read against each institution's broader commitments to multilingual communities, these findings indicate that AI governance and institutional linguistic priorities have not yet been fully integrated. We conclude by proposing a five-dimension continuum for more linguistically responsive and participatory AI governance across domains of governance, language orientation, ethics, responsibility, and innovation.
