TI Object-Control Skills and Cortisol Response During Physical Education
   Lessons in Primary School Children
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE fundamental motor skills; motor coordination; physical education;
   psychomotor performance; stress response
ID PSYCHOSOCIAL STRESS; HEART-RATE; COMPETENCE; REACTIVITY; ASSOCIATIONS;
   TIME
AB Background: Object-control (OC) skills are fundamental movement skills acquired during primary school that may act as either stressors or engagement factors during physical education (PE). This study examined the acute impact of OC exercises on children's stress levels across grade levels. Methods: 124 primary school children (Grades 3-5) participated in two PE lessons, one including OC exercises and one without. Salivary cortisol (C) was measured before and after each lesson. Results: Fourth-grade children showed lower C concentrations than fifth-grade students (p = 0.02). Following PE without OC, third-grade C levels decreased (p = 0.045), fourth-grade increased (p < 0.01), and fifth-grade showed no change. Following PE with OC, C decreased only in fifth-grade children (p = 0.03).Implications for School Health Policy and Practice Because stress-related effects of OC exercises differ by grade level, PE curricula should introduce OC tasks progressively. Conclusions: Primary school children exhibit distinct, grade-dependent neuroendocrine responses after physical activity. High cognitive loads in complex OC tasks may buffer typical cortisol reductions in younger children, whereas mature cohorts find OC activities stress-regulating. Evaluating motor skill development alongside hormonal adaptations can help optimize school health policies and stress management strategies.

TI Solution Strategies and Representational Coherence in Preservice Primary
   Teachers' Fraction-as-Operator Problem Solving
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Fraction as operator; Mathematical representations; Preservice teachers;
   Procedural fluency; Representational coherence
ID MATHEMATICAL KNOWLEDGE; RATIONAL NUMBERS; WHOLE-NUMBER; STUDENTS
AB Developing a robust understanding of fractions, particularly of the fraction-as-operator subconstruct, is essential for prospective primary teachers. This study examines the successful solution strategies of 263 preservice teachers when solving fraction-as-operator tasks varying by operated quantity (whole or fractional) and quantity context (continuous or discrete), each requiring arithmetic and graphical responses. Adopting Kieren's (1976, 1980a) definition of the operator, the study combines quantitative and qualitative analyses to explore success rates, strategies, and representational coherence between arithmetic and graphical solutions. Results show a predominant reliance on direct multiplication in whole-number quantities, while fraction-of-a-fraction problems were associated with greater strategic diversity and reduced use of this method. Graphical representations were generally aligned with the quantity context, rectangular area models for continuous quantities and discrete set models for countable objects, but coherence weakened in structurally more complex tasks, with correct calculations often paired with incomplete or mismatched diagrams. These findings indicate that procedural correctness does not consistently coincide with explicit coordination between arithmetic and graphical representations, highlighting the importance of fostering representational flexibility and explicit structural reasoning in teacher education. Specific challenges, such as translating between symbolic and graphical forms in less familiar structures, warrant targeted instructional attention. By examining preservice teachers' approaches to fraction-as-operator problems across contexts, this study contributes to a more nuanced account of their fraction reasoning and offers insights for improving mathematics preparation in teacher education.

SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom research; learning assessment; scholarship of teaching and
   learning; survey response
ID STUDENTS; EXPERIENCE; VALIDITY; OUTCOMES; FACULTY; IMPACT
AB Determining how students perceive and navigate the physiology classroom is crucial for designing evidence-based pedagogy and a well-informed curriculum. As trained scientists, most physiology instructors are well versed in using quantitative research, a methodology that prioritizes statistical analysis to predict future outcomes. While these methods offer valuable insights into measurable trends, they often rely on assumptions that overlook the "why" and "how" of student learning, which fall into the realm of qualitative research methodologies. TI Exploring flipped classrooms in undergraduate anatomy and physiology
   courses: a systematic review
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic performance; anatomy and physiology; flipped classroom; student
   satisfaction; undergraduate
ID EDUCATION; PERFORMANCE; IMPACT; LEVEL
AB We conducted a systematic review to investigate the effect of implementing flipped classroom designs on academic performance and student satisfaction in undergraduate anatomy and physiology courses. We used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework and searched databases (EBSCO Medline and EBSCO Eric) with the terms "flip* class," "anatomy," and "physiology." Original research articles were limited to peer-reviewed, quantitative, and/or mixed-methods studies published between 2010 and 2025. Three main themes emerged from the 11 articles reviewed, including positive gains in academic performance (n = 10/11 studies reporting; 91% studies) and student satisfaction (n = 10/11 studies reporting; 91% studies). While low effect sizes were found in most studies, none of these studies reported a negative effect for flipped classroom interventions. Structured teaching strategies and curriculum design appear to be important determinants of performance and satisfaction. Studies on flipped classrooms in undergraduate anatomy and physiology courses indicated positive changes in academic performance and student satisfaction linked to a well-designed curriculum. Methodological limitations in the studies reviewed include the absence of demographic analysis, minimal or absent descriptions of flipped classroom curriculum design, inadequate data reporting, and the absence of randomized comparison groups. Future research needs to focus on refining and standardizing the quality of preclass materials and exploring strategies to enhance student compliance and engagement with preclass content. Additional studies could all focus on identifying the factors that contribute to both the successes and limitations of the flipped classroom, particularly in complex courses such as anatomy and physiology, where unique challenges may arise. NEW & NOTEWORTHY Our systematic review shows that flipped classrooms in undergraduate anatomy and physiology courses can boost academic performance and student satisfaction, especially when paired with well-structured curriculum design. These findings highlight both the promise of flipped learning and the need for stronger, more consistent research in this area.

TI BioQueer: educational narratives on sex and gender-a methodology
   for developing, implementing, and evaluating an instructional guidebook
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE constructivist spiral; differences of sex development; instructional
   material; intersexuality; science communication
ID MANAGEMENT; SCIENCE
AB This study evaluates an educational intervention using a constructivist guidebook developed by the authors to teach human development and sex diversity within physiology education. Despite scientific advances, tertiary curricula often maintain binary, pathologizing views that overlook biological complexity. We implemented the BioQueer guidebook in a one-group pretest-posttest study with 44 undergraduate students from Bachelor's and teacher education track (Licentiate) degrees. The intervention focused on hormonal signaling and differences of sex development (DSD) as natural physiological variations. Statistical analysis using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests revealed significant perceived learning across all five dimensions (P < 0.0001), with large effect sizes (r >= 0.64). Cumulative link models indicated that the material reduced disparities in physiological knowledge regardless of baseline levels, whereas cumulative learning patterns emerged regarding gender binarism. Bachelor's students showed higher odds of attaining top-tier posttest categories in specific domains. This approach fosters gender literacy without compromising scientific rigor, situating physiological processes within the broader context of natural variability. Promoting such inclusive frameworks is essential for training future professionals to interpret human biology with greater precision and social responsibility. Future longitudinal research is needed to assess the durability of these conceptual shifts in reproductive physiology education. NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study evaluates the BioQueer guidebook, an educational intervention developed to improve undergraduate understanding of differences of sex development (DSD) and sex and gender concepts. With a one-group pretest-posttest design with ordinal analysis [cumulative link model (CLM)], results showed consistent increases in participant scores. Despite design limitations, findings support the guidebook's clarity and pedagogical potential. This exploratory study informs future research, including a planned randomized controlled trial to assess causal effects in physiology education.

TI Perceived Anthropomorphism as a Mediating Mechanism in Human-AI
   Interaction: Explaining Empathy, Trust, and Perceived Value in Higher
   Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE educational artificial intelligence; higher education; perceived
   anthropomorphism; perceived animacy; perceived intelligence; perceived
   empathy; perceived usefulness; trust in AI; perceived value; PLS-SEM
ID INTELLIGENCE
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly evaluated as both a functional technology and a socially responsive interaction partner. This study examines how academic staff form trust in educational AI and how that trust contributes to perceived value. Its central contribution is to position perceived anthropomorphism as a mediating mechanism through which perceived animacy and perceived intelligence are translated into perceived empathy. A cross-sectional survey was completed by 236 academic staff members, and the model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity. A competing-path analysis provided a more differentiated account of the proposed mediation mechanism. In the final competing-path model, Perceived Usefulness remained the strongest predictor of Perceived Value (beta = 0.586), while Perceived Intelligence strongly predicted Perceived Usefulness (beta = 0.570) and also had a substantial direct effect on Perceived Empathy (beta = 0.465). Perceived Anthropomorphism remained positively associated with Perceived Empathy (beta = 0.238). The direct effect of Perceived Animacy on Perceived Empathy was not significant (beta = 0.104, p = 0.154), whereas its indirect effect through Perceived Anthropomorphism remained significant (beta = 0.095, p = 0.006), indicating indirect-only mediation. For Perceived Intelligence, both the indirect effect through Perceived Anthropomorphism (beta = 0.057, p = 0.020) and the direct effect on Perceived Empathy were significant, indicating complementary partial mediation. Perceived Usefulness and Trust in AI jointly explained 57.3% of the variance in Perceived Value (R2 = 0.573). The findings reveal two complementary routes to valuing educational AI: a functional-cognitive route centered on intelligence and usefulness, and a social-emotional route through which anthropomorphism converts AI features into perceived empathy.

TI From Fragmented Adoption to Institutional Articulation: A Six-Axis
   Framework for Capability-Enhancing Generative AI in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; higher education; institutional
   articulation; institutional coherence; human capability formation;
   assessment validity; AI governance; equity
ID PERCEPTIONS; EMOTIONS
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being integrated rapidly across higher education, yet its educational value depends less on adoption intensity than on the institutional conditions through which its use is organized and enacted. This conceptual study develops a six-axis framework for examining institutional articulation across governance, curriculum, assessment, faculty development, digital ethics, and equity. Drawing on a selective integrative analysis and conceptual synthesis, the framework moves from a dimensional taxonomy of institutional interventions to a configurational account of their interdependence. It distinguishes institutional articulation, the process through which institutional functions are connected, interpreted, resourced, and revised, from institutional coherence, the variable degree of alignment that results. Human capability formation provides the substantive educational criterion for evaluating that coherence, distinguishing capability-enhancing configurations from arrangements oriented primarily toward efficiency, automation, or output production. The framework further situates the six institutional axes within a broader relational architecture in which affect, trust, and perceived legitimacy condition enactment; assessment validity and demonstrable learning provide evidence of capability formation; and credential credibility, professional adaptability, stakeholder trust, reputation, and legitimacy constitute potential system-level consequences. The framework is operationalized through phased institutional transformation and illustrative process, outcome, and alignment evidence, and generates four propositions for future empirical research.

TI Exclusion Through Eligibility: How Administrative Disability
   Certification Limits Access to Special Education in South Korea
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE special education in South Korea; special education eligibility;
   educational exclusion; disability certification; administrative
   gatekeeping
AB South Korea identifies only about 2.2% of K-12 students as eligible for special education, compared with approximately 15% of students receiving services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) in the United States and approximately 27% of Australian students receiving educational adjustments for disability. Existing explanations have largely attributed this disparity to Korea's narrow statutory disability categories. However, this paper argues that disability definitions alone cannot adequately explain Korea's exceptionally low rate of special education eligibility. Instead, it examines how the relationship between disability registration and special-education eligibility may affect access to special education, even though the two are determined through distinct institutional processes. In Korea, registered disability status carries consequences across multiple policy domains, including eligibility for welfare benefits, employer compliance with the mandatory employment quota, and access to supernumerary university admission tracks. Using comparative institutional and legal analysis supported by official national statistics, this paper advances the administrative certification model as a new institutional framework that complements existing medical, social, and human rights models of disability. South Korea is examined as a critical case and compared with the United States, Germany, Finland, England, Japan, Canada, and Australia to examine how differences in certification arrangements relate to access to special education. Because national indicators differ in age range, identification criteria, and reporting conventions, the comparison is descriptive rather than a causal test. The analysis suggests that certification-centered eligibility may contribute to the educational exclusion of medically fragile, neurodivergent, and twice-exceptional students. This paper's theoretical contribution is to identify administrative certification as an institutional mechanism that may shape educational access beyond statutory disability categories. Its practical contribution is to identify greater separation between educational eligibility and disability certification as a potential reform option and to propose an accommodation-based tier of support, informed by Section 504 of the U.S. Rehabilitation Act, for students whose educational needs warrant support but who do not meet the certification threshold.

TI International Students' Perception of the Linguistic Landscape at a
   Hungarian University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE linguistic landscape; multilingualism; internationalisation; higher
   education; cross-sectional comparative research design
ID TRENDS
AB Internationalisation is an ongoing process in higher education institutions worldwide. Sz & eacute;chenyi Istv & aacute;n University (Hungary) has also made it a priority to increase the number of international students, a move that draws attention to language issues. Building on previous research on the linguistic landscape of the university, this study evaluates the results of a questionnaire survey of international students' perceptions of the language environment, conducted during the 2023-24 and 2025-26 academic years. The most significant finding of the cross-sectional comparative survey is the change in international students' perceptions over the years and the steps the institution still needs to take to meet the information needs of its international students. Our findings suggest that students' attitudes towards the linguistic landscape are shaped primarily by their practical experiences of language accessibility rather than by their existing Hungarian-language competency or the number of foreign languages they speak. The results can inform the conscious (re)design of the linguistic landscape at the university in question and help other universities plan their language policies.

TI Early Predictors of Completion and Performance in a Gateway Mechanical
   Engineering Course: A Retrospective Cohort Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; student performance prediction; gateway courses;
   early-warning systems; course completion
ID STUDENTS
AB Gateway engineering courses often expose accumulated gaps in students' foundational knowledge, affecting progression and retention. This study investigates early predictors of completion and performance in Machine Elements, an integrative second-year mechanical engineering course at the University of Zagreb. A retrospective cohort dataset of 2351 students enrolled between 2013 and 2021 was analysed using admission variables, first-year course grades, and exam-attempt indicators. Cohort differences were examined with descriptive statistics and non-parametric tests, while course completion was modelled using logistic regression, LASSO-based predictor selection, and temporal validation. Students who completed the course differed most consistently from non-completers in Strength of Materials performance and prerequisite exam attempts. A reduced five-predictor model retained most of the full model's predictive ability, achieving ROC AUC = 0.749 in the pooled sample and 0.726 in temporal validation. Intervention-oriented evaluation showed that Top-K risk selection provided high precision but low sensitivity under limited support capacity.

TI Attitudes of Preservice Teachers Towards Pedagogical Use of Generative
   Artificial Intelligence: An Italian Study Within a Primary Teacher
   Education Program
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; teacher education programs; preservice
   teachers; lesson plan; formative assessment
ID CONFIDENCE-INTERVALS; FIT INDEXES; TRENDS; OMEGA
AB Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is increasing its influence at all educational levels and specifically, it is affecting how a school and a learning environment can be organized. Consequently, teacher education institutions are investigating how GAI is seen by preservice teachers and whether they consider GAI as a pedagogical partner in their future profession. This study focused on the attitudes of preservice teachers regarding their relationship with GAI. One hundred thirty-two Italian preservice teachers were involved in an experiment aimed at exploring the possible educational affordances of using AI at the primary school level. Before and after this path, preservice teachers were asked to express their ideas about GAI and its potential use at school. Findings indicate that, prior to completing the educational path, preservice teachers recorded low scores in the areas of self-efficacy and social outcome expectations, while performance outcome expectations, self-evaluative outcome expectations, interest, and behavioral intentions were comparatively high. After experimenting with the use of GAI, preservice teachers showed statistically significant increases in self-efficacy, performance outcome expectations, social outcome expectations, and behavioral intentions, while interest and self-evaluative outcome expectations remained stable, having already reached high levels at baseline.

TI Navigating Online Learning: Lived Experiences of Young Adult Students in
   a Historically Disadvantaged South African University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE digital learning; experience; higher education; historically based
   university; online learning
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB The transition from face-to-face to online learning has been problematic, particularly for historically disadvantaged universities (HDUs) shaped by infrastructural inequalities in South Africa. Grounded in connectivism theory, this study explores the lived experiences of young adult students' navigating online learning at an HDU in South Africa. Adopting a qualitative interpretative phenomenological approach, the study purposively selected 20 young adult students from the institution. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Two primary themes emerged: students' experiences and navigation of online learning, and perceived strategies and support mechanisms to enhance online learning. The findings reveal that young adult students' learning experiences are significantly constrained by limited access to critical nodes (such as digital devices), weak network structures, and unstable connectivity. These challenges disrupt the flow of information within learning networks, thereby hindering meaningful academic engagement. Despite these constraints, young adult students demonstrate forms of navigational agency in attempting to connect to available learning resources. This study contributes to the literature and theory by extending connectivism theory into a Global South context, illustrating how digital inequality undermines the formation and sustainability of learning networks in HDU. It moves beyond viewing online learning challenges as purely technical issues, instead framing them as structural and pedagogical limitations. The study recommends that HDUs develop policies that seek to strengthen network connectivity through targeted institutional interventions, including strategic partnerships with telecommunications providers to subsidize data costs and improve access to digital devices for socio-economically disadvantaged students.

TI Learning with ChatGPT: Challenges and Benefits for Diverse College
   Students in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; diverse students; higher education; AI learning
ID INTERSECTIONALITY
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), such as ChatGPT 3.5, presents academic challenges to college student users. Past literature has emphasized using non-diverse student samples, which limits understanding of diverse students' perspectives and experiences in using ChatGPT in the learning process. Diverse students face challenges in addressing their learning needs and seeking additional academic support. As such, this study aims to examine the experiences of diverse students using ChatGPT to identify learning challenges and opportunities in higher education, drawing on Intersectionality Theory and Connectivism Learning Theory. A qualitative methodological approach using a Generic Qualitative Inquiry (GQI) design was employed by interviewing 27 diverse student participants from a public higher education institution. In examining the first research question on learning challenges in using ChatGPT, the findings revealed that diverse students reported reduced critical thinking, research limitations, and difficulties in using it effectively. Findings also revealed that they were becoming dependent on AI answers. Diverse students also acknowledged issues such as inaccuracies and misinformation, as well as adherence to academic integrity. In examining the second research question about the benefits of using ChatGPT, the findings showed that ChatGPT was perceived as practical and accessible, valuable for time management, and useful for gaining a deeper understanding and for studying. ChatGPT was also helpful in language development and proficiency. Findings also revealed that students were using ChatGPT to brainstorm and understand assignments, and to guide them in completing assignments. Implications point to the recognition that ChatGPT provides academic value to the learning experience of diverse students, which they can obtain beyond the realms of the classroom and university settings. Given that ChatGPT also poses challenges for learning, implications for educators include considering strategies to help diverse students navigate their learning expectations of ChatGPT use in their classrooms. Broader theoretical implications are interpreted through Intersectionality Theory and Connectivism Learning Theory, raising considerations for learning equity, institutional policy, and the cultural responsiveness of AI tools. This study provides needed qualitative evidence of diverse students' experiences of using ChatGPT for learning in courses, which can inform efforts toward learning inclusion in academic environments.

TI Negotiating Generative AI-Assisted Academic Writing: Student
   Perspectives on Authorship, Responsibility and Learning
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; academic writing; authorship;
   student agency; cognitive ownership
AB The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in university students' academic writing is challenging established understandings of authorship, academic integrity, and learning. The study investigated how undergraduates negotiate authorship, responsibility and learning within these emerging writing practices. The study used a qualitatively driven mixed-methods design with undergraduate students enrolled in two sections of an academic writing course at an English-medium university in Cyprus. Data comprised 55 written reflections on students' use of GenAI while completing a research paper and 27 responses to an anonymous post-course questionnaire. Reflections were analysed using thematic analysis, with questionnaire data providing additional descriptive and contextual evidence. Findings indicate that students positioned GenAI as legitimate support for brainstorming, organising ideas, language refinement and feedback while resisting its use as a substitute for intellectual engagement. Students constructed authorship through human judgement, locating ownership in verification, evaluation, decision-making, and accountability rather than sole textual production. Ethical GenAI use emerged as boundary work distinguishing assistance from substitution, while meaningful learning was associated with maintaining cognitive ownership of the thinking underpinning academic work. These findings suggest that GenAI can be integrated into academic writing while students continue to locate authorship, ethical responsibility, and meaningful learning in human judgement and intellectual engagement.

TI The Bush Kinder Assessment Tool: Supporting Educators to Understand
   Children's Learning in Nature-Based Early Childhood Education Settings
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment; bush kinder; nature-based education; early years learning
   framework; participatory action research
ID PLAY; AUSTRALIA
AB Nature-based approaches to Early Childhood Education and Care have been popularised since the mid-twentieth century. Grounded in practices from Nordic countries and the United Kingdom, taking preschool children outdoors into forests, parklands and coastal settings has been found to build children's love of nature and risk-taking behaviours. In the Australian context, local adaptations of UK and European forest and nature kindergartens have gained popularity since the mid-2010s. They have flourished in numbers as educators and parents realise the benefits children gain from being outdoors for learning. The 'bush kinder' approach, as it is known in Australia, has challenged early childhood educators to apply pedagogy in new and varied situations. One result of this approach is that educators have been stimulated to find ways to assess children's learning. This paper reports on a small pilot project that applied a participatory action research methodology. The project's participants were three preschool educators, an early childhood pedagogical leader and a bush kinder researcher. This study sought to co-design and test an assessment tool specific to nature-based teaching aligned to Australian curriculum frameworks. This paper draws on data generated through the reflections of the research team as active participants in this study, who applied the assessment tool during bush kinder sessions. Data collection occurred through individual interviews with each educator, led by the researcher. This study's key finding is that the tool developed through this study enables bush kinder educators to deepen their understanding of children's learning in nature, and it confirms the validity of the bush kinder approach for supporting young children's learning.

TI Sustaining Community-Engaged Work-Integrated Learning: A Decade of
   Listening-Centred, Community-Co-Designed Practice
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE work-integrated learning; service learning; education for sustainable
   development; SDG 4.7; global citizenship; listening; community
   engagement; higher education; wise practice; graduate employability
ID POLITICS
AB Work-integrated learning (WIL) is now central to higher education, yet two questions have outrun its expansion: whether it builds the competencies a sustainable future requires, and whether the community-engaged forms that might build them can themselves be sustained. This paper takes up both through a collective case study of thirteen university-led WIL-for-social-impact projects delivered between 2015 and 2025 across social issues, disciplines, three delivery modes and two countries. The evidence is separated into two tiers. Eight projects carry the empirical claims, drawing on interviews, focus groups and surveys collected under institutional human research ethics approval and reported in the associated peer-reviewed literature. Five more-recent projects are used as documented practice only, evidencing implementation and transfer rather than outcomes. A single listening-centred, community-co-designed model recurs across this variation and engages sustainability at five interacting levels-issue, competency, pedagogical, delivery and relational-all held together by an ethic of listening. The findings are stated at the level the evidence supports: the model is structured to support recognised sustainability competencies rather than producing measured outcomes, and its adaptability across institution, scale and border is a claim of portability, not proven efficacy. The principal constraint is pedagogical: the workload, emotional labour and limited recognition the model demands of those who run it, and what that implies for institutional purpose.

AB The development of higher-order cognitive thinking skills has become a central objective of innovative pedagogies. While heutagogy is recognized as an approach that promotes autonomy, self-regulation, critical thinking, and metacognition, little is known about how educators perceive these skills during the planning and implementation stages of innovative schools within traditional cultural contexts. AB Scholarly activity and teaching are recognized components of radiology training, but their distribution across residency years is poorly characterized in Italy. We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional online survey of Italian radiology residents between August and September 2024. Among 176 consenting respondents, we assessed scientific article authorship, congress presentation experience, and formal teaching experience. Scholarly and formal teaching engagement was more frequently reported among later-year residents; longitudinal studies are needed to characterize within-resident development.

AB Background This study examined associations between school-based social relationship quality (school belonging, peer support, teacher-student interaction) and mental health outcomes among high school students in Iran, identifying protective and risk factors for depression, anxiety, and stress.Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted in 2024 among 1200 students from 32 public and private high schools in Tehran-Iran. TI Exploring cognitive-institutional alignment in poetry comprehension: a
   grade 8 case study in Nepal
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory; Cognitive-institutional alignment; ESL/EFL
   curriculum design; Genre-based performance; Poetry comprehension;
   Universal design for learning
ID INTELLIGENCE
AB Poetry is persistently perceived as more difficult than narrative prose among ESL/EFL learners, yet whether this difficulty is intrinsic to the genre or structurally mediated remains undertheorised. This study examined whether Grade 8 ESL/EFL learners' poetry difficulty may be associated with institutional-cognitive misalignment rather than inherent genre complexity. Employing a convergent mixed-methods case study design, eleven Grade 8 students from a private school in Kathmandu, Nepal, completed controlled genre comparison tasks using thematically identical poetic and prose texts, alongside a 50-item Universal Design Learning (UDL)-aligned cognitive engagement instrument mapped onto Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) domains. Within this bounded classroom context, descriptive patterns revealed a performance asymmetry: 54.54% of participants demonstrated at least partial success in prose comprehension, whereas 72.72% of participants failed the poetry task entirely. Cognitive profiling indicated a within-subject pattern of relatively higher engagement in Crystallised Knowledge and relatively lower engagement in Fluid Reasoning and Long-Term Storage and Retrieval, a domain theoretically implicated in poetic interpretation. Because the profiling instrument was purpose-built and was not designed to support between-domain psychometric comparison, this pattern is reported as a relative within-sample profile rather than as evidence of differential cognitive strength. A further metacognitive misalignment was found, suggesting a possible "brevity-as-ease heuristic", wherein learners conflated the poetry shorter length relative to its prose with reduced cognitive demand. These patterns are consistent with a possible role for differential rehearsal of cognitive processes within a prose-dominant, examination-oriented curriculum rather than from inherent textual opacity. The study advances a provisional institutional-cognitive alignment framework to guide future large-scale investigation across examination-driven ESL/EFL contexts.

TI Navigating Affective Cues in Video-Based Instruction: The Role of

SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL vocabulary learning; idiom acquisition; instructor emotion; idiom
   valence; emotional design; and instructional video; learning experience
ID NEGATIVITY BIAS; VOCABULARY
AB EFL vocabulary learning is an emotionally rich process, particularly in video-based instruction where learners encounter multiple affective cues. This mixed-methods study examined whether instructors' emotional expressions and idiom valence influence EFL learners' idiom acquisition and learning experience. A 3 & times; 3 within-subjects experimental design was adopted, manipulating instructor emotion (positive, neutral, and negative) and idiom valence (positive, neutral, and negative). Forty-five undergraduate EFL learners from a university in China participated in the study. After viewing each video, participants completed an immediate idiom recall test, a perceived learning experience scale, the self-assessment Manikin scale, a cognitive load scale and an open-ended questionnaire. These findings provide implications for the emotional design of instructional videos in EFL vocabulary learning.

AB Educational theories of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning include mechanisms absent from reusable platform logs. TI A Study on Improving the Usability of an AI-Based Learning Tool to
   Support English Diary Writing for EFL Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE usability evaluation; AI; ChatGPT; learning (support) tool; EFL diary
   writing
ID FEEDBACK
AB AI-based writing support systems are increasingly being explored as tools for supporting English writing in educational contexts. In English as a Foreign Language (EFL) settings, learners often need support in generating ideas, organizing content, receiving feedback, and revising written texts. However, AI-based writing tools should be carefully designed and evaluated to ensure their usability, reliability, and educational relevance before being implemented in authentic learning contexts. This study aimed to design and evaluate the educational usability of WriteOn, an AI-based writing support system for EFL writing tasks that integrates AI and natural language processing technologies, including GPT-API, NLTK, spaCy, and BERT. Although the system was initially designed to support English diary writing in EFL contexts, its feedback structure and system architecture were intended to be extensible to broader writing tasks. A formative usability evaluation was conducted with eight experts in South Korea with backgrounds in EFL instruction, educational technology, instructional design, and human-computer interaction. A structured questionnaire was used to assess the system's effectiveness, efficiency, learnability, satisfaction, memorability, error prevention, and cognitive load minimization. Based on the expert evaluation results, the system was refined through an iterative design process. The findings provided preliminary evidence of WriteOn's overall usability while identifying several areas for improvement, including clearer feedback, more consistent design features, and enhanced language support in grammar correction modules. In response, the system was refined to include topic and genre selection, rubric-based evaluation, and a more consistent interface. These results suggest that integrating generative AI and natural language processing technologies into EFL writing support can support the development of reliable, scalable, and learner-centered writing tools. The study also highlights the importance of iterative and formative usability evaluation in developing AI-driven writing support systems that promote instructional efficiency, feedback transparency, and learner-centered revision.

TI Strength of character and universal values are essential for the
   effectiveness of entrepreneurial students' intention
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE character strength and virtue; entrepreneurial education;
   entrepreneurial intention; higher education; lecturer's entrepreneurial
   competence
ID EDUCATION
AB Introduction This study aims to present a detailed empirical investigation of the role of entrepreneurship education in building entrepreneurial intention of business students through competencies, character strengths, and virtues. This study focuses on several business students in a higher education environment.Methods The methodology used in this research is associative research with the study of certain dependent, independent, and mediating variables involving business management students from various state universities in East Indonesia. According to the research model, the author chose a structural equation model (SEM) to analyze the data and support using character strength and virtues with six traits: wisdom and knowledge, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.Results The research findings indicate that the six variables shaping character strengths, virtues, and lecturer competencies are effective in developing entrepreneurial intentions among students. TI Introversion in Surgical Residency: A Risk Factor for Burnout?
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; extraversion; introversion; personality traits; surgical
   residents; wellness
ID PERSONALITY; US; SATISFACTION; HEALTH
AB Introduction Burnout among surgical residents continues to present a critical challenge in graduate medical education. The high demands, long work hours, and intense emotional toll of surgical training make this group especially vulnerable to mental health challenges, including disengagement and exhaustion. Previous research has explored factors such as gender, training level, and work hours; however, the influence of personality traits, specifically introversion and extroversion, on burnout has been underexplored. This study seeks to bridge that gap by examining how personality influences burnout among surgical residents at a major academic institution. Methods This study surveyed surgical residents from a large academic medical center representing multiple surgical subspecialties and postgraduate years (PGY1-PGY7). Participants were invited to complete the survey via REDCap. The initial invitation was distributed by program directors, and subsequent reminder emails were sent directly to residents. The survey consisted of 38 items, including demographic questions and 3 validated instruments: the Big Five Inventory, a modified Big Five Inventory, and the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory. Burnout was defined as exhaustion or disengagement and classified as high, moderate, or low according to the criteria described by Demerouti et al. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS software. Results The survey was distributed to 204 trainees, and 116 responded for a response rate of 57%. Sixty-six percent of the participants identified as females and were evenly distributed across residency years. General surgery residents represented the highest number of participants (n = 20), while obstetrics and gynecology represented the fewest (n = 4). No participants reported "high" burnout on the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory scale. Higher extraversion and agreeableness scores were significantly associated with lower disengagement (r = -0.22, p < 0.05) and were not associated with exhaustion (p = 0.25). Agreeableness showed a statistically significant negative correlation with disengagement (p = 0.028). Female gender was associated with higher burnout (p < 0.01), while PGY year was insignificant. A significant difference in exhaustion and disengagement was observed across specialties (p < 0.01), with obstetrics and gynecology residents reporting the highest levels of burnout (both exhaustion and disengagement). In contrast, vascular surgery residents reported the lowest exhaustion rates, and plastic surgery residents reported the lowest disengagement rates. Discussion Our findings suggest that personality traits, particularly extraversion, may play a substantial role in how surgical residents experience burnout. Introverted residents may be more vulnerable to emotional fatigue and disengagement in high-interaction environments like surgical training. In addition to personality differences, our study also found that female residents reported significantly higher levels of exhaustion than their male peers, independent of personality traits. This gender-based difference echoes prior research highlighting the unique challenges faced by women in surgical training, including microaggressions, work-life balance pressures, imposter syndrome, and underrepresentation in leadership roles. Interestingly, PGY year was not a significant factor for burnout in our analysis, contrasting several earlier studies that reported increased burnout among junior residents.
   These findings highlight the need for personality-informed wellness interventions and support systems that align with residents' coping styles and psychological needs. Conclusion Personality traits are associated with burnout in surgical residency. Specifically, extroversion may be protective against disengagement. Residency programs should consider integrating personality assessments into onboarding and wellness initiatives to better support residents at risk, particularly introverts and female trainees.

TI Influence of the professional dimension of vocational training on the
   choice of post-compulsory studies in Spain
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic and professional guidance; Labour market; Multifocal analysis;
   Post-compulsory studies; Professional dimensions; Vocational education
   and training (VET)
ID EDUCATION; TEACHERS
AB Vocational Education and Training (VET) has taken on new importance across Europe, especially in Spain, as a means of connecting education to the labour market. In examining the professional dimension of VET, several categories influence the decision to pursue VET: employability, salary, professional skills, job placement, and emerging professional profiles. This study analyses the impact of these categories on the decision to pursue VET among secondary students and their families, along with the academic and professional guidance shaping these choices. Using a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, focus groups were conducted with third-year secondary students and their families in four Spanish regions. Results show that the baccalaureate is considered versatile, associated with job stability and high income, while VET is linked to job opportunities, skill development, and employability. In this context, providing a skilled workforce should align with the broader socioeconomic role VET can fulfil today and the aim of VET should be to connect the vocational preferences of students with the most in-demand technical professional profiles, making VET a similar alternative to university education.

TI From silence to solidarity: Asian American youth navigating school
   ethnic-racial socialization
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Asian American youth; School ethnic-racial socialization; Asian American
   underrepresentation; AsianCrit theory; Qualitative study
ID CURRICULUM; FOREIGNER; EDUCATION; MINORITY; IDENTITY; PARENTS; HISTORY
AB This qualitative study examined how 30 first- and second-generation Asian American youth navigated school Ethnic-Racial Socialization (ERS) in predominantly White K-12 schools, primarily located in Southern U.S. states with low Asian American population density. We collected data through semi-structured interviews and analyzed them using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Guided by the School ERS and Asian Critical Race Theory, we identified six interconnected themes. Participants vividly recounted persistent pressures from stereotypes such as the model minority and perpetual foreigner, deepening their experiences of marginalization and isolation. Curricular erasures further reinforced feelings of invisibility, portraying Asian American histories as peripheral or entirely absent. Compounding these challenges, institutional silence in response to racial bullying intensified their marginalization. Peers also played a contradictory role, serving both as sources of racialized harm and as spaces of cultural support, where friendships helped participants navigate identity and build belonging. Yet, even amid these structural barriers, participants actively resisted by creating cultural spaces and sharing counternarratives. These strategies demonstrated significant agency, enabling participants to reshape their educational and social environments. This study extends the School ERS framework by revealing students as producers of ERS, moving beyond its traditional top-down emphasis. Through these retrospective narratives, we also captured participants' developmental progression from initial internalization of stereotypes and passive acceptance to active advocacy and identity affirmation. This study represents one of the first detailed explorations of school ERS specifically among Asian American youth, highlighting the dual process by which they navigate persistent marginalization and assert their identities, voices, and cultural presence within their schools.

TI Barriers and Facilitators to Surgical Career Pursuit Among
   First-Generation Medical Students: A Multi-Institutional Survey Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE medical students; medical schools; internship and residency; surgical
   specialties; workforce diversity; career choice; survey
ID HIDDEN CURRICULUM; DIVERSITY; MENTORSHIP; SURGERY; SCHOOL
AB OBJECTIVE: To characterize perceived barriers and facilitators influencing first-generation medical students' pursuit of surgical residency training and to inform targeted interventions to support their success. DESIGN: Cross-sectional, anonymous survey study assessing perceived financial, professional, and structural barriers to pursuing surgical training. Descriptive statistical analyses were performed on quantitative responses, with thematic review of open-ended responses. SETTING: Multi-institutional study of U.S. allopathic medical schools, with participants recruited through national first-generation medical student listservs and online forums. P ARTICIPANTS: A total of 215 self-identified first-generation medical students from 24 U.S. medical schools completed at least 1 survey item. Participants were aged >= 18 years; item-level response rates varied across questions. RESULTS: Of the 215 first-generation medical students from 24 medical schools that participated, most were White (n = 136, 63.3%), female (n = 152, 70.7%) and either "currently interested" (n = 100, 46.7%) or "previously interested" (n = 50, 23.4%) in surgical training. Among the 68 respondents who reported identity-based discouragement and completed the follow-up question, the most frequently cited deterrents were perceived disadvantages in competitiveness (n = 55, 80.8%), lack of personal belonging (n = 39, 57.3%), and limited family support (n = 32, 47.1%). Among 146 respondents, tailored resources (n = 71, 48.6%) and personal connections (n = 123, 84.2%) were identified as facilitators; however, many respondents reported a lack of institutional resources. Financial constraints discouraged pursuit of surgery, with 24 (16.4%) strongly and 39 (26.7%) somewhat agreeing (n = 146). Open-ended responses highlighted costs associated with away rotations, debt burden, and prolonged training. CONCLUSION: First-generation medical students face substantial barriers to pursuing surgical residency and, despite evidence that tailored resources and mentorship are associated with greater interest, persistent gaps in institutional support, limited mentorship, and financial constraints continue to be perceived as barriers to their pursuit of surgery. TI Screen use, health status, and self-perceived academic performance among
   Swedish dental and nursing students: an exploratory cross-sectional
   survey study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic performance; Digital media use; Mental health; Physical health;
   Screen time; Temporomandibular disorders
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; UNIVERSITY; VALIDITY; SLEEP; PREVALENCE; ANXIETY;
   RISK
AB Background This study examined how screen use, physical and mental health, and 3-question temporomandibular disorders (3Q-TMD) screening status relate to self-perceived academic performance among Swedish undergraduate dental and nursing students. Methods Ninety-one first-semester dental and nursing students completed a survey comprising sociodemographic items, estimated daily screen use by purpose, and twelve self-report instruments. Self-perceived academic performance was measured with the Academic Performance Scale (APS) and analyzed as a continuous score. Bivariate group comparisons between lower and higher self-perceived academic performance used the Mann-Whitney U test or Welch's t-test with effect sizes, and the Holm-Bonferroni procedure to control the family-wise error rate within families of outcomes. The primary analysis was a hierarchical linear regression on the continuous APS score, entering demographics, then total screen time, then purpose-specific screen use, then a psychological symptom burden composite and 3Q-TMD screening status. Results Total screen time was unrelated to academic performance in every analysis. Purpose-specific screen use added 19.0% of explained variance beyond total duration (F(3,81) = 6.78, p < 0.001), whereas total duration added 2.2% beyond purpose and was not significant (F(1,81) = 2.37, p = 0.127). In the full model (R2 = 0.341, adjusted R2 = 0.266), academic screen use was positively associated with performance (beta = 0.426, p < 0.001), while work-related screen use (beta = -0.299, p = 0.003) and psychological symptom burden (beta = -0.361, p = 0.001) were negatively associated with performance. Students reporting lower performance also reported poorer health-related quality of life in five of eight RAND-36 domains and were more likely to have a positive 3Q-TMD screening result, although the latter association did not survive adjustment for oral parafunctional behavior. Conclusions Self-perceived academic performance was associated with the purpose of screen use and with psychological symptom burden, but not with total screen-time duration.

TI Exploring perceived fluency in interpreting through a multimodal lens:
   Insights from trained interpreters and target audience members
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multimodality; Perceived fluency; Non-verbal communication; Consecutive
   interpreting; Target audience members; Trained interpreters; Intonation
ID ENGLISH; QUALITY; ASSESSMENTS; ACCURACY; LANGUAGE
AB Fluency is a key component of interpreting quality, yet its perceptual and multimodal nature remains underexplored. This study investigates how verbal and non-verbal elements jointly shape perceived fluency in consecutive interpreting (CI) among trained interpreters (TIs) and target audience members (TAMs). Seventeen raters, including nine trained Chinese-English interpreters and eight English-native audience members without prior formal interpreter training and study of Chinese, evaluated 20 videotaped English interpreting outputs, using a five-point Likert scale across perceived fluency and 21 verbal and non-verbal indicators. Results of Spearman correlation analysis show that both verbal and non-verbal elements are significantly correlated with perceived fluency, with non-verbal elements as a group demonstrating stronger correlations. Results of forward stepwise regression analyses further suggest that intonation, a feature not typically included in traditional utterance fluency frameworks, emerges as one of the important contributors of perceived fluency, with other predictors including speech rate, repair, cohesion, and pronunciation. Additionally, TIs and TAMs show differences in their fluency ratings as well as their rating patterns. TIs tend to rate fluency higher than TAMs, with the former group focusing more on sentence-structural features of interpreting outputs and the latter group relying on a wider range of comprehension-related elements. Research findings suggest that perceived fluency may be better understood as a multimodal construct, underscoring the importance of integrating audience perspectives into fluency assessment, thereby offering implications for both interpreting research and pedagogy.<br /> (c) 2026 Elsevier Inc. TI Assessing Residency Readiness: Patterns of "Not Yet Level 1" Milestone
   Ratings in Emergency Medicine Interns
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID DISCIPLINARY ACTION; STUDENTS
AB Background To characterize the extent and domains of variability in Emergency Medicine (EM) residency preparedness by evaluating "Not Yet Level 1" (NotYL1) Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) Milestones ratings among US MD-graduated interns at mid-year and end-of-year. Method This was a national retrospective analysis of ACGME Milestone assessments for 6893 US MD-graduated EM interns from 2021 through 2024. For each of the 22 EM sub-competencies, we calculated the percentages of interns assigned a NotYL1 rating at both the mid-year and end-of-year assessment periods. Results Overall, NotYL1 ratings were < 4%. At mid-year, the mean NotYL1 percentage across sub-competencies was 2.5% (range: 1.8%-3.3%), decreasing to 0.4% (range: 0.2%-1.0%) at end-of-year. At mid-year, the highest proportions of NotYL1 ratings were concentrated in all Systems-Based Practice (SBP) sub-competencies-including Patient Safety (SBP1; 3.0%), Quality Improvement (SBP2; 3.2%), System Navigation (SBP3; 3.0%), and the Physician Role in Health Care Systems (SBP4; 3.3%)-as well as Pharmacotherapy (PC5; 3.1%) and Accountability/Conscientiousness (PROF2; 3.2%). By end-of-year, nearly all interns achieved Level 1 or higher, though PROF2 remained the highest outlier at 1.0%. Conclusions US MD graduates demonstrate strong overall readiness for EM residency, with most initial gaps resolving by the end of the first year. However, consistent mid-year deficits in systems-based practice and professionalism (accountability/conscientiousness) highlight critical targets for undergraduate medical school accountability, transition-to-residency curricula, and targeted residency onboarding.

TI Enrolling in a consecutive federal vocational baccalaureate program:
   effects of successful career choice, needs-supplies discorrespondences
   and cognitive overload among VET graduates
SO EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Federal vocational baccalaureate; Career adjustment; Career choice;
   Person-environment fit; Needs-supplies correspondence; Ability-ability
   requirement correspondence; Vocational education and training; Secondary
   education; Variety; Educational status aspiration; Qualitative workload
ID WORK; SWITZERLAND; PREDICTORS; EDUCATION
AB In Switzerland, federal vocational education and training (VET) diploma holders may choose to obtain a federal vocational baccalaureate by completing a consecutive federal vocational baccalaureate (FVB2) program. This multiwave study investigated the probability of FVB2 program enrollment within the first 4.5 years after the completion of compulsory school among federal VET graduates. Based on the theory of work adjustment (TWA), we conceptualized FVB2 program enrollment as a form of career adjustment in upper-secondary education. The theory lists perceived discorrespondences between individual needs and environmental supplies as the main predictor of career adjustment. As forms of discorrespondences, we analyzed the predictive effects of lack of achievement-related variety and educational status aspiration at the end of first year in company-based VET. Complementing TWA, we also included qualitative workload as a form of perceived cognitive overload, and to link career adjustment with career choice in lower-secondary education, we investigated the predictive effect of successful career choice in the form of anticipated person-environment fit (i.e., similarity between an individual's characteristics and the characteristics of the chosen upper-secondary environment). Controlling for the effects of school tracking and educational status aspiration in lower-secondary education, structural equation modeling was applied (N = 914). Lack of achievement-related variety and educational status aspiration in VET had positive effects on FVB2 program enrollment, and qualitative workload had a negative effect. Anticipated person-environment fit had a statistically significant negative indirect effect on the probability of FVB2 program enrollment, simply mediated by lack of achievement-related variety. The indirect effects via educational status aspiration in VET and qualitative workload were not statistically significant. Findings shed light on the processes behind one of vocational learners' key paths to university of applied sciences.

TI The supplementary year as a bridge from vocational studies to higher
   education for healthcare students in Norway
SO EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper secondary; Higher education; VET; Healthcare education;
   Transitions; Permeability
ID PERMEABILITY
AB Norwegian upper secondary education allows for permeability between vocational and academic tracks via a supplementary academic year, which grants vocational students access to higher education. This route is particularly common among vocational students in the healthcare programme. However, there are concerns regarding both the academic preparedness of these students for higher education, and the potential impact on the supply of healthcare assistants. Using rich administrative register data, this study compares healthcare students who gain their higher education entrance qualification through the supplementary year with peers from the academic track. To account for selection into programmes, we estimate linear probability models with extensive controls for prior achievement and family background, supplemented by propensity score matching and fixed effects models. The results show that while students in the healthcare programme are less likely to complete upper secondary education within the nominal timeframe in raw comparisons, this difference disappears once observable characteristics are taken into account. In fully specified models, healthcare students are slightly more likely to complete on time than comparable students in the academic track. Moreover, they exhibit higher rates of direct enrolment in higher education, particularly in care-related fields, although these differences diminish over time. However, these advantages do not translate into higher overall completion rates in higher education. Instead, healthcare students are more likely to complete degrees within health-related fields, but less likely to complete degrees outside these fields.

TI 'Pivotal but Not a Priority': Exploring the Process and Affecting
   Factors of Undergraduate Thesis Writing in China
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic literacies; China; EFL; self-regulated learning; supervision;
   undergraduate thesis writing; writing process
ID STUDENTS
AB Undergraduate thesis writing is widely regarded as a capstone of higher education. Yet most research has examined the quality of the finished thesis and has paid little attention to the writing process and the factors that shape it, especially in English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) contexts. This study examined the process of undergraduate thesis writing and its influencing factors among English majors at one Chinese normal university. It framed thesis writing as an academic-literacies practice and drew on self-regulated learning to interpret student engagement. A qualitative-dominant single-case design was adopted. Data came from 121 senior English majors through a structured questionnaire (111 valid responses), one-to-one interviews with 12 students, and their graded theses. The data were analysed through descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis, with triangulation across sources. Thesis writing was pivotal in students' stated beliefs but not a priority in their practice. It was compressed by competing career tasks and undermined by methodological and linguistic difficulties. It was also strongly conditioned by supervisor responsibility, the rigour of institutional management, and students' own self-regulation. The study argues that thesis quality depends less on isolated writing ability than on the alignment of curriculum, supervision, management and student agency. It concludes with implications for EFL thesis pedagogy and quality assurance.

AB Background Rhythmic reading training (RRT) is a rhythm-based intervention designed for individuals with dyslexia. Studies on RRT demonstrated its positive effect on reading abilities on Italian children and adolescents with dyslexia. TI Embedding Rule-Based Augmented Reality Scaffolding in Experiential
   Learning Cycles: An SEM Study of Student Engagement in Lab-Based STEM
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality (AR); experiential learning; kolb's learning cycle;
   lab-based STEM education; rule-based scaffolding; structural equation
   modeling; student engagement; sustainable development goal 4 (SDG 4)
ID ENGINEERING-EDUCATION; SCIENCE; SKILLS
AB Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly used in STEM laboratories, but its pedagogical value depends on how digital guidance is embedded within structured physical learning activities rather than on technological novelty alone. This study examined an AR-supported hydropower laboratory activity designed around Kolb's experiential learning cycle and rule-based instructional scaffolding informed by Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development. A total of 202 participants completed a post-intervention questionnaire measuring learner digital readiness (LDR), perceived AR scaffolding quality (ARSQ), perceived AR experience design quality (AREDQ), and student engagement (SE). The study contributes a transparent design protocol for linking physical laboratory tasks, Kolb-aligned learning stages, rule-triggered AR support, and progressively reduced instructional guidance. Future research should validate the framework using broader measurement scales, objective performance indicators, control-group comparisons, and longitudinal learning outcomes.

TI Through Different Lenses: Connecting Educational Backgrounds to Fermi
   Problem-Solving Pathways
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational background; Fermi problems; Ill-defined problems;
   Problem-solving pathways; STEM education
ID SCIENCE; KNOWLEDGE; INSTRUCTION; TASKS
AB Understanding how educational backgrounds shape problem-solving approaches is essential for developing effective science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) teaching strategies. This exploratory study investigated the relationship between students' educational backgrounds, operationalized as declared majors and prior coursework, and their problem-solving pathways, which are defined here as the sequence of assumptions and decisions made toward a solution. Specifically, this study aimed to identify common pathway patterns in students' solutions to an ill-defined Fermi problem, examine whether an engineering background systematically relates to pathway selection, and characterize individual variations within the identified pathways. Eighty-four Ivy League undergraduate students with diverse majors independently solved a single Fermi problem before engaging in team-based reflection. We analyzed their solution processes using a dimension-based coding approach, extracting dimensions and values from the students' equations and written assumptions. The pathways were categorized and integrated into a structured database to investigate the relationship between problem-solving processes and educational backgrounds. Although participants exhibited substantial individual variation in problem decomposition, underlying assumptions, and parameter settings, statistical analysis suggested that engineering majors were more likely to adopt the bottom-up target-revenue pathway (odds ratio = 3.43). In this pathway, solvers begin with unit-level assumptions, accumulate them into an estimate of potential revenue, and compare this estimated revenue with the tuition-related cost target. Given the single-problem design and limited sample size, these results should be interpreted as preliminary evidence suggesting potential differences in the problem-solving strategies emphasized in science and engineering disciplines.

   between Spain and Costa Rica universities

AB This study evaluated the development of intercultural competencies through Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) in 207 pre-service teacher education students from the University of Granada (Spain) and the Distance State University (Costa Rica). Over seven weeks, participants collaborated in mixed international teams to design learning situations integrating 3D printing as a didactic resource in Primary Education. TI Toward a Multidimensional Science Content Knowledge Framework: An Expert
   Science Teacher's Uneven Development of Pedagogical Content Knowledge
   Through Classroom Teaching Experiences
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE expert teacher; pedagogical content knowledge; teacher professional
   knowledge; teaching experience
ID MEANINGFUL ASSESSMENT; PCK; EDUCATION; LEARNERS; ACHIEVEMENT;
   CONCEPTIONS; INTEGRATION; COMPONENTS; MODELS; IMPACT
AB Contemporary science education advocates instruction that fully integrates the conceptual, procedural, and epistemic aspects of science. Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) is the unique knowledge that teachers use to make content accessible to students. Few studies examine teachers' development of PCK for teaching conceptual, procedural, and epistemic ideas simultaneously. This qualitative case study explored the development of an expert science teacher's PCK across the plan-teach-reflect pedagogical cycle and its impact on student learning. Our conceptual framework drew on the Refined Consensus Model of PCK, which differentiates between pPCK (personal knowledge held by the teacher) and ePCK (specific knowledge and skills utilized while planning, teaching, and reflecting on a lesson), along with the multidimensional aspects of science content knowledge. Data from multiple sources, including teacher interviews, video-recorded lessons, classroom artifacts, and student focus group interviews, were used to reveal the teacher's PCK development and its impact on student learning. Data analysis revealed several features about the expert teacher's PCK and its development: (a) The teacher's PCK extended beyond conceptual ideas to include procedural and epistemic ideas, based on his beliefs about the nature of science; (b) The teacher's PCK developed through classroom teaching experiences, facilitated by his deliberate attention to eliciting and responding to evidence of student thinking in classroom assessments; (c) The teacher's PCK development was uneven, with greater growth in PCK for teaching conceptual and procedural than epistemic ideas. Most of the students interviewed reported learning conceptual and procedural ideas through the lesson activities, reflecting the impact of the teacher's PCK, although few reported learning epistemic ideas. The findings' implications for teacher education to enhance PCK development through classroom teaching experiences are discussed.

TI 'You Left No Crumbs': Student Voices Informing an English Teacher's
   Podcasting Assessment
SO LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom assessment; digital multimodal composing (DMC); English
   language arts (ELA); multimodality; podcasting; student voice
ID MULTIMODAL ASSESSMENT; DESIGN
AB Although writing essays remains hegemonic in English Language Arts (ELA) classrooms, podcasting as a form of digital multimodal composing (DMC) is an empowering alternative for diverse learners to represent learning. However, their privilege to draw on their full communicative repertoires may be constrained by assessment practices that overlook student voices. Situated in Western Canada, this ethnographic case study explored how diverse learners in Grade 8 might have informed an ELA teacher's assessment of podcast episodes they co-created to analyse poetry. Data included student-generated rubric criteria, self-assessment sheets, interviews, teacher feedback and the podcast episodes. Adopting a telling case approach and drawing on sociocultural, critical and multimodal perspectives on literacy assessment, we used thematic analysis to examine one trio's episode. We followed an inductive-deductive approach to examine student input and used constant comparison to juxtapose student input with teacher feedback. Three themes emerged: emphasizing relatability in literary analyses, explaining design choices to engage the audience and foregrounding collaborative troubleshooting. The findings demonstrate how prioritizing student voices legitimizes the intellectual, collaborative and multimodal work potentially overlooked in product-centred assessment. The study invites ELA teachers to position students as dialogic partners in DMC assessment and recognize their reflections as legitimate evidence of learning.

TI Pedagogical Translanguaging Read-Alouds: Making Hidden Comprehension
   Audible in Multilingual L2 Classrooms
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 literacy; multilingual classrooms; pedagogical translanguaging;
   read-alouds; teacher mediation
AB This article reports on a translanguaging-oriented read-aloud implemented in a Malaysian primary classroom where pupils learned English as a second/foreign language (L2) but came from multilingual backgrounds. We observed that English-ready pupils tended to dominate whole-class talk, while other pupils showed understanding only through writing or in their home or first languages. To address this display-language problem, we inserted a brief, teacher-led multilingual turn at pre-identified comprehension points, followed immediately by revoicing into instructional English and a return to the text. The routine was organized around four principles, namely text centrality, pre-performance sequencing, visible teacher mediation, and English residue, so that multilingual processing advanced, rather than replaced, L2 literacy goals. Across lessons, participation widened, text-related inferences became audible, and the subsequent English round was easier to populate. We argue that this design helps teachers reconcile equity and L2 exposure, and we offer a stepwise guide for adapting it to other multilingual literacy settings.

TI Assessing mechanical, morphological, and syntactic error patterns in
   written English grammatical accuracy among English language learners at
   SIMAD University, Somalia
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mechanical errors; Morphological errors; Syntactic errors; Written
   grammatical accuracy; Written morphosyntactic accuracy; Error Analysis;
   SIMAD University
ID MORPHOSYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; AWARENESS
AB This study examined mechanical, morphological, and syntactic error patterns in the written English grammatical accuracy of first-year learners at SIMAD University. Grounded in Error Analysis theory, this study used a descriptive quantitative design and analyzed 223 in-class written essays (100-150 words) to identify, classify, and quantify learner errors. An error identification checklist grouped errors into 11 types and three operational categories: mechanical errors (punctuation, capitalization, and spelling), morphological errors (tense errors), and syntactic errors (word order, fragments, run-on sentences, comma splices, phrasing, prepositions, and general grammar). A total of 2,270 errors were noted. The results showed that syntactic errors were the most frequent category (49.87%), followed by mechanical errors (31.06%) and morphological errors (19.07%). The most frequent individual errors were tense errors (19.07%), punctuation (15.64%), sentence fragments (11.67%), and grammar errors (10.31%). The study concludes that targeted instruction should address sentence-level structure, tense accuracy, and written mechanical conventions separately, rather than treating all errors as either morphological or syntactic. Because the data were limited to short written essays and error counts, the findings were interpreted as evidence of written grammatical accuracy rather than broad English proficiency. Limitations include exclusive reliance on written data and a descriptive design. Longitudinal, cross-institutional, and mixed-method studies are recommended to further explore the development of written grammatical accuracy.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.
