TI Education, Knowledge Communication and Sustainable Governance: An
   Analytical Framework for University Narratives and Digital Knowledge
   Infrastructures
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital cultural heritage; evidential warranting; higher education;
   knowledge communication; knowledge infrastructure
AB Universities increasingly organise and communicate sustainability-related knowledge through reports, databases, digital collections and other knowledge infrastructures. Existing research, however, has focused mainly on institutional narratives, disclosure practices or digital resources themselves, leaving underexplored how specialist knowledge, including material and sonic knowledge, becomes intelligible, credible and usable in educational and public settings. This article develops an analytical framework comprising three interrelated mechanisms: translation, through which specialist knowledge becomes intelligible through classification, contextualisation and interpretation; evidential warranting, through which knowledge claims gain credibility through traceable relations to sources, methods, data and uncertainty; and educational and public circulation, through which knowledge enters new educational and public settings and becomes usable. The framework takes knowledge objects and their movement across settings as the unit of analysis, distinguishing representational, provenance and circulation evidence. Using the Ancient Shu Musical Instrument Knowledge Base (ASMIK) as an illustrative case, the article shows how archaeological objects, acoustic data, organological descriptions, documentary evidence and historical interpretations of instruments, sound and musical practice can be organised within a single digital knowledge infrastructure. It argues that digitisation, access, understanding, learning and governance effects should be treated as distinct processes. University knowledge communication therefore depends on maintaining intelligibility, credibility, usability and revisability as knowledge moves across settings.

TI What the Etude Taught Me: On Music, Surgery, and a Pedagogy Worth
   Borrowing
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgical education; motor learning; deliberate practice; surgical
   training; music pedagogy
ID SURGICAL SKILLS; PERFORMANCE
AB Surgical dexterity is a motor skill, and motor skills are teachable. Surgical education has built an increasingly sophisticated apparatus for teaching them, from mastery-based knot-tying curricula and home skills laboratories to operative video atlases, coaching programs and sensor-derived performance metrics. Serious instrumental music pedagogy has been refining its own methods for far longer, and 3 of its organizing principles are worth examining alongside our own: that a large volume of purposeful repetition is the precondition for automaticity, that accuracy must be consolidated before speed is introduced, and that an internalized representation of the target performance should be built before the hands begin to move. This perspective is written by a clinician who trained seriously at the piano before training in surgery. It argues that these principles are mechanisms rather than metaphors. Surgical education already applies several of them in places, and naming them explicitly would allow them to be applied more consistently and assessed more directly. Three proposals follow: structured preprocedural preparation that pairs video review with deliberate live observation, assessment that sequences accuracy before speed, and explicit recognition of the deliberate practice habits that trainees bring with them, coupled with the faculty development required to teach those habits to trainees who arrive without them.

TI A hybrid collaborative filtering and knowledge graph-based cross-domain
   recommendation method for multimodal teaching resources
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Personalized recommendation; Knowledge graph; Collaborative filtering;
   English teaching resources; Multimodal learning
AB This paper proposes a hybrid recommendation system that integrates collaborative filtering with a pedagogically structured knowledge graph for personalized multimodal English learning resource recommendation. Resources, concepts, and learner attributes are organized into four instructional dimensions, and user-dependent semantic similarities are derived from this structure. On the behavioral side, an interaction matrix is enriched with indices describing learner interest, ability, and progress, which are used to construct feature-based collaborative filtering predictions. An ability- and progress-aware fusion coefficient adaptively balances semantic and behavioral signals for each learner. The recommendation process starts from explicit instructional requirements, performs semantic expansion on the knowledge graph, refines candidates using collaborative filtering, and ranks resources using a hybrid scoring strategy. Experiments on the English subset of the MARS dataset compare the proposed model with six baselines (HMM, SAE, FR, BSA, MLP-DNN, and a deep learning recommender) using NDCG, hit rate, coverage, and cross-domain accuracy. Results show that the proposed model achieves superior offline ranking performance and higher system-level coverage. Additional modality-aware and modality-ablation analyses demonstrate robustness across text, video, and interactive resources, as well as under partial modality removal. Importantly, all evaluations are conducted on historical interaction logs, and the reported improvements reflect recommendation quality rather than educational or learning effectiveness.

TI Caught between silence and truth: Graduate trainees' disclosures of
   microaggressions
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Supervision; Microaggression; Graduate psychology training
ID RACIAL MICROAGGRESSIONS; CLINICAL SUPERVISION; DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMS;
   PERCEPTIONS; PSYCHOLOGY
AB Graduate training in school, clinical, and counseling psychology programs is often shaped by structural inequities that can harm racially minoritized trainees. Guided by Critical Race Theory, this qualitative study used counterstorytelling to explore how 10 racially minoritized graduate students in school, clinical, and counseling psychology programs experienced and disclosed microaggressions to faculty/supervisors during their graduate training. Through thematic analysis, six overarching themes emerged: (a) types of microaggressive experiences, (b) influence on perceptions of program climate, (c) influence on emotional functioning, (d) actions in response to microaggressions, (e) faculty/supervisor responses, and (f) institutional feedback. Findings indicate that disclosure is frequently fraught, influenced by perceptions of safety, previous harm, and institutional silence. We conceptualize trainees as "caught" between the risks of silence and the risks of telling the truth about racialized harm, where "truth" refers to their experiential knowledge of oppression that often conflicts with institutional narratives of equity and safety. While some faculty/supervisors responded with cultural humility and validation, others reinforced systemic oppression through inaction or retaliation. Implications for school psychology include the need to reconceptualize supervision as a political and relational space, integrate antioppressive frameworks into training, and develop institutional mechanisms for accountability and repair. We urge school psychology programs to move beyond symbolic commitments to equity by addressing how racism, whiteness, and other systems of power shape the supervisory context and student well-being.

TI Can teachers identify and overcome content effects in mathematics? A
   conceptual replication study
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher training; Arithmetic reasoning; Problem solving; Content
   effects; Mathematical expertise; Mental models; Arithmetic word problems
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; SCHOOL-PSYCHOLOGISTS; SCIENCE; PCK
AB Our study aims to conceptually replicate and extend findings from Gros et al. (2019), which explored the impact of real-world semantics interference in expert mathematicians' ability to solve 5th-grade level arithmetic word problems. Unlike the original study, our replication examines the performance of secondary-level mathematics teachers, a group with a different kind of expertise. We aimed to determine if teachers, who often need to translate abstract concepts into concrete examples, are less susceptible to semantic interference due to their specific form of pedagogical expertise. Secondary-level school teachers (N = 122) participated in behavioral experiments involving semantically congruent and incongruent arithmetic word problems. Results showed that what we call "semantic incongruence" significantly increased response times and error rates, both among mathematics teachers and non-mathematics teachers, suggesting that pedagogical experience in itself is not sufficient to recognize semantic incongruence when encoding arithmetic word problems. These findings indicate that teachers, despite their pedagogical expertise, fall into the same traps as mathematicians, demonstrating that semantic incongruence interferes with both Content Knowledge (CK) and Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK). We discuss the implications of this replication for educational practices, school psychology, and teacher training and make recommendations to reduce the impact of semantic interference and improve instructional effectiveness.

TI Breaking the mold: Revisiting the impact of teacher-student
   relationships on achievement
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher-student relationships; Academic achievement; Latent change score
   models; Elementary school
ID CHILD RELATIONSHIP QUALITY; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; ELEMENTARY-SCHOOL;
   LONGITUDINAL EXAMINATION; EXTERNALIZING BEHAVIOR; LATENT-VARIABLES;
   MODEL; ENGAGEMENT; CONFLICT; ADJUSTMENT
AB Empirical research has suggested that teacher-student relationships (TSR) and academic achievement are reciprocally associated over time. We suggest these reciprocal associations may be overestimated due to methodological and analytical limitations. The current study aims to reassess prior findings of longitudinal and reciprocal associations between TSR and mathematics achievement during elementary school using latent change score models (LCSM). The aim is to identify and explain the distinct insights that researchers can obtain from LCSM which cannot be independently estimated via longitudinal panel models and growth curve models, methods predominantly used in examining TSR-achievement associations. Latent change models with structured residuals which is a combination of growth curve and autoregressive and cross-lagged modeling of the item-level residuals are used to corroborate findings from the LCSM. Findings from this replication study using a longitudinal dataset of 847 children from the Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development suggest that variability in ratings of TSR Closeness and Conflict did not predict subsequent latent changes in mathematics achievement and vice versa. These findings suggest consistency across data collected from two different generational cohorts. Additionally, the findings underscore the need to engage in replication studies using innovative methodological approaches and analytic techniques with different nonexperimental samples. We compare our findings from the LCSM with results from the other analytic approaches to contextualize our discussion and implications for future research.

TI Exploring the role of context in universal social, emotional, and
   behavioral screening and students' willingness to receive support
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Universal screening; School mental health; Environment; MTSS
ID ADOLESCENT MENTAL-HEALTH; SCHOOL CLIMATE; HELP-SEEKING; DISCRIMINATION;
   CONSEQUENCES; CHILDREN; RACE/ETHNICITY; DISPARITIES; RACISM
AB Universal screening for students' social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) needs is a crucial step in promoting their adaptive functioning and well-being through the provision of supports. Although abundant research emphasizes the significance of contextual factors in child development, there is a gap in understanding how such factors might influence students' SEB functioning within school-based, universal screening and intervention efforts. Addressing this gap requires greater attention to the use of practical, context-relevant measures that not only fit the realities of the school setting but also yield data that can better inform support efforts. This cross-sectional study presents findings from a high school-university partnership designed to examine the relative contributions of school-based contextual variables to students' SEB risk scores and their willingness to receive support. The analytic sample consisted of 539 high school students who completed measures of SEB risk, willingness to receive support, school climate, bullying, and experiences of discrimination. Results from robust multiple regression analyses demonstrated that school-based contextual variables were significantly associated with both SEB risk scores and willingness to receive support. Binary logistic regression analyses further indicated that these contextual variables significantly predicted risk status. Implications for practice and directions for future research are discussed.

TI Replication and validation of the Multidimentional Teacher Victimization
   Scale (MTVS): Evidence from the United States
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Multidimensional teacher victimization scale; (MTVS); Replication study;
   Measurement invariance; Teacher burnout; Psychological distress
ID RACIAL MICROAGGRESSIONS; MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE; PEER VICTIMIZATION; FIT
   INDEXES; VIOLENCE; AGGRESSION; STUDENTS; EXPERIENCES; COVARIANCE;
   COMPETENCE
AB In response to the need for reliable and validated measurement tools to assess teachers' risks of victimization from student aggression and violence across diverse educational settings and to fill gaps in measurement replication research, this pre-registered study replicated the Multidimensional Teacher Victimization Scale (MTVS) in a demographically and geographically diverse U.S. K-12 teacher sample (N = 504) to examine its applicability and validity in the U.S. context. The study aimed to explore the dimensionality of teacher-targeted victimization and measurement invariance across race, gender, and grade level, as well as its correlation with teacher burnout and psychological distress. The findings revealed that a five-factor correlated model of victimization (physical, verbal, relational, cyber, and property offenses) best fit the U.S. data, suggesting that the original six-factor structure may not fully capture the complexity of teacher victimization in the U.S. context. Notably, the sexual harassment factor did not emerge as a distinct sub-dimension. Strict measurement invariance was achieved across White and non-White teacher groups with no significant latent mean differences. Strong measurement invariance was achieved across genders (male vs. female) and grade levels (elementary and middle combined vs. high schools), with latent mean differences indicating that male teachers reported more frequent social/relational victimization, and elementary and middle school teachers reported more frequent physical victimization than high school teachers. Correlational analyses revealed that social/ relational victimization was most strongly associated with teacher burnout and psychological distress, aligning with previous studies on the emotional toll of teacher victimization. Implications for adapting MTVS across diverse school contexts and teacher populations are discussed.

TI Pre-service mathematics teachers' collaborative work: Tensions between
   the individual and the collective
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics teacher education; Collaborative work; Communitarian ethics;
   Dialectical-materialistic analysis; Group debates
ID EDUCATION; COMMUNITIES
AB This study problematizes the instrumental character of collaborative work of pre-service mathematics teachers (PMTs) in neoliberal university contexts, such as that in Chile. We research how such work comes about when PMTs participate in training activities oriented towards collective learning. From the principle of learning of the theory of objectification (TO), we undertake a dialectical-materialistic analysis of four episodes that show collaborative work by two groups of PMTs around debates regarding the TO's principles of being and communitarian ethics. These findings suggest a shift towards training practices that move beyond instrumental logics and merely discursive or prescriptive approaches in initial mathematics teacher education.

TI Academic educators' leadership styles and their associations with
   student engagement and critical thinking disposition among Saudi health
   sciences students: a mixed-methods study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educator leadership; Student engagement; Critical thinking disposition;
   Health professions education; Mixed methods
AB Background Educator leadership behaviors are widely recognized as an important component of the classroom environment and may be associated with student engagement and critical thinking disposition. In health sciences education, these competencies are fundamental to clinical reasoning and evidence-based decision-making. However, empirical evidence examining the associations among educator leadership styles, student engagement, and critical thinking disposition remains limited. Methods This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was conducted at a Saudi health sciences university. Quantitative data were collected from a stratified random sample of 351 undergraduate students across four health sciences colleges using the Leadership Style Questionnaire, the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale, and the University Student Engagement Inventory. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlations, multiple linear regression, and bootstrapped cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis. Qualitative data were subsequently collected from 58 unique participants through 40 semi-structured interviews and four focus group discussions (28 participants, including 10 who also participated in interviews) and analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results Students reported mean student engagement and critical thinking disposition scores above the scale midpoint. Democratic leadership demonstrated the strongest positive bivariate associations with student engagement (r = .363, p < .001) and critical thinking disposition (r = .402, p < .001), whereas laissez-faire leadership demonstrated comparatively weaker associations. In adjusted regression analyses, democratic leadership remained independently associated with student engagement (beta = 0.39, p < .001) and critical thinking disposition (beta = 0.15, p = .007), whereas laissez-faire leadership showed no statistically significant independent association with either outcome after adjustment for the remaining leadership styles. Bootstrapped indirect-effect analysis indicated that student engagement statistically accounted for part of the association between democratic leadership and critical thinking disposition. Qualitative findings converged with and expanded the quantitative results, with students describing participatory teaching behaviors, open dialogue, constructive questioning, collaborative learning, and clear instructional guidance as supporting engagement and reflective thinking. Conclusions Democratic educator leadership demonstrated the strongest positive associations with student engagement and critical thinking disposition. These findings suggest that participatory teaching approaches may represent valuable components of faculty development and educational practice. Longitudinal and multi-institutional studies are warranted to further examine the temporal relationships among educator leadership, student engagement, and critical thinking disposition.

TI Beyond the classroom sample: Validating a STEM biographical data measure
   with online adult learners
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; Biographical data; Exploratory factor analysis; Social
   cognitive career theory; Digital learning platforms; Measure validation;
   Childhood experiences
ID CHILDHOOD EXPERIENCES; BACKGROUND DATA; SCIENCE; STUDENTS; CAREER;
   PREDICTORS; RECOMMENDATIONS; INTERESTS; VALIDITY; BIODATA
AB Higher education research in STEM is a critical and evolving domain. However, it often relies heavily on college student samples, particularly those who have already signaled STEM interest via their majors or extracurricular activities, limiting the generalizability of findings. New digital learning platform based research infrastructures offer advantages that complement traditional recruitment and data collection approaches. We utilized OpenStax Kinetic to validate a biographical data (or biodata) measure of STEM and other early academic life experiences, recruiting online adult learners with no specific predisposition toward STEM. This sample spans broader interests and a wider age range than traditional college-aged STEM students. As with many measure validation studies, our current instrument is relatively long, raising concerns about participant fatigue and data quality. Kinetic enables administration of convergent and discriminant validity measures (vocational interest, STEM interest, and personality traits) at different times, reducing common-method variance and respondent fatigue. We conducted an exploratory factor analysis of a seven-factor model with online adult learners (n = 467), finding that five factors (general parental support, STEM parental support, teacher support, math extracurricular engagement, and science extracurricular engagement) loaded as expected, while the remaining two were reconceptualized into factors comprising items that capture community STEM engagement and intrinsic hands-on engagement with STEM. We describe our interpretability assessment process and item refinement decisions for future validation efforts. Finally, we highlight additional advantages and considerations for researchers and learning scientists using large-scale platforms for measurement studies.

TI Comparing global competence of native and immigrant students: A network
   analysis of countries with different immigration policies
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Global competence; Native students; Immigrant students; Immigration
   policies; Psychometric network analysis; PISA 2018
ID INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION; SELF-EFFICACY; MODEL; MULTICULTURALISM;
   CITIZENSHIP; PERSONALITY; INTEGRATION; DIMENSIONS; CENTRALITY; AWARENESS
AB Transnational challenges such as the climate crisis, forced migration, regional conflicts, and digital threats have increased the need for schools to support students' global competence. However, how the components of global competence relate to one another and how these relational patterns vary across countries with different migration and integration approaches remain insufficiently understood. Overall, the study offers a relational and cross-national perspective on where efforts to strengthen these dimensions might begin across diverse migration and integration contexts.

TI Spatial mismatch and logical transition of basic education resource
   allocation in South Korea
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE School-age population; Educational resource allocation; Local Indicators
   of Spatial Association; Low fertility; Spatial mismatch; South Korea
AB Against the backdrop of sustained demographic decline driven by ultra-low fertility, the long-standing assumption that educational facility provision responds proportionally to local population change has become increasingly contested. Using annual time-series data from 228 basic local governments in South Korea between 2014 and 2024, this study examines how changes in the school-age population are associated with adjustments in overall school supply, encompassing both public and private schools as a proxy for local public service provision. Combining ordinary least squares regression, a dual-indicator classification framework, and spatial autocorrelation analysis, the study identifies temporal and spatial inconsistencies between changes in the school-age population and changes in the number of schools. The results reveal pronounced regional divergence: while school-age population has declined nationwide, more than half of local jurisdictions exhibit changes in the number of schools that are misaligned with demographic trajectories, most notably in the form of "overadjustment," where school expansion or retention occurs despite population contraction. Spatial analyses further show an increasing concentration of school-age population in the Seoul Metropolitan Area and major industrial centers, whereas school supply adjustments display a polarized west-east pattern. These findings point to a growing decoupling between demographic demand and educational infrastructure allocation, suggesting that the number of schools is increasingly shaped by planning priorities linked to industrial strategies and urban development policies rather than by population size alone. By empirically documenting this shift, the study contributes to broader debates on public service allocation and spatial governance under conditions of sustained population decline.

TI Semiotics Theory of Borders: Proposal of a Theoretical Model for
   Interdisciplinarity in STEAM Education
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interdisciplinarity; STEAM education; Semiotics; Borders; Fibonacci
AB This paper proposes the semiotics theory of borders (STB) as a theoretical framework for understanding interdisciplinarity in STEAM education. While existing research often conceptualises disciplinary boundaries as sites of integration, STB focuses on borders as semiotic spaces in which meaning is actively constructed through interaction. The study illustrates the framework through the analysis of an interdisciplinary workshop involving 45 STEAM teachers, centred on a modelling task connecting mathematics and physics through the Fibonacci sequence. The analysis, guided by Habermas's rationalities and semiotic functions of borders, shows how interdisciplinary collaboration unfolds through processes of differentiation, mediation, and transformation. The findings highlight how teachers initially rely on discipline-specific approaches, then negotiate meanings through dialogue, and finally develop shared understandings that reconfigure disciplinary knowledge. The contribution of the paper is threefold: it provides a theoretical lens for analysing meaning-making at disciplinary borders, offers design principles for interdisciplinary tasks, and contributes to understanding teacher professional development in STEAM contexts.

TI Applying the 6E Learning byDeSign™ Model to Support Collaboration in a
   STEM-Integrated System Analysis and Design Course
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Collaboration; STEM education; 6E Learning byDeSign (TM) model;
   Interdisciplinary learning; Knowledge integration; Team-based learning;
   System analysis and design
ID SCIENCE
AB This mixed-method case study examined how the 6E Learning byDeSign (TM) model was implemented to support collaboration, interdisciplinary knowledge integration, and STEM competency development in an undergraduate System Analysis and Design course. The study included 137 students who completed the course and worked in 20 stable project teams that they formed at the beginning of the semester. After the final projects, two industry mentors classified nine existing teams as Honored (H) and 11 as Registered (R). These labels were not disclosed to the students. Quantitative course-performance and survey data were aggregated into equal-weight team means and analyzed using Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with exact p-values and family-specific Bonferroni adjustment. These data were supplemented by qualitative student reflections and project documentation. The surveys yielded 125 valid midterm responses and 126 valid final responses. After adjustment, H teams had higher midterm and final raw team-project scores than R teams, whereas differences in the other course-performance outcomes did not remain statistically significant. Across all 20 teams, final ratings were higher for all four STEM indicators and for Explain, Engineer, and Evaluate. Engage, Explore, and Enrich and all direct H/R change-score comparisons were nonsignificant after adjustment. The findings suggest that the 6E model can provide a practical structure for collaborative and interdisciplinary STEM learning.

TI Tertiary English Education in the GenAI Era: Chinese English Majors'
   Cognitive Appraisals, Employment Anxiety, and Informal Digital Learning
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE challenge-hindrance appraisal; English education; English majors; future
   employment anxiety; GenAI-IDLE; parallel mediation
AB The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified employment anxiety among Chinese English majors, posing new challenges for foreign language education and career development. However, how their cognitive appraisals of GenAI shape engagement in GenAI-mediated informal digital learning of English (GenAI-IDLE) remains underexplored. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory and the challenge-hindrance stressor framework, this study examined the mediating role of four-dimensional future employment anxiety (personal ability, knowledge application, career replaceability, social relations) in the relationship between challenge/hindrance appraisals and GenAI-IDLE. A valid sample of 526 Chinese English majors completed an online questionnaire, and data were analysed using PLS-SEM. Both challenge and hindrance appraisals were directly positively associated with GenAI-IDLE. Challenge appraisal was indirectly associated with GenAI-IDLE through reduced career replaceability anxiety. Hindrance appraisal was positively associated with all four anxiety dimensions, but only two indirect pathways were significant: negative through career replaceability anxiety and positive through personal ability anxiety. Knowledge application and social relations anxiety did not mediate significantly. These findings reveal that the cognitive appraisal-future employment anxiety-GenAI-IDLE behaviour chain operates through differentiated, anxiety-specific pathways. The results offer pedagogical implications for foreign language education, including curriculum design that reframes GenAI as an augmentative tool, integration of digital resilience training, and development of career-oriented interventions to mitigate maladaptive employment anxiety while fostering self-directed informal learning among English majors.

TI 'You Care More if You Work Yourself to Death': Exploited Altruism and
   Other Adverse Factors Affecting the Culture Within an English Higher
   Education Initial Teacher Training Team
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE altruism; higher education; initial teacher training; micro-resistance;
   relationships; trust
ID OCCUPATIONAL BALANCE
AB This paper shares the ways in which Higher Education Lecturers (HELs) in Initial Teacher Training (ITT) at an English university perceive their workplace culture. Data from 15 questionnaires and 12 semi-structured interviews underwent thematic analysis. The findings suggest that culture was a preoccupation, with trust, relationships and idealism featuring as sub-themes within that focus. The attitudes and perceptions underpinning the sub-themes contributed towards a sense of altruism being exploited by systems and leadership structures. This appeared to be counter-balanced through reliance upon upstairs/downstairs bonding and exclusions. Micro-resistance was therefore apparent, but with little impact on improving the strategies and space of ITT. From this study, suggestions are therefore made for all stakeholders in ITT to reflect on their occupation of place, space, strategies and tactics, with an emphasis on developing compassionate leadership.

TI L2 Teachers' Work Engagement in AI-Enhanced Teaching Environments:
   Harnessing a Phenomenological Approach to Uncover Its Personal and
   Contextual Determinants
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-enhanced teaching environments; artificial intelligence (AI);
   descriptive phenomenological approach; L2 teachers; work engagement
ID BURNOUT
AB Adopting a descriptive phenomenological approach, this study sought to unravel the determinants of L2 teachers' work engagement within artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted instructional contexts. To this end, 49 English language teachers were purposefully selected from Chinese educational contexts to complete an open-ended questionnaire online. Data were thematically analysed using MAXQDA (v. 2024), revealing that teachers' work engagement has been shaped by specific personal traits-adaptability, AI literacy, self-efficacy, resilience and emotional regulation-and contextual conditions, including leadership behaviours, professional development opportunities, colleague support and learner engagement. These findings highlight how these individual and environmental factors together have influenced teachers' ability to remain engaged while navigating AI-mediated teaching demands. By uncovering these personal and contextual determinants, the study offers practical insights for educational leaders and policymakers seeking to support L2 teachers in effectively integrating AI tools into instruction.

TI More than getting the answer: How students engage with generative AI in
   technical problem solving
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce complete solutions and explanations for quantitative STEM problems, raising questions about the forms of cognitive engagement students enact when using these tools. Although prior research has examined AI use, perceptions, and performance, less is known about how students engage with GenAI during structured technical problem solving.Results This study examined 38 undergraduate students in an operations management course who first solved a linear programming problem manually and then used GenAI on the same task. Student reflections were analyzed using deductive thematic analysis guided by the ICAP framework, with available AI interaction records used to validate classifications and develop illustrative cases. Three engagement patterns were documented. Passive engagement involved receiving AI-generated output without using the interaction to compare, verify, reinterpret, or extend understanding. Active engagement involved using AI to check or confirm previously completed reasoning, whereas Constructive engagement involved seeking explanation or conceptual interpretation, particularly around sensitivity analysis, shadow prices, and binding constraints. No reflection or available interaction record provided sufficient evidence of Interactive engagement, including in cases involving multiple conversational turns.Conclusion The findings show that students can position GenAI differently within the same technical task, from receiving answers to verifying existing reasoning or seeking conceptual explanation. These distinctions suggest that STEM educators should attend not only to whether students use GenAI, but also to the forms of engagement that instructional tasks and expectations invite.

TI Linguistically and Culturally Responsive Reading Conversations:
   Understanding and Fostering Children's Reading Engagement
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment for learning; cultural responsiveness; English language
   learners; linguistic responsiveness; multilingual learners; pedagogical
   translanguaging; reading engagement
AB Reading engagement is a key factor in children's literacy development, yet it often receives limited attention in classroom practice. Linguistically diverse learners may face added challenges when formal reading education and assessment focus only on the language(s) of schooling. Understanding reading engagement across its behavioral, cognitive, affective, and social dimensions helps teachers see how learners interact with and respond to texts and identify where additional support could strengthen both literacy skills and engagement. In this article, we introduce Linguistically & Culturally Responsive Reading Conversations, an Assessment for Learning approach developed and piloted with seven teachers and 38 learners aged 4-11, across four primary schools in the Netherlands and Australia. This approach treats home languages and cultural knowledge as assets, giving teachers a fuller picture of learners' reading engagement. We share practical strategies, including for teachers who do not speak or understand learners' home languages. In doing so, we show how valuing and capitalizing on learners' home languages and cultural backgrounds can also support their enjoyment of reading, identity development, and well-being, fostering more equitable and inclusive reading education.

TI Career Development in Pediatric Emergency Medicine Fellowships: A
   Qualitative Study
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID MENTORSHIP; SUPPORT
AB Objectives Effective career development guidance during fellowship is essential to prepare pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) fellows for diverse career paths. However, little is known about how PEM fellowships structure and deliver career development support. Our objectives were (1) To describe how PEM fellowship Program Directors (PDs) provide career development support to their fellows and (2) To explore how PEM junior faculty (JF) experienced career development during fellowship and how the process could be optimized.Methods In this qualitative study, we recruited PEM PDs and JF for semi-structured 1:1 interviews, purposively sampling across United States geographic regions and program sizes. We developed an interview guide to explore perceptions of career development. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, coded, and analyzed thematically to identify key themes in PEM fellowship career development. Participants completed a survey collecting demographic data and information on fellowship career development curricula.Results We conducted 39 interviews (20 PDs and 19 JF) and identified 12 themes across four career development domains: exploration and niche development, academic versus non-academic careers, mentorship, and transition to employment. PDs described individualized career development opportunities, whereas JF expressed a desire for more explicit structure and early scaffolding around niche exploration and mentorship assignment. Both groups noted a strong emphasis on academic careers, with limited exposure to non-academic pathways. Job search preparation included guidance on applications and networking, but JF described less clarity around hiring timelines, negotiation, and contracts. Across domains, participants highlighted that fellow initiative is required to drive their career development.Conclusions By integrating both PD and JF perspectives on career development, this study identifies a dynamic interplay between program support and fellow initiative. Earlier scaffolding, specifically in niche exploration and mentorship, broader exposure to diverse career pathways, and greater transparency in job search preparation may strengthen how career development is provided during PEM fellowship.

TI Principles of interval training: a practical and physiological teaching
   guide for educators
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE exercise; intensity; intermittent; interval; training
ID BLOOD LACTATE CLEARANCE; ACTIVE RECOVERY; HEART-FAILURE; SPECIAL
   RECOMMENDATIONS; EMPIRICAL PRACTICE; MIDDLE-DISTANCE; LOW-VOLUME;
   INTENSITY; EXERCISE; ADAPTATIONS
AB We teach that physical activity, exercise, and exercise training are good for us and that the positive effect is better if we exercise with intensity; the greater the intensity, the greater the effect. Indeed, there is clear and irrefutable evidence of intensity dependence of effect, stemming from a dose-response relationship between effort going into the exercise and the result coming out of it. This leads to the situation where we generally and practically prescribe exercise as intensely as possible, for as long as possible, but this comes in conflict with the speed/power:duration relationship that dictates how long high-intensity exercise may be sustained. The solution we have is high-intensity interval training, referred to as HIIT or just interval training. This is a modality of exercise training that with repeated bouts of high-intensity exercise interspersed by active/passive recovery periods permits accumulation of intense exercise beyond that which would be achievable in a single exercise bout. This is then applied to a range of exercises and locomotion modes. However, while we often refer to and teach concepts of intensity dependence of exercise training effects, we rarely describe the basics of the actual exercise. Here, we introduce interval training, and by association, intensity, for the physiology-savvy, but nonexercise science educator. We conceptualize the principles of interval training and provide a practical framework and lesson plan for teaching appropriate interval training.

TI Student Performance and Instructional Complexity Across Team-Based and
   Mastery Learning Course Formats
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mastery learning; Team-based learning; Competency-based education;
   Active learning; Instructional complexity
ID TASK COMPLEXITY; EDUCATION; GUIDELINES
AB Objective: To compare cumulative final examination performance between mastery learning (ML) and team-based learning (TBL) and conduct an exploratory characterization of differences in instructional complexity between the 2 models. Methods: This retrospective study compared 7 years of student performance data from a TBL course format (2012-2018, n = 996) with 7 years following implementation of ML (2019-2025, n = 1078). Course content, sequencing, learning objectives, and cumulative examination blueprint remained relatively stable across years. The primary outcome was student performance on a cumulative final examination. Final examination scores were compared between instructional models using Welch's independent-samples t test. The exploratory instructor-informed complexity analysis suggested that TBL concentrated relative instructional complexity within synchronous classroom coordination and team management, whereas ML concentrated complexity within assessment infrastructure, reassessment processes, and individualized learner support. Conclusion: Both TBL and ML were associated with high cumulative final examination performance despite substantial differences in instructional organization and operational demands. Selection of an instructional model should depend on alignment among learning goals, institutional resources, and implementation context rather than small differences in examination outcomes.

TI Comparative analysis of short answer questions and multiple-choice
   questions in formative assessment of first-year medical students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multiple-choice questions; Short answer questions; Psychometric
   analysis; Item difficulty; Item discrimination
AB Background Assessment methods are essential for evaluating medical students' knowledge and cognitive skills. Multiple-choice questions (MCQs) are widely used because of their objectivity and efficiency, whereas short answer questions (SAQs) are considered better suited for assessing higher-order cognitive skills. However, evidence comparing the psychometric performance of these formats in formative undergraduate medical assessments remains limited. This study aimed to compare the difficulty index (P), discrimination index (DI), and overall test performance of SAQs and MCQs in a formative assessment of first-year medical students. Methods A descriptive analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 178 first-year medical students enrolled in the Medical Parasitology course within the Locomotor and Skin module at Ain Shams University during the 2024-2025 academic year. Students completed content-matched SAQ and MCQ examinations, each comprising 20 items aligned with the same intended learning outcomes. Psychometric analyses included item difficulty, discrimination, reliability, and comparisons between formats. Results Students achieved significantly higher scores on MCQs than SAQs (13.5 vs. 11.1/20, p < 0.001). MCQ items were significantly easier (mean p: 0.67 vs. 0.55, p < 0.001), while discrimination indices were comparable (0.44 vs. 0.41, p = 0.398). Both formats demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.85 for MCQs and 0.83 for SAQs) and strong discrimination between high- and low-achieving students. Pass/fail concordance was 68.0%, with more students passing MCQs but failing SAQs (p = 0.012). Item difficulty correlated strongly across formats (r = 0.71), whereas discrimination showed a weak, non-significant correlation (r = 0.01). Clinical SAQs were associated with lower performance among low-achieving students. Conclusions Both MCQs and SAQs demonstrated sound psychometric properties. MCQs were easier and yielded higher scores, whereas SAQs provided a more challenging assessment with comparable discrimination. Using both formats together may enhance assessment quality in undergraduate medical education.

TI Tolerance of uncertainty and reflection ability among medical students
   in Germany
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Uncertainty tolerance; Reflection ability; Medical students; Medical
   education
ID AMBIGUITY
AB Background With growing recognition of uncertainty tolerance (UT) and reflection ability (RA) as core competencies for healthcare professionals, targeted promotion of these skills has become increasingly important in medical education. However, research on the associations between UT and RA and students' individual characteristics, such as age and gender, remains limited, and existing findings are inconsistent. Addressing this gap, the present study assesses UT and RA among medical students at entry to medical school, examines their associations with age and gender, and explores implications for the tailored design of educational interventions. Methods All first-year medical students at Ludwig Maximilian University and the Technical University of Munich were invited to participate in the survey during a compulsory joint course, Introduction to Clinical Medicine. The questionnaire, administered via EvaSys, included the Groningen Reflection Ability Scale, the Uncertainty Tolerance Scale, and demographic data. Results A total of 761 participants were included in the analysis. The age could be determined for 384 participants, and the gender for 493 participants. Measuring UT resulted in a mixed picture: while students reported openness toward novel experiences, they simultaneously expressed a preference for predictability and routine. Linear regression analysis revealed no significant association between overall UT scores and age or gender (all p > 0.05). However, statistically significant gender differences emerged at the item level, with female students reporting lower tolerance of uncertainty. Regarding RA, linear regression analysis similarly revealed no significant association between overall GRAS scores and age or gender (R & sup2; = 0.002; all p > 0.05). However, statistically significant gender differences were identified at the item level, with female students reporting a higher level of self-underestimation and self-doubt. Conclusions Although overall UT and RA scores were not significantly associated with gender or age, exploratory item-level analysis suggested gender-specific differences in certain aspects of both constructs. Given the high proportion of female students, these differences may warrant further investigation and consideration in curriculum development to promote equitable opportunities and optimally prepare all students for clinical practice.

TI Teachers' desired mobility to disadvantaged schools: Do financial
   incentives matter?☆
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher mobility; Financial incentives; Stated preferences; Rank-ordered
   choices; Disadvantaged schools
ID HIGH-POVERTY SCHOOLS; STUDENT-ACHIEVEMENT
AB This article exploits a 2018 reform of financial incentives for teachers to work in French disadvantaged schools. Based on administrative personnel records from an educational authority, it evaluates the impact of those incentives on stated preferences to move to such schools. This quasi-experimental source of variation of financial incentives, namely a gradual doubling of the annual stipend from & euro;2,300 to & euro;4,600 in these schools, enhanced their attractiveness. The estimated effect on teachers' desired mobility is substantial and equivalent to a 34-minute reduction per trip. However, this effect is heterogeneous among teachers, notably higher for those with less experience and who already work in such schools.

TI Exposure to simulators and early surgical practice in medical students:
   A cross-sectional study
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical students; Simulation exercise; Surgical procedures
ID SKILLS; SURGERY; IMPACT
AB Introduction: Early surgical exposure and simulators in medical schools are fundamental in the education process. These techniques allow students to practice and subsequently improve their skills in clinical and surgical practice. The aim was to determine early exposure to an active surgical clerkship among medical students and identify their viewpoint to improve surgical education. Materials and methods: This cross-sectional observational study was carried out among medical students (N = 80) in the 5th and 6th year. A 5-item Likert-scale questionnaire assessing surgical exposure, clerkship characteristics, and simulator use was validated via a pilot test (Cronbach's (alpha) > 0.70). Statistical analyses, including Wilcoxon rank-sum and Fisher's exact tests, were conducted using Stata. Results: A significant difference was observed regarding skill development perceptions (p = 0.008), with Ecuadorian students (n = 63) reporting higher satisfaction than international students (n = 17). No significant differences were found for career motivation (p = 0.298), with 82.4% of international and 66.7% of Ecuadorian students strongly agreeing that hands-on rotations increase surgical interest. Active rotations were fully recommended over observerships by 82.4% of international and 87.3% of Ecuadorian respondents (p = 0.468). Exposure to simulators trended higher among international students (35.3% vs. 15.9%; p = 0.093). Conclusion: Early surgical exposure could help students develop skills during their clinical placements, and students choose to participate in these placements because they achieve learning objectives during their rotations. In addition, simulation and virtual learning were recommended by a large proportion of students. (c) 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Espa & ntilde;a, S.L.U. TI Developing writer identity through authorial voice in EAP writing: A
   mixed-methods case study of Chinese postgraduates in an Australian
   university
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE EAP writing; Writer identity; Voice; Study abroad
ID ENGLISH; LANGUAGE
AB This mixed-methods case study examines how five Chinese postgraduate students in an Australian university developed writer identity through EAP writing tasks over one academic year. Drawing on textual analysis of written assignments and semi-structured interviews, it traces changes over time in individual, collective, and depersonalized voice, based on Lehman and Su & lstrok;kowski's (2020) framework. The findings suggest uneven patterns of writer identity development, marked by increased individual positioning, strategically deployed collective voice, and selective use of depersonalized expression. Motivation, perceived reader expectations, and language proficiency shaped students' voice choices in the English-medium academic context; these choices also varied with the rhetorical demands of different task genres. The study contributes to EAP writing research by showing how authorial voice functions as a textual and social resource through which multilingual students negotiate academic participation. Pedagogically, it highlights the need for explicit instruction on voice, clearer assessment expectations, and lexical and rhetorical scaffolding for novice L2 academic writers.

TI The association between neighborhood safety, parenting, and
   victimization
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer victimization; Parental overprotection; Neighborhood safety;
   Moderation
ID PEER VICTIMIZATION; BULLYING VICTIMIZATION; SCHOOL; ADOLESCENCE;
   CHILDREN; CHILDHOOD; FAMILY; RISK; OVERPROTECTION; CONSEQUENCES
AB Scholars across multiple disciplines have identified peer victimization is a critical area of research. The current study investigates how parental overprotection is linked to victimization, moderated by the perception of neighborhood safety. Bronfenbrenner's socio-ecological model provides a theoretical framework, emphasizing the interconnectedness of individual, family, school, and neighborhood influences. Although many researchers have focused on individual characteristics and micro-level factors like parenting and school environment, the exosystem-specifically neighborhood dynamics-has been understudied. We hypothesize that overprotective parenting may increase the likelihood of victimization, with stronger effects in neighborhoods perceived as unsafe. Additionally, we posit that perceived neighborhood safety may have a greater impact than, for example, crime in the neighborhood. Data will be collected from elementary and secondary school students in northern Germany, with a sample size of 119. Findings from this research will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how ecological factors, such as neighborhood safety, shape bullying dynamics, offering insights for more comprehensive intervention strategies.

TI A cross-country comparison of student and school level variables in
   online reading achievement
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Confidence in reading; Emphasis on academic success; Online reading
   achievement; Engagement in reading lessons; Digital resource shortage
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; ENGAGEMENT; PERFORMANCE; LITERACY; CLIMATE; PAPER
AB No research has yet comparatively examined student-and school-level variables related to online reading achievement. This study investigated the student-and school-level variables associated with online reading achievement in a cross-country comparison of fourteen countries based on data from the latest ePIRLS (e-reading component of the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study). Based on a correlational research design, this study employed hierarchical linear modeling to gauge the associations hierarchically for each country in the sample independently. The full model including both student-and school-level variables was statistically significant for ten countries but not for Denmark, Georgia, Italy, or Slovenia. The student-level variables accounted for 10%-33% of online reading achievement. When the student-level variables were controlled for, the school-level variables explained 8%-32% of the variance. The study offers specific findings for each country that could be used to better understand the nature of online reading achievement and design education policies and points to further research on cultural differences.

TI Higher-order thinking skills in STEM education: A systematic review of
   HOTS constructs, assessment methods, and chatgpt-assisted coding
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; Higher-order thinking skills; Assessment; Systematic
   review; ChatGPT; AI-assisted coding
ID LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS; STUDENTS; TECHNOLOGY
AB Higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) are important learning outcomes in STEM education, but their assessment has not been systematically synthesized. This study reviewed 88 empirical studies published between 2003 and 2025. For the first research question, two human researchers independently coded HOTS-related constructs from assessment instruments and evidence sources, synthesized assessment methods, and examined patterns across STEM domains. For the second research question, we explored ChatGPT's feasibility on two structured coding tasks: classifying research participants and categorizing research methods. The six most frequently identified HOTS-related constructs were problem solving, analyzing, evaluating, critical thinking, creating, and creativity. Researcher-developed instruments were the most frequently used assessment method, followed by rubric-based performance assessments, validated scales, and qualitative analyses; standardized tests were used less frequently. HOTS emphases varied across STEM domains. ChatGPT supported the preliminary classification of research participants and research methods, but the latter still required human verification.

TI GenAI-assisted language teaching (GenAILT): Approach, design, and
   procedure
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Language teaching; Language teaching methods; Pedagogical
   design; Teacher decision-making
AB Since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has been rapidly taken up in second language teaching and learning. Much of the existing literature reports on perceptions, tools, techniques, and short-term outcomes; however, the broader question of what kind of pedagogy is emerging has received less attention. This conceptual paper addresses that question by analysing GenAI-assisted Language Teaching (GenAILT) through Richards and Rodgers' (2014) framework of Approach, Design, and Procedure. At the level of Approach, we demonstrate that GenAI is deployed under quite different theoretical assumptions, and we distinguish declared theory from the commitments GenAI enacts through its training data, which favour dominant language varieties unless teachers counter them. At the level of Design, we argue that objectives in GenAILT are better understood along a product-process continuum, that GenAI functions as a flexible resource for realising existing syllabus types, and that activity design must build in strategic, critical and ethical engagement with GenAI output. We further propose a fourrole matrix for learners along the dimensions of learning orientation and instructional scaffolding, examine how teacher work is redistributed, reframe instructional materials in terms of form and quality assurance, and discuss classroom assessment as a design decision. At the level of Procedure, we illustrate that competent GenAILT depends on teacher decision-making. We close with implications for teacher education and research.

TI Calibrating self-regulated learning: Convergence and divergence in EFL
   university teachers' and students' perceptions in blended learning
   environments
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; EFL university teachers and students; Blended
   learning
ID SKILLS
AB This qualitative case study examines how Chinese EFL university students and teachers perceived self-regulated learning (SRL) in a blended learning environment. Drawing on interviews with 20 students and 18 teachers, reflective journals, and classroom observations, the study identifies shared understandings and persistent misalignments. Both groups viewed SRL as involving learner responsibility, especially goal setting and resource selection. However, teachers emphasized guidance, monitoring, feedback, and self-evaluation, whereas students relied more on peer interaction and practical resource use during online and out-of-class learning. Student interviews and reflective journals indicated that practical strategy use often emerged through task completion and peer exchange, whereas teacher interviews and classroom observations showed that these strategies were rarely taught explicitly as transferable SRL practices. Interpreting these findings through a sociocultural lens and in relation to Confucian heritage traditions, the study highlights the need for more explicit, socially supported, and pedagogically integrated SRL in blended EFL courses.

TI A square peg in a round hole: Overqualification as a double-edged sword
   effect on teachers' professional development
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive stress appraisal; Job burnout; Overqualification; Perceived
   competitive climate; Self-efficacy; Teachers' professional development
ID CONSERVATION; MOTIVATION; SELF; BIAS
AB This study examines the double-edged association between overqualification and teachers' professional development (professional identity and job burnout), with cognitive stress appraisal (challenge and threat appraisal) as mediators and perceived competitive climate and self-efficacy as moderators. Based on a questionnaire survey of 569 teachers in Shanghai, the results show that overqualification positively relates to professional identity and negatively relates to job burnout, with direct effects via ability-job fit. Challenge appraisal and threat appraisal play differentiated mediating roles: challenge appraisal enhances overqualification's positive effects, while threat appraisal weakens them. Perceived competitive climate moderates the overqualification -> cognitive stress appraisal pathway, and self-efficacy moderates the conversion of cognitive stress appraisal to professional identity and job burnout. The combination of low perceived competitive climate and high self-efficacy optimizes overqualification's positive effects. This study enriches overqualification research in education, providing practical insights for schools to support overqualified teachers and teachers to use their advantages.

TI Sustaining teachers' epistemic agency in AI-supported instructional
   design: An exploratory design-based study of a conversational-function
   approach
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Design-based research; Student-centered planning; Knowledge building;
   Epistemic agency; Conversational functions
ID GENERATIVE AI; KNOWLEDGE; CONSTRUCTION; EDUCATION
AB The increasing use of generative AI in instructional design raises concerns about cognitive outsourcing, as lesson planning may become overly shaped by algorithmic outputs. Because learning is situated and personalized, sustaining teachers' epistemic agency-responsibility for instructional decisions-is essential for student-centered planning. This exploratory study uses a design-based research approach to examine how a conversational-function framework can support teachers' epistemic agency in AI-assisted instructional design (AIID). Nineteen in-service teachers participated in two iterative intervention cycles in which structured conversational functions scaffolded teacher-AI interaction. Teachers' AIID scores showed substantial within-context improvement across the two cycles, accompanied by changes in score variability. These outcome patterns, together with network and sequential analyses of teacher-AI dialogues, suggest that conversational functions may support more coherent teacher-AI interaction patterns that sustain teachers' epistemic responsibility for instructional decisions.

TI Using an Automated Evaluation System to Improve Medical Student
   Evaluation Response Rate and Reduce Administrative Burden
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Background: Email reminders facilitate timely task completion but can create substantial administrative burdens for clerkship staff. In our emergency medicine (EM) clerkship, third-year medical students initiate digital evaluation requests after each clinical shift, requiring frequent manual reminders to maintain completion rates. The time-intensive nature of this process highlights the need for a more efficient and scalable approach. Methods: This multi-site, pre-post study evaluated clinical performance evaluation completion rates and time to completion during the required EM clerkship over 48 weeks before and after implementation of an automated reminder system in September 2024. The system integrated existing survey functionality with Microsoft Excel and Microsoft Power Automate to track evaluation requests and completion and generate reminders every 2 days for up to 28 days. Primary outcomes were evaluation completion rate and time to completion. A theoretical cost analysis compared estimated personnel costs of the manual reminder process, based on administrator time and median salary estimates, with projected programming development and maintenance costs over 3 years. Results: A total of 5747 evaluations were sent during this period to attending and resident evaluators. Overall completion rate rose modestly post-intervention (71.4% to 75.1%, p < 0.001), with attending evaluation rate demonstrating greater improvement from 73.9% to 81.6% (p < 0.001). Conversely, both resident (median 2.67 to 3.98 days) and attending completion time increased (median 2.59 to 2.74 days), p = 0.002. Based on the state salary estimates and our institutional experience, the automated approach could yield estimated net savings of $2850 in the first year and $9560 over 3 years. Conclusions: Automated reminders improved evaluation completion but did not improve timeliness of completion, which may not translate into meaningful formative benefits if feedback is delayed. Further studies should focus on the impact on cognitive burden and evaluation quality before large-scale automated systems can be optimized and sustainably integrated into medical education.

TI Procedural Confidence Among Graduating Emergency Medicine Residents:
   Implications for Training and Assessment of Clinical Readiness
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID COMPETENCE; SIMULATION; SKILLS
AB Background The current numerical standards for procedural competency in Emergency Medicine (EM) lack strong evidentiary support. In the absence of more validated competency standards, self-reported confidence has been used as a learner-centered measure of perceived procedural readiness. Characterizing procedural confidence, patterns across procedures, and factors associated with confidence may help inform improvements in residency curricula and assessment.Objective To characterize self-reported confidence in key emergency medicine procedures, identify patterns across procedures, and examine associated residency program factors among graduating EM residents.Methods A cross-sectional survey of graduating EM residents was conducted in June 2025, from 20 programs recruited to be intentionally diverse. The survey underwent content and response-process validity assessment and pilot testing before distribution. Residents rated their confidence in 17 essential EM procedures using a 5-point Likert-based scale; program contacts provided program-level characteristics through a separate questionnaire. Survey data was analyzed to determine procedure-specific confidence levels and examine associations between overall procedural confidence and select program characteristics. Additionally, hierarchical clustering was used to identify patterns of confidence across procedures.Results A total of 103 residents (41%) from 20 programs completed the survey. Confidence was highest for intubation (100%) and central line placement (98.1%), and lowest for pericardiocentesis (33.0%). Program-level variables, including program length and emergency department volume, were not significantly associated with confidence. Hierarchical clustering identified three broad domains of procedural confidence: critical invasive procedures, core procedural skills, and resuscitation procedures.Conclusion Graduating residents reported near universal confidence in performance of select skills, but meaningful confidence gaps remained for rare procedures and some core procedures. Procedural confidence clustered into clinically recognizable domains, while examined program characteristics were not consistently associated with confidence. These findings identify potential targets for curricular and assessment efforts while reinforcing that self-reported confidence should complement, rather than replace, objective measures of procedural competence.

TI Leading Australian early childhood education and care through crises and
   complexity
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Early childhood education and care; Complexity leadership theory;
   Leadership; Crises; Complexity; Leading
ID LEADERSHIP
AB This qualitative study investigated how leadership in early childhood education and care (ECEC) is enacted during times of crisis and complexity including the COVID-19 pandemic, climate disasters, and community tragedies. Sixteen Australian ECEC leaders participated in the study that comprised twelve Dialogic Caf & eacute; sessions over six months. The participant-driven inquiry foregrounded their experience of leading through crises. Using complexity leadership theory as an analytical lens, the study revealed adaptive, enabling, and administrative leadership practices that foster resilience, innovation, and community care. Although this study has an Australian context, findings and implications hold relevance internationally where escalating climate and political crises imply growing complexity for ECEC leaders. This study is foundational for future research into complexity leadership, emotional labour, and crisis-responsive policy in ECEC.

TI "My ticket is punched": exploring the retention of rural principals in
   New South Wales, Australia, through the push-pull-mooring turnover
   framework
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Leadership; Principal turnover; Retention; Rural education
ID SCHOOLS
AB A growing body of literature focuses on the attrition of principals in Australia as a result of stress related to increased workloads and work intensification. Rural schools face a looming shortage of leaders and the associated high-turnover of principals in the rural context highlights the challenges associated with ensuring educational equity between urban and rural schools in Australia. This paper examines the turnover perspectives of ten rural principals in the state of New South Wales through the push-pull-mooring framework. Interview data revealed that the push factors encouraging the principals to leave their schools were an increase in compliance-based work whilst leading complex rural communities. Pull factors for the principals were retirement and seeking change through the incentive transfer system. Mooring factors encouraging retention were an anchoring to rural communities and professional networks. To inform future policy, more insights need to be generated related to the attrition of rural principals across the state, differentiating between a total exit, transfer within the system, and natural attrition through retirement.

TI Informed Trust, Epistemic Dependence, Elitism, and the Challenge of
   Misinformation: A Response to Potvin et al. (2025)
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Informed trust; Epistemic dependence; Expertise; Elitism; Misinformation
ID SCIENCE; EXPERTISE
AB In this commentary, we respond to Potvin et al. (), explaining the flaws we find in their critique of our vision of twenty-first -century science education (Osborne & Allchin, ). Principally, our response argues that they have not considered fully the social nature of knowledge, our dependence on specialized experts, or how we cope with knowledge claims that lie beyond our ability to detect all possible sources of error. We argue that reliance on the expertise of others does not foster elitism; rather, it should engender respect for others who know more than we do. This does not imply deference but rather indicates a need to educate students in science media literacy and for them to learn precisely when and why such trust is justified, or well informed.

TI From classroom to apprenticeship: vocational teachers' pedagogical
   approaches to apprenticeship preparation in three vocational fields in
   Norway
SO EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE School-to-work transition; Apprenticeship preparation; Vocational
   teachers; Workplace expectations; Domain-general competencies
ID SCHOOL; WORK; PERCEPTIONS; BOUNDARY; INSIGHTS
AB Transitions from school to apprenticeship represent a critical stage in vocational education and training (VET), yet little is known about how vocational teachers prepare students for this shift. Drawing on focus groups and individual interviews with 37 teachers across three vocational programmes in Norwegian upper secondary VET, this study examines pedagogical approaches to apprenticeship preparation and how they are shaped by expectations of working life, vocational field characteristics and school context. We identified four recurrent approaches: classroom simulations of workplace settings, experience-based storytelling, mock interviews and biographical self-work, and facilitated reflection and discussion. Across programmes, teachers foregrounded domain-general competencies, such as punctuality, reliability, communication and cooperation, while embedding these in field-specific tasks and interactions. In Norway's 2 + 2 model, this emphasis may appear counterintuitive, given that two years of school-based VET precede apprenticeship. The findings show how employer expectations are translated into situated teaching practices and underscore both the importance of school-based preparation and the need to scrutinise the prominence of behavioural regulation.

TI Making Innovation Learning Accountable: Intellectual Property Governance
   and Integrity-Oriented Judgement in University-Industry Collaboration
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; innovation education; institutional accountability;
   integrity learning; intellectual property governance; openness and
   protection; university-industry collaboration
ID STUDENTS
AB University-industry collaboration has become a central way through which higher education seeks to make innovation learning authentic, applied and professionally relevant. Yet the very authenticity of such collaboration changes the institutional condition of learning. When students participate in externally connected projects, incubators, sponsored work, entrepreneurial programmes or technology-transfer environments, their learning becomes entangled with ownership claims, disclosure rules, university resources, external interests and commercial possibilities. This article theorises university-industry collaboration as an integrity-sensitive educational condition. It argues that intellectual property should not be treated merely as legal literacy or entrepreneurial competence, but as a form of governance through which the accountability conditions of innovation learning are made visible, teachable and contestable. The article develops the concept of integrity-oriented innovation judgement to describe the capacity students need when knowledge becomes simultaneously educational, collaborative, institutional and potentially commercial. This judgement consists of three interrelated dimensions: boundary judgement, accountability judgement and integrity judgement. The article contributes to higher education research by reframing innovation education as a problem not only of capability formation, but of accountable participation in the governed production of knowledge.

TI From Content Knowledge to Informal Reasoning: The Mediation of Modeling
   Competence in Socio-scientific Issues
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Content knowledge; Informal reasoning; Modeling competence; Path
   analysis; Socio-scientific issues
ID SOCIOSCIENTIFIC ISSUES; ARGUMENTATION SKILLS; STUDENTS DEVELOPMENT;
   SCIENCE; LABORATORIES; LITERACY; TEACHERS; ENERGY
AB Contemporary science education emphasizes the role of content knowledge (CK) in students' informal reasoning (IR) within socio-scientific issues (SSI). However, students may not automatically apply scientific knowledge when reasoning about complex and open-ended SSI. Drawing on literature on modeling competence (MC), this study examined whether MC, operationalized through students' modeling practices, statistically mediated the association between foundational scientific CK and science-based IR in a climate-related SSI task. 443 tenth-grade students participated in an online inquiry activity on climate change and methane emissions. Data were collected through a standardized CK assessment, a stock-and-flow MC task, and a written policy decision-making IR task. Results showed that students performed relatively well on foundational scientific CK and basic modeling practices involving source-sink identification and net-flow calculation, but showed weaker performance in model prediction and science-based IR. Path analysis indicated significant positive associations among CK, MC, and IR. The indirect association from CK to IR through MC was statistically significant and accounted for approximately 45.8% of the total CK-IR association. These findings suggest that students' MC-related modeling practices may represent a meaningful statistical pathway linking foundational scientific CK and science-based IR. The study highlights the potential value of integrating content instruction with modeling practices in SSI learning and supporting IR that more explicitly incorporates scientific evidence and causal explanation.
