TI Primary Mathematics Preservice Teachers' Reflections on Lesson
   Study-Inspired Collaborative Planning: A Didactical Suitability
   Perspective
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Didactical Suitability Framework; Lesson planning; Lesson study;
   Reflection
ID FRAMEWORK; CRITERIA
AB This study investigated primary preservice teachers' (PSTs) reflections on participating in a collaborative planning model inspired by lesson study (LS). The planning model includes collaboratively brainstorming lesson ideas, planning a lesson, discussing a classroom video on the planned content, receiving feedback, revising the lesson, and writing a reflection. PSTs submitted a reflection related to planning, and the data were collected for this study. Thirty-six reflection entries were input into Excel for analysis. PSTs made different decisions regarding their revisions, from keeping them as is to adding new components with justifications based on their interpretations of learning theories and principles. Discussions about how collaborative planning that maintains LS's essential features and uses DSC can support PSTs in reflecting on salient teaching and learning features are included.

TI Identifying (Mis)conceptions About Genetic Information: Perspectives of
   Current and Future Teachers and Psychologists
SO MIND BRAIN AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE determinism; education; genetic attitudes; genetic literacy;
   heritability
ID FREE WILL; KNOWLEDGE; HERITABILITY; EDUCATION; LITERACY; ATTITUDES;
   METAANALYSIS; BELIEFS
AB Rapid advances in genomics may soon enable low-cost predictions of children's academic potential. To ensure this knowledge is used responsibly in educational settings, stakeholders require sound genetic literacy. This study assessed genetic knowledge, perceived heritability, and genetic attitudes in preservice teachers (n = 236; 83% female), practicing educators (n = 247; 93% female), and psychology students (n = 225; 87% female). Higher genetic knowledge was associated with greater openness to genetic applications for medical treatment and research, but not with personalized education or trait enhancement.

TI Prior knowledge of normal ECGs enhances accuracy in ECG interpretation
   among medical students
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ECG interpretation; eye-tracking; medical education
ID EYE TRACKING
AB Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are frequently misdiagnosed, with potentially serious consequences, yet evidence for effective teaching strategies remains limited. Eye-tracking offers insight into the perceptual processes behind accurate interpretation. We conducted an eye-tracking study among medical students to assess whether priming with normal ECGs improves diagnostic accuracy. We hypothesized that participants viewing normal ECGs before interpreting unknown ECGs would perform more accurately. This between-subjects priming study presented students with one of three image types before an ECG task: normal ECGs with instruction that they were normal, normal ECGs without instruction, or chest X-rays (control). The diagnostic task comprised 30 ECGs across six conditions. The study was built with Experiment Builder, and eye movements were recorded with an EyeLink 1000 Plus system. Students performed well above chance, with accuracy comparable to the 54% reported in meta-analysis. Atrial fibrillation was most often identified correctly, whereas left bundle branch block was the most challenging. Across groups, faster responses and finally fixating the primary abnormality (PA) predicted accuracy, although inaccurate participants spent longer overall on the PA area of interest. Students who were informed that the priming ECGs were normal responded faster and more accurately than those primed unknowingly or with chest radiographs. ECG-primed groups also showed longer fixations in nonrelevant areas, whereas explicitly primed students showed no significant related secondary abnormality fixation sequences and more dispersed spatial attention. These early findings suggest that targeted priming with normal ECGs may support learning. Variation in diagnostic difficulty across conditions indicates that tailored training approaches may be required.

TI A storytelling approach to type 1 diabetes mellitus community health
   education to promote early recognition in underserved populations
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE chronic disease education; community health engagement; health literacy;
   storytelling; underserved populations
AB The incidence of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) has increased worldwide over recent decades. Early disease recognition reduces the occurrence of complications. This study aimed to determine if a community health education intervention utilizing a storytelling teaching method could increase knowledge and awareness regarding T1DM among underserved communities to promote early recognition. Six pharmacy students delivered educational sessions at various venues using standardized materials, including pamphlets, poster boards, and a narrative case titled "Recognizing the Signs: Bella's Story." The story illustrated the progression of unrecognized T1DM leading to complications, and discussions about common symptoms, risk factors, and management. Pre-and postsurveys assessed knowledge and perceived awareness and confidence. A paired t test was used to determine statistical differences. A total of 124 individuals attended the sessions, with 100 completing both surveys. Mean knowledge scores were 54.41% +/- 24.19 vs. 87.47% +/- 16.32, pre-vs. postsurvey, respectively, with improvements observed across all knowledge-based questions. Participants demonstrated substantial gains in self-reported awareness of symptoms and confidence in recognizing warning signs. Approximately 90% of participants indicated that the storytelling method was effective, and 87% reported learning new information. These findings suggest that storytelling-based community education is an effective strategy to enhance knowledge and awareness of T1DM and may support earlier recognition and prevention of severe complications in underserved populations.

TI Trainee Autonomy in Emergency Hernia Repair: Educational and Clinical
   Outcomes From a Propensity Score-Matched Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emergency surgery; trainee autonomy; competency-based training; hernia
   repair
ID RESIDENT PARTICIPATION; SURGERY; IMPACT; COMPLICATIONS
AB BACKGROUND: The role of graduated autonomy in surgical training remains a central challenge in competency-based education, particularly in emergency settings where supervision may be indirect. This study evaluates whether senior trainees can safely perform emergency abdominal wall hernia repairs within a structured autonomy framework. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included adult patients undergoing emergency abdominal wall hernia repair (2010-2024). Cases were classified as trainee-led or attending-led. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using preoperative clinical variables. The primary outcome was 90-day postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo classification). Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of complications. RESULTS: A total of 592 patients were included, of whom 426 remained after propensity score matching (213 per group). Baseline characteristics were generally well balanced between groups. Overall 90-day complication rates were similar between trainee-led and attending-led surgeries (33.8% vs. 38.0%, p = 0.420). Major complications (Clavien-Dindo >_ III) were more frequent in the attending-led group (12.2% vs. 5.6%, p = 0.027). Attending-led cases were also associated with higher intensive care unit admission rates and longer hospital stays. No significant differences were observed in mortality, readmission, or recurrence rates. On multivariable analysis, trainee-led surgery was not independently associated with postoperative complications (odds ratio 1.06, 95% confidence interval 0.68-1.66, p = 0.801). Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index and longer operative duration were independently associated with increased complication risk, while mesh use was protective. CONCLUSIONS: Within a structured training environment, senior trainees performing emergency hernia repairs achieved outcomes comparable to attending surgeons. These findings support competency-based progression and the safe implementation of graduated autonomy in emergency surgical education. ( J Surg Ed 83:104177. TI Preference Signaling and Interview Invitations in the First 15-Signal
   General Surgery Cycle: A National Analysis of Program-Level Variation
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE preference signaling; general surgery application; interview invitation;
   15 signal era
AB BACKGROUND: Designed to align applicant intent with program selection, residency signaling has been studied mostly through individual program outcomes. This study shifts focus to the national level, analyzing how signaling influences interview invitations after adjusting for program characteristics. METHODS: We queried all Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education-accredited general surgery programs from the Residency Explorer database. The 2024 to 2025 application cycle was analyzed, representing the first year that applicants received 15 signals. To evaluate the impact of signaling on interview invitations, we performed a single-predictor logistic regression and mixed-effects multivariable logistic regression with a program-level random effect, adjusting for program characteristics. Signaling status was modeled categorically, and program-level covariates included setting, region, cohort size, and accreditation. The signaling rate was defined as the proportion of signaled applications resulting in an interview. RESULTS: Of 363 programs, 252 (69.4%) reported signaling information, encompassing 275,765 applications and 58,851 signals. The overall signaling rate was 21.3% (median 18%, 14.5-24.0). In a single-predictor logistic regression, signaled applications had a 23.7% interview rate compared with 5.0% for nonsignaled applications (odds ratio [OR] 5.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 5.79-6.12, p < 0.001). After adjusting for signaling status, university programs were less likely to offer interview invitations than community programs (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.91-0.98, p = 0.001). Programs in the Pacific (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.38-1.52), Mountain (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.30-1.43), and West North Central (OR 1.41, 95% CI 1.33-1.49) regions had increased odds to offer interviews overall, independent of signaling, whereas larger programs (>6 residents) were less likely to do so (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.82-0.94). In multivariable analysis, signaling remained the strongest predictor of interview offers (OR 6.63, 95% CI 6.44-6.82, p < 0.001), with regional and program-type variation persisting. CONCLUSIONS: Signaling was the strongest predictor of interview offers. The adjusted odds of receiving an interview invitation were 6.6 times higher for signaled than nonsignaled applications, corresponding to observed interview rates of 23.7% and 5.0%, respectively. TI Building AI companions that prioritise learning over performance
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; AI in education; Adaptive learning; Learning companions
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; GENERATIVE AI;
   KNOWLEDGE; ANALYTICS; AUTOTUTOR; FRAMEWORK; MODELS; IMPACT
AB Generative AI, currently most visible in education through large language models (LLMs), is increasingly embedded in students' everyday learning practices, supporting tasks such as writing, coding, reasoning, and analysis. Yet its educational value remains uncertain because systems designed to improve immediate task performance may also weaken the cognitive and metacognitive processes that support durable learning. This paper addresses this learning-performance paradox by asking how AI systems can be designed to support learning rather than merely produce better outputs. To address this, in this paper, we make three contributions. First, we synthesise current LLM-based study support with earlier traditions in artificial intelligence in education to develop a contemporary account of AI learning companions systems that are pedagogically grounded, adaptive, trustworthy, embedded in authentic learning environments, and oriented toward durable learning rather than short-term performance. Second, we propose a design framework for building AI learning companions organised around three interrelated foundations: a pedagogical foundation concerned with how students learn with AI, an adaptive foundation concerned with how AI learns about students, and a responsible design foundation concerned with transparency, accountability, privacy, inclusion, and trust. Third, we apply the framework to five case studies across diverse educational contexts, levels, and tool designs, illustrating both the promise and current limitations of companion-like systems. We posit that the central design challenge is not to make LLMs more helpful or productive, but to make them educationally accountable: capable of strengthening learner agency, supporting metacognitive growth, adapting to learner development, and being evaluated by what students can understand, transfer, and do independently after AI support is withdrawn.

ID SCIENCE; FRAMEWORK; HYPOTHESES; ENGAGEMENT; REVISION
AB This study examines how generative AI can support middle school scientific inquiry in a rural agriculture-STEM classroom. Using a mixed-methods design with concurrent data collection and sequential analytic integration, we analyzed 42 eighth-grade students, organized into 12 groups, as they used Aspen, a custom AI chatbot, to revise scientific research questions and hypotheses around a sustainable agriculture problem. Data sources included group project journals, AI interaction logs, and peer discussion transcripts. First, a two-dimensional profiling method categorized the 12 groups into four analytic profiles: Struggling, Most Improved, Perfectionists, and High Achievers, based on initial artifact quality and criterion-aligned revision. Second, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) modeled the structural patterns of Aspen's pedagogical support across profiles, and directed qualitative content analysis of peer discussions contextualized the ENA findings for low-initial-quality groups. Results indicate that AI-student interaction patterns varied across profiles. The Struggling profile exhibited a fragmented pattern, with ENA showing strong connections between foundational scaffolding and irrelevant/off-task responses, alongside frequent cognitive offloading and collaborative impasse. In contrast, the Most Improved profile showed a more integrated pattern, with strong ENA connections among coaching, modeling, and reflection and frequent model uptake in group discussion. These findings suggest that, in this context, effective AI support may depend not only on providing models but also on facilitating a complete pedagogical cycle that connects guidance, modeling, and metacognitive reflection.

TI Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning theory; Human-AI interaction; Agentic AI; Generative AI; Agency
ID AI
AB Learning theories have historically changed when the conditions of learning evolved. Generative and agentic AI create a new condition by allowing learners to delegate explanation, writing, problem solving, and other cognitive work to systems that can generate, recommend, and sometimes act on the learner's behalf. This creates a fundamental challenge for learning theory: successful performance can no longer be assumed to indicate learning. Learners may complete tasks effectively with AI support while developing less understanding, weaker judgment, and limited transferable capability. We argue that this problem is not fully captured by existing learning theories. Behaviourism, cognitivism, constructivism, and connectivism remain important, but they do not directly explain when AI-assisted performance becomes durable human capability. We propose Agentivism, a learning theory for human-AI interaction. Agentivism defines learning as durable growth in human capability through selective delegation to AI, epistemic monitoring and verification of AI contributions, reconstructive internalization of AI-assisted outputs, and transfer under reduced support. The importance of Agentivism lies in explaining how learning remains possible when intelligent delegation is easy and human-AI interaction is becoming a persistent and expanding part of human learning. The theory yields six testable propositions and suggests that teachers preserve opportunities for learner judgement while researchers distinguish AI-assisted performance from capability that endures beyond immediate support.

TI Can learning experience in pharmacy school shape a competent leader? A
   cross-sectional study on leadership development, mental wellbeing, and
   Islamic values
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy students; Leadership; Curriculum; Mental health;
   Extracurricular activities; Islamic values in pharmacy; Malaysia
ID STUDENTS
AB Background and purpose: The contemporary healthcare landscape dictates that pharmacists demonstrate comprehensive leadership competencies alongside advanced clinical expertise to navigate complex patient-care environments effectively. While academic curricula and extracurricular engagements are recognized as primary mechanisms for cultivating these professional proficiencies, the psychological impact of assuming such roles-particularly the manifestation of academic burnout and stress-remains critically underexplored within the literature. This study investigates undergraduate pharmacy students' perceptions of how curricular frameworks and extracurricular activities contribute to leadership development, concurrently evaluating the mental wellbeing of student leaders and exploring the mitigating influence of culturally integrated ethical frameworks on psychological resilience. Educational activity and setting: A cross-sectional study was conducted among undergraduate pharmacy students (Years 2 to 4) at the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM). To optimize professional identity formation, pharmacy education programs must balance rigorous leadership training with robust, preemptive wellbeing support mechanisms. Furthermore, the integration of culturally specific paradigms, such as the Islamic concept of moderation (wasatiyyah), offers a valuable pedagogical framework for sustaining student resilience, preventing overcommitment, and navigating the complexities of modern pharmacy practice.

SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Advanced theory of mind development; Traditional education; Inclusive
   education; Primary education
ID INCLUSIVE EDUCATION; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; MIDDLE
   CHILDHOOD; PEER POPULARITY; FIT INDEXES; LONELINESS; METAANALYSIS;
   DEAFNESS; AUTISM
AB The aim of this study was to replicate and extend a previous study on the role of the educational setting in the development of advanced theory of mind (AToM). The previous study had shown that the children's AToM developed significantly faster in inclusive classes rather than the traditional type, which houses only typically developing students. We analysed longitudinal data on 614 typically developing children, who were learning in 24 inclusive (n = 285 children) and 21 traditional (n = 329) primary school classes. Moreover, we demonstrated, at least to some extent, a possible mechanism behind the difference. In inclusive classrooms, teachers' practices are focused mostly on the development of AToM abilities among children with weaker skills, while in traditional education classrooms, teachers tend to work with children whose abilities are stronger.

AB OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to characterize the emotional experiences of surgical residents during the preparation and presentation of morbidity and mortality conferences (MMCs), examining how such experiences influence learning, professional identity formation, and growth. SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION

DT Article
DE health professions education; medical education; mentorship;
   professional identity formation; qualitative research; surgical
   education
ID SURGERY; PROGRAM; TIME
AB OBJECTIVE: To investigate why surgical residents pursue dedicated formal training in medical education and to identify the factors that enable or hinder their ability to complete it. DESIGN: A qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews using the Framework Method. SETTING: Virtual interviews conducted via Zoom within the United States. PARTICIPANTS: General surgery residents and surgical faculty who were currently or recently enrolled in a health professions education graduate program and/or surgical education fellowship undertaken during dedicated, non-clinical time within an Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education-accredited general surgery residency program. RESULTS: Eighteen participants completed interviews. Analysis generated 4 interrelated categories of factors: structural, interpersonal, personal, and symbolic (the SIPS framework), which shaped both why residents pursued education training and how they were able to do so. Female participants, who comprised the majority of the sample, often described pursuing a degree to demonstrate competence relative to male peers. CONCLUSIONS: Residents' ability to pursue medical education training is shaped most by the modifiable factors of program structure, mentorship, and funding. As interest in surgical education grows, programs should develop structured pathways, mentorship, and financial support to broaden access. Strengthening this pipeline may expand the community of well-trained surgical educators who advance surgical education and research. ( J Surg Ed 83:104197. TI Sex moderates the association between self-reported autism and cognitive

AB Background: This study investigated the neurocognitive profile of individuals with self-reported autism within a massive cohort of 50,002 university students and examined the propensity for analytic reasoning and introducing relevant multivariate controls. AB Background: This study investigates the predictors of reading fluency in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) by adopting a multidimensional framework that integrates cognitive, linguistic, and behavioral factors. Methods and procedure: The sample comprised 30 typically developing (TD) children, 35 children with ASD (without intellectual disability), and 36 children with ADHD, matched for age and IQ. TI How to fast-track the early identification of pre-school autistic
   children? By comparing diverse machine learning methods with
   resting-state fNIRS features
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Rs-fNIRS; Machine learning; Feature selection; The change in the
   Binary Entropy
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; TEMPOROPARIETAL JUNCTION; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY;
   DEVELOPMENTAL-CHANGES; IMAGING DURATION; BRAIN; NETWORK; CORTEX;
   SPECTROSCOPY; ATTENTION
AB Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) combined with machine learning (ML) has been increasingly applied to distinguish autism spectrum disorder (ASD) based on resting-state (rs) hemodynamic fluctuations. This study constructed rs-fNIRS datasets comprised of multi-2-minute oxy-hemoglobin (HbO), deoxy-hemoglobin (Hb), and total hemoglobin (HbT) signals (two-or four-times collection for each child) from 50 fNIRS channels. Four evolutionary computation channel selection algorithms (GA, DE, PSO, PBIL) and 12 classifiers (KNN, RC, NB, DT, ET, LSVM, RBF-SVM, RF, ADA, XGB, E-KNN, E-SVM) were firstly employed to test 12 features (mean, std, kurtosis, skewness, BinEn, ApEN, zmean, zstd, zkurtosis, zskewness, zBinEn, zApEN) of the HbO,Hb and HbT. The 3 s time series curve closely aligns with the 2-minute original data, and zBinEn being the optimal discriminative feature. The combination of E-SVM and E-KNN ensemble classifiers with the PBIL algorithm achieved the best performance across HbO, Hb, and HbT data. Validation experiments demonstrated the method's robustness, with an average classification accuracy exceeding 90% and identified key contribution channels (CH1, CH11, CH20, CH24, CH27, CH33, CH42). These findings revealed that rs-fNIRS-ML can serve as an efficient clinical tool for early ASD diagnosis in preschoolers.

TI An opportunity-performance trade-off and institutional strategies: The
   role of secondary school characteristics
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Tracking; Trade-off; Opportunity; Performance; School quality; School
   relative preferences
ID EDUCATION; ACHIEVEMENT; IMPACT; INSPECTIONS; INEQUALITY; TRACKING;
   MOBILITY; GENDER; CHOICE; SES
AB Secondary schools aim to provide students with opportunities to develop their talents and ensure minimum levels of academic performance. These two goals may conflict in practice. This study examines how schools navigate this potential trade-off using data from the Netherlands Cohort Study on Education (NCO). We argue that schools can be ranked on two different analytical dimensions. The first one is quality, the extent to which schools can achieve both goals simultaneously. The second one is relative preference, the extent to which the educational practices in a school favour one goal (opportunity) over the other (performance). Our results suggest that institutional features critically shape how schools balance educational aims. In particular, practices favouring less-strict tracking are associated with quality, that is achieving both aims simultaneously.

TI Understanding what supports self-directed learning in flexible
   educational contexts: A scoping review of interventions and underlying
   mechanisms
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-directed learning; Flexible education; Higher education;
   Educational interventions; Curriculum design; Learner autonomy
ID STUDENTS PERCEPTIONS; OUTCOMES; SKILLS
AB Self-directed learning (SDL) is increasingly emphasized in flexible higher education contexts that require learners to make learning decisions. However, insight into how educational interventions are assumed to support SDL, and through which mechanisms, remains fragmented. This scoping review synthesizes studies reporting SDLsupportive interventions in flexible higher education contexts. Across 29 studies, interventions were identified at curriculum, educator, and student levels. Reported interventions included problem-based learning, programmatic assessment, and authentic learning. Although these interventions were associated with SDL-related outcomes, the mechanisms through which they were assumed to support SDL were often vaguely or implicitly articulated. Reported mechanisms primarily focused on individual-level processes, such as monitoring, feedback seeking and use, and reflective self-appraisal, with limited attention to interpersonal or social-emotional processes. The findings reveal a persistent gap between intervention design and explanatory evidence, highlighting the need for explicit articulation and empirical examination of mechanisms underlying SDL-supportive interventions in flexible learning environments.

TI Enhancing STEM pedagogy through professional development with
   Kazakhstani teacher educators: A qualitative study

AB This study tests Guskey's model of teacher change with STEM teacher educators (TEs) in Kazakhstan's higher education context, addressing the scarcity of systematic TE professional development in non-Western settings. TI Can students identify AI? - A cross-sectional quantitative study about
   AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year
   undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Digital assessment; Large language models; AI; MCQ;
   Key feature question
ID EDUCATION
AB Background Beyond technical feasibility of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated multiple-choice questions (MCQs), their educational value in assessment remains unclear. This study aims to evaluate whether students can distinguish between AI-MCQs and National Licensing Exam (NLE) questions in an exam setting and if they align with the curriculum. Methods In this cross-sectional study 119 year five medical students completed a Family Medicine MCQ tablet-based exam. Participants answered 30 AI-generated and 30 NLE MCQs. AI questions were generated from digital learning materials using ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro. Experts accepted 82% of the questions, with minor edits to retained items and removing those needing major changes. During the exam, students were asked about the question source and whether each item aligned with the course curriculum. Statistical analyses were obtained using Jamovi 2.3.28.0. Results No significant difference in correct attribution of AI or NLE MCQs (t(29.6) = -1.24, p = .225; t(29.6) = 1.18, p = .246) was observed. No significant correlation was found between item difficulty and recognition (tau_b: p = .534). Distractor distributions did not differ across ChatGPT, Google Gemini and NLE (chi(2)(2) = 2.61, p = .271, U p > .05 for all comparisons). Item difficulty did not differ significantly between AI and NLE items; however, exploratory source-specific analysis showed an overall difference among ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and NLE items (chi & sup2;(2) = 6.71, p = .035), with a difference between Google Gemini and NLE items (p = .028). Student-perceived curricular alignment did not differ significantly between AI and NLE or among ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and NLE. Conclusions Students' recognition did not differ between AI-generated MCQs and NLE MCQs. Easier MCQs are generally perceived as more aligned with the curriculum. AI-MCQs may provide a feasible approach to item drafting within a structured human-review process.

TI Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE School belonging; Cross-cultural comparisons; Culturally responsive lens
ID STUDENT MOTIVATION; PERSONAL INVESTMENT; SELF; ACHIEVEMENT; VALUES;
   SENSE; BELIEFS; SUCCESS; CONTEXT
AB School belonging has become a central focus in educational psychology. The present topical collection, curated by Christopher S. Rozek and Carlton J. Fong, advances this scholarly conversation by bringing together contributions that broaden conceptualizations of school belonging, foreground the role of broader social contexts, and encourage more intersectional approaches to understanding students' experiences. However, despite these advancements, the sample of school belonging literature remains geographically concentrated, with much of the evidence base derived from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) contexts. This commentary argues that culture should be moved from the margins to the center of research on school belonging. It first highlights the dominance of WEIRD perspectives that continue to shape the questions researchers ask, the samples they study, and the conclusions they most often draw. This commentary argues for a more context-sensitive and globally inclusive science that takes both cross-cultural similarities and differences seriously. It further clarifies that a cultural perspective should not displace race, gender, social class, or other identity-based factors, but rather deepen our intersectional understanding of how belonging is experienced within and across cultural contexts. The commentary concludes by outlining recommendations for more culturally responsive school belonging research, including broader cross-cultural sampling, stronger methodologies, explicit multilevel theorizing, and greater use of qualitative and mixed methods. School belonging is a critical issue for students worldwide, and we hope that research can also incorporate voices from around the globe.

AB Higher education students, particularly at community colleges, often perceive core mathematics courses such as College Algebra, Precalculus, and Statistics as disconnected from their academic and career goals, contributing to low motivation and engagement. This systematic literature review investigates the integration of technology in mathematics education as a potential solution, with a focus on programming languages, computational thinking (CT) platforms, and interactive applications. TI Why Safety Planning Matters in School Social Events: Lessons From a
   Special Education Case
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE emergency preparedness; risk ecology; school health; school safety;
   special education
ID DISASTER; DISABILITIES; CHILDREN; LIFE
AB Background Emergencies during school social activities are often overlooked, as these events are typically assumed to be covered by general safety plans.Methods This study examined an emergency during a school-wide social event in a special education school using qualitative interviews. TI Deconstructing the constructs of learning-oriented assessment (LOA) from
   teachers' perspectives: a scale development and validation study
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL teachers; Instrument validation; Learning-oriented assessment; Scale
   development; Teacher perception
ID NOVICE
AB The present study aimed to develop and validate the learning-oriented assessment teacher perception scale (LOATPS) to assess language teachers' perceptions of LOA. Thus, a tentative 53-item scale was piloted with 408 novice and experienced Iranian EFL teachers across a range of institutional contexts. Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis (EFA, CFA), the results of the analyses led to the removal of 13 items, leaving the instrument with 40 items on a five-point Likert scale. Moreover, the results revealed that the construct of LOATPS comprises five components, including "teachers' LOA knowledge", "teachers' LOA beliefs", "teachers' practices of feedback and interaction", "teachers' practices of using a variety of assessments", and "teachers' practices of sharing with others". Furthermore, the psychometric properties were confirmed, with composite reliability (CR) values ranging from 0.76 to 0.92, average variance extracted (AVE) reaching acceptable values (around 40 to 50% explained by components), and maximum shared variance (MSV) and the Fornell-Larcker criterion acknowledging discriminant validity. The LOATPS serves as a practical tool for teacher educators to design effective teacher education programs, and for EFL teachers and assessment scholars by raising their awareness of implementing LOA and its underlying components across diverse instructional settings.

   to Reinforcement Learning

LA English
DT Article
DE AI-enhanced simulation; engineering education; hardware-in-the-loop;
   intelligent trajectory planning; neural network kinematics; robotics
AB Undergraduate robotics education faces a widening gap between classical kinematic/dynamic theory and contemporary AI-driven industrial practice. While simulation tools bridge theory and practice, most lack native support for data-driven algorithm development. This paper presents an AI-enhanced virtual-real integrated simulation platform built on MATLAB/Simulink and deployed via VxWorks real-time hardware-in-the-loop. TI Learning in GenAI-Mediated Education: A Hybrid SEM-PNA Approach to
   English Majors' Smart Service Interactional Experience and Anxiety
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE anxiety; English majors; GenAI; pedagogical intervention; smart service
   interactional experience
ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL learning, yet its extensive use has also produced distinctive anxieties. Few studies have examined how such anxiety emerges from the holistic interaction between learners and intelligent systems and fewer still have drawn pedagogical implications. Guided by Hassenzahl's Model of Pragmatic and Hedonic Quality of User Experience, we investigated how eight smart service interactional experience (SSIE) dimensions related to GenAI-mediated EFL anxiety among 478 English majors across three Chinese universities. Using SEM (AMOS 24) and psychological network analysis (PNA, R 4.5.3), it was found that Ease to Use and Flow significantly and negatively predicted anxiety, whereas Efficiency and Newness unexpectedly exerted positive effects. In the network, only Flow maintained a stable negative association with anxiety and emerged as the primary bridging node linking SSIE dimensions to anxiety, while Ease to Use functioned as the global hub of the overall SSIE network. These findings suggest that the anxiety-inducing effects of Efficiency and Newness may operate via disrupting Flow. Pedagogically, cultivating English majors' deep engagement in GenAI-assisted tasks is more critical for anxiety reduction than optimizing efficiency or novelty, with instructional design favouring uninterrupted, learner-paced interaction and metacognitive training to decouple self-evaluation from system output.

TI Peer relationships and intraindividual change in school attitudes during
   adolescence: A longitudinal investigation of trust, communication, and
   alienation
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School climate; Peer relationship; Adolescence; Longitudinal; True
   intraindividual change
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; ACHIEVEMENT; RESILIENCE; ATTACHMENT; QUALITY;
   SUPPORT; STRESS; AGE
AB School attitudes are dynamic during adolescence and are significantly influenced by peer relationships. While research has established the importance of peer support for school engagement, the specific mechanisms through which trust, communication, and alienation shape intraindividual changes in school attitudes remain understudied. This study examined how specific dimensions of peer relationships (trust, communication, and alienation) predict intraindividual changes in students' attitudes toward school during adolescence, moving beyond group-level comparisons to focus on within-person developmental processes. Participants comprised 120 German students aged 10-16 years (M = 12.60, SD = 1.35) from lower secondary schools, with balanced gender distribution (50% female). A longitudinal design with two measurement points six months apart was employed. True Intraindividual Change (TIC) modeling was used to examine baseline levels and change in school attitudes. Peer relationships were assessed using the Inventory of Parent and Peer Attachment (IPPA), and school attitudes using the Bielefeld Longitudinal Study questionnaire. School attitudes demonstrated substantial temporal stability. Communication and trust significantly predicted higher baseline school attitudes. Unexpectedly, alienation positively predicted attitude change, while age negatively predicted change in the alienation model. Peer relationships significantly influence both baseline school attitudes and their development over time. The counterintuitive finding that alienation predicted positive attitude change suggests potential resilience mechanisms, highlighting the complex dynamics of adolescent peer relationships and school engagement.

AB Background People with intellectual disabilities face persistent health inequalities and limited access to health promotion services. TI "The best of both worlds": exploring a hybrid coworking and early
   learning environment
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Childcare; Coworking space; Early childhood education; Hybrid design;
   Portraiture; Third space
ID WORK
AB This study examines the Work & Fun Hub, a hybrid coworking and early childhood environment designed to support adult productivity and children's development. Drawing on 12 months of ethnographic fieldwork and 175 hours of participant observation, the study investigates how caregivers, children, and staff experience and negotiate the physical, psychosocial, and pedagogical conditions of this out-of-school setting. The study shows that hybrid learning environments are shaped not simply by locating work and play in the same facility, but by how boundaries, visibility, movement, authority, and sensory conditions are designed and negotiated. The findings provide transferable analytical parameters for intergenerational environments integrating care, learning, and productivity.

TI Initial evidence that intellectual humility contributes to metamemory
   for sources of conflicting claims on the Internet
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Intellectual humility; Judgment of learning; Metamemory; Multiple
   sources
ID COMPREHENSION; OPENNESS; WISDOM; VIEWS; MODEL
AB Given the abundance and diversity of information available online, individuals must monitor and control operations on their memories about the various information sources they encounter. The current study examined whether Intellectual Humility (IH) plays a role in these processes. IH's multiple dimensions reflect an individual's willingness to accept that memory can be limited and fallible; respect for others' perspectives; openness to revising one's understandings, and less perceptions of threats to one's ego when facing new, possibly conflicting perspectives (Krumrei-Mancuso & Rouse, 2016). One-hundred and seventy-six undergraduates made item-by-item judgments during reading reflecting the extent to which they would remember source information (authors' occupations, publication venues) associated with a series of claims from different perspectives. Ratings were then related to performance on a memory test for the same information sources, which was completed after reading. Students also self-reported how much they endorsed IH. After controlling for prior topic attitudes and interest, the results indicated greater IH predicted more accurate source memory performance, better absolute and relative monitoring accuracy, and less problematic overconfidence in memories for online information sources. Future examinations of IH-related affordances for Internet reading are discussed.

TI Testing the dependency of metacognitive monitoring and executive
   functions in children: A cross-sectional and longitudinal study
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacognition; Executive functions; Inhibition; Working memory;
   Cross-sectional; Longitudinal
ID WORKING-MEMORY; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; PERFORMANCE; JUDGMENTS;
   COGNITION; ACCURACY; VALIDITY; BEHAVIOR; TASKS; TIME
AB Accurate metacognitive monitoring is crucial for effective regulation of learning and performance, yet little is known about its cognitive determinants in childhood. The present study investigated the role of executive functions - specifically inhibition and updating of working memory - in children's metacognitive monitoring accuracy. While prior research has established correlational links between executive functions and metacognitive skills, the current experimental study aimed to provide insight into the causal nature of these relationships by systematically manipulating executive function demands within a task and examining the impact on local monitoring judgment accuracy. Sixty children from two age groups (7 and 9 years) participated, providing cross-sectional data; children in the younger cohort were reassessed approximately 17 months later, contributing longitudinal data. Data were analysed using linear mixed effect models and the results indicated that executive functions and metacognitive monitoring have a dependent relationship in childhood. Moreover, this dependency strengthened with age for inhibition and with repeated task exposure for both inhibition and working memory. These findings are consistent with a competition for resources account of the association between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring, suggesting that when cognitive resources are occupied resolving cognitive conflict or maintaining items in memory, fewer resources remain for monitoring processes and monitoring accuracy suffers. Results are also interpreted within the cue-utilization view of metacognitive monitoring, suggesting developmental changes in the cues children rely on when forming monitoring judgments and a differential dependency of these cues on executive functions.

   Online Eye-Tracking Study

AB While presenting perceptual cues (e.g., spatial proximity or color) in arithmetic expressions can affect participants' problem-solving performance, the attentional mechanism underpinning these perceptual cues remains unclear. TI Predictors of Successful Integrated Vascular Surgery Residency Match: A
   Texas Star Database Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE residency; match; integrated vascular surgery; predictors of matching;
   interviews
AB OBJECTIVE: This study aims to determine factors predictive of successful matching into vascular surgery residency. This has been studied in other fields, but there is a paucity of data specific to vascular surgery. This information can be helpful in guiding medical students interested in applying for this competitive field. METHODS: The Texas Seeking Transparency in Application to Residency database was used to analyze self-reported demographics, match results, and application variables from 2017 to 2025. Multiple characteristics of matched applicants were compared to unmatched applicants. Categorical variables were analyzed using the chisquare test, while continuous variables were assessed with nonparametric tests. Univariate and multivariate logistic regressions were performed to identify predictors of successful matches. RESULTS: A total of 170 applicants responded to the survey, 138 (81%) of whom matched. Those who matched had higher numbers of programs applied to (55 vs 46, p = 0.031), interviews offered (29 vs 20, p = 0.004), interviews attended (21 vs 13, p < 0.001), received an MD vs DO degree (82.5% vs 25%, p = 0.024), and had a vascular rotation at their home institution (85.0% vs 28.6%, p = 0.006). The number of interviews attended was the only significant predictor of matching (OR = 1.96, p = 0.021), with each additional interview attended increasing the odds of matching by 9%. The number of abstracts, posters, and presentations is independently associated with a higher number of interview offers (b = 0.86, p = 0.01), with each additional abstract, publication, or poster associated with an average increase of 0.86 interview invitations. CONCLUSIONS: This study reinforces the idea that going on more interviews increases the chances of matching. Applicants with a higher number of abstracts, posters, or presentations received more interview invites. Geographic signaling, USMLE exam scores, clerkships with honors, and honorary membership in societies were not associated with a higher chance of matching. (J Surg Ed 83:104175. TI Camouflaging and self-esteem in neurodivergent women: A cross-sectional
   comparison across autism, ADHD, and dual diagnosis
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; ADHD; Camouflaging; Masking; Self-esteem;
   Women; Dual diagnosis; CAT-Q; Assimilation
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; DISORDER
AB Background: Camouflaging of neurodivergent traits is increasingly recognized as a strategy used by women with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet comparative evidence across diagnostic groups remains limited. Objectives: This study examined camouflaging levels and self-esteem in adult women with ASD, ADHD, dual diagnosis (ASD+ADHD), and those undergoing diagnostic assessment. We also explored associations between camouflaging subscales and self-esteem and examined the role of sociodemographic factors. Methods: A total of 155 adult women (M = 33.9 years, SD = 9.15) completed an online survey including the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale and a Polish-language translation of the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q). Participants were recruited via social media support communities in Poland. Groups comprised women with self-reported diagnoses of ASD (n = 39), ADHD (n = 42), dual diagnosis (n = 45), and those in the diagnostic process (n = 29). Results: Women with ASD and dual diagnosis reported significantly higher overall camouflaging, compensation, and assimilation scores than women with ADHD. No significant differences emerged between diagnosed women and those undergoing assessment. Self-esteem was negatively associated with overall camouflaging (r = - .29, p < .001) and most strongly with assimilation (r = - .45, p < .001); compensation showed no significant association. Descriptively, the strongest associations were observed in the dual diagnosis group. In exploratory analyses, older age and motherhood were associated with lower camouflaging; the association with motherhood remained significant after adjustment for age, although this finding should be interpreted with caution. The Polish CAT-Q demonstrated good internal consistency in this sample (alpha =.72-.90); full psychometric validation remains to be completed. Conclusions: Assimilation strategies showed the strongest negative association with self-esteem in neurodivergent women. In descriptive terms, women with dual diagnosis reported the highest levels of camouflaging, although they did not differ significantly from women with ASD alone. Diagnosed women did not differ from women undergoing diagnostic assessment in camouflaging or self-esteem, suggesting that diagnostic status alone was not associated with these outcomes; post-diagnostic support focused on reducing camouflaging pressure and building self-acceptance may therefore be warranted.

TI Developmental trends in subject length and complexity in Japanese
   learners' English writing
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Japanese English learners; Longitudinal study; Sentence subject; Noun
   phrase complexity; English writing
ID NOUN PHRASE COMPLEXITY; SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY
AB This study investigates developmental changes in grammatical subjects in the English writing of Japanese learners, focusing on subject position as an index of syntactic growth. Previous L2 assessment research has emphasized clausal subordination and global complexity indices; noun phrase complexity has attracted growing attention, but the subject position itself has rarely been isolated as a unit of analysis. Drawing on a longitudinal corpus of 26,399 texts written by 1086 Japanese high school students over three years, subjects were automatically extracted and annotated using SubjEx, a dependency-parsing system developed for this purpose (accuracy: 93.5%). Mean subject length increased steadily across grades and CEFR proficiency bands, with clearer differentiation from B1 onward; a mixed-effects model with a random slope further indicates increasing divergence in learners' growth trajectories. Subjects shifted from pronoundominant forms toward more complex noun phrases, with greater use of adjectival modification, compound nouns, and prepositional phrases, while lexical analyses showed a decline in firstperson subjects and a rise in informationally dense nominal patterns. Subject position thus emerges as a sensitive indicator of L2 writing development, reflecting a shift from personal expression toward condensed informational packaging, with implications for complexity research and proficiency assessment.

TI The problem with defining teachers' digital competency for deep
   learning: A rhetorical absurdity
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital competency frameworks; Educational technology use; Generative
   artificial intelligence; Hybrid learning environments
ID BELIEFS; TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE; INTEGRATION; FRAMEWORK
AB This conceptual paper interrogates the mismatch between policy rhetoric and classroom practice concerning teachers' digital competence for deep learning. The notion of rhetorical absurdity is used as a conceptual lens to describe the recurring contradiction between competency frameworks that promise technology-enabled deep learning and the persistent difficulty of translating these frameworks into situated educational practice. In this paper we synthesise literature across learning sciences, educational technology and teacher professional learning, and present contemporary technological constellations of Generative Artificial Intelligence and hybrid learning spaces as illustrations of the complexities with technology integration for deep learning. We argue that many teacher competency lists risk reinforcing a checklist mentality rather than enabling adaptive, epistemic and ethical capacities required for deep learning. We conclude with two rejoinders that explore shifts from static competencies to dynamic capability models with local translation into authentic educational settings. This multiauthored paper represents a joint intellectual effort originating from a working group convened at the UNESCO EDUsummIT 2025 in Dublin, Ireland.

TI How internationalization in pharmacy education is delivered: A scoping
   review of experiences and lessons learned
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; International collaboration; Global pharmacy;
   Internationalization; Globalization
ID STUDENTS; IMPLEMENTATION; OPPORTUNITIES; LEADERSHIP; UNIVERSITY;
   PROGRAMS; IMPACT
AB Background: In pharmacy education, global outreach initiatives take diverse forms, each with distinct advantages and challenges. This scoping review examines the literature on international collaborations among pharmacy institutions, highlighting key outcomes, challenges, and insights for future partnerships. Methods: A systematic search of Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, and Embase was conducted up to March 2024. The study adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist. Data were extracted using structured tables, independently reviewed, and cross-checked in two groups of two researchers. A final review of the table was performed by a designated reviewer, and the extracted data were subsequently structured into broader categories. Results: Seventy-one studies were included, with forty four full-text articles analyzed in detail and the remaining conference abstracts summarized in tables. Eight collaboration types were identified. Thematic analysis yielded nine outcome categories and nine challenge categories. The most frequently reported outcome categories were "teaching-learning activities and curriculum" (65.9%), "personal growth and professional development" (61.4%), and "global health and community engagement" (47.7%). The most frequently reported challenges were "logistical and operational issues" (68.2%) and "cultural and language barriers" (47.7%). Different international collaboration models contributed to various professional, educational, institutional, personal, and healthcare-related outcomes. Implications: This review indicates that more well-supported international learning structures may help pharmacy programs achieve more durable educational benefits. Future studies should explore the long-term impacts of such approaches and identify strategies to overcome barriers to sustaining international partnerships.

TI Live and learn: Student pharmacists' perceptions of a pharmacy resident
   led NAPLEX® prep bootcamp

DT Article
DE NAPLEX; Pass rate; Pharmacy education; License preparation
AB Background: Amid declining NAPLEX (R) pass rates, a resident-led, low-resource preparatory bootcamp was implemented to support fourth-year pharmacy students through flexible, student-centered sessions. TI Development and evaluation of a simple structured rubric for grading
   short answer questions
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Constructed-response questions; Rubric development; Educational
   assessment; Interrater reliability; Pharmacy education; Qualitative
   study
ID RELIABILITY
AB Background Constructed-response questions (CRQs) effectively assess pharmacy students' therapeutic reasoning but are underutilized due to inconsistent and resource-intensive grading. This study describes the development and evaluation of a simple, structured rubric template designed to address these challenges. Methods A 6-level rubric used in a Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum was modified into a 3-to-4-level rubric based on a single-point rubric design. It focused on defining "borderline pass" criteria and incorporated three specific therapeutic reasoning domains (making a decision, analytical skills, and content knowledge). It was implemented across three integrated organ-system courses in the 2023-2024 academic year. Perceptions of graders, item writers, and course directors were evaluated via a survey and focus groups. Interrater reliability between expert (faculty) and non-expert (residents) graders was evaluated using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) across 50 randomly selected student answers for 8 CRQs. Results The survey response rate was 96%. Respondents reported high clarity regarding borderline criteria (95.7%), and over 90% of inexperienced graders found the rubric easy to use. Pre-grading calibration sessions using live student answers were highly valued (>90%). Focus group themes highlighted improved grading efficiency and item writing, alongside challenges in defining borderline criteria for basic science items. The grading consistency between expert and non-expert graders was good (ICC = 0.85; range: 0.82-0.87). Conclusion The simple, structured rubric template was successfully implemented, demonstrating high clarity and good grading consistency between expert and non-expert graders. The rubric may help optimize resource utilization and support the expanded use of CRQs in pharmacy education.

TI Investigating the effect of input modality in L2 integrated writing
   tasks for academic purposes: A writing product and process approach
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 integrated writing; Input modality; Audiovisual input; Video-based
   writing tasks; Writing strategy use
ID WORKING-MEMORY; VIDEO; PERFORMANCE; CONSTRUCT; STUDENTS; FEATURES;
   COMPREHENSION; COMPLEXITY; QUALITY; SCORES
AB This study investigated the effect of input modality on L2 learners' writing performance and process in audio-based (AB-IW) and video-based (VB-IW) integrated writing tasks for academic purposes. Using a counterbalanced within-subjects design, 49 tertiary-level EFL learners completed two integrated writing tasks with different input modalities. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were conducted on their writing products and strategic behaviors. Results showed that L2 learners performed better in the VB-IW task in content coverage, organization, and source use, while no difference was observed in language use. Textual analyses further revealed taskspecific profiles: the VB-IW task elicited greater syntactic complexity, textual fluency, and cohesion, whereas the AB-IW task resulted in higher lexical complexity. Language accuracy did not differ between the two tasks. Notably, the relationship between writing performance and strategy use varied by task: organizing strategies served as the primary predictor of scores in the AB-IW task, whereas all strategy types contributed in a more balanced manner to performance in the VB-IW task. Additionally, most participants preferred the VB-IW task, reporting that the audiovisual input facilitated listening comprehension, improved writing quality, and enhanced task engagement and motivation. These findings help to advance our understanding of the role of input modality in integrated writing and offer important implications for task design and strategy instruction.

TI Cluttering: Discussion of issues relevant to the community
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Cluttering; Lived experience; Stigma and self-stigma; Psychosocial
   impact
AB A roundtable discussion entitled "Cluttering: Discussion of Issues Relevant to the Community," held at the 2025 Oxford Stuttering and Cluttering Research Conference, brought together individuals who clutter, clinicians, and researchers to examine key concerns related to the challenges of living with cluttering. Guided by the Three-Pronged Approach to the conceptualization of cluttering (Myers et al., 2018), which emphasizes the importance of lived experience in diagnosis and intervention, the session provided a collaborative dialogue among all stakeholders. Clutterers identified and explored core questions related to employment impact, perceived and internalized stigma, coping with negative emotional consequences, the development of support systems, avoidance behaviors and associated guilt, the use of speech management strategies, and perceived differences between cluttering and stuttering. Perspectives shared during the discussion, considered alongside emerging literature, informed three position statements relevant to the cluttering community. First, the lived experiences of individuals who clutter should be recognized as valid and essential evidence in research and clinical practice. Second, stigma and self-stigma must be explicitly addressed in assessment, intervention, and research. Third, cluttering presents unique characteristics and psychosocial concerns that distinguish it from stuttering and warrant differential consideration. These perspectives highlight the value of a shared approach that involves clutterers as true partners in research design, clinical services, and public education to ensure that professional efforts reflect the priorities and lived experiences of the community.

TI Maintaining vocational readiness during summer vacation: A two-group
   pilot evaluation of a culturally adapted digital parent-mediated
   programme for autistic adolescents and young adults in Saudi Arabia
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Vocational readiness; Transition to adulthood; Parent-mediated
   intervention; Digital intervention; Summer skill maintenance;
   Neurodiversity-affirming practice
ID NEURODIVERSITY; TRANSITION; FRAMEWORK
AB Background: Summer vacation may reduce opportunities for autistic adolescents and young adults to practice vocational readiness skills when structured educational and transition supports decrease. This two-group pilot programme evaluation examined the feasibility, acceptability, and implementation of the 8-week Summer Advocacy and Vocational Opportunities for Readiness (SAVOR) Programme, a culturally adapted digital parent-mediated intervention in Saudi Arabia, and estimated preliminary between-group differences in parent-reported vocational readiness and transition-related functioning. Methods: Sixty-four parent-participant dyads involving autistic adolescents and young adults aged 15-21 years were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to the immediate intervention (n = 32) or waitlist comparison group (n = 32) using a computer-generated allocation sequence. SAVOR comprised eight asynchronous parent micro-learning modules and structured home-based vocational readiness activities. Feasibility, acceptability, and implementation were assessed using retention, intervention exposure and adherence indicators, the SAVOR Parent Feedback Questionnaire (SPFQ), and qualitative parent feedback. Parents completed the SAVOR Career Readiness Skills Checklist (SCRSC) and Transition Planning Inventory-Arabic Version (TPI-AR) at baseline and post-intervention to provide preliminary between-group estimates. Exploratory direct feedback was additionally obtained from five autistic participants. Results: Fifty-eight of the 64 allocated dyads completed the post-intervention assessment (29 per group; retention = 90.6%). Among intervention completers, 89.7% completed all eight modules, 93.1% completed all weekly implementation checklists, and 82.8% reported an average daily practice duration of at least 15 min. Parent-reported usability, acceptability, feasibility, and confidence were favorable, and the mean likelihood-to-recommend rating was 9.1/10. Preliminary intention-to-treat estimates also favored SAVOR for parent-reported vocational readiness (adjusted mean difference = 6.1, 95% CI [1.2, 11.0]; Cohen's d = 0.58, 95% CI [0.10, 1.06]). Exploratory domain-level estimates were largest for self-management and time-management skills, while the estimate for transition-related functioning was directionally consistent but less precise. Exploratory autistic participant feedback highlighted accomplishment, independence, structured routines, task-initiation challenges, and interest in broader community-based activities. Conclusions: SAVOR demonstrated favorable feasibility, acceptability, and implementation among participating families. Preliminary between-group estimates provide a signal of potential benefit for parent-reported vocational readiness but are not intended to establish programme effectiveness. Further evaluation is warranted in a fully powered, prospectively registered study with longer follow-up, systematic autistic participant-reported outcomes, and multiple outcome sources. The study was not prospectively registered. Following completion of data collection and analysis, the study was retrospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; GUID: qajs8).

TI Beyond academic merit: motivation, sociodemographic, and institutional
   factors on persistence in teacher education in Chile
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher education; Persistence; Dropout; Retention; Motivation
AB This study examines the effects on student persistence of a policy that raised academic admission requirements for initial teacher education (ITE) programs in Chile. Using Hierarchical Generalized Linear Models with a probit link function, data from 44 506 students enrolled between 2017 and 2020 were analyzed, incorporating individual and institutional predictors. The results indicate that motivation, measured through students' preference rank for the ITE program at admission, is a key predictor of persistence, significantly moderates the effect of scores on the national standardized university selection test (PSU), and functions as a protective factor in more selective institutions. These findings challenge the assumption that academic credentials alone are a sufficient mechanism to ensure retention and quality in teacher education. Access to student financial aid and female gender are positively associated with persistence, while internal regional migration and enrollment in a regional institution are associated with a higher risk of dropout.

TI ChatGPT for interdisciplinary learning: Does it equally benefit STEM and
   non-STEM students
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Interdisciplinary learning; ChatGPT; Equity; Engagement; STEM and
   non-STEM; Generative AI
ID ENGAGEMENT; FRAMEWORK; TRENDS
AB While studies on using generative AI for education are increasing, research on whether it benefits STEM and nonSTEM students, who tend to have different technology acceptance and AI literacy, in the interdisciplinary learning context is rare. To respond to this gap, this exploratory quasi-experiment study engaged 130 undergraduate students in interdisciplinary learning for two weeks (some used ChatGPT and some did not). We collected participants' physical, emotional, and cognitive engagement using surveys and quantified their interdisciplinary learning quality based on their written online posts. Results showed that STEM students' physical engagement was higher in the ChatGPT condition, whereas non-STEM students' physical engagement was higher in the non-ChatGPT condition; students from non-STEM disciplines showed greater cognitive engagement than those from STEM fields; and the non-ChatGPT condition students showed higher diversity and integration in their online notes than their counterparts in the ChatGPT condition. Our findings suggest that STEM and non-STEM students did not equally benefit from ChatGPT in terms of physical engagement, cognitive engagement, or the interdisciplinary learning quality manifested in their online notes, indicating students' disciplinary backgrounds need to be considered to optimize the use of ChatGPT.

TI Piloting generative AI in pharmacy education: Student experiences,
   resistance, and redesign
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Writing instruction; Instructional design; Transparency in learning and
   teaching (TILT); Student perceptions; AI literacy
AB Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into pharmacy education, with calls for intentional, ethical instruction to support AI literacy and professional competencies. Educational activity: We piloted a semester-long sequence of seven scaffolded assignments supporting an argumentative synthesis paper in a required first-semester PharmD course, permitting allowed and disclosed AI use across multiple stages of the research and writing process. Evaluation findings: Quantitative data demonstrated consistently high student performance across assignments, with average scores near maximum values, and widespread but variable AI use across tasks. Transparent purpose, intentional sequencing of AI use, and preservation of student autonomy may enhance engagement and perceived learning value. Conclusion: A TILT-informed, student-partnered approach offers a practical framework for integrating AI into pharmacy education while supporting meaningful learning and AI literacy development. Future evaluation will examine student experiences via focus groups and interviews and survey data will examine changes in AI literacy.

TI Bridging distances by delivering rural pharmacy education through a
   virtual elective course
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Rural pharmacy education; Virtual course; Community engaged learning;
   Rural health
AB Introduction: Rural communities across Canada experience healthcare inequities that health professional programs can address, yet rural-specific courses are limited in pharmacy education. This case report describes a virtual rural pharmacy course and examines students' perceptions of rural practice and students' and community partners' (CPs) experiences with the course. Methods: In 2024, the first elective on rural pharmacy practice launched in the Entry-to-Practice PharmD Program at the University of British Columbia. This primarily asynchronous online course included a virtual community-engaged learning (CEL) project where students worked with CPs that served rural communities. Using a qualitative descriptive design, three students and two CPs participated in semi-structured interviews (25% and 67% response rates, respectively). Transcripts were analyzed through inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Students reported shifts in rural practice perceptions after completing the course. The asynchronous, self-paced aspect drove disengagement, while multi-modal delivery involving rural voices fostered engagement. Students' experiences with the virtual CEL were shaped by the project's output, peer collaboration, and level of perceived CP support. CPs discussed needing to intentionally bridge connections between students and rural communities in virtual partnerships. CPs perceived the CEL projects' health resources as contributing to knowledge mobilization for their organizations and the communities they serve. Conclusion: Virtual delivery and CEL can offer meaningful and accessible rural pharmacy education to students, with reciprocal benefits for CPs. Intentional synchronous opportunities could address limitations with student engagement and community connections. These findings offer insights for integrating rural health content into pharmacy education through virtual course and CEL approaches.

TI Teacher agency and generative AI: A cultural-historical analysis of
   contradictions in planning, instruction, and assessment
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI); Cultural-Historical Activity
   Theory (CHAT); Contradiction; Artificial Intelligence in Education
   (AIED); Teacher agency; Natural Language Processing (NLP); Sentiment
   Analysis (SA)
ID PROFESSIONAL AGENCY
AB Scholars have traced diverse contradictions of GenAI's potential to seemingly both help and harm education back to the origins of AI in Education (AIED), thereby broadening the discussion to include a cultural-historical perspective. Generative AI (GenAI) is being analyzed for its impact on student achievement through personalized learning, and concerns about the potential devaluation of educators' skills and expertise. However few studies have examined AIED's impact on teacher agency, particularly through the lens of its perceived exchange value. This pilot study applies a third-generation CHAT framework to explore how GenAI mediates teacher agency and generates contradictions across the activity systems of planning, instruction, and assessment. GenAI is perceived to increase teacher agency in planning, but constrains it during instruction and assessment due to emergent contradictions. A primary contradiction was identified indicating that AI is being perceived as a helpful tool in the delivery of learning while also being perceived as negating the development of teacher agency. A secondary contradiction consisting of a dilemma between efficiency and agency was also found.

ID READING-COMPREHENSION; COGNITIVE LOAD; LANGUAGE; LEARNERS; DIFFICULTIES;

TI Estimating VO2max With the Timed Mile Run: An Updated Equation for
   Today's Youth
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE BMI; representative sample; school-based physical fitness testing;
   VO2max prediction equation
ID FITNESS; EXERCISE; IMPACT; PREDICTION; STANDARDS; CHILDREN
AB Background School-based physical fitness testing (SB-PFT) is an important tool to address youth physical inactivity. However, the widely used Fitnessgram equation that converts timed mile run performance into estimates of cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max) may not be valid for today's diverse US adolescent population. This study evaluated its validity, developed updated prediction equations, and examined the effect of omitting sex and/or BMI.Methods A diverse sample of middle school students (n = 177) provided demographic information and timed mile run data and completed lab-based VO2max testing. Prediction accuracy for the Fitnessgram equation and newly-developed equations was assessed using root mean square error (RMSE), Pearson's correlation, and sensitivity and specificity.Results In this diverse sample, all four new VO2max prediction equations outperformed the Fitnessgram equation, including equations excluding sex and/or BMI.Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity When evaluated on a diverse sample of adolescents, the Fitnessgram misclassifies many adolescents as being in the healthy fitness zone despite having cardiorespiratory fitness levels associated with elevated health risk.Conclusions The Fitnessgram VO2max prediction equation should be updated to reflect contemporary US demographics and schools' concerns about collecting BMI data.

TI Promoting Students' Chemical Literacy and Cultural Awareness Through
   Culturally Responsive Teaching Oriented Toward Green Chemistry in
   Stoichiometry Learning
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Culturally responsive teaching; Green chemistry; Chemical literacy;
   Cultural awareness; Stoichiometry
ID EDUCATION; PERSPECTIVES; SCIENCE
AB This study aims to investigate the effect of culturally responsive teaching (CRT) oriented toward green chemistry on high school students' chemical literacy and cultural awareness. A quasiexperimental design with pretest-post-test was employed, involving 216 tenth-grade students from two senior high schools in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, selected using cluster random sampling. Three experimental classes implemented CRT integrated with local cultural practices, including bersih desa tradition, natural-dye batik production, and traditional herbal medicine (jamu), while three control classes followed the scientific approach aligned with the national curriculum. The intervention consisted of six 90-min sessions covering chemical equations, basic laws of chemistry, and the mole concept. Data were collected using the Stoichiometry Chemical Literacy Test (SCLT) and the Cultural Awareness Scale oriented toward Green Chemistry (CAGC), and analysed using descriptive statistics and MANOVA. The results showed that students in the experimental group achieved higher improvements in chemical literacy and cultural awareness compared to the control group. MANOVA confirmed a significant difference between groups with a large effect size, indicating that CRT oriented toward green chemistry effectively enhances both cognitive and affective learning outcomes. This study highlights the potential of integrating cultural and sustainability contexts in chemistry education to foster meaningful learning experiences.
