TI Orthopaedic surgeons using 3D printed models to prepare for surgery: a
   qualitative investigation
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Surgical planning; Surgical training; Medical 3D printing; Working
   memory; Cognitive load; Theatre
AB Purpose With the recent accessibility of 3D printing (3DP), many orthopaedic surgeons have taken up 3DP for pre-operative planning and rehearsal. The aim was to label and categorize perceived benefits of using 3DP anatomical models in preparation for surgery, and how they regard its future use in training.Methods We employed a qualitative explorative design using a phenomenological approach. In-depth, semi-structured interviews with 10 orthopaedic surgeons based at a training hospital were transcribed and imported into ATLASti for analysis. We used an inductive coding approach performed by three of the authors. Individual coding was compared and adjusted by an iterative process.Results Two main themes emerged: perceived benefits and surgeon attitudes. Four subthemes included: pre-operative benefits, intra-operative benefits, post operative benefits and effect on competence and training. All the surgeons reported that having 3DP models of patient imaging positively influenced surgical preparation. Most described the models as an adjunct to image interpretation. In several cases, participants reported rehearsing a procedure more than once to test out strategies and implants. Intra-operative benefits included increased confidence in the theatre and a sense of 'd & eacute;j & agrave; vu' when operating. Many participants mentioned a perceived increase in surgeon skill and 3DP being a valuable training tool. Several surgeons mentioned a perceived decrease in theatre times and a perceived increase in surgical accuracy. Surgeon attitudes to medical 3DP were most frequently about how the models can be modified for improved pre-operative rehearsal. Most mentioned that they are expecting the technology to develop, and this co-occurred with an intention to proactively engage with the technology. Other ideas that occurred were that planning with 3DP is not essential for all cases, but that it would become essential for some cases.Conclusions Recent publications about the use of 3DP in healthcare have risen dramatically and the use in pre-operative planning is a major theme. However, most studies focus on more objective outcomes like operative time, blood loss, fluoroscopic usage and surgical accuracy. However, blood loss, fluoroscopic usage and hospital stay were not mentioned by participants. A benefit of using 3DP might be that it moves critical decision-making points to the pre-operative phase, decreasing cognitive load experienced in theatre. There was very often an overlap in the discussion of 3DP for surgeon training and for experienced surgeons preparing for something new and complex, which underscored the concept of surgical practice being a continuous embodied process. Future directions for research could investigate how perceived benefits link with existing models of cognitive load and fatigue accumulation in theatre, linking it to more measurable outcomes.

TI Positioning Mathematical Routine Enactments Along the Ritual-Explorative
   Continuum: The Case of Prospective Teachers' Fraction Ordering
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Commognitive framework; De-ritualization; Prospective teachers;
   Mathematics teacher education; Fractions
ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB Learners may solve the same mathematical task correctly using the same solution strategy while engaging in qualitatively different mathematical participation. Such variation is difficult to identify through correctness-based assessments alone, limiting insights into students' mathematical learning. Drawing on Sfard's commognitive framework, this study investigates how three prospective teachers enacted the shared common denominator routine while solving the same fraction-ordering task. Using the ritual-explorative continuum as a cross-sectional analytic framework, we analyzed four discursive characteristics-bondedness, substantiation, objectification, and agency-and reconstructed each participant's construed task from observable discourse. The findings indicate that differences in routine enactment were associated not with procedural performance but with how participants construed the task, connected and justified mathematical actions, and positioned mathematical authority in their discourse. These findings demonstrate the value of the ritual-explorative continuum for cross-sectional analyses of mathematical participation, identify three analytic prototypes of routine enactment, and suggest that routine enactment is multidimensional, with mathematically successful performances differing substantially in their learning potential despite producing the same correct solution.

TI Beyond Enabling Perspectives: How Organizational Conditions Shape
   Intertwined Forms of Professional Agency in Health and Social Care
SO VOCATIONS AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional agency; Organizational conditions; Health and social care;
   Interprofessional collaboration; Reflective work; Changing work
   environment
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; WORKING LIFE; OUTCOMES
AB The need to deepen our understanding of how organizational conditions shape the enactment of professional agency in the context of rapidly changing health and social care organizations is growing. Professional agency is understood in this study as a temporally embedded, relational, and situated process through which professionals shape their work and work-related identities while individually and collectively interacting with the sociocultural conditions of their practice, including in interprofessional collaboration. Specifically, the present study examined how professional agency is enacted in two Finnish settings-adolescent psychiatry and adolescent residential care-using semi-structured interviews with 14 professionals to explore how organizational conditions shape agency in complex care environments. The interview transcripts were abductively analyzed, revealing three interrelated dimensions that influence the enactment of professional agency: managerial and leadership practices (i.e., how leaders act and communicate), structural and professional developmental conditions (i.e., resources and processes, such as training), and organizational climate and interprofessional collaboration (i.e., relational conditions, including trust). These organizational conditions individually and jointly shape the forms that professional agency takes, ranging from proactive and collective to constrained and compensatory. The findings also highlight reflective work, encompassing both reflection and reflexivity, as a cross-cutting process through which professionals navigate tensions and make sense of organizational demands. Importantly, agency was expressed not only through participation and development-oriented action but also through professionals' active negotiation, adaptation, and improvisation in response to organizational constraints. These insights deepen our understanding of professional agency by extending conceptualizations of agency beyond enabling organizational conditions and positive expressions.

TI Scaffolding problem-based learning in postgraduate immunology: a
   pyramidal mind-mapping approach to teaching complex immune mechanisms in
   COVID-19
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19 immunity; immunology education; learning scaffolding; mind
   mapping; problem-based learning
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB Problem-based learning (PBL) is an effective strategy for developing higher-order cognitive skills in biomedical education; however, structured exposure is often introduced late in postgraduate immunology curricula, leaving students insufficiently prepared for complex, independent learning tasks. Teaching immunity to COVID-19 presents additional challenges due to the need to integrate innate, adaptive, and cytokine-mediated immune pathways. The objective of this study was to quantitatively evaluate the effect of a pyramidal PBL intervention using structured mind mapping on academic performance, conceptual organization, and learner engagement among postgraduate immunology students. The intervention group (n = 18) replaced a scheduled didactic lecture with an intergroup pyramidal PBL activity involving domain-specific mind mapping, iterative peer and facilitator feedback, and whole class synthesis, while a comparable control cohort (n = 20) received conventional lecture-based instruction. Knowledge retention was assessed using a delayed summative examination administered 2 wk postintervention, and student perceptions were measured using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire. The intervention group achieved significantly higher examination scores than controls (means +/- SD: 73.5 +/- 4.4 vs. 66.2 +/- 6.5), with a mean difference of 7.3 percentage points [95% confidence interval (CI): 3.8-10.7; P < 0.001] and a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.30). Questionnaire findings demonstrated high acceptability and perceived effectiveness, with most participants reporting improved conceptual understanding, communication skills, and engagement with complex immunological content. These findings indicate that pyramidal mind-mapping-based PBL produces educationally meaningful improvements in learning outcomes and supports earlier scaffolding of problem-based learning within postgraduate immunology curricula.

TI GutMove: a new educational game for active learning and assessment of
   competencies on gastrointestinal motility
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; assessment; gamification; gastrointestinal motility;
   teaching innovation
ID RETRIEVAL PRACTICE; PHYSIOLOGY; STUDENTS; PUZZLE; SYSTEM; TEACH
AB We described our first-ever gastrointestinal (GI) motility game (GutMove), designed to enhance teaching and assessment of knowledge on motility across the GI tract. The game has seven sections: 1 (pregastric regions), 2 (upper stomach), 3 (lower stomach), 4 (small intestine and its transition), 5 (large intestine), 6 (stimulating hormones), and 7 (inhibiting hormones). Sections 1-4 have 8 cells each on the left side, and 12 e-tokens each scattered on the right side, although only 8 e-tokens are correctly matchable to the corresponding left cells, while the remaining 4 e-tokens are distractors to enhance critical thinking. Other sections have varying numbers of left cells and correctly matchable e-tokens versus scattered e-tokens (16 vs. 20 in section 5; 9 vs. 14 in section 6; and 18 vs. 23 in section 7). The game is played by a registered individual by tapping or dragging each e-token from the right repository and dropping it in the appropriate cell of the game board on the left, until completely filled. The game displays the play results after each round and reshuffles the e-tokens for the next rounds. The results can be verified via a dedicated link, and it provides feedback on right and wrong answers after every three wrong trials. Users of this game reported its positive impact on retrieval learning and assessments. This game can be used for improved teaching, assessment, and practical simulation of GI motility by tutors across the globe, irrespective of the structure of the curriculum used in an institution. NEW & NOTEWORTHY There is currently no educational game dedicated to learning and assessment of motility across the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. This study describes our first-ever GI motility game (GutMove), designed to promote the Active Learning of students and serve as an effective tool for assessing students' knowledge on the motility across the GI tract. Users have reported the benefits of this game in learning and assessment on this topic.

TI Classroom implementation of Hill's force-velocity relationship using
   accessible materials in resource-limited educational settings
SO ADVANCES IN PHYSIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biomechanics education; force-velocity relationship; Hill's
   force-velocity model; low-cost teaching; muscle physiology
AB The force-velocity relationship, originally described by Hill (Proc Biol Sci 126: 136-195, 1938), is a foundational concept in muscle physiology and biomechanics. Despite its theoretical relevance, its instructional application remains limited in educational settings without laboratory infrastructure. Here, we present a low-cost strategy for teaching the force-velocity relationship using accessible materials and commonly available software. The procedure was implemented in a regular classroom environment and involved estimating velocity from the number of repetitions performed with different loads over a fixed time interval. Classroom-derived data were used to construct force-velocity and power-velocity curves, with the objective of illustrating expected biomechanical patterns, without evaluating learning outcomes. The activity emphasized biomechanical reasoning and graphical interpretation, incorporating simplified measurement tools as part of the instructional process. The strategy is adaptable to resource-limited contexts and may be extended to other biomechanics topics that require the operationalization of theoretical relationships. NEW & NOTEWORTHY This paper describes a low-cost, classroom-tested instructional strategy for teaching Hill's force-velocity relationship using accessible materials and commonly available software. Classroom-derived data are used to construct force-velocity and power-velocity curves, enabling the operationalization of classical biomechanical concepts without laboratory-grade equipment. The approach is adaptable to resource-limited educational settings and supports hands-on exploration of muscle mechanics.

   Canadian Neurosurgical Attrition

LA English
DT Article
DE attrition; postgraduate medical education (PGME); high workload; poor
   work-life balance; gender-related challenges for women; structural;
   cultural; and individual factors intersect to shape attrition
ID GENDER DISCRIMINATION; SURGICAL RESIDENCY; MEDICAL-EDUCATION;
   SEXUAL-HARASSMENT; PERSPECTIVES; SPECIALTY; WORKFORCE; COHORT
AB OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to determine the current level of attrition from neurosurgical residency programs in Canada and to identify the factors contributing to this phenomenon. DESIGN: The study employed a mixed-methods approach. First, a national cross-sectional descriptive survey collected program-level data from all 14 Canadian neurosurgery residency programs to determine resident attrition rates across Canada between 2013 and 2023. Subsequently, guided by critical constructivist theory, semistructured virtual interviews were conducted and iteratively coded through reflexive interpretivist analysis to construct an analytical framework. SETTING: Fourteen accredited neurosurgical residency programs across Canada, representing a national postgraduate medical education setting. PARTICIPANTS: Attrition data were requested from all 14 Canadian neurosurgery residency programs. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 7 neurosurgery program directors and 7 former neurosurgery residents who had left training between 2013 and 2023, representing 7 Canadian residency programs. RESULTS: Data from 8 of 14 programs revealed an average institutional attrition rate of 14.1% (range, 0%-28.6%). CONCLUSIONS: Attrition from neurosurgical residency is a multifaceted issue shaped by structural, cultural, and individual factors. Applying this holistic perspective enables a systematic approach to formulating interventions. Structurally, efforts should optimize resident workload, protect educational time, and support women and minoritized trainees through mentorship and equitable policies. Culturally, programs should promote role modeling, address gender inequities, and prioritize wellbeing alongside professional demands. Individually, mentorship, career counseling, and transparent communication about training realities can help align expectations and strengthen retention. ( J Surg Ed 83:104184. TI From familiarity to safety-by-design: Teaching Preliminary Hazard
   Analysis through a fried-egg micro-process
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Inherent safety; Process safety education; Pedagogical tool;
   Experiential learning; Risk assessment
ID CHEMICAL-ENGINEERING EDUCATION; FRAMEWORK; FEEDBACK
AB Preliminary Hazard Analysis (PHA) is often introduced to students as a structured table applied to a process that has already been defined. This can hide its educational value: helping engineers shape safer systems before design choices become fixed. This paper presents a short, low-cost preparatory scaffold in which students learn early-stage PHA through an everyday micro-process: cooking a sunny-side-up fried egg. The activity is not intended to reproduce industrial complexity; it prepares students to approach later industrial case studies, accident reports and plant-scale scenarios with a clearer reasoning structure. Students define the system, specify the target product, identify flows, recognise hazards and hidden failure modes, build accident scenarios, and translate safeguards into operating, degraded-mode and emergency instructions. The activity was implemented as a two-hour individual mini-project with 71 eighth-semester food-engineering students; 69 complete retrospective self-assessment responses were collected. Across nine items, self-ratings as Acquired or Mastered increased from 11.6% to 23.2% before the activity to 81.2-87.0% after it. These descriptive data indicate perceived progress rather than objectively verified performance, but they suggest that familiar micro-processes can support early process-safety reasoning.

TI Transformational leadership, innovation, and organizational performance
   in higher education institutions: A systematic review and meta-analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Transformational leadership; Innovation; Organizational performance;
   Higher education institutions; Systematic review; Meta-analysis
AB Background: Transformational leadership (TL) is a critical determinant of organizational success. However, there is a lack of evidence on how TL operates specifically in higher education institutions (HEIs), where innovation and organizational performance are shaped by academic autonomy, shared governance, and stakeholder accountability. This review, therefore, draws on existing evidence to further understand how TL affects innovation and organizational performance in HEIs, and which TL dimensions are most influential, and through which mechanisms these relationships are explained. Methods: A systematic review of 65 peer-reviewed studies published between 2011 and 2024 was conducted using academic databases. Qualitative synthesis and quantitative meta-analytic techniques were employed to investigate the direct and indirect ways in which TL influences innovation and performance outcomes. Results: This systematic review and meta-analysis consolidate that TL has a significant positive effect on both organizational innovation and performance in HEIs. The influence is attributed to the leaders' abilities to provide a supportive organizational environment, fostering employees' motivation, collaboration, participatory decision-making, and risk-taking. Of the TL dimensions, inspirational motivation and individualized consideration emerged as the most influential drivers of organizational performance, while inspirational motivation showed the strongest effect on innovation. Emotional intelligence was identified as a critical enabler of individualized consideration, underscoring the affective foundations of effective TL in academic contexts. Conclusion: This study advances the understanding of how TL operates in HEIs by highlighting specific leadership dimensions, mediators, and contextual moderators as key mechanisms linking TL to innovation and performance. Implications for future empirical and theoretical research, as well as practical initiatives for HEIs, are provided.

TI Caregiver-endorsed intervention strategies for sensory reactivity
   symptoms in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; ASD; Sensory; Sensory processing; Sensory reactivity;
   Sensory-based interventions
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; CHILDREN; ATTENTION
AB Purpose: Sensory reactivity differences are a common feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and related neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Sensory-based interventions (SBIs) are commonly implemented to address sensory needs, yet empirical support remains limited. This study examines the frequency of caregiver-reported SBI use and caregiver-rated helpfulness of SBIs across sensory modalities (visual, auditory, tactile, and multisensory/vestibular) among autistic children and children with other NDDs. We also explore the relationship between perceived helpfulness and child age, sex, and the presence of intellectual disability (ID). Methods: Caregivers (N = 219) completed an online survey about their child's sensory response patterns, specific SBIs, and perceived helpfulness. Results: Caregivers frequently implement SBIs, though most were perceived as only sometimes helpful. Vestibular strategies (e.g., trampoline and swing exercises), tactile input (e.g., massage) and auditory reduction (e.g., noise-cancelling headphones) were most commonly used. Massage and swing exercises were also rated as among the most helpful, while brushing protocols and weighted vests, despite frequent use, had the lowest helpfulness ratings. Age and sex were not significantly related to helpfulness ratings; however, caregivers of children with ID rated brushing protocols as significantly less helpful than caregivers of children without ID. Conclusion: Findings highlight the need for targeted trials to align research with real-world caregiver experiences.

AB This study examined how different dimensions of teacher formative assessment literacy (TFAL) relate to student formative assessment practice in the Chinese Mainland. TI Ethical principles of AI in education: Exploring teachers' contextual
   ethical reasoning through an STS lens
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Ethical principles of AI in education; Socio-technical systems;
   Low-resource context; In-service STEAM teachers; Secondary schools;
   Phenomenology
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
AB The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education (AIED) promises significant pedagogical transformations. However, it also raises concerns that have intensified global discourse on the ethical principles guiding its design and use. Despite this growing discourse, limited empirical evidence exists from the Global South, where little is known about how teachers in low-resource contexts conceptualize AI ethical principles. Addressing this gap, this study investigates in-service secondary school STEAM teachers' conceptual understanding of the Ethical Principles of AI in Education (EPAI-Ed). We propose EPAI-Ed as a collective term for the principles guiding the governance of AIED. Guided by Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, a two-stage qualitative design was adopted. Participants engaged in think-aloud (TA) protocols (n = 30) and follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 10). Data were analysed using sentiment coding and reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that, despite lacking formal training on AI ethics, teachers in this context are not "ethics empty." Instead, they rely on common sense and professional experience-based ethical reasoning shaped by professional identities, classroom realities, cultural norms, and contextual vulnerabilities to conceptualize and practice responsible AIED. This study is one of the first to provide novel insights into teachers' ethical reasoning in low-resource contexts, addressing a critical gap in global AIED discourse. It also used the STS theory as an interpretive lens to explain how ethical reasoning co-emerges with socio-technical constraints. The findings offer practical implications for aligning teachers' context-based ethical beliefs with global frameworks to mitigate increasing AIED-related risks in educational spaces.

TI Comparing the predictive effects of three programming self-efficacy
   components on pre-service teachers' intention to integrate computational
   thinking
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational thinking; Self-efficacy components; Block-based
   programming; Robot programming; CT integration intention
ID SOCIAL COGNITIVE THEORY; OUTCOME EXPECTATIONS; PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY;
   HEALTH-BEHAVIOR; TECHNOLOGY; ROBOTICS; BELIEFS; VALIDATION; MOTIVATION;

AB This study compares the predictive effects of self-efficacy components (i.e., efficacy expectation, performance outcome expectation, and affective outcome expectation) on preservice teachers' intention to integrate Computational Thinking (CT) in their teaching. TI How dilemmatic spaces are constructed: Assuming, assigning, and
   justifying positions in early career teachers' literacy teaching in low
   socio-economic status schools
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Dilemmatic space; Early career teacher; Literacy; Professional learning;
   CHAT; Sociocultural
ID SATURATION; INTERVIEWS; EDUCATION
AB Early career teachers (ECTs) in low socio-economic status (LSES) primary schools often teach literacy under strong accountability and benchmark pressures. Prior research has commonly treated these challenges as discrete problems solvable through better instructional decisions. Drawing on dilemmatic space theory and CulturalHistorical Activity Theory (CHAT), this study reconceptualises ECTs' literacy teaching as shaped by intensified contradictions within and across activity systems. Semi-structured interviews with twelve Australian ECTs identified five recurrent dilemmatic spaces concerning curriculum narrowing, student capability, leadership data demands, parent-teacher responsibility, and year coordinator support and monitoring. The findings show that these spaces were constituted through ECTs' self-assumed and other-assigned positions and made visible through the justificatory accounts by which teachers explained competing obligations. The study extends dilemmatic space theory by showing how systemic tensions are mediated through ECTs' positioning in LSES literacy contexts.

TI Does teacher-student closeness mediate the effect of teacher enthusiasm
   on self-efficacy? A diary study among Chinese teachers
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chinese teachers; Teacher enthusiasm; Teacher self-efficacy;
   Teacher-student closeness; Dynamic structural equation modeling
ID POSITIVE EMOTIONS; WORK ENGAGEMENT; RESOURCES; OUTCOMES; BELIEFS
AB Teacher self-efficacy is critical for effective teaching, highlighting the importance of identifying its predictors. Drawing on the Broaden-and-Build Theory of positive emotions and the Prosocial Classroom Model, this study examined whether teacher enthusiasm predicts teacher self-efficacy and whether teacher-student closeness mediates this association. A two-week diary study was conducted with 132 Chinese primary and secondary school teachers, yielding 1293 daily reports. Data were analyzed using multilevel structural equation modeling and residual dynamic structural equation modeling. Teacher enthusiasm positively predicted teacher self-efficacy at both the between-person and same-day within-person levels, and teacher-student closeness mediated this association. However, lagged analyses showed that teacher enthusiasm negatively predicted next-day teacher self-efficacy, and teacher-student closeness did not mediate this association. These findings suggest that the relationship between teacher enthusiasm and teacher self-efficacy differs across temporal levels, highlighting the importance of adopting multilevel and temporal perspectives to understand teachers' emotional and motivational functioning.

TI Collaborative action research as professional development to support
   educational change in the UAE
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teachers' practice; Educational change; Collaborative action research
   (CAR); Professional development; Impact; United Arab Emirates (UAE)
ID STUDENT VOICE; TEACHERS; PRESERVICE; WORKPLACE; CONTEXT; IMPACT
AB Despite substantial investment in professional development to support educational reforms in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), concerns remain about its effectiveness. Collaborative Action Research (CAR) has emerged as a promising model, prompting this study to examine Arab teachers' perceptions of CAR and its impact on practice. Using a multiple-case study design, 20 teachers from four public schools participated in a one-year CAR project following a four-day preparatory workshop. Working in collaborative groups, teachers applied an iterative cycle of planning, acting, observing, and reflecting to address classroom challenges. Data were collected through interviews, reflective journals, and a researcher's diary, and were analysed thematically. Findings indicate that CAR facilitated meaningful changes in teaching practice by creating a supportive environment, focusing on relevant challenges, fostering reflective habits, and promoting professional dialogue. This study addresses a gap in Middle Eastern research and highlights CAR's potential as a context-sensitive, teacher-driven approach to professional learning.

TI How early well-being sustains work engagement across a one-year
   placement: A longitudinal mixed-methods study of rural volunteer
   teachers
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher well-being; Psychological capital; Work engagement; Rural
   volunteer teachers; Conservation of resources theory; Longitudinal study
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; CONSERVATION; RESOURCES
AB Drawing on Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined the longitudinal relationships among wellbeing, psychological capital, and work engagement, and whether AI use moderated them. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, we combined a two-wave survey of 642 teachers, spanning the full oneyear placement, with interviews of 20 teachers. Cross-lagged models showed that early well-being prospectively predicted later psychological capital and work engagement, with psychological capital partially mediating the association between early well-being and later engagement, whereas reverse and reciprocal paths were unsupported. The association between early well-being and later psychological capital was stronger among teachers with prior AI use experience. Interviews contextualized these patterns, portraying psychological resources as developing incrementally and AI as a potential facilitator of resource development. The findings reposition wellbeing as an initiating resource, suggest a predominantly forward pattern of resource development during a oneyear teaching placement, and inform support for rural volunteer teachers.

TI How Does Technical Background Shape Teachers' Epistemic Framings,
   Reflection, and Conceptualisation of Digital Competence?
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE disciplinary epistemologies; knowledge representation; self-reflection;
   socio-technical systems; teacher's digital competence
ID EXPERTS
AB As digital technologies increasingly shape education and social life, teachers are expected to exercise Teachers' Digital Competence (TDC) as professional agency across pedagogical, organisational, and ethical dimensions. While policy frameworks such as DigCompEdu articulate this breadth, how teachers interpret and enact these dimensions in reflective practice remains insufficiently understood. This qualitative study examines how teachers with and without an undergraduate computer science background conceptualise TDC by mapping how their distinct disciplinary backgrounds act as epistemic lenses through two guided reflective interventions: the SELFIEforTEACHERS (SfT) self-assessment tool and a subsequent collective reflection focused on ethical and socio-technical issues. Moving away from a linear skill-accumulation model, this study uses an expertise-informed analytical lens to analyse differences in knowledge organisation, reflective orientation, and metacognitive engagement. The findings suggest that disciplinary enculturation shapes the reflective trajectory and epistemic framings of TDC. While SfT supports structured, multidimensional reflection aligned with policy intentions, deeper developmental engagement (particularly with ethical judgement) is strengthened when reflection foregrounds socio-technical complexity. The study contributes to conceptualising TDC as epistemic resilience within evolving educational systems.

TI Leveraging digital platforms to advance global orthopaedic education and
   collaboration
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global surgery; Virtual education; Surgical education; Global
   orthopaedics
ID SURGERY
AB Purpose Musculoskeletal pathologies disproportionately affect populations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where access to subspecialty training and peer support is limited. Our organization developed a moderated international online community and video library to support ongoing orthopaedic education and near-real-time clinical collaboration. This study characterized their reach, engagement, and perceived educational value.Methods We performed a mixed-methods descriptive study of a global orthopaedics online community (organized on WhatsApp) and an affiliated video library (hosted on YouTube). Online community chat exports (March 2024-October 2025) were analyzed using Python to quantify message volume, case submissions, and geographic distribution. A REDCap survey circulated within the community assessed engagement, perceived usefulness, and impact on clinical decision making. YouTube Studio analytics (August 2020-October 2025) were used to evaluate video library composition, viewership, watch time, subscriber growth, and audience demographics.Results The online community comprised 1754 members from 95 countries. 1166 clinical cases from 26 countries were discussed (mean 5.3 cases/week), though participation was concentrated with the top 10 contributors accounting for 30.3% of all messages. Among 106 survey respondents from 42 countries, 92% found the community useful for clinical learning or decision making, and 80% reported using community advice in real clinical cases. The video library comprised 334 videos in English (56.0%), Spanish (23.6%), and French (20.4%), accumulating 10,549 subscribers, 560,400 views, and 32,212 watch hours from viewers in 92 countries. Viewership was geographically concentrated, with five countries, led disproportionately by India, accounting for 54.9% of all views, and a single introductory video accounting for 52.4% of total channel views.Conclusions When extensively curated, moderated, and maintained, free digital platforms can expand access to high-quality orthopaedic education and support near-real-time clinical decision making across LMICs. However, the success of such platforms depends not only on access and scale, but on intentional community building and sustained efforts to foster meaningful engagement among the audiences they aim to serve.

TI AI-Driven Instruction and Its Influence on Learners' Educational
   Engagement: The Parallel Mediation Analysis on the Role of Self-Efficacy
   and Grit
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-driven instruction; educational engagement; EFL learners; grit;
   self-determination theory; self-efficacy
AB The quick progress of technology, namely Artificial Intelligence (AI), within the language teaching sphere has widened the research domain on learners' educational engagement; however, a research gap remains regarding the basic psychological tools specifically the interaction between non-cognitive traits through which AI interventions influence this engagement. Based on self-determination theory (SDT), addressing a need for empirical evidence on the effect of technological integration, this research contributes by examining the role of grit and self-efficacy in AI-enhanced settings. Within 6 weeks, two groups, the Experimental group (EG) and the Control Group (CG), received the same curriculum content; however, the former were engaged with an AI chatbot using TalkAI that provided adaptive learning support, quick feedback and personalized encouragement. Contrarily, the latter received conventional teacher-oriented teaching through conventional teaching. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to estimate the direct and indirect relationships among the study variables simultaneously. The significance of the mediation effects was examined using the bootstrapping procedure. Based on the results, AI-driven teaching significantly and positively affected English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students' engagement. In addition, grit and self-efficacy had a mediating effect on this relationship. Although self-efficacy is proven to be a better mediator, both elements assisted in explaining the way AI-based instruction improved students' engagement. Finally, the present research underscores the capacity of AI-based instruction to improve the emotional and cognitive aspects of language learning, providing worthy information for learners, teachers and other stakeholders preferring to use new technologies aiming to integrate AI to boost learners' engagement.

   creativity through play-based coding
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Coding education; Computational thinking; Motor creativity; Early
   childhood education; Preschool
ID MOVEMENT; CHILDREN; CEREBELLUM; SYSTEM
AB This study examines the effectiveness of a coding education program for preschool children, focusing on its impact on motor creativity and computational thinking, two key domains in early development. Rooted in constructivist learning theory and creative cognition frameworks, the intervention incorporated developmentally appropriate, play-based coding activities to foster motor creativity (fluency, originality, imagination) and computational thinking (mathematical and critical thinking). Standardized instruments (TCAM and TechCheck-K) were used to assess outcomes, and follow-up measures were conducted to evaluate retention. Analyses showed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in all motor creativity and computational thinking subdomains. Retention data also indicated sustained gains across all measured domains, including motor creativity (fluency, originality, imagination) and computational thinking (critical and mathematical thinking). These results suggest that early coding education, when aligned with age-appropriate pedagogies, can offer meaningful and durable benefits beyond digital literacy. The findings support integrating coding into early childhood education to promote both motor creativity and computational thinking. Practical implications for educators and policymakers include the need for consistent, reflective, and movement-based coding approaches.

AB Creative thinking (CT) is becoming increasingly significant as a crucial component of personal core competitiveness in the modern day. TI Crossing metrics: are PISA, national tests, and grades measuring the
   same?
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bifactor model; Multitrait-multimethod (MTMM); National tests; PISA;
   Student achievement; Teacher-assigned grades
ID TEACHER-ASSIGNED GRADES; GENERAL INTELLIGENCE; READING-ACHIEVEMENT;
   SCHOOL; MOTIVATION; ABILITIES; GENDER
AB Background Understanding the relationship between International Large-Scale Assessments such as PISA and national school achievement measures is important due to the potentially significant influence of PISA outcomes on national educational policy reforms. While PISA was developed to assess achievement based on the OECD's literacy framework and is low-stakes for individual students, national tests and teacher-assigned grades measure students' attainment relative to the national curriculum and carry higher stakes for students. This study used Swedish data to examine the interrelationships and latent structure of achievement measures from PISA, national tests, and school grades in the domains of reading, mathematics, and science. Methods The data came from the Swedish sample of PISA 2022 (N = 6072), which was linked to register data containing students' final grades and national test results from Grade 9. We examined the intercorrelations among the observed measures and estimated a series of confirmatory factor analytic models, with the final model specified as a bifactor model with a multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) structure. Results The association between PISA and school achievement measures was moderately strong, and the PISA domains themselves were highly intercorrelated. (r > 0.80). Further, results from the bifactor MTMM model indicate that grades and national tests differentiate similarly across subjects and show little method-specific variance. In contrast, PISA exhibits limited differentiation across subjects and substantial method-specific variance, suggesting that PISA captures achievement according to its own literacy-oriented framework rather than the subject-specific curricular learning reflected in national tests and grades. Conclusions The extent to which PISA, national tests and school grades capture socially relevant learning is a normative question that lies beyond the scope of this study. However, it is important for policymakers to recognize the differing characteristics of PISA and national school achievement measures when making educational policy decisions. While PISA provides a valuable benchmark for cross-national and trend analyses, its literacy-oriented approach and assessment design limit the extent to which subject-specific inferences can be drawn.

TI Grade retention and psychoeducational resources: evidence from PISA 2022
   using propensity score matching
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Grade retention; PISA; Propensity score matching; Psychoeducational
   resources
ID COMPULSORY SECONDARY-EDUCATION; CAUSAL INFERENCE; VARIABLES
AB Background Grade retention is often justified as a compensatory measure that gives low-achieving students additional time to master school content. However, research on grade retention has focused mainly on academic achievement whereas studies of non-academic outcomes have generally examined individual constructs separately. This study examined adjusted cross-sectional associations between grade retention and seven psychoeducational resources among Spanish students participating in PISA 2022.Methods We used data from the Spanish PISA 2022 sample, including 29,775 students aged 15-16 years. Of these students, 5642 were classified as retained (18.95%) and 24,133 as non-retained (81.05%). Retained students were compared with non-retained students who were similar in observed background characteristics. The seven psychoeducational resources were sense of belonging, perceived quality of student-teacher relationships, self-directed learning self-efficacy, perseverance, curiosity, emotional control, and stress resistance. To reduce imbalance in observed background characteristics, we applied propensity score matching across five imputed datasets and then estimated survey-weighted regression models that accounted for the complex sampling structure of PISA.Results Retained students reported lower levels of six of the seven psychoeducational resources analysed than their matched non-retained peers. Grade retention was negatively associated with sense of belonging, student-teacher relationships, self-directed learning self-efficacy, perseverance, curiosity, and emotional control. By contrast, the association between grade retention and stress resistance was not statistically significant.Conclusions These findings suggest that retained students reported lower levels of several psychoeducational resources than observationally similar non-retained students. Although the results should be interpreted as adjusted cross-sectional associations rather than causal effects, they identify relational, learning-related, and emotional domains that may warrant closer attention in future research on the support provided to retained students.

AB Background Compassionate communication is a critical skill when caring for patients experiencing early pregnancy loss (EPL) in the emergency department; however, medical learners often have limited opportunities to practice this skill in a psychologically safe, low-stakes environment before interacting with patients experiencing a loss in the clinical setting.Objective The goal of this innovation was to develop a novel simulation experience using forum theatre techniques to enhance empathy, confidence in communicating about loss, and compassionate communication skills of emergency medicine (EM) residents when diagnosing an EPL, delivering the diagnosis, and discussing management options while providing emotional support.Methods Using forum theatre (i.e., an experiential learning technique that uses interactive theatre for exploring and performing transformative actions), we developed an innovative training for first-year (PGY-1) and second-year (PGY-2) EM residents to practice compassionate communication strategies. TI The myth of best practice: how understanding the site changes what best
   fits
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Best practice; Practice theory; Professional learning conversations;
   Site ontology
AB This article problematises the discourses of 'best practice', and despite the prevalence of the term in educational media and policy, there is a general lack of consensus how it is reconciled by teachers as they seek to understand and develop their pedagogical practices. By applying practice theory as a site-ontological lens through which to understand education practices, analysis of observations of teacher professional learning conversations and follow-up interviews and focus groups, an empirical basis to reframe best practice as best-fit practice is proposed. Findings from one case selected from a two-year ethnographic case study conducted in seven schools show how a site ontological perspective reframes best practice not as a universal set of rules, procedures or programs but as best-fit practices, those that are uniquely relevant to particular places, at particular times and with particular groups of learners (both teachers and students). This reframing asserts a principled, dynamic, site-based and responsive approach to practice, ever open to focused professional critique and reflection. Findings establish that a deep sense of site is critical for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the nature and particularity of the practices and practice architectures that shape how education is experienced (produced and reproduced) in each and every site. Conclusions have important implications for understanding the rhetoric of 'best' in terms of recognising and valuing teacher expertise, development, and pedagogical decision-making as teachers are expected to increasingly grapple with system mandates and compliance.

TI Timing matters: exploring the impact of pre- and post-draft rubrics on
   students' written assignments
SO INSTRUCTIONAL SCIENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Rubrics; Cognitive load; Feedback; Writing task
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; HIGHER-EDUCATION; FEEDBACK; MODELS
AB Rubrics are widely used in education to clarify expectations and guide student performance. However, the optimal timing of rubric presentation - whether before, after, or at both stages of a task - remains underexplored. This pre-registered experimental study aimed to determine whether rubrics function more effectively as pre-task guides or post-task feedback tools by examining differences in writing performance and cognitive load. Additionally, it explored potential differences between sixth and eleventh graders. Participants included 271 students from a private school in the Northeastern United States, with 141 eleventh graders and 130 sixth graders. Students wrote persuasive essays under one of four conditions: rubric before, rubric after, rubric before and after, or no rubric. Performance was assessed at two time points: the initial draft (T1) and the revised draft (T2). Cognitive load (perceived difficulty and effort) was also measured. Results revealed that rubrics provided before did not have any effect on the initial draft quality (T1), while rubrics provided after or at both stages enhanced revision outcomes (T2). Eleventh graders showed greater improvement than sixth graders. Cognitive load varied across conditions, with earlier rubric access reducing perceived difficulty. Thus, the timing of rubric presentation significantly influences writing performance and cognitive engagement. Rubrics are most effective when provided after the task, serving as an effective post-task feedback tool.

TI Collaborative agency in rating scale development for L2 academic writing
   assessment
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Collaborative agency; Analytic rating scale co-construction; L2 writing
   assessment; Formative classroom assessment; Learner involvement;
   Teacher-student collaboration
ID SCORING RUBRICS; PEER ASSESSMENT; FEEDBACK; STUDENTS; FOCUS
AB Calls for greater learner involvement in assessment have highlighted a need for rating scales that are not only technically sound but also pedagogically meaningful. However, in second language (L2) writing, students are largely absent from scale design, with most instruments being developed by teachers or test developers. Previous co-construction studies have often positioned students as the primary agents, with comparative underuse of teacher expertise and limited curricular alignment. This study addresses this gap by investigating how collaborative agency between teachers and students can inform the development of a rating scale for academic writing in a Saudi higher education context. Drawing on a multi-source framework, four meshed teacher-student focus groups and a followup focus group were conducted to negotiate the scale criteria, properties, and level descriptors. Through cycles of debate and compromise, the process yielded a five-level analytic rating scale with six criteria grounded in curricular objectives and stakeholder perspectives. This study shows how collaborative agency was enacted through a dialogic process of negotiating and integrating teacher and student perspectives in rating scale development. It extends participatory assessment research in L2 writing by illustrating a context-sensitive, theoretically informed, and curriculum-aligned approach to analytic rating scale co-construction for classroom use.

SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT

DT Article
DE Family Socioeconomic Status; Parental Involvement; Educational
   Achievement; Wage Returns; Individual Heterogeneity
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; PARENTAL INVOLVEMENT; SELECTION BIAS; FAMILY
   INCOME; SCHOOL; QUALITY; COLLEGE; TRANSMISSION; EXPECTATIONS; MOBILITY
AB This study utilizes linked data from the Taiwan Education Panel Survey (TEPS) and its follow-up survey (TEPS-B) to examine how family background is associated with educational attainment and early-career wage outcomes, while accounting for selection bias and individual heterogeneity. We construct a dual-channel framework distinguishing between a structural resource channel (parental education and family income) and a behavioral socialization channel (four distinct dimensions of parental involvement). The selection-adjusted estimates reveal a clear division of labor between these mechanisms across the lifecourse. Consistent with the socialization hypothesis, parental social involvement is associated with a higher likelihood of attending a selective public university, even after controlling for cognitive ability and personality traits. However, this socialization effect fades during the labor-market transition, operating instead through mediated educational credentials. In contrast, the resource channel exhibits long-term structural persistence: family income remains directly and positively associated with adult wages, even when accounting for complete educational profiles and individual attributes. Individual heterogeneity, including tested ability and independence, remains crucial throughout both stages. Overall, this study contributes new empirical evidence from Taiwan's expanded higher education environment, demonstrating that while active parental socialization supports qualitative tracking within the school system, it cannot fully neutralize the direct occupational and networking advantages conferred by structural economic resources.

TI From 5 to 15: The Impact of Increased Program Signals in the 2024 to
   2025 General Surgery Application Cycle
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE interview invitations; program signals; residency recruitment; residency
   match
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the change from 5 program signals to 15 program signals in General Surgery using data from the 2024 to 2025 cycle using AAMC ERAS (R) application, Thalamus interview, and NRMP ranking and matching data. DESIGN: Data collected by the NNBME, AAMC, Thalamus, and NRMP were analyzed to assess the impact of program signals on: interview invitation, placement on a program's rank order list (ROL), ranking in the top quartile of a program's ROL, and applicants matching into programs. SETTING: The 2024 to 2025 residency application cycle. PARTICIPANTS: Applicants applying to and ranking programs in General Surgery during the 2024 to 2025 residency application cycle. RESULTS: A significant decrease in the average number of applications per applicant between the 2024 and the 2025 cycle was noted. Candidates were more likely to get an interview invitation and be placed on a program's ROL at a program they signaled when compared to a program they did not signal. Signaling positively impacted candidate median match rate. CONCLUSIONS: These data suggest that program signals are being used by both applicants and programs to help place the right applicant in the right program. The shift to large number of signals may have encouraged applicants to submit fewer applications and it did not negatively impact interview or match outcomes. Ongoing research in this area is critical to better understand the impacts of program signaling on residency and resident selection and to assess any unintended negative consequences. TI Primary school pre-service teachers' ability to understand and use
   dashboard data and associations with their data literacy knowledge,
   beliefs and experience
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning analytics; Dashboard; Primary education; Data literacy; Teacher
   competence
ID DECISION-MAKING; EFFICACY; SENSE
AB Teacher dashboards can support instructional decision-making, but teachers often struggle to interpret dashboard data. This study examines pre-service teachers' situation-specific skills for using dashboards, including perceiving relevant data, interpreting information, and making pedagogically appropriate decisions. We investigated how these skills relate to data literacy knowledge, beliefs, and individual characteristics. 412 pre-service primary teachers completed a dashboard task, a knowledge test, and Likert-scale items to measure beliefs and experience. Findings highlight the need to strengthen data literacy and support data-informed decision-making in teacher education.

TI Language learning motivations by age and socio-economic status: A
   cross-sectional comparison of Taiwan's high school students
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Language learning motivation; L2MSS; Socio-economic status (SES); Taiwan
ID SELF-REGULATORY STRATEGIES; FOREIGN-LANGUAGE; ENGLISH; LEARNERS; SES;
   PERFORMANCE; ATTITUDES; DYNAMICS; SYSTEM; SELVES
AB This paper provides quantitative comparisons between language learning motivations of students at transitional periods of high school in Taiwan: the final year of junior high (grade 9) and final year of senior high school (grade 12). Representative samples of students at each level provided responses to a motivational questionnaire delivered in conjunction with the Ministry of Education in Taiwan. The total sample comprised 5645 candidates (Grade 9: n = 2994; Grade 12: n = 2651). This large, robustly sampled dataset distinguishes it from many previous motivation studies. With Ford's (1992) Motivational Systems Theory (MST) as the overarching framework, this study draws upon eight distinct motivational constructs, with additional insights gleaned by incorporating socio-economic status (SES) information. Multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to compare levels of, and associations between, different motivators across groups. Grade 12 students exhibited a stronger sense of the instrumental and outward-looking communicative value of language learning than grade 9 students, however relationships between internalised and externalised motivators were found to be weaker amongst this group. Within both grades, motivation levels of higher SES students were reported to be systematically higher than those of their lower SES peers. Implications are highlighted for policy and teaching.

TI Prepared to stay: Arts-based pedagogies, generative discomfort and
   teacher durability in sexuality and relationships education
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arts-based pedagogies; Initial teacher education; Sexuality and
   relationships education; Teacher retention; Professional formation;
   Generative discomfort
AB Arts-based pedagogies (ABP) offer innovative pathways for pre-service teachers' professional formation in sexuality and relationships education (SRE), yet their integration into initial teacher education (ITE) remains limited. This qualitative study examines how ABP shapes professional confidence, relational readiness, and emotional preparedness for teaching SRE. Drawing on interviews and reflections from pre-service teachers in a Victorian ITE unit, alongside retrospective accounts from in-service alumni, we offer a theoretically informed interpretation of how professional dispositions formed during ITE may persist into school practice. Applying Ahmed's (2017) theorisation of generative discomfort, we argue that ABP creates structured encounters with the relational challenges SRE demands, and theorise the outcome as a form of professional durability: a disposition participants describe as sustaining, not depleting. As the alumni data is retrospective and the study is nonlongitudinal, we frame professional durability as an interpretive claim, not a demonstrated one, with implications for SRE preparation design in contested curriculum areas.

TI Critical Reflections and Third Spaces in the Secondary English Classroom
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE dialogic classroom; hybridity; polyphony; third space; writing
   instruction
AB This article examines a pedagogical shift in how student writing is conceived, from a solitary, evaluative demonstration of finished argument toward a recursive, dialogic, collaborative process of knowledge construction. This shift is enacted through the Critical Reflection, a short-form, open-ended, frequently-executed writing assignment grounded in Homi Bhabha's hybrid third spaces and Mikhail Bakhtin's polyphonic chronotopes. Through a practitioner-research analysis of student submissions, peer annotations, and meta-commentaries from a single secondary classroom, the author traces how this approach fostered syntactic fluidity, theoretical integration, a shared class lexicon, and productive uncertainty, alongside the uneven outcomes and tensions that accompanied it. The Critical Reflection emerges as a pedagogical third space in which most students moved from passive reporters toward active critics, offering transferable principles for reconceiving writing as dialogic and recursive.

TI Automated Scoring of Long-Context Essays Using Linear-Complexity
   Language Models
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
AB Automated essay scoring (AES) increasingly uses pretrained language models, but many operational systems still impose fixed input limits that truncate essays and may weaken score validity. We study how truncation and model architecture affect scoring for long-form writing using more than 20,000 responses. We compare a modern Transformer encoder, ModernBERT, with a linear-time state-space model, Mamba-130M, which supports efficient long-context processing. Evaluation follows the standard framework for the evaluation of automated scoring using Quadratic Weighted Kappa, exact agreement, and standardized mean difference. A paired permutation test (1,000,000 resamples) confirms that truncation produces a statistically significant reduction in QWK for both architectures (), although the effect size is modest. To assess truncation-related bias, we also examine Kullback-Leibler divergence on propensity score-matched samples and Jeffrey's divergence. Our results show that truncation harms not only scoring accuracy but also construct validity by forcing models to judge incomplete evidence of writing quality. By contrast, the state-space model shows favorable distributional behavior and much lower inference latency as sequence length grows, while maintaining competitive scoring performance. Overall, the findings highlight an important trade-off between efficiency and validity in AES and suggest that linear-time architectures are a promising basis for more faithful evaluation of long-form writing.

TI Teacher-Centered Action Research for Professional Development in Science
   Education: A Systematic and Critical Review
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher-centred action research; Professional development; Science
   education; Practitioner-led inquiry
ID COLLABORATIVE ACTION RESEARCH; MATHEMATICS; STRATEGIES; PROGRAM
AB This review explores the potential of teacher-centred action research as a professional development strategy in science teacher education. By examining 18 peer-reviewed systematically selected, peer-reviewed research articles, we identified the contexts, support mechanisms, success factors, and challenges associated with this approach. Through a thematic analysis, our findings reveal that teacher-centred action research is adaptable across diverse educational settings and levels, emphasising its general applicability and flexibility. Key success factors include authentic collaboration, continuous support, and the acquisition and integration of research-based knowledge. The identified challenges include significant time investment and additional workload. The review further emphasises the importance of structured support, including the active participation of mentors and facilitators, to provide help in navigating such challenges. Moreover, our findings indicate that dissemination of research findings beyond local communities remains limited, highlighting the necessity for initiatives that promote broader mobilization of developed knowledge. Future research should prioritise innovative support mechanisms and measure long-term impacts of teacher-centred action research on professional development, as well as on student outcomes. This review conclusively establishes that according to the available and relevant literature, teacher-centred action research significantly improves teaching practices and supports the professional growth of science educators.

TI Borrowed but Not Implemented: Educational Policy Borrowing and the
   Implementation Gap in Centralized Systems
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE borrowed reforms; Kuwait; policy implementation; reform patterns
ID CHALLENGES
AB This study examines why borrowed educational reforms in Kuwait have failed. It is based on in-depth interviews with 20 key figures from the Ministry of Education (MOE), including former Ministers, and administrators from the Kuwait National Center for Education Development (NCED). The study found prior research suggesting that the failures of Western education not being a suitable fit for Kuwait were incorrect, and that a weakness in following correct implementation patterns was the main reason. The study recommends that reforms should include orientation and planning, collaboration with stakeholders, modification of the reforms to fit the local socio-cultural context, and effective ongoing monitoring and tracking systems.

DE Assessments; Education; Artificial intelligence; Large language models;
   Simulation; Psychometric
ID RESIDENT
AB Background Artificial intelligence systems increasingly generate performance feedback for surgical trainees. While existing validation focuses on classification accuracy (novice vs. expert identification), no widely adopted frameworks measure whether feedback appropriately reflects performance level (analogous to validity) or adapts consistently to performance changes (analogous to reliability). We sought to develop a psychometric framework measuring AI feedback quality through two complementary metrics: Calibration (does the tone of the feedback match how well the resident performed?) and Feedback Robustness Index (when scores go up or down, does the feedback tone move in the same direction?), and to identify assessment design factors associated with AI feedback performance.Methods Assessments from nine PGY-2 general surgery residents per station, selected to span the performance range, were drawn from five standardized simulation stations (FLS Knot Tying, FLS Circle Cutting, Vascular Anastomosis, Endostitch, and Imaging Interpretation) with scoring rubrics ranging from minimal (time and accuracy only) to detailed, behaviorally anchored descriptors. Feedback was generated by an open-source LLM Qwen3 4B, on a local machine. For each assessment, we systematically modified each resident's scores in five controlled ways: global improvement, global decline, targeted weakness correction, targeted strength deterioration, and minimal change. We measured: (1) Calibration (R2): correlation between feedback sentiment and performance scores; (2) Feedback Robustness Index (FRI): percentage of times feedback direction correctly matched performance changes. Sentiment was quantified using TextBlob (general purpose) and VADER (lexicon and rule-based) algorithms.Results Across 225 baseline-perturbed comparisons, AI feedback quality varied substantially by rubric design. Two assessments with detailed, behaviorally-anchored rubrics showed the strongest calibration and robustness (FLS Knot Tying: R2 = 0.40, FRI = 84%; Vascular Anastomosis: R2 = 0.37, FRI = 73%). Stations with structured but not behaviorally anchored rubrics showed moderate robustness but near-zero calibration (EndoStitch: R2 = 0.00, FRI = 64%; Imaging: R2 = 0.00, FRI = 69%). The station with a minimal, two-item rubric showed near-zero calibration and robustness no better than chance (FLS Circle: R2 = 0.03, FRI = 49%). Across assessments, feedback more often moved in the right direction than matched the resident's overall level of performance (mean FRI = 68% vs mean R2 = 0.16).Conclusions This study proposes a psychometric evaluation framework for measuring AI feedback appropriateness and consistency in surgical education, offering candidate metrics analogous to validity and reliability evidence. AI feedback quality was closely associated with assessment rubric design. Programs implementing AI feedback should evaluate systems with calibration and robustness metrics, alongside expert review, before educational use, and should ensure that assessment rubrics include detailed performance criteria.
C1 [Baloul, Mohamed S.; Giri, Oviya; Mehta, Aashna; D'Angelo, Jonathan] Mayo Clin, Dept Surg, 200 1st St SW, Rochester, MN 55905 USA.
   [Cui, Daniel] Univ Wisconsin, Madison, WI USA.

   MOTIVATION; ABILITY
AB A differentiated understanding of the motivational trajectories of international students in Germany is crucial to support their study success. Drawing on the Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT), we investigated the development of international students' expectations and value beliefs over the study course. We also investigated interindividual differences in developmental trajectories by gender, subject group (STEM/non-STEM), parental academic background, students' cultural background and their intersectional interplay. The findings offer a differentiated understanding of the long-term motivational trajectories in the heterogeneous group of international bachelor's students in Germany and provide indications for tailored interventions to support their study motivation and success.

TI Surgical performance anxiety (SPA) among general surgery residents in a
   tertiary care hospital
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Surgical performance anxiety; General surgery residents; Resident
   wellbeing; Sports competition anxiety test (SCAT); Surgical education
ID BURNOUT; SPECIALTIES
AB Purpose Surgical performance anxiety (SPA) is a common but under-studied phenomenon among surgical trainees, with potential implications for both resident well-being and patient safety. This study assessed the prevalence, severity, and triggers of SPA among general surgery residents in Pakistan. Methods A descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Surgery at a tertiary care teaching hospital, Peshawar, from 1 to 31 May 2026. All 145 general surgery residents were invited to participate (census approach). SPA was assessed using a modified 10-item Sports Competition Anxiety Test (SCAT), adapted from a prior study in orthopedic trainees, alongside a checklist of technical, environmental, and non-technical stress triggers adapted from a UK-based study of surgeons. Data were analyzed using t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Pearson's Chi-square tests, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results Of 145 residents, 122 (84.1%) responded. The mean SCAT score was 17.28 +/- 3.05 (95% CI: 16.73-17.83), with 45.9% (n = 56) showing low anxiety, 53.3% (n = 65) average anxiety, and 0.8% (n = 1) high anxiety. Scores were highest among PGY-3 residents (18.29 +/- 3.65). The most frequently cited triggers were complex or high-risk cases (66.4%), equipment issues (64.1%), and fear of negative evaluation by colleagues (56.3%). Acute complications as a trigger varied significantly by training year (p = 0.047), and female residents were significantly more likely to cite personal/family issues as a stressor than male residents (p = 0.011). Conclusion Most general surgery residents reported low-to-average SPA, though specific stressors varied by training level and sex, suggesting a need for tailored wellness interventions.

TI Association of Teacher Well-Being With Student Motivation and
   Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher well-being; Student motivation; Student achievement;
   Meta-analysis; Educational psychology
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; MENTAL-HEALTH; MODEL; EXHAUSTION; ENGAGEMENT;
   PSYCHOLOGY; EDUCATION; EFFICACY; GOALS; STATE
AB In this meta-analysis, we examine the association between teacher well-being and ill-being with student motivation and achievement. Based on 186 articles, 811 effect sizes, and data from 355,637 teachers, we investigate these relationships through the lens of the Job Demands-Resources Model, Transactional Stress Model, Self-Determination Theory, and the PERMA model. Using three-level meta-analytic models, we found small to moderate associations between student outcomes and teacher well-being (r = .18) and ill-being (r = -.13). These associations were similarly patterned across student motivation and student achievement, with no significant differences by outcome type. Associations were also comparable across domains of teacher functioning with no significant differences by domain. Moderator analyses indicated stronger associations in secondary school settings. Associations were also larger when teacher and student variables were reported by the same informant, although this difference reached conventional significance only for teacher ill-being and approached significance for teacher well-being. These findings suggest that teacher well-being and ill-being show reliable but modest associations with student motivation and achievement across a diverse body of research, though the evidence remains largely correlational. Given this correlational nature and the influence of measurement source, future longitudinal and intervention research is needed to clarify causal mechanisms and the direction of effects.

TI Social and emotional learning programs in Australian primary schools: a
   systematic review
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Social and emotional learning (SEL); Student wellbeing; Primary
   education; Education policy; Collaborative for academic, social, and
   emotional learning (CASEL)
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; INTERVENTIONS; CHILDREN; STUDENTS; SKILLS; METAANALYSIS;
   RESILIENCE; IMPACT; TRIAL; RISK
AB Social and emotional learning (SEL) is increasingly embedded in Australian primary schools, yet the evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to identify evaluated SEL programs in Australian primary schools, examine effects across emotional, behavioural, and social outcomes, and map program content against the CASEL-5 competencies. Searches were conducted in ERIC, APA PsycINFO, Embase, MEDLINE, and Scopus in August 2024, with supplementary searches of Be You-listed programs and KidsMatter Primary program names updated via Google Scholar in May 2026; the protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251117280). Fifteen studies involving 7814 students aged 5-12 years were included. Effects were predominantly null or mixed across emotional distress, problem behaviour, and positive social behaviour. Evidence was limited by heterogeneity in designs, measures, and content, as well as variable methodological quality. Competency mapping showed stronger emphasis on Self-Awareness and Self-Management than on Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making. Australian primary school SEL evaluations provide inconsistent evidence of effectiveness and uneven competency coverage. These findings underscore the need for Australian SEL research and policy to more explicitly account for how program design, evaluation expectations, implementation conditions, and school delivery realities shape evidence of effectiveness.

TI An Omitted Variables Approach to Disentangling Differential Prediction
   in College Admissions
SO EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT-ISSUES AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE college admissions; differential prediction; omitted variables;
   predictive bias; race/ethnicity; SES
ID TEST BIAS; COGNITIVE-ABILITY; COURSE-TAKING; PERFORMANCE; VALIDITY;
   GRADES; TESTS; ACHIEVEMENT; SCORES; SAT
AB Standardized tests used in college admissions have raised fairness concerns, with critics arguing bias against underrepresented groups. Recent research suggests that apparent differential prediction may reflect omitted variables (OVs), which are unmeasured factors that systematically differ across groups and influence performance. We examined 499,622 Black and White SAT takers across 142 institutions to test whether OVs help account for prediction differences in forecasting first-year GPA using SAT scores, high school GPA, and both. Black students' college grades were overpredicted by .11-.24 GPA points, while SES showed smaller effects. Adding omitted variables reduced Black overprediction by 54%-72%. Our findings highlight that typically unmeasured differences that shape academic performance, rather than flaws in traditional predictors, account for a substantial portion of differential prediction.

   dynamics; South Africa; taboos; Zambia
AB This study explored the under-researched phenomenon of taboos in doctoral education within the unique contexts of Zambia and South Africa. Guided by three core objectives, the research aimed to: (1) systematically identify specific taboos related to research topics, methodological biases, and supervisory power dynamics; (2) analyse their effects on students' mental health, academic performance, and innovation; and (3) develop student-centred recommendations for reform. Employing an interpretive phenomenological design, the study collected data through semi-structured interviews and, for participants who were unavailable for a live interview, open-ended Google Form questionnaires structured around the same interview guide, with 35 doctoral students (30 from Zambia, 5 from South Africa) from diverse disciplines. Data were analysed using interpretive thematic analysis, drawing on Bourdieu's concept of symbolic violence and a postcolonial critique to frame the findings. Key findings revealed that taboos in doctoral education function as systemic control mechanisms, including the prohibition of challenging supervisors, institutional silencing of complaints, enforced concealment of struggle, and gendered stigmas. The impact of these taboos is severe, manifesting as epistemic constriction (suppression of critical inquiry), psychological distress (isolation, anxiety), and systemic academic delays. Participants advocated for structural transformations, including mandatory training on power dynamics, safe channels for reporting misconduct, and a shift towards supervisory partnerships informed by principles like ubuntu. The study concludes that these taboos perpetuate colonial hierarchies and stifle intellectual decolonization, necessitating urgent institutional action to create supportive, equitable, and intellectually liberating doctoral environments. This study contributes to doctoral supervision literature by demonstrating how addressing these taboo-laden dynamics is essential for decolonizing supervisory practice and fostering a culture of openness and accountability. Future research should investigate policy effectiveness and the manifestation of taboos across other contexts and disciplines.

AB This study aimed to determine the profiles of refugee students regarding their perception of school climate and their relationship with mathematics achievement, gender, and length of stay as a refugee. AB Background This mixed methods study examined the social networks of adults with intellectual disability (ID), alongside a matched group of typically developing (TD) adults, with 'friends' defined from their perspectives.Methods Participants identified their friends among those they interacted with in their day-to-day and former contexts, and described what a friend meant to them.
